PREFACE TO THIRD EDITION 

In order to inaugurate the new plan by which it is proposed to issue yearly pocket supplements, and due to the period of time that has elapsed since the former edition over six years ago, it has been thought wise to bring out this third and revised edition of Orphans' Court 

Practice. 

All new reported cases, it is believed, have been added down to date, together with the Acts of Assembly to the close of the year 1937. The sections relating to investments by fiduciaries and the distribution of extraordinary dividends and the like have been completely revised and enlarged to keep pace with the trend of the latest decisions.

There has also been added to the Appendix in aid, we hope, of the active practitioner, a list of the acts relating to investments, cases on the apportionment of extraordinary dividends, etc., with a cross reference to Purdon's

Statutes Annotated, Title 20. 

No great change has been made in the forms included in the second edition, but the author again notes his gratitude to David G. Hunter, Esq., of Philadelphia, by whose kind consent numerous forms have been used as drafted by him in the fourth edition of his valuable work published by the Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company. 

The writer acknowledges the great assistance rendered him by Robert M. Boyle, Esq., in connection with the chapters on practice before the Register; Edward S. 

Morris, Esq., on matters relating to inheritance taxes; 

William H. S. Wells, Esq., on the sections relating to 

Federal estate tax, and Robert Brigham, Esq., for his collaboration in the work on cases relating to the apportionment of extraordinary stock dividends, etc. Also the great help rendered by his son, Henry C. Remick, Esq., in listing and verifying citations. 

April 14, 1938.

R. M. REMICK. iii

PART I  CHAPTER I. 

WHEN AND WHERE LETTERS SHOULD BE GRANTED. 

1. THE FACT OF DEATH. 

It would scarcely seem necessary to state that the first requisite in the administration of a decedent's estate is the actual death of its owner, but strangely enough cases have arisen where letters have actually been granted by the register on the estate of a supposed decedent who afterwards was shown to have been living. Letters thus granted are, of course, absolutely void,' as are also any of the acts of an administrator or executor thus appointed except when done under the protection of a decree of court.²

Letters, however, once granted "are not only in all cases prima facie evidence of the death of the person on whose estate they are granted, but when there is no plea to them and consequently no issue made upon the grant they are conclusive evidence of the fact of death."" Under the present status of the law, with its elaborate machinery for the grant of letters on the estate of a presumed decedent, the situation arising from the grant of letters on the estate of a living person could hardly arise, and in its event the rights of all parties are amply protected."

Though fortunately of rare occurrence, it sometimes happens that two or more persons die as the result of a 

1 Devlin v. Comm'th, 101 Pa. 273. 2 Id. 

3 Sharswood, J., in Cunningham v. Smith's Admr., 70 Pa. 450, 458. 

4 See Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 6, infra Secs. 54-66. 

5 See sections 65 and 66, infra. 1

common disaster so that difficulty arises in ascertaining which was the first to die. On the determination of this fact devolution of real or personal estate may depend. 

In all such cases the fact is determined by the orphans' court in moulding its decree of distribution." 

2. SETTLEMENT OF ESTATES BY AGREEMENT. 

Having thus, of necessity, first actually determined the fact of death, the next step for determination is whether or not letters must be secured or the estate settled by the heirs without such formality. If it be ascertained as a matter of fact that the decedent had no creditors and left no assets which cannot be transferred by delivery, such as cash in hand, furniture, negotiable securities and the like, it is possible, though rarely advisable, to distribute the estate among the next of kin by agreement." 

Care should be taken to see that the funeral and burial expenses are met out of the estate and the inheritance tax paid prior to such distribution.

In the case of inheritance tax settlement it is customary for the state appraiser to aid such settlement when desirable by accepting in one document an affidavit by the next of kin describing and appraising the decedent's property and itemizing the deductions therefrom for the computation of the tax.

Care should be taken by each heir to receive from all the heirs an itemized receipt for all property of the decedent thus distributed, each agreeing to defray pro rata any debts of the decedent which may afterwards develop Needless to say settlement of an estate by this method is only permissible under the clearest circumstances and 6 "In the absence of substantial evidence warranting a definite conclusion as to survivorship of those perishing in a common disaster, they will be treated as dying at the same instant and property rights adjudged accordingly"; Kimmey's Est., 326 Pa. 33, af 'g. 27 D. & C. 608, and citing

For like purpose and to the same effect the court is wont to approve family agreements for the settlement and distribution of estates held in trust.11 

3. WHEN LETTERS SHOULD BE GRANTED. 

It is quite customary among registers to refuse to grant letters until after the burial of the decedent and such a custom though not imposed by statute certainly follows the dictates of orderly procedure and a proper respect for the dead. It allows sufficient time for the parties in interest, usually those nearest of kin to the deceased, properly to dispose of the dead before turning their attention to the rights and property of the living as his heirs. "Whilst a rush for letters of administration and the granting of the same on the day of the death of the decedent, in the absence of some imperative necessity shown, should be held to be scandalous," there is "no authority on which they can be declared void, as against public policy." 12 

The dictates of decency having been met, and also opportunity granted for the filing of a caveat 13 should such be warranted, application for letters should be made as soon as practicable after the funeral.

 4. WHERE LETTERS SHOULD BE GRANTED. 

In the great majority of cases the official appointment of some proper person or corporation to administer the decedent's estate either under the intestate laws or under a will is found to be not only advisable but necessary. 

No formal act of administration can be successfully performed without it.

For the grant of such letters the service of the register of wills is a prerequisite and in determining which register in the Commonwealth shall have jurisdiction the law clearly states that in the case of a resident¹ of Pennsylvania: "Letters testamentary and of administration shall be grantable only by the register of wills of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent at the time of his decease.'' 15 66 While ordinarily the determination of a decedent's 'family or principal residence" is a simple matter nevertheless instances occur from time to time when it is a question of considerable doubt.

Petitioners for letters on a decedent's estate have a duty cast upon them to serve the interests of the commonwealth and must aid in the collection of taxes due upon the transfer of estates. CHAPTER II. 

LETTERS OF ADMINISTRATION. 

5. THE RIGHT TO ADMINISTER. 

The statute sets forth in particular language those who successively have the right to administer an intestate's estate. "Whenever letters of administration are by law necessary, the register having jurisdiction shall grant them in such form as the case shall require, to the [widow] surviving spouse, if any, of the decedent, or to such of his or her relations or kindred as by law may be entitled to the residue of his or her personal estate, or to a share or shares therein, after payment of his or her debts, or he may join with the [widow] surviving spouse in the administration such relations or kindred,28 or such one or more of them as he shall judge will best administer the estate, preferring always, of those so entitled, such as are in the nearest degree of consanguinity with the decedent [and also preferring males to females]; and, in case of the refusal or incompetency of every such person, to one or more of the principal creditors of the decedent applying therefor; or to any fit person, at his discretion: 

Provided, That if such decedent was a married [woman, her husband] person, the surviving spouse shall be entitled to the administration, in preference to all other persons: And provided further, That in all cases of an administration with a will annexed, where there is a general residue of the estate bequeathed, the right to administer shall belong to those having the right to such residue, and the administration in such case shall be granted by the register to such one or more of them as he shall judge will best administer the estate." 25

"When the class primarily entitled to administration consists of several persons, it is the duty of the register to grant letters to such one or more of them as he shall judge will best administer the estate. He may thus grant letters to them all jointly, if they so desire; or in his discretion, he may select one of them and commit the administration to him alone, to the exclusion of the others; and when properly exercised, his discretion is not the subject of review.....He is not bound to select the oldest in preference to the youngest of the class entitled to administration. Primogeniture gives no right of preference, so as to weigh against the wish of the majority of interests; yet if things are precisely equal, if the scale is exactly poised-being the elder brother, would incline the balance, and the same principle applies to the elder of two sisters.....among children the right does not depend on seniority: it is entirely in the discretion of the register; but when he has exercised his discretion by selecting one of the sons, it is no longer in his power to revoke the letters thus granted and issue them to another, except for sufficient cause. When administration has been committed to any of the next of kin, others, even in the same degree of kindred, have during the life of the administrator no title to a similar grant.'' ³¹

CHAPTER III. 

PROBATE OF WILLS. 

12. PRODUCTION OF THE WILL. 

Obviously the first step in the grant of letters on the estate of a resident testator is the production before the proper register 62 of the original will. Ordinarily this is done by the custodian thereof, or the parties interested, as a matter of course.

There is no limit of time for offering a will for probate. "The last will of any decedent may be offered for probate at any time: Provided, That if such will shall not have been offered for probate within three years from the date of the death of the testator, the same shall be void and of no effect against a bona fide conveyance or mortgage of the real estate of said decedent, duly recorded before the date of the offering of said will for probate." 63 

If, as often happens, the will has been lodged for safe keeping in the safe deposit box of the decedent, the bank or trust company in charge will permit the opening of such box by the next of kin or the executor named, if known, for the purpose of searching for the will, and if found, will deliver such document to the executor named upon proper receipt therefor, or, according to the custom of some companies, will deliver it to the register. 

Care should be taken to have the will lodged with the register or have him formally notified of its existence immediately upon the death of the testator to prevent the grant of letters to persons not entitled thereto.

14. CERTIFICATION OF RECORD TO ORPHANS' COURT. 

Under the former practice and the Act of 1832," it was provided that if the respondent refused to comply with the order of the register he should "be liable to an in dictment as for a misdemeanor, or to an action for damages by the person aggrieved." 70 This proved to be ineffectual.

It has therefore been provided that if the respondent "shall conceal or withhold such writing, during the space of fifteen days, after being personally served with a citation issued in the manner aforesaid, it shall be the duty of the register forthwith to certify the record of the proceeding to the orphans' court of said county, and the said court, upon petition" of any person interested, shall proceed to enforce obedience to said citation by attachment as in cases of citations issued from said court."' 72 to Register for citation; (2) citation by Register requiring person in possession or control of will to produce and deposit it for probate; (3) personal service of citation; (4) if answer filed denying possession or control of will, Register must certify record to Orphans' Court. No provision for Register to take testimony or make decree in such case. Court must hear and determine issue raised by petition and answer. Where alterations in a will are made prior to the execution of a codicil, the will as altered is by the codicil republished and validated.

A will was properly admitted to probate, when, after their names had been marked out by pencil marks, the attesting witnesses appeared before the register and on oath declared that testatrix was of sound mind and memory and that they subscribed their names as witnesses to the will in her presence and at her request and they also gave further proof that they knew nothing about the " erasures or additions to said will." Her signature remained untouched.

In a petition to the orphans' court to set aside the probate of a will by the register of wills, petitioner alleged that by inter lineations and marks of cancellation and obliteration appearing upon the face of the writing and that by crossing out and drawing lead pencil lines through the signatures of the two attesting witnesses, testatrix had indicated her intention to revoke her will in its entirety. Preliminary objections to petition sustained and petition to set aside dismissed.

An order revoking the probate of an alleged will and setting aside the grant of letters testamentary was affirmed on appeal, where it appeared that the alleged will consisted of three pages fastened together and exhibiting complete continuity in expression, but unsigned, and a separate page, signed and witnessed, but not following the last of the bound pages in sequence of thought.

Testamentary intent may be evidenced by several papers only one of which is signed at the end thereof, provided they are connected either physically, or by logical and grammatical sequence, by their internal sense, by coherence or adaptation of parts.

The order of connection must manifestly appear upon the face of the will; it cannot be established by extrinsic proof. 

In determining whether or not a will was validly executed, the question is not what a testator mistakenly thought he was doing, but what he actually did. Bryen's Est., 328 Pa. 122.

"In order to establish the validity of a nuncupative will, seven distinct requisites must affirmatively appear and be clearly proven: "1. It must relate to personal property. "2. It must be made during the last sickness of the testator and in such extremity as precluded a written will. "3. It must be made in the house of testator's habitation of dwelling or where he has resided for the space of ten days or more before the making of such will, except where such person shall be surprised by sickness, being from his own house, and shall die before returning thereto. "4. Where the sum or value bequeathed shall exceed one hundred dollars, it shall be proven that the testator at the time of pronouncing the bequest bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will or to that effect. "5. In all cases the foregoing requisites shall be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making of such will. "6. The decedent must have intended to make a will which was to be a nuncupative one. "7. The testimony relating to the said will or the substance thereof must be committed to writing within six days after the making of such will." 92

Register. 

If the register had jurisdiction and no appeal is taken from the decree of probate within two years,¹ such decree is conclusive as to both real and personal estate. 

It is a judicial act the legality of which cannot be collaterally impeached.2

There is a presumption from the probate of a will that all the essential facts necessary to sustain the probate are present. The law provides the procedure necessary to overthrow that presumption if it is in any way challenged, and it must be followed. 

Probate of a will is conclusive of the fact that it is the will of the deceased person whose estate is under consideration, that it was made with all the statutory requirements physically present or supplied by proof,that is, form, execution, capacity, proper age, or, if made by a mariner under age, that he was at sea.³

But probate is not conclusive as to extraneous matters, or matters dehors the record; nor is it conclusive as to 

1 Register of Wills Act of 1917, (P. L. 415) Sec. 16 (a); Act of 

June 25, 1895 (P. L. 305), 1 Purd. 1072-3 (e-i). See also Purd. Stat. Ann.

Tit. 20, Sec. 1886. 

2 See 1 Purd. 1072 (b-d).

A register is a judge and the admission of a will to probate is a judicial decision. His judgment if it be in favor of the will, is evidence of its validity in all respects whatever, conclusive as to personal property and presumptive as to real. Such judgment can only be set aside on appeal, and is unimpeachable in any other proceeding. Robinson's Est., 13 Erie 60.

After the lapse of the statutory period, with no action at law duly pursued to contest a will, the decree of probate, which had been but prima facie to that time, becomes conclusive, and, therefore, affects the title to land. Way v. Hooton, 156 Pa. 8, 20; McCay v. Clayton, 119 Pa. 133; 

Broe v. Boyle, 108 Pa. 76. Terry's Est., 7 D. & C. 350, and see Sebik's

PROBATE OF FOREIGN WILLS. 

Where it becomes necessary to probate in Pennsylvania a copy of a will which has theretofore been originally probated in another state or foreign country the appropriate procedure is set forth in detail in the statute: "Copies of wills and testaments proved in any other State, Territory or possession of the United States of America, or any foreign country according to the laws thereof, and duly authenticated, may be offered for probate before any register having jurisdiction; and proceedings thereon may be had with the same effect, so far as respects the granting of letters testamentary, or of administration with the will annexed, as upon the originals; and if the executor or other person producing any such copy shall produce also therewith a copy of the record of the proceedings for the probate of the original, and of the letters testamentary, or other authority to administer, issued thereon, attested by the person having power to receive the probate of such original in the place where it was proved, with the seal of office, if there be one, annexed, together with the certificate of the chief judge or presiding magistrate of the State, country, county or district where such original was proved; that the same appears to have been duly proved, and to be of force, and that the attestation is in due form; such copies and proceedings shall be deemed sufficient proof, unless the contrary be shown, for the granting of letters testamentary or of administration with the will annexed, as the case may require, without the production or examination of the witnesses attesting such will." 996 The method of exemplifying the will and record of probate in other states of the Union under the Act of Con-

22. USE OF CERTIFIED COPIES. 

Properly to disclose of record in other counties of the state where the property of the decedent may be located the disposition made thereof by the testator, the law provides: "In any case in which a last will or testamentary paper shall have been duly proved before the register of wills for any county of this Commonwealth, and shall relate to real estate in any county thereof, it shall be lawful to take from the office of such register a copy of said will or paper and of the probate thereof, duly certified by such register under his seal of office to be a full and perfect copy of the same, and to file the said copy in the office of the register of wills in any county in which any of the real estate owned by the testator may be, which said register shall forthwith record the said copy. And the record of such copy shall be, and is hereby declared to be, as valid and effectual in law as the original will or paper after probate, or its duly certified copy, or its record would be for all purposes of vesting title, of evidence, and of notice. "Like proceedings may be had at the instance of any party interested, to obtain the certification of all subsequent proceedings appearing in the records of the regis ter of wills concerning such probate." 13

23. TIME AND METHOD OF APPEAL.

This act is not a statute of limitations; it declares a rule of evidence, which, after the lapse of the time limited without proceedings instituted, makes that conclusive which before was prima facie only; it provides for the greater certainty of title; it affects the title to the realty and not merely the remedy for it recovery.24

Under this section an appeal lies from the act of the register in revoking letters of administration; Moninger's Est., 3 Wash. 88.

This section of the Register of Wills Act does not dominate Secs. 18 and

It was error for the orphan's court to issue an order to the register of wills to allow an appeal from the probate of a will without furnishing a bond, in that the register of wills act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 415, expressly provides that an appeal cannot be taken unless a bond be filed. 

The right of appeal was unknown to the common law but it is a process of the civil law and is wholly dependent upon statutory authority. 

It is within the power of the legislature to prescribe the cases in which and the courts to which parties shall be entitled to bring a cause for review; and to impose such conditions and restrictions as it may see fit. 

In so doing neither the XIV amendment nor article I, section 9, of the 

Pennsylvania constitution is infringed. Polke's Est., 85 P. L. J. 641, 51 

York 103, 30 D. & C. 521 holding: "in Bailey's Est., 281 Pa. 392, where the bond was not signed by the sureties within the time prescribed, the appeal from the register was dismissed. In discussing the act of 1917 our supreme court in a per curiam opinion said, (395): The terms of the act of assembly referred to make a strict compliance therewith necessary; the bond executed by the appellants alone does not comply with the law, and the register should have dismissed the appeal. The statute is specific as to when the appeal may be taken and as to how it is to be perfected. 

Ample time is given to comply with these requirements. The required conditions have not been met in the case at bar and the situation is as if no appeal had been filed.''

In order to prevent the needless and sometimes intentional delays which have often occurred in the prosecution of proceedings before the register the Commission of 1915 introduced a new statutory provision: "Where a caveat is entered against the probate of any last will or testamentary paper, or where there is a dispute as to such probate or as to the granting of letters testamentary or of administration, the orphans' court of the county in which said will or testamentary paper has been offered for probate or said letters testamentary or of administration have been applied for, may, by general rule or by special order in the case, on the petition" of the register of wills of said county or of any party interested, direct said register to certify the entire record thereto pertaining to said court, which shall then determine whether the will or testamentary paper shall be admitted to probate or an issue devisavit vel non be directed to the court of common pleas of said county, or whether said letters testamentary or of administration shall be granted, in like manner as if the said will or testamentary paper had been admitted to probate, or said letters testamentary or of administration had been granted by said register and an appeal been taken to the orphans' court from his decree. There is also a provision for such certification directly by the register where there are difficult or disputable matters: "Where objections are made, or a caveat is entered, against the probate of any last will and testament, and no precept for an issue is directed by the register into the court of common pleas as aforesaid, or where objections are made to the granting of letters testamentary or of administration to any person applying therefor, or where any question of kindred or other disputable and difficult matter, comes into controversy before any register, he may certify the entire record thereto pertaining to the orphans' court of the county, for the determination by said court of such disputable and difficult matter, giving convenient notice of the time when the matter will be heard in said court to all persons interested."¹

Cross's Est., 278 Pa. 170, where the following rules were promulgated: 

1. The orphans' court has power of its own volition to send any issue of fact to the common pleas. (Miller's Est., 39 Lanc. 380.) 

2. Where a substantial dispute exists on a material point of fact concerning the status of an alleged will or testamentary writing, and the evidence is of the probative value required by our decisions, the orphans' court must send such issue to the common pleas when requested so to do by any party in interest, if that request is made in due season. (Dahlstrom's 

Est., 44 Montg. 258; Stewart's Est., 45 Montg. 216.) 

3. After judgment entered on the verdict in the common pleas, so long as the judgment stands undisturbed, the findings of fact by the jury of

§ 29 

"When the register of wills has certified to the orphans' court for its determination an application for an issue devisavit vel non, that tribunal may appoint one of its members to hear the evidence produced and report his conclusion thereon to the court in banc. "To his report exceptions may be filed by the parties in interest, or some of them, whereupon the court in banc should hear argument thereon, and enter such a decree as to right and justice shall belong. "The hearing judge acts as a chancellor in such cases, and his findings are entitled to the weight of a jury's verdict, and, where supported by evidence, though in dispute, are controlling in the appellate court. This is particularly so where the decision of the case depends on the testimony of witnesses whose credibility must be weighed and passed upon, especially if the hearing judge saw and heard those who testified for and against the matters under consideration. that tribunal are conclusive on the orphans' Court, (a) whenever the issue is of the class mentioned in Rule 2,-whether sent to the common pleas on request or otherwise, or (b) when it involves the decision of a fact upon which depends the jurisdiction of the orphans' court. 

4. When the issue is in neither of the classes mentioned in Rule 3, and merely involves facts as to which the tribunal sending it desires advice, the result in the common pleas is not conclusive in any sense, but, when the judgment on the verdict is not appealed from, if followed by the orphans' court, the Supreme Court may consider the findings of the jury as acquiesced in by the appellant. 

5. In cases falling within Rule 3, the date of the entry of the judgment in the common pleas marks the time from which the six-months' period for taking an appeal runs, while, in cases within Rule 4, the date of the final decree in the orphans' court marks the date from which the judgment on the issue in the common pleas becomes final for purposes of appeal. 

6. In the class of cases covered by Rule 4, where the verdict is not binding, the refusal of an issue will not be reviewed on appeal (Thompson's 

App., 103 Pa. 603, 607); but when the issue is granted, and the facts found thereon are adopted as the basis of a final decree by the orphans' court, the party thus aggrieved may appeal from such decree and at the same time appeal from the judgment of the common pleas on the feigned issue (Green v. Mills, 103 Pa. 22). 

7. The refusal of an issue in cases covered by Rule 2 will be reviewed on appeal when the record shows, by evidence of the probative value required by our decisions, that a substantial dispute on a material question of fact exists, but not otherwise (Fleming's Est., 265 Pa. 399, 406;

"In a will contest the hearing judge sitting as a chancellor must consider all the evidence. "The right to an issue under the statute, depends upon whether there is a substantial dispute upon a material matter of fact, and unless there is the proponent is not entitled to an issue on any of the questions raised. Such substantial dispute exists only when the court, after weighing the evidence impartially, feels that the ends of justice call for a verdict against the will, or it is so uncertain on this point that it could conscientiously sustain a finding either way on one or more of the controlling issues involved."' 8

A substantial dispute upon a question of fact exists if a verdict that might be reached by a jury, even if at variance with the opinion of the judge conducting the hearing, would not have to be set aside as judicially untenable because contrary to the weight of the evidence.

cept for an issue to the court of common pleas 19 of the county for the trial thereof." 20 "It is the duty of the hearing judge sitting as a chancellor, after weighing the evidence impartially, to refuse to present the question to a jury, unless he feels the ends of justice call for a verdict against the will, or he is so uncertain on this point that he could conscionably sustain a finding either way on one or more of the controlling issues involved. "It is the function of the chancellor to decide whether there is a substantial dispute upon a material fact, but he may not decide the case as he would if acting in the capacity of an ultimate fact-finding tribunal. "A substantial dispute exists, requiring the grant of an issue devisavit vel non, if a verdict that might be reached by a jury, even at variance with the opinion of the chancellor, would not have to be set aside as judicially untenable because contrary to the weight of the evidence. In reviewing a chancellor's refusal of an issue devisavit vel non the question for the appellate court to decide is not whether it would have

§ 69 

Lack of space prevents an exhaustive study of the evidence admissible, its weight and probative value.5 54 reached the same result had it been acting as chancellor, but rather whether a judicial mind, on due consideration of the evidence as a whole, could reasonably have reached the conclusion of the chancellor; in other words, the chancellor's decision will not be reversed unless an abuse of discretion on his part appears. Dible's Est., 316 Pa. 553 rev'g 112 Super. 23 and af'g 81 P. L. J. 263; Taylor's Est., 316 Pa. 557; Moore's Est., 317 Pa. 42.

In the trial of an issue to determine the validity of a will, the judge sits as a chancellor; the evidence is addressed quite as much to him as to the jury, and he cannot permit the jury to do what he, as a chancellor, would not do. 

If the judge feels that the ends of justice call for a verdict against the will, or he is so uncertain on this point that he could in good conscience support a finding either way on one or more of the controlling issues involved, the question should be submitted to the jury, and unless, on reexamination after verdict, the evidence proves insufficient to support their finding, that conclusion should stand, even though its effect be to set aside the will.

In such case where the action of the chancellor is based on a consideration of the evidence, there is, in effect, a judicial determination, independent of the finding of the jury, that the verdict ought to stand; to reverse this judgment, in a stronger sense than is commonly applicable to a disappointed suitor, the laboring oar is on the appellant. On petition for an issue devisavit vel non the opinion of the physician who attended the decedent that he did not have testamentary capacity if opposed to facts established by reliable evidence is not entitled to overcome such evidence. Sapp's Est., 43 Lanc. 681.

Expert medical opinions are of little weight when based upon insufficient facts or an erroneous conception of testamentary capacity, and should be entirely disregarded when contrary to established facts revealing mental capacity.

opposed to established facts are not entitled to much respect in proceedings devisavit vel non.

Testimony given freely at an original hearing by the scrivener of a will acting also as a subscribing witness, and his stenographer, to the effect that a testator's mark was affixed before his name, cannot be overcome by testimony of the same witnesses at an additional hearing subsequent to the adjudication, which appears to have been given in a studied effort to show ratification or adoption. Bobbitt's Est., 19 Erie 391.

On the trial of an issue as to testamentary capacity and undue influence, evidence of declarations by testatrix several years after the execution of the alleged will and of declaration of the principal beneficiary several years prior thereto is properly excluded. Devereux's Estate, 18 D. & C. 289.

When the testimony of friends and acquaintances of the testatrix is conflicting in a proceeding to contest a will of an aged person, it appears to raise a substantial question as to mental capacity which should be submitted to a jury for determination. Kelly's Est., 28 Sch. 275.

Evidence that testator had declared he would never make a will and that the will was not produced until some time after his death is not sufficient to warrant an award of an issue devisavit vel non, when there is detailed evidence by the scrivener and witnesses regarding the execution of the will and some evidence that the existence of the document was disclosed to certain members of the family shortly after its execution. Catania's 

Est., 20 D. & C. 656.

In a will contest involving the questions of testamentary capacity and undue influence, prior wills of undisputed authenticity are admissible and relevant evidence, as showing the basis of the will under attack and testator's purpose in making it. Peterson's Est., 18 D. & C. 429.

The testimony of an absent witness, given at a former hearing when the witness was subject to cross-examination, may be impeached when offered in evidence at a later trial by statements made by the witness, out of court and not under oath, subsequent to the first hearing, the admission of such evidence being entirely within the discretion of the trial judge. Curtis's 

Est., 27 D. & C. 31.

The operation of a decree adjudicating a person to be weak-minded and appointing a guardian for his estate, is prospective only, and in and of itself cannot nullify a prior will executed by such person through the proceedings in which the decree was entered were begun on the same day on which the will was executed. Taylor's Est., 316 Pa. 557.

In a case where the question of the forgery of an alleged will depends upon the credibility of witnesses, it is especially proper to grant an issue devisavit vel non and award a precept to the court of common pleas for the trial and determination of the disputed question of fact. Boland's Estate, 34 Lack. 158.

Experts, and others acquainted with decedent's signature, may if duly qualified, express an opinion as to whether or not the signature to the will

§ 71 

is in the handwriting of decedent; but such testimony will be of little or no weight as against the testimony of credible and disinterested witnesses who actually saw the decedent sign his or her name to the will. Lowe's 

Est., 318 Pa. 497, and see Brooks' Est., 27 Del. 140 and cases there cited.

In a proceeding to determine the authenticity of a will, the signature to which is alleged to have been forged, the testimony of handwriting experts is admissible, although standing alone such evidence is insufficient to sustain a finding of forgery in the face of direct and credible evidence to the contrary. 

On appeal from a decree dismissing an appeal from the probate of a will, filed on the ground that the signature to the will was a forgery, it was held that the evidence of the witnesses on behalf of the proponents of the will who testified that they saw the actual writing of the signature by decedent was not so credible and trustworthy as to overcome all the opposing evidence in the case, and that, taking into consideration the will itself, the surrounding facts and circumstances, and the direct evidence of forgery produced by contestants, it was an abuse of discretion on the part of the orphans' court to refuse to award an issue. DeLaurentiis's Est., 323 Pa. 70. "On a hearing before the orphans' court on an application for an issue d. v. n. opinion evidence standing alone as to the forgery of the signature to the instrument will not sustain a finding of forgery in the face of the direct and credible evidence of witnesses who saw the signature written: 

Henry's Est., 276 Pa. 511. "The Act of May 15, 1895, P. L. 69, while declaring the relevancy of expert evidence and its scope where there is a question as to any writing, does not attempt to define its weight: Ibid., See also, McWilliams's Est., 259 Pa. 526. "Osborn on Questioned Documents (2d ed.) at page 314, states that 'Marks as signatures are sometimes questioned and present some unusual problems. The law reports contain sharply conflicting views on the subject, but generally hold that a "mark" does not contain identifying characteristics.' "No Pennsylvania case was submitted for our consideration, and we have failed to find one as to technical testimony regarding the genuineness or lack of genuineness of a cross-mark in the execution of a will." Olszewski's 

Est., 35 Lack. 47. "To authorize the admission of the writing offered as a test or standard, nothing short of evidence by a person who saw the party write the paper, or of an admission by such party of its being genuine, or evidence of equal authority is sufficient: Baker v. Haines, 6 Wh. 283. This rule has been adhered to in later cases (Cohen v. Teller, 93 Pa. 123), and was not changed by the act of 1895 [May 15, 1895, (P. L. 69)]. The case of Sweigart v. 32. RIGHT TO LETTERS, RENUNCIATION. 

The execution of a valid will having been thus established, letters testamentary will be granted to the executor or executors named therein if of age 55 and otherwise competent, unless such executor renounce," whereupon letters of administration c. t. a. will be granted to those entitled thereto.58 56

70 The grant of ancillary letters of administration is necessarily based on the assumption that the domicile of the testator at the time of his death was in another jurisdiction. Taylor's Est., 15 D. & C. 281, af'd in 301 · 

Pa. 7.

A native of Pennsylvania who moved to California two years before her death was a resident of the latter state, where, during her residence there, she had frequently expressed her satisfaction with her new place of abode and said she never expected to reside again in Pennsylvania. The fact that she kept her funds deposited in a Pennsylvania bank and preferred to conduct her business through it, as well as that she desired to be buried at her old home, would not prevent California from administering her estate.

Ancillary letters to administer on any assets in Allegheny County, Pa., were granted, where the evidence showed that at the time of her death, testatrix was a resident of California. Under these circumstances, the orphans' court in Pennsylvania refused to take original jurisdiction. 

Charitable bequests void in Pennsylvania would be distributed according to the law of the state of her residence. Kerin's Est., 82 P. L. J. 108.

Where a Pennsylvania creditor of a nonresident decedent fails to petition for the appointment of an ancillary administrator for over eight years after the decedent's death, and in the meantime all of decedent's real estate in Pennsylvania (which was his only asset therein) has been sold and the proceeds distributed in accordance with the laws of the State of domicile, and there are no unadministered assets, either real or personal, within Pennsylvania, an application for an order upon the domiciliary fiduciaries to pay over alleged assets within the jurisdiction to the ancillary administrator must be dismissed.

The proper procedure for determining whether a mortgagee of real estate belonging to a nonresident decedent is a creditor of the estate is by an audit of the ancillary administrator's account, even though the account 75

"Where land is located in Pennsylvania and the domicile of decedent is in another state and an ancillary administrator is appointed here, the land would then be sold by such administrator for the payment of local or foreign debts. After the payment of our domestic creditors the surplus would be remitted to the legal representatives in the domiciliary jurisdiction for the payment of its creditors: Middleby's Est., 249 Pa. 203, 207. Wolfe v. Lewisburg T. & S. D. Co., 305 Pa. 583.

A Pennsylvania orphans' court has no discretion, upon the audit of an ancillary administrator's account, to remit Pennsylvania creditors, including .lawyers and the accountant as to her claim for commission, to the State of domicile, whether they be creditors of the decedent or of the ancillary executrix; only after such claims have been taken care of has it discretion to remit the balance to the domicile or to retain it and distribute the entire fund.

Where it appears that the estate of a nonresident, as to which ancillary administration proceedings are pending in Pennsylvania, may be insolvent, the proper procedure is to adjudicate the claims of Pennsylvania creditors and administration claimants, to award distribution to them and to Pennsylvania legatees if any, and then to suspend payment thereof until it has been judicially determined in the State of domicile how much of the fund should be remitted to the domicile to satisfy claimants there. "At common law, upon the death of an executor, the executorship devolved upon his executor; and upon the death of one or more joint executors it devolved upon the survivors, and passed ultimately, upon the death of the last survivor, to his executor. Upon the death of the executor of an executor, the executorship passed to his executor, and so long as the chain of representation remained unbroken by an intestacy, the ultimate executor represented every preceding testator." 89 This is still the law of England, and some of the American states.

Where no administrator pendente lite has been appointed, and no application for such an appointment has been made until after probate of the will has been refused, the register of wills may refuse to appoint an administrator pendente lite but appoint a full administrator.³

Administrators durante minoritate are appointed by the register where the executors named in the will at the time of the death of the decedent or the next of kin of an intestate are minors. His powers and duties are similar to that of an administrator pendente lite and his appointment terminates when the executor named in the will or such next of kin reach majority, whereupon the administrator temporarily appointed should file his account and the balance found thereby turned over under proper award to the executor or administrator. 

Administrators durante absentia are appointed when the executors named in the will or the next of kin of an intestate are out of the jurisdiction, as for instance, traveling abroad and cannot return within a reasonable time for the assumption of their duties. Upon return to the jurisdiction and qualification as executor or administrator, the duties of the temporary administrator cease and the procedure is as outlined above.

41. GRANT OF LETTERS AFTER TWENTY-ONE YEARS. 

A lapse of twenty-one years after the death of the decedent affects the original jurisdiction of the register in the grant of letters either of administration or testamentary. In such case the law provides: "No letters testamentary or of administration shall in any case be originally granted upon the estate of any decedent, after the expiration of twenty-one years from the day of his decease, except on the order of the orphans' court upon due cause shown.”’7

This act applies not only to cases in which no letters of administration have previously been granted, but also to cases in which prior letters have been issued. "No 6 When a will is properly proved and an executor is named therein, if of age, the register has no discretion but must issue letters to the appointee of the testator.

A testator has the right to provide for a second executor in case of the death of the first one and his rights must be respected. Crandall's Est., 6 Erie 59, 2 Som. 258. 

7 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 2 (b), derived from Sec. 

21 of the Act of March 15, 1832 (P. L. 135), 1 Purd. 1075 (u-v). See also 

Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 342.

This applies to the grant of letters only, not to the probate of a will. 

Comm'th v. Fisher, 2 D. & C. 300. "The intent of this statute is that any disputable matter should be disposed of by the orphans' court in the first instance rather than by the register. When it appears quite clear from the petition that the petitioner is a party in interest, that there is a vacancy in the office, and that there are unadministered assets, it has been our practice to grant such leave ex parte without notice to the parties in interest. If any dispute should later appear, the parties will not be concluded by our decree made without notice, and may raise the point before the register. Experience has shown that in the great majority of such cases a citation to parties in interest will be useless paper work. But when there appears to be a doubt on the face of the petition, the parties interested should be notified by citation, and be heard in the usual way, before the leave is granted." 

The register of wills will not be authorized ex parte to grant letters of administration d. b. n. c. t. a. on the estate of a decedent who has been dead more than 21 years, upon petition of one claiming to be a party in interest, alleging that the trust company which was the original administrator has ceased to exist, if it does not set forth how petitioner happens to be a party in interest or what other parties in interest there may be, and an answer has been filed alleging that the original trustee is still in existence. Penrose's Est., 24 D. & C. 647. 

8 Hanbest's Est., 21 Super. 427.

§ 85 

authority is conferred upon the Court to grant the letters: nor is the original jurisdiction of the Register's in the least degree interfered with. But he is not to issue the letters, except upon order of the Court, due cause having been shown. By that it is intended, it must appear, that the decedent has been dead more than twenty-one years, that there is no executor or administrator of his estate, and assets of his estate still remain uncollected and unadministered." Such letters, if granted without an order, are not absolutely void; the sureties on the bond are liable to the parties in interest.10 And a stranger cannot appeal from a decree of the register, granting letters of administration on the estate of one who has been dead more than twenty-one years. 11 It will be noted that the court does not attempt to name the persons to whom such letters should be granted, as that would be an interference with the register's prerogative.

CHAPTER VII. 

BONDS OF ADMINISTRATORS AND EXECUTORS. 

42. BONDS OF ADMINISTRATORS. 

"It shall be the duty of every register¹ upon his granting any letters of administration, domiciliary or ancillary, of the goods and chattels of any person dying intestate, to take a bond or bonds, from the person or persons receiving such letters, with two or more sufficient individual sureties, or sufficient corporate security; or the register may, in his discretion, permit any corporation to which letters are granted to give its own bond without surety. In fixing the amount of any bond, respect shall be had to the value of the estate; and all bonds shall be in the name of the Commonwealth." 15

On an appeal from the decision of the Register of Wills of Allegheny County revoking letters of administration issued on a decedent's estate, it appeared the decedent died in Philadelphia County and letters of administration were issued by the Register of Wills of that county to a foster son of the decedent. 51. PROCEDURE TO OPEN DECREE OF PROBATE. 

It frequently happens that after a will has been probated a codicil is discovered which should have been probated with the will, as its effect may be to change the terms of the will or republish it with a consequent effect on the distribution of the estate.

The procedure thereupon is greatly similar to that necessitated in the actual contest of a will. That is, an appeal must be taken from the decree of probate and the proceedings certified to the orphans' court." In this and the following section are considered those cases involving no question of the validity of the after discovered document. 

All the parties whose interest will be affected by the probate of the codicil must either join in the petition or be cited as respondents. In the latter case the form of petitions would of course be varied, eliminating the statement of joinder, changing the prayer to request a citation and a decree should be attached."9 

If the matters of fact set up in the petition require denial, an answer should be filed.

In either case if no answer be filed the matter is ordered down for hearing and the court, upon merely formal proof of the after-discovered codicil, will enter a decree¹ pro forma.

PART II PRESUMED DECEDENTS CHAPTER IX. 

METHOD OF PROCEDURE. 

54. THE PRESUMPTION OF DEATH. 

It has been noticed that letters granted on the estate of a living person are void" yet prior to 1885 no method was available to determine the fact of death under the presumption arising at common law from an absence of seven years. It became obvious to the legislature that such power should exist somewhere, as the Supreme 

Court had observed: 68 "It is not in the interests of order or good government that property should lie ownerless or open to conflicting claims. If the absentee be really dead it is conceded that the proceeding to administer his estate is unimpeachable. 

But if he be dead, so far as can be learned, though death be not absolutely proved, yet the effect to the state is the same, there is property in its charge without a recognized owner. It must have power to meet such a case or one of its chief functions as a government must go unperformed. 99 69 To correct this situation a series of laws have been enacted" which provide “a complete system for the dis- 

67 See Sec. 1, supra. 

68 In the absence of proof that a person was confronted with any peril that might reasonably be expected to destroy his life, or that he was in any particular or immediate danger, it will be presumed that he lived until the expiration of seven years from the time he was last heard of and that his death occurred at the end of the seventh year. Levering's Trust, 9 D. & C. 328.

Otherwise the petition is substantially identical in form and thereafter the proceedings are similar. 78 Thereupon the court will enter a decree appointing a master in the form set forth in the foregoing section. 

57. NOTICE AND ADVERTISEMENT. 

Actual notice of all master's meetings should of course be given to counsel for the petitioner in the proceedings. 

The minimum notice" by advertisement is set forth in the act, that is, in addition to that required by rule of court, if any, in a legal periodical,8° notice shall be given "in a newspaper published in said county, once a week for four successive weeks.' 

Such other advertisement is permissible as may be found expedient, especially in the case of a non-resident where like notice should be given in the locality of his last residence and in such other places as he may have been last seen since his disappearance.

As to the evidence and testimony admissible, the act provides: "At the hearing in either of the cases provided for in the preceding clauses of this section, the orphans' court shall take such legal evidence as shall be offered, for the purpose of ascertaining whether the presumption of death is established; 81 or may appoint a master to take such testimony and report his findings thereon; and no person shall be disqualified to testify by reason of his or her relationship as husband or wife to the presumed decedent, or of his or her interest in the estate of the presumed decedent." 82

In such proceeding obviously the widest latitude is given for the production of any evidence which may throw light upon the inquiry.

After all available testimony and evidence has been deduced the court will render its decision or the master his report finding as a fact either for or against the presumption of death. 83 To such findings exceptions may be filed by any party in interest and will be disposed of in due course. 84

If alive when last heard from at his new domicile, the presumption is that life continues: Francis v. Francis, 180 Pa. 644.

63. DISTRIBUTION ON REFUNDING BONDS. 

In the case of direct distribution of an estate of a presumed decedent resident of this commonwealth, the statute provides for protection to the presumed decedent against the possibilities of his continuance in life: "Before any distribution of the proceeds of the estate of such presumed decedent, the persons, other than creditors, entitled to receive the same shall, respectively, give sufficient real or personal security, to be approved by the orphans' court having jurisdiction, in such sum and form as the court shall direct, with condition that if the said presumed decedent shall in fact be at the time alive, they will respectively refund the amounts received by each on demand, with interest thereon." CHAPTER X. 

VACATION OF PROCEEDINGS. 

65. PROCEDURE TO VACATE DECREE AND EF. 

FECT THEREOF. 

If the presumed decedent is in fact alive and such fact is proved to the satisfaction of the court prior to final decree the preliminary decree is vacated as heretofore shown.Ⓡ

If, however, such fact is not established until after the final decree has been entered and letters granted, the act provides an adequate remedy. On petition "The orphans' court may revoke the said letters and vacate the decree that the presumption of death has been established, at any time, on due and satisfactory proof that the presumed decedent is in fact alive." 10

Thereupon a hearing is had¹¹ before the court, or where possible before the same master who officiated in the original proceedings, and if the facts alleged are proven a decree¹² is entered vacating the former decree and revoking the letters.

The statute specifically provides the rights and remedies of all parties under these circumstances: "After such revocation all the powers of the executor or administrator shall cease, but all receipts or disbursements of assets, and other acts previously done by him. shall remain as valid as if the said letters were unrevoked. The executor or administrator shall settle an account of his administration down to the time of such revocation, and shall transfer all assets, remaining in his hands, to the person as whose executor or administrator he has acted, or to his duly authorized agent or

66. PROCEDURE ON PRODUCTION OF WILL OR LATER WILL. 

If after letters of administration are granted a will of the presumed decedent is discovered, or after letters testamentary are granted on a will, a later will is found, the act provides an ample remedy: "Whenever, hereafter, letters testamentary or of administration shall be issued upon the estate of any person, presumed to be dead, on account of absence of seven years or more from the place of his last domicile, in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this section, the person having custody of any will which may have been left by such presumed decedent, in case letters of administration have been issued, or of any later will, in case letters testamentary have been issued, or any creditor or any person interested in the estate, may file a petition in the orphans' court in which the proceedings to establish the death by presumption have been held, as aforesaid, setting forth the facts of the case, a copy of said will or later will, or an averment that such will exists, and the names of all persons interested in the estate of the presumed decedent. Upon the filing of such petition, said court, after due notice to all parties in interest, may enter an order directing the register of wills to receive proof in support of the averments of said petition and, if established, to admit said will or later will to probate; and, if an executor be named in said will, to revoke said letters of administration, or, in case an earlier will shall have been admitted to probate, to set aside such probate and revoke the letters testamentary issued thereunder.'' 15

It will be noted that the method of procedure on the discovery of a later will is precisely the same as that heretofore described in such circumstances during the administration of a testator actually known to be dead.10

PART III  CHAPTER XI. 

RIGHTS BEFORE GRANT OF LETTERS. 

67. ACCESS TO SAFE DEPOSIT BOX. 

If the decedent is supposed to have made a will the executor named therein, if known, or the next of kin if an executor is not known to have been appointed, are authorized to visit and search the safe deposit boxes owned by the decedent in an endeavor to locate such document if the same cannot readily be found among the personal effects of the deceased.

Such a right is generally recognized by safe deposit companies who will open the box for this purpose and examine its contents, but in so doing they usually require, as a safeguard, the presence of the next of kin. 

If found the will is delivered to the executor named, or if none, or if the executor be deceased or unable to qualify, to the next of kin and his or their receipt taken therefor, or lodged with the register for probate. 

68. SAFEGUARDING ASSETS. 

It very frequently occurs that a portion of the decedent's property requires immediate attention to prevent its loss or waste as in the case of livestock or growing crops or articles of a very perishable nature, such as food stuffs, and the like.

Necessarily, in most cases,21 a certain interval must elapse between the decedent's death and the grant of letters and during that period certain important duties devolve upon the next of kin who are presumptively en- 

21 See Sec. 3, supra. "The true representative is bound by those acts of an executor de son tort which are lawful and such as the true representative would be bound to perform in the due course of administration, but not by any other acts of the intermeddler." Sherly's Est., 19 Erie 486, 117

titled to letters in the event of intestacy of if no executor is known to have been appointed. Of course, if such executor is known, the same duties devolve upon him. 

Any acts of the next of kin, or even a stranger, if no kin are available, done to protect such property, will be confirmed on grounds of ordinary good sense or from humanitarian principles, pending the official appointment of an administrator or executor. 

69. FUNERAL AND BURIAL OF DECEDENT. 

Since the statute as hereinafter shown, puts the duty of paying the decedent's debts, of which funeral expenses have priority, on the administrator or executor, "the duty to determine when, where and in what manner the body shall be buried rests with the executor or administrator. But his right is not absolute nor his judgment conclusive. The determination must rest * * * 6. 'upon considerations arising partly out of the domestic relations-partly out of the universal sentiment-that the dead should repose in some spot where they will be secure from profanation; partly out of what is demanded by society for the preservation of the public health, morality and decency; and partly often out of what is required by a proper respect for and observance of the wishes of the departed themselves.' Under the statute in Pennsylvania the right to administration belongs first to the surviving husband or widow. To such survivor, therefore, belongs the right of control of the body for interment, and a waiver of the right to administer will not include a waiver of such right of control unless it be express and absolute. In the exigencies of business and the interests of the estate it is not unfrequently desirable that a stranger, or even a creditor should administer, but no court would sanction a disregard by such an administrator of the wishes of a widow or even of the next of kin, as to the place and manner of burial.

As a practical matter it is rarely that a funeral can be arranged or conducted by an administrator in his official capacity as ordinarily letters will not be granted until after the burial of the deceased. If the will can be produced and opened, prior to burial, the desires of the decedent, if any, therein expressed with reference to his interment should be followed.24 "How far the desires of the decedent should prevail against those of a surviving husband or wife is an open question, but as against remoter connections, such wishes especially if strongly and recently expressed, should usually prevail."

Deceased had been a member of a relief association of a fire company and upon his death the association admitted an obligation to pay $461 as benefits. The by-laws provided that payments were intended for the immediate relief of the "family" of the member "for funeral and incidental expenses" and were payable to the family, if any; otherwise to his administrator or executor.'' The fund was claimed by the executor, and by the children and grandchildren. On a framed issue the testimony showed that decedent's children had not lived with him since 1919; that an unfriendly feeling existed; that they never visited him even during his last illness; did not attend his funeral, and neither paid nor incurred expenses in connection therewith. There was no testimony that decedent contributed to their maintenance by allowance, gifts or otherwise. Held, that the family relationship did not exist between decedent and the children or grandchildren within the intent of the by-law; that they were not entitled to share in the relief fund; and that it should be decreed to the executrix. 

The fact that there were other funeral funds, such as insurance policies on decedent's life is immaterial to the issue and the fact that the funeral expenses had been actually paid out of insurance money does not warrant a decree of the fund in question to the children and grandchildren. Stitzel v. Smith, 28 Berks 26.

70. ADVERTISEMENT OF GRANT OF LETTERS. 

"The executors or administrators of every decedent shall, immediately after the granting of letters testamentary or of administration to them, cause notice thereof to be given in one newspaper, published at or near the place where such decedent resided, and in the legal periodical, if any, designated by rule of court for the publication of legal notices, once a week, during at least six successive weeks, together with their names and places of residence; and in every such notice they shall request all persons having claims or demands against the estate of the said decedent to make known the same, and all persons indebted to the said decedent to make payment to them without delay."' 31 33 Care should be taken that the required notice 32 is inserted not only in a public newspaper of the locality but also in the legal periodical, if any, required by the rules of the orphans' court of the county where the decedent died. It is also of importance that the requirement of the act that notice be given "immediately" be strictly followed. A delay in doing this will cause a corresponding delay in filing the account which can only be done after at least six full months have expired since the date of the first complete insertion of the advertisement.35 34 Neglect to advertise is no defense to a citation to file an account as in such case an accounting will be or- 36

After the advertisement has appeared for six successive weeks the administrator should procure from the newspaper office what is technically known as a "proof of publication"; that is, an affidavit showing a copy of the notice and setting forth the time and manner of its publication. In most jurisdictions this "proof of publication" must be produced and exhibited to the court when the administrator's or executor's account is audited. 

71. NOTICE TO CORPORATE BENEFICIARIES. 

A special duty devolves upon executors with reference to corporate beneficiaries under the will. In such case the law provides: "Whenever a devise or bequest shall be made to any corporate body by any last will and testament, the executors thereof shall, within three months after they undertake the execution of such will, make known, by letters addressed to such corporate body, the nature and amount of such devise and bequest, together with their names and places of residence." 39

While the main object of this section is, seemingly, notice to charitable corporations, yet the act does not so limit it and in terms it applies to any corporation. 

Common courtesy would seem to require like notice to all beneficiaries whose whereabouts are known.

 74. POWERS OF ADMINISTRATORS D. B. N. 

From the very nature of their office and the purpose of their appointment, in addition to their ordinary duties of administration, such administrators have special duties to perform with reference to the acquisition and administration of the estate of the decedent not previously administered. As to such administrators, the law provides: "Administrators de bonis non, with or without a will annexed, shall have power to demand and recover from their predecessors in the administration, or their legal representatives, all moneys, goods and assets remaining in their hands due and belonging to the estate of the decedent; and to commence and prosecute actions upon promises made to such predecessors in their representative character; and to take and defend appeals and sue forth and defend writs of scire facias and writs of execution upon judgments, obtained by or in the name of the executors or administrators into whose place they may have come; and also to proceed with and perfect all undistribute the proceeds among legatees, the power belongs to them virtute officii and may be exercised by an administrator c. t. a. This is so whether there be an absolute direction, so as to work a conversion, or the power be discretionary, and whether the distribution is to be immediate, or upon the expiration of a certain time, or upon the uncertain contingency of a life or lives.

Where no trust is created by a will, the administrator d. b. n., c. t. a. cannot be regarded as a substituted trustee, and it is immaterial whether the distribution of the proceeds of a sale is to be immediate or on the expiration of a certain period of time. 

Where real estate left by a testator is subject to a power of sale given by him for the benefit of more than one of his distributees, a judgment recovered against one of them will be divested by a sale of the land under the power. Kemerer v. Johnstone, 318 Pa. 526, (af'g. 25 North. 54) cit’g:

CHAPTER XIII. 

THE INVENTORY AND APPRAISEMENT. 

76. WHEN AND WHERE TO FILE INVENTORY. 

One of the first principal duties of an executor or administrator is to prepare and file an inventory.56 As to this the law provides with respect to a resident decedent: “It shall be the duty of the said executors or administrators to make a true and perfect inventory of all the goods, chattels and credits of the deceased, as far as they may know or can ascertain them, and file the same in the register's office 57 within thirty days from the time of administration granted.'' 58 

And in the case of a nonresident: "That in the case of a will of a decedent, not resident, at the time of his decease, within this Commonwealth, proved in another state or in a foreign country, whereof letters testamentary or of administration with the will annexed may be granted in this state, or in a case of ancillary administration of the estate of a nonresident intestate, the inventory herein mentioned shall be of the goods, chattels and credits of the deceased within this 

Commonwealth.'' 58 "The obvious purpose for which an inventory" is re- 56 With this document there would also be filed certain affidavits relating to personal property taxes. Sec. 133a, infra.

The executor who himself causes an inventory to be prepared and filed has the burden of proof in any subsequent effort to show that the assets thus listed were not in fact the property of the decedent. "Of course, an inventory and appraisement is not conclusive, but is prima facie evidence of the extent and value of the estate and of the personal representative's liability therefor. However, a personal representative may show that, through inadvertence, ignorance or mistake, property has been therein erroneously included which does not in fact there belong: Stewart's Estate, 137 Pa. 175; and along such line the personal representative can go even so far as to establish that certain items listed as belonging to the deceased belonged in reality to such personal representative individually; but the law requires that such claims shall be supported by the clearest and most satisfactory evidence: Stewart's Estate, 137 Pa. 175.'' Cummings' Est., 25 Lack. 214, 38 York 94.

An administrator, in the absence of negligence or bad faith, is chargeable only with real values when ascertained by a proper sale, notwithstanding the fact that the sum realized by the sale is much less than the values at which the assets were inventoried and appraised, especially where it was not shown that more could have been realized at some other time. Inasmuch as ordinarily real estate is not an asset with which the administrator or executor has any concern, it will not be included in the inventory.80 Where, however, such real estate is under contract of sale by the decedent in his lifetime and the sale is completed by the administrator or executor acting under the provisions of the statute there is a conversion effected and the real estate becomes personal property and the proceeds of the sale should be included in the inventory. 

The inventory "is more likely to omit what it ought to contain, than to contain what ought to be omitted. It is, as the Act of Assembly declares, to be 'of all the goods, chattels, and credits of the deceased so far as he may know or can ascertain them,' and should not include anything with which the executor or administrator, as such, is not chargeable, as, for example, real estate, which, in fact, not being 'goods, chattels, or credits,' is excluded by the language of the act; and while it is true that lands which the will directs to be sold are regarded in equity as personal estate, as they cannot be distributed until actually converted, and the ownership of the decedent is shown by the public records, there seems to be no reason for setting them forth in the inventory, and still less for bringing them into the account. 

After all, however, utile per inutile non vitiatur, and no great harm can result from their introduction.'' 82

The general rule is to include no real estate in the inventory. It is quite a common mistake to do so, but in a great majority of cases there would be no occasion for so doing. Only two cases would appear to arise, the one where the will works a conversion and the other where the decedent in his lifetime contracted to sell real estate and died before the delivery of the deed. In the former the Act of Feb. 24, 1834, (P. L. 70) 1 Purd. 1090 (o), 1089 (e). See also 

Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 449.

Where an administrator fails to include assets of the decedent's estate in an inventory and final account, the court will require such administrator to file a supplemental inventory and account, embracing such omissions and fully accounting for all assets discovered subsequent to the filing of the first inventory. Riblet's Est., 7 Erie 10.

 81. METHOD OF APPRAISEMENT-FORM OF IN- VENTORY. 

In the usual case the preparation of the inventory is a simple matter. Bank accounts are given with interest added to the date of death. Personal effects are valued at the figure they would probably bring at public sale. 

Stock is given at the last market quotation and the same applies to bonds, though in the case of the latter interest accrued to the date of death must be added. In the case of personal effects of a technical nature, or where articles of great value or of rare quality such as valuable gems or old masters are involved the services of an expert should be engaged. In appraising securities it is frequently advisable to consult a responsible banker or broker.

All assets of whatsoever nature should be appraised at their value as of the date of death.

On all interest bearing securities such as bonds and mortgages, interest must be calculated up to the date of the decedent's death. The official tax appraisers throughout the state in their valuation of securities rely on the quotations published weekly in the "Commercial and Financial Chronicle" and an adjustment of values by the appraisers with those given therein will save any controversy with the official state appraisers in regard to the inheritance tax assessment.

The proper and exact valuation 87 of a decedent's effects is of the greatest importance not only as a matter of right for the information of creditors and distributees but as a matter of precaution for the administrator, as his liability is fixed by the valuation thus ascertained. 88 

An appraisement is only prima facie evidence of value, and where the discrepancy between the appraisement and the amount realized is great, and the consequences serious, an executor should be given full oppor- 87 Personal effects are valued at the figures they would bring at public sale. A lumping appraisal including the contents of certain rooms in a single amount is not a true and perfect inventory and appraisement. 

Merten's Est., 14 Erie 240, 47 York 27. 

88 And it may be objected to as being too high or too low by creditors or other persons having an interest in the estate. Johnson's Est., 8 Erie 

249, rel❜g on Sample's Est., Steven's App., 189 Pa. 385, 343. See sec. 79, supra.

§ 81 

tunity to show that the discrepancy was not the result of any fault of his.89

The duties of the executor or administrator in accomplishing the appraisement are thus outlined: "It shall be the duty of the executors and administrators, having given convenient notice to the appraisers of the decedent's estate, of a time and place for making the inventory and appraisement thereof, to produce or make known to them, in the presence of such of the persons interested in the estate as may attend, the whole of the personal estate of the decedent, which may have come to their possession or knowledge.'

It will be noted that the law requires that the actual appraisement shall be made "in the presence of such of the persons interested in the estate as may attend." 

Compliance with this provision will prevent any criticism of the acts of the administrator or the appraisers in performing this duty. It is a provision, however, that would seem rarely to be observed.

While a decedent in his lifetime has a perfect right to enter upon any lawful business however venturesome or speculative, the right of the executor or administrator of his estate is otherwise.10 It is the duty of the latter "not to make money for the estate by hazardous ventures, but to save that which came into his hands for creditors and heirs by prudent business management.” ¹¹ 

An executor, however, if given ample power and discretion under the will may continue to carry on the business of the decedent after his death and thereby subject the assets of the estate to debts contracted for that purpose.¹2 contracts whether named therein or not, and whether the breach occurs in his lifetime or afterwards.

Where decedent during his lifetime executed an agreement of indemnity, accompanying an application to an indemnity company for a completion bond, and, relying upon such agreement, the indemnity company bound itself to the proposed obligee to issue the bond, a liability attached to decedent which, even though contingent, survived after his death and bound his representatives when determined. Fullmer's Est., 319 Pa. 360.

Such rule is based upon the proposition that the representatives or trustees may sell the property rather than suffer such loss, or, if they are required to carry on the business or cannot sell it, they may always refuse to act as executors.
