84. INCORPORATION OF DECEDENT'S BUSINESS. 

Where the decedent either alone or as a partner was engaged in an active business the liquidation of which is impracticable without great loss the statute provides adequate procedure for its protection by incorporation: "Fiduciaries may themselves, or jointly with others, organize a corporation to carry on the business of the decedent, whether he die testate or intestate, whether the business was owned solely by him or in partnership with others, if such business be one for which a charter could have been obtained in the lifetime of the decedent, and may contribute all or part of the property of the estate which was invested in the business at the time of the death of the decedent, as capital to such corporation and accept stock in the corporation in lieu thereof." 22 

20 Woodward, J., in Brown's App., 89 Pa. 139, 147. 

21 Stern's App., 95 Pa. 504. 

22 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 42 (a). 

This and the two following clauses are based upon Sec. 1 of the Act of April 22, 1889, (P. L. 42) 4 Purd. 4928, extended to cases of guardians and administrators and to cases where the will does not authorize or direct the continuance of the business. Cases where the testator was a partner with others are also included, and the phraseology has been modified. 

In offering this provision the Commissioners of 1915, in their report, said: "The Commissioners have considered that the provisions of the Act of 1889 might well be extended in this way. Very often the testator is engaged in a profitable business and its incorporation will obviously be af great benefit to the cestuis que trust interested in the estate, or when the decedent dies intestate the interests of his minor children can best be conserved by an incorporation of the business. In the present state of the law this cannot be done by trustees or guardians without possible risk to them personally; and in cases of a partnership dissolved by death, where the partnership articles do not sufficiently protect the estate of the deceased partner, a forced liquidation may be disastrous. "As the incorporation must be effected under the supervision of the court, it is conceived that the interests of all parties concerned will be properly safeguarded."' 

See also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 807.

§ 149 

The procedure also is clearly outlined: "No such corporation shall be organized without the approval of the orphans' court having jurisdiction of the accounts of such fiduciaries first had and obtained,23 upon petition" filed setting forth all the facts and circumstances and the proposed terms and conditions of the organization. Such notice as shall be prescribed by said court shall be given to all persons having any beneficial interest, vested or contingent, in the estate of the decedent, who are in being at the time of the filing of such petition; and the said court shall approve such organization only after inquiring into the circumstances and the proposed terms and conditions of such organization, aided, if necessary, by the report of a master, and only with the written consent of all persons interested who shall be sui juris, and of the guardians or committees of such as shall be under age or non compos mentis." 25 It will be noted that the consent of all parties interested is a prerequisite.20 If all such parties join in the petition this will be sufficient. Otherwise the form given should be changed by praying for a citation on the parties who do not join to show cause why the petition should not be granted.

Unless the matter is so clear and manifestly advantageous as to induce the court to act in the first instance, it is almost the universal custom to refer the petition to a master to inquire carefully into the facts and circumstances involved, and the court's action will be largely governed by his report.

We are not, however, without authority in Pennsylvania on this subject. "The law casts the legal ownership of personal property of a deceased intestate upon his administrators. 

They are sometimes said to be trustees, but they are such for administration. Their primary duty always is to dispose of the personal property, and therewith pay the debts of the intestate and make distribution amongst his next of kin. A sale and transfer of stocks by them is therefore in the line of their duty. There is no cestui que trust having a right to interfere and prevent such a transfer. Hence, letters of administration are always sufficient evidence of authority. "A trustee of an insolvent debtor would seem to stand on the same footing. And so, generally, does an executor. His primary duty is administration. He is to pay debts and legacies out of the personal estate, and use even specific legacies to pay debts if necessary. His letters testamentary, therefore, show an apparent right to dispose of the stocks of the testator. Even if the stock has been bequeathed specifically, a transfer agent has no means of ascertaining whether it is needed to pay debts. 

He can inquire only of the executor, the very person who proposes to make the transfer. If he inquire of the specific legatee, he can learn nothing, for the legatee may be ignorant, and to require evidence of authority beyond the letters testamentary, might greatly delay and embarrass the executor in the discharge of his duties. It has, therefore, generally been held that transfer agents may safely permit a transfer of stock by an executor without looking for his authority beyond his letters."' 31

It is the primary duty of an administrator of an estate to preserve the assets of the estate, and not to endeavor to increase them by speculation. 

Where, as the result of an agreement between all the claimants of an estate, one of them is made a preferred distributee, and demand is made by the preferred distributee that the administrator sell the securities intrusted to it so that her share of the estate may be paid to her, it is the duty of the administrator to sell the securities though the secondary distributees insist that the securities be held so that, when the market rises, they may yield sufficient to take care of their distributive share in the estate also, and upon failure of the administrator to do, he may be surcharged. 

In such case the amount of the surcharge is the difference between the market value of the securities at the time they should have been sold and the amount for which they were actually sold. 

Market value is the price which an article will bring when offered for sale in the market. Mellier's Estate, 312 Pa. 157, af'g 18 D. & C. 595.

An agreement entered into by the executors for sale of decedent's interest in a corporation will be set aside when the evidence shows that the price as stated in the agreement was simply based on the liquidation value and such value is inadequate and the agreement must be set aside and the executor enjoined from consummating the sale and all monies received on account must be returned to the purchaser.

The primary duty of an executor is administration, i. e., liquidation of debts and distribution.

While under the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, it is the duty of an executor to convert personal property and file his account within six months from the grant of letters, the rule is not an unbending one where the result of compliance would be to divest an executor of a large part of the discretion which the testator gave him and which the law imposes. 

The paramount duty of an executor is to exercise, in the sale of personal assets, as in other matters, common prudence, caution and skill. He is presumed to need to sell and is expected to sell within the six months period. He should not sell for the mere sake of selling within six months.

If he holds beyond the period, the burden of justifying his act is cast upon him. Brusstar's Est., 27 Berks 242.

While a fiduciary must exercise his discretion in disposing of nonlegal securities, particularly in a falling market, and will not be surcharged if he has acted with common skill, prudence and caution, this rule is subordinate to the requirement that such securities must be converted within six months after the grant of letters, unless unusual circumstances warrant an exception to the rule, and it is the fiduciary's duty to ascertain in sufficient time whether a beneficiary will agree to distribution in kind; if he fails to do so and the beneficiary refuses to accept non-legal securities, he must take the consequences.

A fiduciary is not bound at all events to sell immediately sufficient securities of the estate to pay debts, administration expenses and pecuniary legacies, unless there is a danger that the value of the securities may shrink to such an extent that it will be impossible to pay those items or unless the securities are pledged as collateral.

The amount of the surcharge of a fiduciary for failure promptly to sell non-legal securities included in the estate is the difference between the amount received therefor and the last sale price on the last day when he might properly have sold them, or if there was no sale of a particular security on that date, then the bid price of that date or of the next subsequent day. Curran's Est., 18 D. & C. 103, citing Borell's Est., 256 Pa.

CHAPTER XV. 

ADMINISTRATION OF REAL ESTATE. 

88. GENERAL DUTIES. 

Ordinarily the personal representative of a decedent has no cause to meddle with the real estate of the deceased.50 Title passes at once upon the death either to the heirs and next of kin under the intestate laws 51 or under the will to the devisees, either specific or residuary, and these alone are entitled to occupy, sell, lease or otherwise dispose of the same.

Where, however, the rents or the corpus of the real estate are required for the satisfaction of creditors, or the decedent in his lifetime has contracted with reference to real estate, or an equitable conversion is effected 52 or

See Morrison's Est., 196 Pa. 80; Herron v. 

Stevenson, 259 Pa. 354, 356. When an administrator assumes to act in his representative capacity in the management or control of real estate, he is merely the agent of the heirs, who alone can call on him to account: Appeals of Fross and Loomis, 105 Pa. 258, 269; Morrison's

Generally in the absence of an order or decree of the court, an administrator has nothing to do with the realty: Kelley's Est., 297 Pa. 17, 21; Huff's Est., supra. Possibly one of the earliest cases on the subject is M'Coy v. Scott, 2 Rawle

The duties of an executor and trustee are separate and distinct. 

The executor must take charge and make an inventory of the personal estate, collect monies due the estate and pay the decedent's debts and obligations, and make distribution of the balance to the persons entitled thereto, whether heirs, legatees or trustees. Except when necessary to pay decedent's debts, he has nothing to do with the real estate unless so directed by the will. He is appointed by the testator and derives his authority to act from the will.

The duties of a trustee, on the other hand, have been said in general terms to be to protect and preserve the trust property and to see that it is employed solely for the benefit of the cestui que trust. 

The provisions and the conditions of the instrument creating the trust, make the law by which the conduct of the trustee, in the management and disposition of the trust property must be regulated and controlled. Reed

If an estate in trust be conveyed to a volunteer, he will be bound by the trust, although he had no notice of it, and if the grantee of such an estate for full value has notice of the trust, he is bound just as the grantor is bound. 

A power to sell real estate does not confer upon an executor or trustee the right to bind the estate by an option contract (as in a lease, Moore v. Trainer, 252 Pa. 367).

Where a trustee for a continuing trust, with power to sell real estate and invest the proceeds, conveys real estate to creditors after the lien of their debt has expired and after the trust estate becomes insolvent, the sale is without valuable consideration and void and a reconveyance will be decreed. Bucklen v. Bucklen, 24 Del. 266.

A written contract for the purchase price of realty will be specifically enforced on the application of either party, if the terms thereof are clearly specified in the writing and they have been fully complied with by the party seeking specific performance. 

A written agreement to transfer a property to a named person who already has an interest in it, when the intended transferor receives a specific sum from the rents collected by him, is not an agreement to make a gift of the property to the named transferee, but is an agreement of sale for the specified consideration. Patterson's Est., 316 Pa. 241.

Where an option clause in a lease of real estate provides that the lessor may offer the property for sale during the term of the lease with ninety days' notice to the lessee, who may within such period accept the option or purchase the property at the price fixed by a bona fide purchaser, if such offer is for a less sum than a sum stated, such option may be exercised by the optionee after the death of the lessor, and the orphans' court has jurisdiction under the Act of June 17, 1917, (P. L. 447) specifically to enforce the contract after the option is declared. 

On a petition in the orphans' court for specific performance of a contract for sale of land, the executor in his representative capacity, is not a necessary party to the proceeding, until a decree is entered. He must then make the deed and receive the purchase money.

Where an option to purchase real estate in a lease is exercised after the lessor is dead, a decree for specific performance will not be avoided because the widow did not join in the lease, and this is especially so where it appears that the widow had not elected to take against her husband's will, and that the period for so doing had expired. 

If, in such case, the widow has any claim on any account, she can assert it thereafter in appropriate proceedings. Cardon's Est., 278 Pa. 153.

Where both the vendor and vendee of the real estate are deceased, intestate, upon proceeding in the orphans' court by the administrator of the vendor to enforce the specific execution of the contract, the administrator and heirs of the vendee and all persons deriving title under them, or interested in the contract should be made parties, and notice should also be given to the heirs of the dcceased vendor"; where, however, the vendor alone has died intestate, it has been held a decree for specific performance entered on petition by the administrator with the consent of the vendee was conclusive though no notice had been given to the widow and heirs.78 

Where the purchaser institutes proceedings it is necessary in order to give full force and effect to the decree entered in such proceedings that the heirs and devisees of such real estate should be made parties to the proceedings as the decree is of no effect as to those not notified." 

Under the plain provisions of the act as they now stand, however, notice would apparently be mandatory in all cases to all parties in interest. It would at least seem to be the safer course to pursue.

Section 1401 of the Fiscal Code of April 9, 1929, P. L. 343, which provides that all state taxes settled against any person shall be a first lien upon the property of such person, does not repeal, by implication, section 13 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, which states the order of distribution of an insolvent decedent's estate and declares that debts due the Commonwealth shall be last paid.

Section 1802 of the Fiscal Code provides that the provisions of the act, so far as they are the same as those of existing laws, shall be construed as a continuation of such laws, and not as new enactments. 

A later law, which is merely a reënactment of a former, does not repeal an intermediate act which qualifies and limits the first one, but such intermediate act will be deemed to remain in force, and to qualify or modify the new act in the same manner as it did the first. 

A statute will not repeal another by implication unless the two cannot stand together; the legislative intent to repeal must be clear. 

It was unnecessary in this case to determine the difference in effect of the mandatory phrasing of Act of April 14, 1827, (9 Sm. L. 433), and of the permissive words of section 1404, Act of April 9, 1929, (P. L. 343). Fergu son's Est., 325 Pa. 34, af 'g 26 D. & C. 421.

95. THE LIEN OF DEBTS. 

Prior to the Act of April 19, 1794 (3 Sm. L. 143), the debts of a decedent were liens upon his real estate against all the world for an indefinite period of time. To remedy the inconveniences recited in the preamble the second section of that act limited the lien of debts, "except they be secured by a mortgage, judgment, recognizance or other record," to seven years. The Act of February 24, 1834, Section 24 (P. L. 70), reduced the period of lien of debts to five years, "except they be secured by mortgage or judgment." The Act of June 8, 1893 (P. L. 392), further reduced the period of lien to two years, which is the same period as provided by the Act of June 14, 1901 (P. L. 562).¹4

Title is not marketable unless so free from difficulty as to law and fact that on a resale an unwilling purchaser should be unable to raise any question which may appear, to a judge sitting in equity, so doubtful that a title involving it ought not to be enforced. 

Title to real estate of a decedent is not good and marketable for a period of one year after decedent's death, because of the lien of his debts, unless relieved of such lien by appropriate proceedings. Fisher v. Green, 28 D. & C. 195. 

The statutory liens of general creditors are for one year after decedent's death and where nothing has been done to continue them, the land is free from the enforcement of such claims. Where the administrator has paid such claims he stands in no better position than the original creditor. 

Robbins's Est., 8 Erie 197.

There is no authority by a nunc pro tunc order to set aside the limitation enacted by the statute, and thus breathe the breath of life into dead liens, thereby making these debts once again claims against the real estate, without the consent of its owners. "The effect of the statute is that, unless suits are brought as provided in section 15, the creditors no longer have any legal right to look to the real estate for payment of their claims and to collect the same from it. Bowman v. Knorr, 206 Pa. 272; Cooper's 

Estate, 206 Pa. 628. Even the making of a conveyance in fraud of creditors will not prolong the statutory lien: Sherman v. Farmers' Bank 

5 W. & S. 373;" Kiehl v. Fauset, 16 Wash. 130.

It was early the settled law of Pennsylvania that the lands of a decedent were assets for the payment of his debts, and his heirs, legatees and devisees took only such of the estate as remained after the payment of the debts, with no limitation on the time in which claims should be brought; but, later on, for the security of purchasers, heirs and legatees, statutes were enacted limiting the period in which a lien must be enforced against decedent's real estate, the latest reducing the period to one year. 

While the Orphans' Court is a court of equitable jurisdiction, it is a statutory court, and its jurisdiction is limited by statute so it is without the power to order a sale of a decedent's real estate, in the case of a claim for the payment of which proper proceedings have not been begun during the statutory period of limitation, which is one year from the date of the death of a decedent. Catanzaritti's Est., 37 Lack. 199. 

Where the decedent died December 30, 1925, an amicable action and confession of judgment by the administrator in favor of a creditor entered on December 31, 1926, is too late to continue the lien against real estate. 

The statute provides that suit must be brought "within' one year. Excluding the day of decedent's death, the year expired December 30, 1926. 

Kline's Est., 20 Berks 149.

A decree or judgment rendered either by the common pleas court or by the orphans' court is conclusive and free from collateral attack in the other.

Where an action upon a claim against the executors of a decedent is instituted in a court of common pleas, such court has jurisdiction over questions relating to the indexing of the action in the judgment index in accordance with section 15 of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, (P. L. 

447), and all other matters contained in or incident to the litigation. 

Whether failure of the prothonotary to index an action against a decedent's estate in the judgment index, upon the filing of a præcipe to do so, may be corrected by the court, and whether the prothonotary, as an officer of the court, can voluntarily index the action nunc pro tunc, not determined. 

Tourison's Est., 321 Pa. 296, rev'g 22 D. & C. 704.

If the prothonotary fails to enter on the judgment index an action brought against the executors of a decedent's estate, notwithstanding an order by plaintiff to make such an entry pursuant to section 15 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, the entry may be made by the prothonotary upon his attention being called to the error or the court may make an appropriate order upon the prothonotary on application by plaintiff for that purpose.

Where the prothonotary neglects to enter in the judgment index a suit brought to preserve the lien of a creditor's claim against decedent's real estate, and part of the realty is sold to an innocent grantee, an entry subsequently made in the judgment index upon discovery of the error is not binding upon the grantee, who may be relieved from the effect thereof on proper application to the court. 

Any person injured by failure of the prothonotary properly to enter the record of a suit on the judgment index may, upon showing that fact, recover against the prothonotary for any damage sustained or, upon appropriate petition, may be released from the lien created upon his property by an entry on the judgment index nunc pro tunc. 

A creditor instituting suit to preserve his lien against real estate of his deceased debtor, may, if he has done all that he is required to do, recover

A general creditor who fails to continue the lien of his claim against the land of the decedent by instituting an action against the personal representatives of the decedent within one year of his death and properly indexing such action, in accordance with the requirements of section 15 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. (447), as amended by the 

Act of June 7, 1919, (P. L. 412), may not thereafter proceed against the land of the decedent, and this is so although it is alleged that the decedent fraudulently conveyed the land to another during his lifetime. 

Section 15 (a) of the Act of 1917 is a statute of repose and not merely of limitation.

The requirements of the Act of 1917 must be strictly complied with 

Central-Penn National Bank &c. v. Culp, 320 Pa. 358.

In determining whether or not a debt due by a decedent has been duly kept alive as a lien upon land of which he died seized, there are but two basic questions to be answered: (1) Was plaintiff a creditor of decedent at the time of his death? and (2) If he was, was the lien kept alive in the way prescribed by paragraphs (a) and (b) of Sec. 15 of the Fiduciaries 

Act as amended?

Where a will directs that testator's debts shall be paid out of his estate, real and personal, which he devises subject thereto, the orphans' court has power to enforce the sale of his realty in order to obtain a fund to pay the creditors. Pyles v. Bosler, 313 Pa. 548, af'g 11 D. & C. 38 (s. c. 308 

Pa. 297 and 22 D. & C. 10.)

A decree of the orphans' court, awarding certain real estate of a decedent's widow as her exemption, cannot be collaterally attacked on the ground that she sold the property a few days after the award for a sum greatly in excess of that at which it had been awarded to her, in a suit in the common pleas, under section 15 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act, to continue the lien of a debt of the decedent against the real estate. 

Benner v. 

Benner, 23 D. & C. 350.

An orphans' court is without jurisdiction to direct, on petition, that a sum due a widow under an antenuptial agreement is to be a lien upon decedent's real estate; any such proceeding must be brought in the court

that the debt due or damages exceeds the sum of one hundred dollars. If an action for the recovery of a debt be brought as aforesaid, it shall be deemed to have been duly prosecuted to judgment if award in favor of the plaintiff be made by an auditor or the orphans' court, or if the claim be included in a schedule of distribution and the latter be confirmed by the court." 24

The institution, indexing, and prosecution of an action against the executor or administrator of a decedent's estate in the court of common pleas, under this section of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, does not estop the creditor from presenting and providing his claim in the orphans' court or oust the jurisdiction of that court in respect of the claim.

Loesch's Est., 23 D. & C. 606.

Under section 15 (d) of the Act of 1917, relating to indexing by the prothonotary, a transferred judgment may be indexed by the filing of a præcipe in conformity with that section of the Act.

 97. STAY PENDING SALE IN ORPHANS' COURT 

"In every case of an execution against the executors or administrators of a decedent, whether founded upon a judgment obtained against such decedent in his lifetime, or upon a judgment obtained against them in their representative character, if it shall be made to appear, to the satisfaction of the court issuing such execution, that there is reason to believe that the personal assets and the rents of real estate are insufficient to pay all just demands upon the estate, such court shall thereupon stay all proceedings upon such execution, until the executors or administrators shall have made application to the proper orphans' court for the sale of the real estate of the decedent, or for the apportionment of the assets, or both, as the case may require. 99 41 upon which he has a prior lien, and out of personal property pledged as collateral security for the debt. 99. JURISDICTION OF ,- APPOINTMENT OF MASTER. 

"The orphans' court which possesses jurisdiction of the accounts of an executor or administrator shall have power to authorize a sale or mortgage of real estate by such executor or administrator in the following cases, viz.: "I. On the application of the executor or administrator, setting forth that the personal estate and the rents of real estate of the decedent are insufficient for the payment of debts. "2. On the application of such executor or administrator, or of any creditor of the decedent, setting forth that on the final settlement of the administration account, it appears that the personal assets together with the rents of real estate of the decedent are insufficient to pay the balance appearing to be due from the estate of such decedent, either to the accountant or creditors.'' 56 

Of course, having power to order, the court may, with equal authority ratify a sale previously made 57 though such procedure is not recommended.

The procedure under this section of the act is for the executor or administrator to present in the orphans' court having jurisdiction of his accounts, a petition substantially similar in form to that hereinafter set forth reciting and describing however the real estate in the other county and the prayer should be for leave to apply to the orphans' court of such other county where the real estate is situated for leave to raise the necessary funds by a sale or a mortgage of said real estate, or to complete a proposed private sale, as set forth in the petition, with a decree accordingly.

Thereupon a petition is presented in the usual form substantially similar to that hereinafter set forth embodying therein the essential facts of the former procedure and having annexed thereto a certified copy of the decree entered on the former proceeding of the court having original jurisdiction.

The act also provides for the somewhat rare contingency of the real estate being divided by a county line: "When application shall hereafter be made to the orphans' court having jurisdiction of the accounts of any executor or administrator for leave to sell or mortgage the real estate of a decedent or any part of the same for the payment of debts of such decedent under the provisions of this section, and any part of said real estate is situated partly in the county where said application shall be made and partly in one or more other counties, by reason of a county line or lines running through the same, the said court shall have power to order and direct the sale or mortgage of the whole or any part of said tract of land, irrespective of the county boundary lines, and such sale or mortgage shall be as effectual to pass the title of such real estate to the purchaser or mortgagee as if the whole of said tract of land had been within the boundaries of the county having jurisdiction of the accounts of the executor or administrator. Notices of said sale or mortgage, as required by this section, shall be given in all the counties in which the land is situated, and a certified copy of all proceedings in connection with said sale or mortgage shall be filed in the orphans' court of each county in which said land is situated. " The law also provides: "No authority for the sale or mortgage of real estate, for the payment of debts of a decedent, shall be granted until the executor or administrator shall have exhibited to the court having jurisdiction of his accounts a true and perfect inventory and conscionable appraisement of all the personal estate whatsoever of the decedent," together with a full and correct statement of all the real estate of such decedent, wherever situated, which has come to his knowledge, and of the rental value of such real estate; and also a just and true account,72 upon oath or affirmation, of all the debts of the decedent which have come to his knowledge." 73

In this State the surplus from a sale of land for the payment of debts, after debts are paid, is distributable as the real estate would have descended or has been disposed of by will." 80 "When an orphans' court sale of devised real estate is made for the payment of debts of the testator, the proceeds of such sale are distributable as realty. Any record liens against the testator's title that were divested by the sale, and the statutory lien of his general debts, are of course first payable, their payment being the purpose of the sale, and they being paramount to the rights of the devisee and the latter's creditors. But the surplus remaining after payment of the testator's debts, while in the form of money, is to be regarded as real estate for the purpose of determining who is entitled to it, although the distributees thereof so ascertained will take and hold their distributive shares as personalty, so that in the event of their death it will be descendible from them as personal estate.81 Accordingly if there be any liens against the devisee's title, in favor of the latter's creditors, these will be subject to the rule that the effect of a judicial sale is to divest liens from the land sold and transfer them to the fund produced by the sale, and the holders of such liens will participate in the distribution in accordance with relative priorities. 104. ENTRY OF SECURITY, 

Corresponding to the uniform practice in all cases of sales of real estate by a fiduciary under order of court, the law provides: "In all cases°¹ where the carrying out of any decree of the orphans' court under the provisions of this section shall involve the receipt of money by the person carrying it out, the court shall direct the person acting under the decree to file a bond 92 to the commonwealth in a sufficient amount 93 conditioned for the proper application of all moneys to be received, which bond shall inure to the benefit of all parties interested and be executed by two individual sureties or by one corporate surety, approved by the court, and no such decree shall be executed until such bond, with sureties as may be required, shall be filed: Provided, That where a corporation, duly authorized by law, shall be designated to carry out any such decree, the court may, in lieu of security as aforesaid, permit such corporation to enter its own bond without surety."' 94 

90 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 16, (n) (see Purd. Stat. 

Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 573). The Commissioners of 1915 in their report recommending this section, said: 'This is a new section, introduced in order to make the practice uniform and free from doubt. "Where authority is given to a fiduciary to make public sale of real estate, obviously the fiduciary should make return of his doings to the court and have the sale confirmed; but the same reason would not apply where, as in the case of a private sale, the price and terms of sale and the name of the purchaser appear in the petition. The court having approved the sale and directed that it be carried out, it seems unnecessary for the fiduciary to report to the court and obtain a confirmation of what he was instructed to do."'

The orphans' court has jurisdiction to set aside a sale made by an executor or an administrator, in case of gross inadequacy of price, when this is manifestly to the interest of the estate. Huber's Est., 11 Leh. 189, 39

106. MORTGAGES,-PROVISION FOR REFUNDING. 

It has been noted heretofore that where possible a mortgage will be preferred to an outright sale. This is especially true where the entire value of the property is not required to liquidate debts and from the nature of the estate there is a possibility of procuring the ultimate repayment of the mortgage.

The practice and procedure is exactly similar to that described in this chapter with reference to sales, with the necessary changes in the phraseology of the petition. 

The statute also provides for the refunding of a mortgage thus authorized when it falls due. "When a mortgage authorized under the provisions of this section shall fall due or shall be about to fall due, the orphans' court which authorized such mortgage may, on the application" of the executor or administrator or of any party in interest, and although the period of the lien of the decedent's debts may have expired at the time of such application, authorize the refunding of such mortgage and the making of a new bond and mortgage, the proceeds of which may be used for the payment and satisfaction in whole or in part of the said existing mortgage and necessary expenses. Such new mortgage may be for such period and on such terms as to said court shall deem advisable."' 98

110. SALE OR MORTGAGE TO FIDUCIARY. 

If the executor or administrator desires to bid at his own sale or act as mortgagee, the act provides an adequate means for doing so: "Whenever any orphans' court, having jurisdiction under this section to decree a sale or mortgage of real estate, shall issue its order to any executor or administrator to sell or mortgage such real estate, and shall, in any case within its jurisdiction, give authority to any executor or administrator to bid at such sale, and shall confirm the sale to such fiduciary, or shall authorize the making of such mortgage to any executor or administrator, the said court may make an order directing its clerk to execute a deed or mortgage, as the case may be, for said real estate to such purchaser or mortgagee, who shall give security and shall account for the amount of said purchase money or mortgage money, in the settlement of his accounts, to said court.'' 13

REMOVAL OR INCAPACITY OF FIDUCIARY. 

If the person to make the sale or mortgage is removed or becomes incapacitated his successor may act, as the law provides: "In all cases where the sale of real estate shall be made by an executor or administrator under an order of, or confirmed by, the orphans' court, or where the making of a mortgage by such executor or administrator shall be authorized by said court, under the provisions of this section, and the letters testamentary or of administration shall be revoked, or the executor or administrator shall be removed by the court, or shall die, or become insane, or otherwise be incapable, before a conveyance is made to the purchaser, or before a mortgage is executed and delivered, it shall be lawful for the successor of such executor or administrator, having first given security, to be approved by the said court, for the faithful appropriation of the proceeds of such sale or mortgage, to execute and deliver to the purchaser a deed of conveyance for the estate so sold, on the purchaser's full com-

Where the executor or administrator refuses to carry out the sale or mortgage, an adequate remedy is provided: "The like proceedings may be had where an executor or administrator shall neglect or refuse to execute and deliver such deed or mortgage for the space of thirty days after due notice of an order of the court requiring him to execute and deliver the same."" 19

The rule which makes the pleadings in a judicial proceeding absolutely privileged may properly be applied to a will in which there is no apparent purpose to injure the reputation of anyone but merely a purpose to insure the distribution of the testator's estate to his intended beneficiaries and to protect it from possible claims of persons whom he does not desire to share in the distribution.

A statement made in good faith relating to a subject in which the person making the communication is interested, or in regard to which he has a social or moral duty, when made to one having a like interest or duty, is privileged, and in such case the burden of proof rests on the party claiming to have been libeled to show that the communication was malicious.

The act has no bearing on the right of a plaintiff, in a suit in trespass brought jointly against three defendants to discontinue, at the trial, as to one of the defendants who had died in the interim. Shearer v. Rasbridge, 28 Berks 150.

The purpose of this section of the Act of 1917 "is to provide a procedure whereby the defendant can compel the next of kin of a plaintiff to take out letters testamentary or of administration in order to substitute the personal representative for the deceased plaintiff, and provides a penalty for failure so to do, after a rule has been issued, of the abatement of the suit. It is not intended to cover a situation where a laches for failure to prosecute is the question involved, this being a substantive matter of defense and not procedural." Washington Borough Auditors' Appeal, 11 

Wash. 146.

Smith v. Brown, 46 York 196.

As to suits instituted by or against fiduciaries abatement is prevented under any circumstances by the provision that: "No action or other legal or equitable proceeding, commenced by or against fiduciaries, or in which fiduciaries are parties, shall abate or be otherwise defeated, by reason of the death, dismissal, removal, resignation or renunciation of any one or more of them, nor by reason of the annulling or revoking of the letters or powers granted to them, or any of them; but such suit or proceeding may be prosecuted to final judgment or decree, by or against such other person or persons as may have been joined with them in the administration or trust, or the fact of death and to substitute the personal representative as plaintiff on the record; in such a case, the cause of action survives under Sec. 18 of the Act of April 15, 1851, (P. L. 669, 674) and the measure of damages is the same as that recoverable by the original plaintiff. Spiegel, Guardian, v. Magill, 15 D. & C. 566.

Such actions are maintained by the dependents in their own right; as the deceased had no right of action for his own death, there was nothing to survive to his executor or administrator under section 35 (b) of the

While a deceased person who was killed in an automobile accident is presumed to have exercised due care and therefore not to have been guilty of contributory negligence, this does not in any way lessen the burden which falls upon the plaintiff of proving the defendant's negligence to have been the proximate cause of the death. 

The Act of June 7, 1911, (P. L. 678) provides that the only persons entitled to sue for damages resulting from a death caused by negligence are husband, widow, parents or children, and the administrator of the deceased cannot maintain the action. Markley v. Aldrich, 17 Erie 250.

This Act of 1911 amended the Act of April 26, 1855, (P. L. 309) Sec. 1, to read: "Section 1. Be it enacted, &c., That the persons entitled to recover damages for any injuries causing death shall be the husband, widow, children, or parents of the deceased, and no other relatives; and that such husband, widow, children, or parents of the deceased shall be entitled to recover, whether he, she, or they be citizens or residents of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, or citizens or residents of any other state or place subject to the jurisdiction of the United States, or of any foreign country, or subjects of any foreign potentate; and the sum recovered shall go to them in the proportion they would take his or her personal estate in case of intestacy, and that without liability to creditors under the laws of this Commonwealth." 

The Act of April 1, 1937 (P. L. 196), added thereto the following provi sion effective as of its date: "If none of the above relatives are left to survive the decedent, then the personal representative shall be entitled to recover damages for reasonable hospital, nursing, medical, funeral expenses, and expenses of administration necessitated by reason of injuries causing death.'' 

This statute being remedial, acts prospectively, not retrospectively. Moser v. Merring, 26 North, 195.

An action for damages for personal injuries may be maintained by the injured party against the executors of the wrongdoer. The Fiduciaries Act of 1917 repealed the Act of June 24, 1895, P. L. 236, and authorizes such a proceeding. Strain v. Kern, 277 Pa. 209, distinguished; Renard v. Kier, 73 P. L. J. 4, 6 D. & C. 375.

Under Section 35 (b) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, as amended executors and administrators are liable to be sued only in such actions which might have been maintained against the decedent if he had lived. 

An unemancipated minor is not permitted to sue its parent, because of the very vital interest which society has in preserving harmony in domestic relations and in not permitting families to be torn asunder by suits for damages by children against their parents for real or fancied grievances. 

The guardian of an unemancipated minor may not maintain an action in trespass against the administrator of the deceased mother of the minor. 

The maxim that when the reason for a rule ceases the rule itself ceases, does not apply to such a case. York Trust Co. v. Blum, 48 York 159, 83 

P. L. J. 169, 22 D. & C. 313.

Suit was brought by administratrix of decedent, averring that death resulted from a motor accident caused by the negligence of defendants' driver, to recover for funeral expenses connected with the burial of the decedent and for damages to decedent's car. 

It was held that the plaintiff was entitled to sue for damages to the decedent's car, but not for the expenses of burial. 

An administrator has no right of action for personal damages resulting from his decedent's death. The right to bring such actions is entirely statutory and only the persons designated in the statutes upon the subject can assert it.

In discussing the right of an administrator to bring suit for damages to personal property of the decedent, the court considered the question raised as to whether Section 35 (b) of the Act of June 7, 1917, authorizing such actions, was void by reason of the fact that the title of the Act did not include sufficient wording to make it applicable and the effect of the repealing section including an express repeal of Section 28 of the Act of February 24, 1834, which authorized executors and administrators to commence and prosecute such actions. It was held by the court that the purported repeal of Section 28 of the Act of 1834 should not be given the effect of abrogating the rule enacted by the statute of 1834, and carried from it into the Act of 1917.

The plaintiff's right to sue for a tortious injury to her decedent's automobile, if not supported by the Act of 1917, is sustainable upon the Act of 1834; and that, even if the latter were held to be repealed, the right

"All such rights of action which were not barred by the statutes of limitation at the time of the death of decedent may be brought against his executors or administrators at any time within one year after the death of the decedent, notwithstanding the provisions of any statutes of limitation whereby they would have been sooner barred." 46 could be rested upon the law as it existed previous to 1834. Under section thirty-five (b) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, as amended by the Act of May 2, 1925, (P. L. 442) a right of action against a decedent not barred by limitation at the time of death may be asserted against his personal representative within one year thereafter; the statute of limitations is not tolled by the grant of letters testamentary but the filing of an account has the same effect as a pending suit and the rights of creditors are fixed as of the date when it is filed. Frascone's Est., 17 D. & C. 664.

In an action against the administrator to recover damages caused by the negligent operation of a motor vehicle by defendant's decedent in the county in which the action is brought, service may be made under the Acts of

Wiesheier et al. v. Kessler, 311 Pa. 380, and see cases there cited.

In an attachment execution, in the absence of service of the interrogatories upon the garnishee during his lifetime, the proceedings against him as garnishee terminate with his death and do not survive against his personal representatives. A dead man cannot be a party to an action, and any such attempted proceeding is completely void and of no effect. 

An amendment the effect of which is to bring in new parties after the running of the statute of limitations will not be permitted. 

Allowance of amendment to caption of action of trespass to recover for personal injuries alleged to have been suffered by the minor plaintiff as a result of defendant's negligence, instituted after the death of the stated defendant, by substituting the executors of the decedent as parties defendant, held error, and action against executors of decedent held barred, where petition for amendment was not filed, and no other proceedings against executors were instituted, within one year of decedent's death. Section 35 (b) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, (P. L. 447) as amended, does not confer authority on an executor or administrator to begin an action for personal injuries to his deceased where the latter did not commence it in his lifetime.

Under Article II, Section 21, of the Constitution of 1874, as amended, the legislature is authorized to prescribe for whose benefit actions to recover damages for death shall be maintained. Potter &c. Co. v. Petcoff, 122 

Super. 540.

A suit may be maintained in a Pennsylvania court by an administrator, appointed in this State, of a decedent who was killed in the State of New York by the negligent act of defendants. 

The general rule is that the law of the place where the tort resulting in death is committed determines whether an action can be brought therefor, and the party who is to bring it. 

The right of action given arises not under our law, but under that of New York. Such right is enforced here under the doctrine of comity, the public policy of New York being the same as our own. Dickinson, Admrx. v. Jones, 309 Pa. 256 and cases there cited.

116. SUIT OR DISTRESS FOR RENT, ETC. 

In order to give a specific remedy for the collection of such rent as may be an asset of the estate at the time of the death, the act provides: "The executors or administrators of every person who was the proprietor of any rent-charge or other rent or reservation in nature of a rent,49 in fee or otherwise, as mentioned in Section 11, clause (f), of this act,50 shall and may have an action for the arrearages of such rent due to the decedent, at the time of his decease, against Strawbridge, Executrix, 4 D. & C. 297. The defendant in this case has met this requirement. Kerr v. Vallely, 12 Wash. 97. 

Judgment will not be entered against an executor for want of a sufficient affidavit of defense where the facts alleged in the statement are not specifically admitted by the affidavit of defense and there are not sufficient additional facts admitted in the affidavit to authorize the entry of judg ment. Hardinge Co. v. Whitaker's Exrs., 42 Lanc. 381, 45 York 91, 15

D. & C. 66. 

While an executrix is required to file an affidavit of defense, the penalties of Sections 6 and 17 of the Practice Act of 1915 do not apply. An executrix is specifically exempted from penalty by the terms of the sixth section of the Practice Act. 

A failure of decedent's representative to deny specifically is not an admission and plaintiffs are not relieved from proof of their allegations. 

Schaaf v. Burger, 8 Erie 91.

It is not sufficient for a fiduciary to file an affidavit of defense using the words of Section 7 of the Practice Act of May 14, 1915, (P. L. 483) without stating the facts upon which he bases his belief that there is a defense to the plaintiff's claim. Thorpp's Sons Co. v. Peoples Trust Co., 6 D. & C. 362.

Jurisdiction over a "cause of action," has reference solely to the competency of the particular court to determine controversies of the general class to which the case then presented, belongs. 

The court of common pleas has jurisdiction in a pending suit, over a nonresident executor of the defendant, and may cause him to appear by writ of scire facias as prescribed by the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) as amended by the Act of March 30, 1921, (P. L. 55).

In such case the sheriff of the county in which the suit is pending, may deputize the sheriff of the county in which the executor resides, to serve the writ of scire facias. 

The service of a writ of scire facias on a nonresident executor, under the Fiduciaries Act, will not be set aside because the court did not direct such service to be made.

Where service of a writ is required to be allowed or directed by the court, service will not be set aside because such allowance was not procured, but will be ratified by the court rather than to provide for a useless task of again serving the writ.

Where a nonresident fiduciary is both executor and trustee, service of the scire facias will not be set aside but the question of jurisdiction over the party as trustee will be determined at the trial or hearing.

118. EFFECT OF FAILURE TO PLEAD. 

Frequently the personal representative of a deceased defendant is greatly hampered by lack of knowledge of certain facts which the decedent in his lifetime might have successfully pleaded. To prevent any improper advantage arising from such a situation the act provides: "The omission of an executor or administrator to plead to any action brought against him in his representative character, that he has fully administered the estate of the decedent, or any other matter relative to the assets, shall not be deemed an admission of assets to satisfy the demand made in such action; also the omission of the plaintiff to reply to any such matter when pleaded, shall not be deemed an admission of the want of assets as aforesaid, nor shall such omission otherwise prejudice either party; and no mispleading, or lack of pleading, by executors or administrators, shall make them liable to pay any debt or damages recovered against them in their representative character, beyond the amount of the assets, which in fact, have come or may come or should have come into their hands.'' 64

119. SUITS AGAINST FIDUCIARIES IN OTHER COUNTIES. 

If the fiduciary should not reside in the county where he must account, suits may be maintained and prosecuted there under the act which provides: administrators, "In all cases where executors, guardians or trustees shall not reside within the county the orphans' court of which has jurisdiction of their accounts, proceedings may be had and suits may be brought against them by creditors and others interested in the estates, in the counties where such accounts are to be settled, and process may be served on said fiduciaries, in any other county by the sheriff of such other county, who shall be deputized for that purpose by the sheriff of the county in which the process issues, or process may be served upon any surety on the official bonds of such fiduciaries.'' 65

121. SUITS BETWEEN FIDUCIARIES. 

Where one of several executors or administrators is indebted to the decedent, action may be brought by the co-executor or co-administrator under the provisions of the act: "Where one of two or more fiduciaries shall be personally or individually indebted, obligated or liable to the estate which he represents, it shall be lawful for the other fiduciaries, or either of them, to institute an action at law, bill in equity, or other appropriate legal or equitable proceeding, on behalf of the said estate, against such fiduciary, individually, to recover or enforce the said indebtedness, obligation or liability, in the same manner as though such fiduciary were not connected with the said estate: Provided, That this shall not in anywise affect the duty or liability of such fiduciary to account therefor in the office of the register of wills or in the orphans' court in the manner now provided by law, the remedy herein provided being in addition to other remedies, legal or equitable, already existing." 67

CHAPTER XIX. 

A. 

SETTLEMENT OF TAXES. 

Transfer Inheritance Tax. 

123. PROPERTY SUBJECT TO INHERITANCE TAX. 

Since 1826 collateral inheritances have been subject to tax in this Commonwealth and since 1917 a tax has also been imposed on direct inheritances. Until 1887 the procedure was governed by the Acts of April 7, 1826, 9 

Sm. L. 146; April 22, 1846, (P. L. 486), Sec. 14, [as amended Jan. 23, 1850, (P. L. 7)]; April 10, 1849, (P. L. 

570), Secs. 10-16, and March 11, 1850, (P. L. 170).73

These acts were all codified and included in the Act of May 6, 1887, (P. L. 79) which with its supplements imposed a flat tax of five per cent on all collateral bequests which in the aggregate equaled or exceeded $250. 

Transfers to the father, mother, husband, wife, children, lawful lineal descendants and wife or widow of a son were not taxed.

This act as supplemented and amended" from time to time remained in force until 1919. The Act of July 11, 1917, (P. L. 832) was substantially similar in its terms to the Act of 1887, except that it added a flat tax of two per cent on all transfers to persons theretofore exempted from collateral tax.

Both of these acts were superseded by the present Transfer Inheritance Tax Act of June 20, 1919, (P. L. 

73 1 Purd. 603, et seq. In 1928 the Penna. Leg. Reference Bureau published its Bulletin No. 28, of which Secs. 167-208 cover the subject matter of inheritance tax in a most admirable fashion with copious annotations.

L. 521) as amended. 

The tax imposed by the Act of 1919, is not a tax on the transfer of securities in the ordinary sense of the word, but is a tax on the succession or right of inheritance of a decedent's estate.

The appropriation by the state to itself of any portion of the property of a decedent, whether such appropriation be designated an inheritance tax, an estate tax, a succession tax, a death duty, or otherwise, is not, in its essence, a tax on the decedent's property or any component part of it, or on the transaction of transferring it, but is an excise on the privilege of inheritance.

The share of the decedent's estate appropriated by the state is taken from the clear value of the estate for distribution, and the nature or identity of the component parts of the estate from which such net balance results is wholly immaterial.

Exemptions from taxation must be strictly construed. Tack's Est., 325 

Pa. 545, af'g. 26 D. & C. 237.

Inheritance Tax

Taxes assessed under this act but caused by reason of the existence of assets other than those from which the tax is paid may be prorated against the respective funds under the Act of July 2, 1937 (P. L. 2762).

The "normal" state inheritance tax is assessed separately on life interests and remainders.

The "normal'' state inheritance tax on remainders is not assessed pur suant to Article II, Section 10 of the Act of June 20, 1919, (P. L. 521) at the testator's death. The life tenant, however, is not personally liable for the tax but it is payable out of the first income which he receives. 

The "normal" state inheritance tax on remainders is not assessed or payable until the remainderman comes into actual possession, but he is permitted, under Section 3, Article I of the Act of June 20, 1919, (P. L. 521) to anticipate the payment.

The federal transfer inheritance tax and the "additional" state inheritance tax imposed by the Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, as amended by the 

Act of May 16, 1929, P. L. 1782, are "'estate" taxes and must be paid out of the general funds of the estate. 

Where, in order to reduce the amount of the "additional" state inheritance tax, the "normal" state inheritance tax is paid by an executor on

As a practical matter in the settlement of estates the property which is thus subject to tax becomes a matter of serious moment and the question is not always free from doubt.80 postponed life estates and remainder interests in advance of payment to the beneficiaries, the remaindermen have no standing to object to payment of the tax on the life estates out of the corpus. Crane's Est., 109 Super. 91, af'g 17 D. & C. 199, af'd in 314 Pa. 193.

In computing the additional inheritance tax under Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, the Commonwealth may not refuse to allow as credit to an estate an amount previously permitted by it as rebate for prompt payment of normal inheritance tax. Commonwealth having given credit of five per cent for such prompt payment, and having receipted therefor cannot at a later date set up that the credit was not proper. Markle's Est., 27 Luz. 131, af'd in 311 Pa. 472.

Where the executors of a decedent's estate duly paid to the Commonwealth the normal transfer inheritance tax due thereon, and no effort was made either by the register of wills or by the Auditor General to collect the additional tax due under the provisions of the Act of May 7, 1927, (P. L. 859) for a period of more than 5 years and until a claim for overpayment of tax to the Federal Government was barred by article 99, sec. 

319, of the Federal Revenue Act of 1926, no interest is collectible upon such excess tax due the Commonwealth.

Failure of the register of wills or of the Auditor General to commence suit against a decedent's estate within 5 years from the date of his death for the collection of the additional tax due under the Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, does not relieve the executors from payment of that tax. Caflisch's Est., 21 D. & C. 282, 16 Erie 26. 

80 A compromise settlement by all persons interested in a decedent's estate, whereby one claiming as widow is to be paid a certain sum from the estate, the settlement being approved by the court at the audit of the estate, when the Commonwealth was represented, is a determination binding upon all parties, including the Commonwealth, to the extent of the sum paid the alleged widow, that she was in fact decedent's widow, and the Commonwealth is estopped to compute the tax on that sum at a higher percentage than that imposed upon a bequest to a widow, especially where the adjudication awarded inheritance tax to the Commonwealth in accordance with its provisions, which included approval of the settlement. Kuh's Est., 22 D. & C. 311. And see Cherry's Est., 29 D. & C. 378.

A compromise settlement by all persons interested in a decedent's estate, whereby one claiming as widow is to be paid a certain sum from the estate, the settlement being approved by the court at the audit of the estate, when the Commonwealth was represented, is a determination binding upon all parties, including the Commonwealth, to the extent of the sum paid the alleged widow, that she was in fact decedent's widow, and the Commonwealth is estopped to compute the tax on that sum at a higher percentage than that imposed upon a bequest to a widow. Snodgrass's Est., 22 D. & C. 598.

In the case of wills or intestacies the period of the date of the death of the decedent whose estate is being administered determines the act under which the tax, if any, is to be calculated, assessed and paid.81 

The Act of 1887, which as before stated, was a codification of all previous laws in force on the subject, introduced no new subject of taxation.82

Where a testator devised a farm to his wife and daughter in common for life, with remainder to the daughter's children if she survived her mother leaving children and the daughter survived her mother and left an only child, it was held on the settlement of the daughter's estate that the farm was not subject to transfer tax, as her daughter inherited it not from her mother but from her grandfather. Hershey's Est., 39 Lanc. 539.

Where a testator bequeathed the residue of his estate to his widow with further direction to divide it among his three children after her death, thus giving her the right to consume, and giving the children what was left, the amount of the legacy which passed to the widow should be deducted from the appraisement of her estate for transfer inheritance tax purposes and not be taxed again as part of her estate. Haller's Est., 40 Lanc. 419.

A specific sum of money payable to the wife of decedent under an antenuptial agreement by which she was to receive said sum "from his estate as his wife, in the event of her surviving him . . . unless he shall by will give or bequeath to her a larger sum, is not subject to transfer inheritance tax. Fridenberg's Est., 8 D. & C. 705. Contra, where a bequest is made in compliance with such agreement. Cooch Est., 29 Sch. 12.

A promise to pay a specified sum to a charitable institution within one year after promisor's death, in consideration of benefits received as a member of the religious body controlling the institution, does not constitute such a debt as may properly be deducted in computing transfer inheritance tax upon the promisor's estate. Butler's Est., 19 D. & C. 172.

Where the insured named his wife, "her administrators, executors or assigns" as the beneficiary of his life insurance policies, reserving the unrestricted right to change the beneficiary at any time, and his wife dies intestate in the lifetime of the insured, her interest, at the time of her death, in the proceeds of the policies, no change of beneficiary having been made, was a mere expectancy with no vested right or interest. 

Where, in such case, the proceeds of the policies are paid, upon the subsequent death of the insured without changing the beneficiary, to the administrator of the deceased beneficiary, the transfer of the fund to the heirs of the deceased beneficiary is not subject to the transfer inheritance tax for the reason that the beneficiary was not seized or possessed of the fund at the time of her death and there was no transfer from her. The administrator was a mere conduit through which the fund passed to the heirs of the deceased beneficiary.

A gift causa mortis'' is one made in contemplation of death.

It is not necessary where a transfer is made of property by a decedent within one year from the date of his death for the Commonwealth clearly to show that the decedent made the transfer because of a fear of impending death to secure the inheritance tax. The burden of proof in such case is on the appellant.

The burden of proof is not met by the appellant in this case where the testimony clearly shows that the decedent was ill for a number of years, was unable to attend to any of her own affairs, and actually said that "she won't be here long." Trout's Est., 45 Lanc. 505, 51 York 83.

Real estate conveyed to the grantor's son, by a deed acknowledged and delivered more than a year and a half prior to her death and while she was in good health, is not subject to the imposition of transfer inheritance tax as part of the grantor's estate, in the absence of other evidence that the transfer was conditional or in contemplation of death. 

Neither failure of the grantee to record a deed until after the grantor's death a year and a half later, nor the payment of rent by a tenant of the premises so conveyed by a check drawn to the grantor's order, shows that the transfer was in contemplation of death or was not complete when the deed was delivered. A joint tenancy exists where a single estate in property, real or personal is owned by two or more persons under one instrument or act of the parties. 

Joint tenancy and tenancy in common are alike in that both are held by unity of possession. The essential difference in the two relationships is that joint tenants hold the property by one joint title and by one right, whereas tenants in common hold by several titles or by one title and several rights.

 124. CALCULATION AND ASSESSMENT OF TAX. 

Ordinarily the duty to ascertain and pay the amount of tax due by an estate as regards the personalty falls upon the executor or administrator. The basis of ascertaining the gross value of the estate is, of course, the inventory filed with the register of wills. The valuations, however, therein contained, are not conclusive upon the commonwealth. It is the duty of the Department of 

Revenue to appoint an official appraiser as occasion may require. If the inventory has been prepared with due care with a special regard to the appraisement of securities, there will be little or no difficulty in settling any controversy which may arise with these appraisers with reference to the inventory values. 

Unless by reason of its conversion into personalty' the real estate has been included in the inventory, the duty of paying the inheritance tax on real estate does not devolve upon the executor or administrator, but is imsuch power and diverts the estate from the ultimate beneficiaries named in the deed, the estate is thereby made subject to inheritance tax at the rate specified at the time that the will becomes effective, the Act of May 16, 1929, (P. L. 1795) having no application to such a situation. Williamson's

14 The question of the value of real estate needs no involved reasoning. 

It requires only fairness and the application of a good business judgment. 

It is obvious that any appraisement is not a precise, infallible and exact determination of the thing valued.

It is not the policy of the law to permit the commonwealth for taxation purposes to assess the taxable value of real estate at the highest value it might possibly bring.

The law requires that the value of real estate for the purpose of taxation shall be determined upon the basis of market value, or rather actual value, limited and defined by market value under all the circumstances. 

The statute contains no express provision as to the basis to be adopted for determining the clear value or as to the manner to be pursued by the appraiser in arriving at the sum he considers to be a fair value. 

For inheritance tax purposes the future, anticipated or potential value of real estate is not a matter of concern. The test is value at the date of the death. Haggerty's Est., 34 Lack. 21, af'd in 311 Pa. 503. And see Gerber's Est., 43 Lanc. 433; Smith's Est., 21 Erie 23. 

15 The actual value of stock as limited and defined by the fair market value of the said stock is the test as the value fixed by the Commonwealth and being offered in evidence makes out a prima facie case for the Commonwealth. 

Before setting this valuation aside the Court must be convinced that the appraisal is manifestly unfair and unconscionable. 

If the appraiser erred in his appraisal, he failed to do his duty and his appraisal would be unfair.

The valuation fixed by the Commonwealth will be set aside, when credible witnesses familiar with the stocks in question and their values place a different value upon the same.

The weight of such testimony will overcome the official appraisement. 

Though findings of fact made below are as binding in the Appellate Court as would be the finding of a jury, where there is evidence to support its conclusions reached, yet, if not based on proper proofs, or if they merely give expression to an inference or deductions from that offered, no such effect follows. Stirling's Est., 15 Erie 108.

In determining the "clear value" of stock in a close corporation having no market value, neither book value nor liquidation value is controlling, but the court must also consider the record of corporate earnings and whether the stock to be valued constitutes a majority or minority interest. Stern's

The proper method of ascertaining the amount of inheritance taxes to be paid out of a decedent's estate under the Acts of June 20, 1919, (P. L. 

521) and May 15, 1925, (P. L. 806) is for the debts and administration expenses to be deducted from the gross estate, thus arriving at "the clear value of the property subject to such tax." 

It is improper to calculate the ratio of the debts and expenses to the gross estate and then apportion them amongst the legacies, and direct that the tax shall be calculated upon the result ascertained.

Where a final appraisement of an estate has been made for the purpose of assessing the inheritance tax due therefrom, a second appraisement is without authority of law.

Article IX, Section 1, of the Constitution of the State, expressly author izes the unlimited classification of subjects for the purpose of taxation, but the legislature alone can make the classification.

Within the classification made by the legislature all taxes must be uniform, and this applies to inheritance taxes as well as to all others. If they are not uniform within the classes, the statute is at least pro tanto unconstitutional.

If a taxing statute is reasonably capable of two interpretations, one of which would provide for uniform taxes and the other not, the former interpretation is to be preferred. Rowell's Est., 315 Pa. 181; af'g 20 D. & C. 42.

L. 521, the tax upon a bequest which is to take effect in possession after the expiration of a period of years is not payable until the legatee comes into actual possession by the termination of the prior estate and is assessed upon the value of the estate at such time, but it is the duty of the owner of such estate to make a return of the same within one year from the death of the decedent, and, in case of failure to do so, the tax is immediately payable, that is, at the termination of the year. 

Where, in an appraisement for inheritance tax on a legacy payable after a period of years, the particular estates are not separately appraised, and the appraisement is not made with knowledge of, or notice to, the legatee, the appraisement is not conclusive upon the latter, nor is he precluded by failure to make a return within a year from the death of decedent from subsequently objecting to the amount of tax paid by the executor. Youngblood's Est., 117 Super. 550.

When interest is charged on a delinquent tax it is in the nature of a penalty and is not part of the tax. 

The Department of Revenue has no authority to impose any interest penalty with respect to inheritance taxes accruing under the provisions of the Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, as amended. (Sec. 123, n. 79, supra.) 

The provision of the Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, that taxes imposed thereunder shall be collected "in accordance with the provisions of the transfer inheritance tax laws of the Commonwealth' applies only to the procedure of collection and has no reference to interest provisions, nor could the provisions of the prior law as to interest be constitutionally incorporated by reference only, since any such incorporation would be viola tive of Article III, Sec. 6, of the Constitution. 

While the contrary is true with respect to Federal taxes, it is a wellestablished rule that interest is not recoverable on delinquent taxes due a state or political subdivision thereof unless it is expressly so provided by statute. 

Where the legislature amends an act without making any change in the administrative construction placed thereon its action in so doing is at least persuasive of its recognition and approval of the administrative construc tion. Inheritance Tax Penalties, 30 D. & C. 189, 85 P. L. J. 807.

The power of the Board of Finance and Revenue, under paragraph (b), Sec. 1102, Art. XI, of the Administrative Code of June 7, 1923 (P. L. 

488), at 551-2, to "revise any settlement made . . . by the Auditor General or any other agency of the state government charged with the settlement of state taxes,'' does not apply to the collection of an inheritance tax by a register of wills appraised by appraisers duly appointed. 

The word "settlement," in its technical sense, cannot be considered as synonymous with the word "appraisement, as used in the Act of June 20, 1919, (P. L. 521). As construed by the courts and understood in prevailing practice, it means an adjustment or determination of an amount. 

Neither the State Treasurer nor the State Board of Finance had jurisdiction or authority to refund transfer inheritance taxes alleged to have been erroneously assessed and paid to the state, where the error was discovered more than three years after the payment was made. The only remedy, if any, would be by the passage of a refunding act by the Legislature.

 128. PAYMENT OF TAX BY NON-RESIDENTS, RECIPROCITY 

Real estate situated in Pennsylvania unless conversion is worked by the will has always, under all of the acts, been subject to inheritance tax, even though owned by a nonresident. The present act, however, taxes per- 66 Code of 1929, so as to extend the period within which application may be made for a tax refund.

The provisions of section 503 of the Fiscal Code of 1929, extending the time for an application for tax refund in the event of litigation "by reason whereof there was an overvaluation of that portion of the estate on which the tax was assessed and paid, which overvaluation could not have been ascertained within said period of 2 years, ," refers to any involvement in litigation which postpones until its termination the ascertainment of the true value of the net taxable estate, whether there is involved the true value of admitted assets, the inclusion of certain property as an asset of the estate, or the amount of deductible liabilities.

In order to suspend or extend the period of limitations provided by section 503 of the Fiscal Code of 1929, litigation relating to overvaluation of the estate must have been commenced within that period; a claim for refund filed with the Commissioner of Internal Revenue after expiration of the period does not create a right to refund of the State tax. While the residence set forth in the will and reaffirmed in the codicil is not conclusive, yet being signed and executed by the testatrix in the formal and solemn manner required in the execution of a last will and testament, it is in our opinion entitled to at least as much weight as decedent's declarations made to her sisters, as to her intended residence. 

A declaration (as to domicile) that is self-serving and not followed by acts in accordance with the declaration will not be regarded as conclusive, but will yield to the intent which the acts and conduct of the person clearly indicate.

Every person must have a domicile somewhere and a man cannot elect to make his home in one place for general purposes of life and in another place for the purposes of taxation.

129. METHOD OF APPEAL.

B. Federal Estate Tax. 

130. LIABILITY FOR TAX. 

Nature of Tax. 

Current federal estate taxation consists of (1) the es tate tax imposed by the Revenue Act of 192676 as amended, and (2) the additional estate tax imposed by the Revenue Act of 1932 as amended. Section 301 of the 

75 Act of June 20, 1919 (P. L. 521), Sec. 27. 

See Form No. 112, App., p. 124. 

76 The Federal Estate Tax was first imposed by the Act of September 8, 1916. This law was amended by the Act of March 3, 1917 (Title III), and the Act of October 3, 1917 (Title IX). These two statutes increased the rate of tax. The Revenue Act of 1918 (Title IV), which became effective 

6:55 p. m., Washington, D. C., time, February 24, 1919, reduced the rates applicable to the smaller net estates as compared with those of Title IX of the Revenue Act of 1917, and contained a number of provisions not found in any of the prior acts. The Revenue Act of 1921 (Title IV) be came effective at 3: 55 p. m., Washington, D. C., time, November 23, 1921.

The Revenue Act of 1924 became effective June 2, 1924, while the Revenue 

Act of 1926 became effective at 10: 25 a. m. (Wash., D. C., time), Feb. 26, 1926. It supplants all prior acts as to the estates of decedents dying after the effective date thereof, embodies certain changes, but continues many of the provisions of the earlier acts. The Revenue Act of 1928 which became effective May 28, 1928, amended certain sections of the Act of 1926 and embodied certain provisions not appearing in any of the earlier acts. 

Public resolution No. 131, 71st Congress approved 10:30 p. m., March 3, 1931, amends certain provisions of the Revenue Act of 1926. The Revenue

6, 1932, and imposed a tax upon net estates of decedents dying after the effective date thereof, in addition to the tax imposed by the Revenue Act of 1926. The Revenue Act of 1934, which became effective 11: 40 a. m., Washington, D. C., time, May 10, 1934, amended and supplemented the 

Revenue Act of 1926 and the Revenue Act of 1932. The Revenue Act of
