302 (d) (1) of the Revenue Act of 1926 as amended.

§ 130 

Revenue Act of 1926 (29) imposes an estate tax on the transfer of the net estate of every decedent dying after the passage of the act. This tax is the basic federal estate tax and is graduated beginning, with 1% on the first $50,000 in value of the net estate and running as high as 

20% on an amount in excess of $10,000,000.00.

The Revenue Act of 1932 imposed an additional tax on the transfer of the net estate of every decedent dying after the passage of the act. This tax is also graduated and the rate of tax varies in accordance with the provisions of the amendment to the act in force at the date of the death of the decedent.

Both the basic estate tax and the additional estate tax are imposed upon the transfer of the net estate and are measured by the value of the property transferred. The subject of the tax is the transfer of the net estate and it is, therefore, neither a legacy nor an inheritance tax.768

The value of the net estate is determined by computing the value of the gross estate in accordance with the provisions of Section 302 of the Revenue Act of 1926 as amended and deducting therefrom the applicable deduc tions as authorized by Section 303 of the Revenue Act of 1926 as amended. Such basic provisions as those relating to the composition of the gross estate are set forth in the Revenue Act of 1926 as amended and are not repeated in the act which imposes the additional estate tax. 

After the amount of the gross estate has been determined the second step is to subtract from the value of the gross estate the total amount of the deductions authorized in order to arrive at the value of the net estate. Gross Esate The gross estate includes all property of the decedent whether real or personal, tangible or intangible, except real estate situated outside the United States. If the decedent was a resident, or a nonresident citizen who died prior to the Act of 1934 the value of all personal property owned by him should be included, wherever situated. If the decedent was a resident alien, or, re- 

76a Eichenlaub 's Est., 13 Erie 234; Ely's Est., 28 D. & C. 663; see also

Article 3, Treasury Regulations 80.

§ 291 

gardless of citizenship, was a nonresident who died prior to the Act of 1934, the value of so much of his personal property as had its situs in the United States at the time of his death should be included. In addition to all property which is actually a part of decedent's estate, there must be included under the provisions of the act in determining the value of the gross estate, any property passing under a general power of appointment exercised by the decedent (1) by will, or (2) by deed executed in contemplation of or intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after death, except in the case of a bona fide sale for an adequate and full consideration in money or money's worth. There must also be included in computing the value of the gross estate any property, or interest therein, of which the decedent has at any time made a transfer, by trust, or otherwise, in contemplation of or intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after his death, except, however, property which has been transferred as the result of a bona fide sale for an adequate and full consideration in money or money's worth. This applies only to transfers made by a decedent after the Act of 1916. As originally enacted Section 

302 (d) of the Act of 1926 contained a provision that a transfer of over $5,000 made to any person within two years prior to death should, as to such excess, be conclusively deemed to have been made in contemplation of death. This provision of the Act of 1926 as amended was held to be unconstitutional.70b 

Under the present law there is a rebuttable presumption that a transfer was in contemplation of death if it was a "transfer of a material part of his property in the nature of a final disposition or distribution thereof" made without an adequate consideration in money or money's worth.

A transfer intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after the decedent's death includes the following: (1) transfers to the extent that title remains in the decedent at the time of his death and the passing thereof was conditioned upon his death; (2) transfers 

76b Hall et al. v. White, 58 Fed. 2nd 1060; Certiorari denied 285 U. S. 553.

§ 130 

under which the decedent reserves or retains (in whole or in part) the use, possession, rents or other income or enjoyment of the transferred property, for his life, or for a period not ascertainable without reference to his death, or for a period of such duration as to evidence an intention that it should extend to his death; including also the reservation or retention of the use, possession, rents or other income, the actual enjoyment of which was to await the termination of a transferred precedent interest or estate; (3) transfers under which the decedent retained the right, either alone or in conjunction with another person or persons, to designate who should possess or enjoy the property or the income therefrom; and (4) transfers under which the enjoyment of the transferred property was subject at decedent's death to a change through the exercise, either by the decedent alone or in conjunction with another person or persons, of a power to alter, amend, revoke, or terminate or such a power was relinquished in contemplation of decedent's death.

Property held jointly by the decedent and other persons, or by the decedent and spouse as tenants by the entirety, or deposited with any person carrying on a banking business in their joint names and payable to either or the survivor, is included in the gross estate to the extent of the decedent's interest in said property." Any part of such property, however, as may be shown to have originally belonged to such other person and never to have been received or acquired by him from the decedent for less than a fair consideration in money or money's worth shall not be included as a part of decedent's estate. 

The Revenue Act of 1926 as amended provides that all insurance receivable by the executor of the estate under policies taken out by the decedent upon his own life and all insurance receivable by beneficiaries other than the executor, in excess of $40,000, under similar policies should be included in computing the value of the gross estate. Where, however, the decedent during his lifetime has not retained the legal incidents of ownership in the 

77 Tyler et al., adms., v. U. S.; U. S. v. Provident Trust Company et al., adms.; Lucas v. Girard Trust Company et al., exrs., 281 U. S. 497, held such provisions of the statute to be constitutional.

policies of insurance, as for example, the right of the insured or his estate to its economic benefits, the power to change the beneficiary, to surrender or cancel the policy, to assign it, to revoke an assignment, to pledge it for a loan or to obtain from the insurer a loan against the surrender value of the policy, etc., the proceeds of such policies may or may not be subject to tax, depending upon when the policy was issued or when the decedent gave up the legal incidents of ownership in the said policies.""

It is evident from the above that in computing the value of the gross estate, in accordance with the provisions of the act, certain property must be included which, under the law of Pennsylvania, does not form a part of the decedent's estate.

Valuation 

Unless the executor elects otherwise, at the time that the return is filed, all property included in the gross estate must be valued as of the date of the decedent's death. 

The date of the decedent's death is the only valuation date permitted for the estate of a decedent who died. prior to August 31, 1935. Section 302 (j) of the Revenue

Act of 1926 as added by Section 202 (a) of the Act of 

1935 contains a provision whereby the amount of tax otherwise payable may be lessened when, within one year following the decedent's death, the gross estate has suffered a shrinkage in its aggregate value. Executors of decedents dying on or after August 31, 1935, now have the option of valuing the estate as of the date of death or within the year following the decedent's death. An election as to the valuation date must be made by the executor at the time the return is filed and cannot thereafter be rescinded. The election applies to all property, included in the gross estate on the decedent's death and cannot be applied to a portion thereof.

If an executor elects to adopt the valuation authorized by subdivision (j) of Section 302 of the Act of 1926 as added by Section 202 of the Act of 1935, the property which was included in the gross estate on the date of decedent's death may be valued as of the applicable dates 

77a See Citations in Commerce Clearing House, 1937 Fed. Tax Service, Vol. 3 (p. 233), under Article 27 of Regulations 80.

§ 130 

as follows: (a) any property distributed, sold, exchanged or otherwise disposed of within one year after the decedent's death is valued as of the date of such distribution, sale, exchange or other disposition, whichever first occurs; (b) any property not distributed, sold, exchanged or otherwise disposed of within such one-year period is valued as of the date one year after the date of the decedent's death; (c) any property, interest or estate which is affected by mere lapse of time, is valued as of the date of decedent's death; except an adjustment may be made for any difference in its value not due to such lapse of time, as of the date of one year after the date of decedent's death, or as of the date of its distribution, sale, exchange or other disposition, whichever first occurs.

Interest-bearing obligations, such as bonds and notes, embody two promises, one to pay principal and the other to pay interest, and both promises are a part of the gross estate at the death of the decedent. If the valuation date is that of the decedent's death, the principal of the obligation and interest then accrued and unpaid thereon are to be valued as of that date. If the valuation date is subsequent to the decedent's death, the principal and interest then accrued and unpaid are to be valued as of that date. Like rules apply to other obligations such as those calling for the payment of rent or royalties. 

When corporate stock is a part of the decedent's gross estate at the decedent's death, a dividend paid on or before the date as of which the stock is to be valued, will be valued as of the date of its payment, but earnings of the corporation neither declared as a dividend nor paid between decedent's death and the valuation date of the stock, is reflected in the value of the stock. A dividend declared prior to the valuation date of the stock but payable subsequent thereto will not be so reflected if " exdividend" on the valuation date of the stock, but is to be valued as of that date.

Properties, interest or estates which are affected by mere lapse of time include patents, remainders, reversions and other like properties, interest or estates. 

In every case where the election is exercised the return must set forth (1) an itemized description of all prop-

§ 295 

erty included in the gross estate on the date of decedent's death together with the valuation of each item as of that date, (2) an itemized disclosure of all distributions, sales, exchanges, and other dispositions of any property during the one-year period after the decedent's death together with the dates thereof, and (3) the value of each item of property determined in accordance with the provision of the statute. The return must also show the amount of income accrued and unpaid, the date of death, the amount of any income collected or otherwise realized after the date of death and prior to the date as of which the item of principal, is to be valued, and the amount of any income accrued and unpaid at such subsequent valuation date. 

Specific Exemptions 

Under the Act of 1926, as amended, and also under the Act of 1932, as amended, specific exemptions are granted as deductions in determining the net estate of residents subject to tax. The specific exemption deductible in determining the net estate upon which the tax is imposed by the Act of 1926 is $100,000. The specific exemption deductible in determining the net estate upon which the additional tax is imposed by the Act of 1932 is $50,000, in the estates of decedents dying prior to August 31, 1935, and $40,000 in the case of decedents dying on or after August 31, 1935.

In the case of the estate of a citizen, regardless of residence, if the decedent died after the effective date of the Act of 1934, a deduction may be taken for the specific exemptions granted under the Act of 1926 and the Act of 1932. No specific exemption is authorized in the case of the estate of a nonresident alien and no specific exemption is authorized in the case of the estate of a nonresident, regardless of citizenship, if the decedent died prior to the effective date of the Act of 1934. 

Deductions 

In determining the net estate there are allowed as deductions in the case of a citizen or resident of the United States, funeral expenses, administration expenses, claims against the estate (not including, however, income tax

§ 130 

on income received after death by the decedent and not including succession, estate or inheritance taxes) unpaid mortgages upon or any indebtedness in respect to property to the extent that such claims, mortgages or indebtedness were contracted bona fide for an adequate and full consideration in money or money's worth; actual losses sustained during the period of settlement from fire, storm, shipwreck, or other casualties or from theft not compensated for by insurance or otherwise; amounts reasonably required and actually expended during the period of settlement for the support of those dependent upon the decedent as allowed by the laws of the jurisdiction under which the estate is administered, etc. 

There is also allowed as a deduction in the case of a citizen or resident of the United States in computing the value of the net estate, an amount equal to the value of any property forming a part of decedent's estate, which property formed a part of the estate situated within the United States of any person dying within five years prior to decedent's death or which was transferred to the decedent by gift within five years prior to his death. In order to obtain this deduction the property must be identified as having been received by the decedent from such donor by gift or from such prior decedent by gift, bequest, devise or inheritance, or which can be identified as having been acquired in exchange for property so received, and the property must have been subject to a gift tax or subject to an estate tax as a part of the estate of the previous decedent. If the decedent died after the effective date of the Act of 1934, no such deduction in respect to the property or property given in exchange therefor must have been allowable in determining the value of the net estate of the prior decedent. In no case can the deduction for such previously taxed property exceed the value at which such property was previously taxed. 

There is also allowed as a deduction the amount of any legacy, bequest or transfer, (1) to or for the use of the

United States, any State, Territory, any political subdivision thereof, or the District of Columbia, for exclusively public purposes, or (2) to or for the use of any corporation or association organized and operated exclusively

§ 297 

for religious, charitable, scientific, literary or educational purposes (including the encouragement of art and the prevention of cruelty to children or animals). In order to obtain such deduction, however, it is necessary that no part of the net earnings of such corporation or association shall inure to the benefit of any private stockholder or individual, and that no substantial part of the activities of the same involves the carrying on of propaganda, or otherwise attempting, to influence legislation. Legacies to trustees or to a fraternal society, order, or association operating under the lodge system exclusively for any of the above purposes are also deductible. This deduction is not limited in the estates of residents (or of citizens who died after the enactment of the Act of 1934) to transfers to domestic corporations or associations or to trustees for use in the United States. The deduction is, however, limited in the case of nonresident aliens (or to nonresident citizens who died prior to the enactment of the Act of 1934) to bequests to be used in the United States.

Under the provisions of the Act of 1926 as amended, a credit is allowed for inheritance, succession, legacy or estate taxes actually paid to any State, Territory or the District of Columbia in respect of any property included in the gross estate, not exceeding, however, 80% of the Federal Tax.77b In order to obtain this credit it is necessary that the taxes be paid and credit therefor claimed within four years from the filing of the return. No such credit is allowed against the additional tax imposed by the Acts of 1932 and 1934. 

In accordance with the Act of 1926, as amended, and the Act of 1932 as amended, a credit is also allowed for gift taxes paid by the decedent in respect of property included in his gross estate. This credit is, however, subject to the provision that it shall not exceed an amount which bears the same ratio to the gross estate tax computed under the provisions of the Revenue Act of 1926, under the Revenue Act of 1932 and the Revenue Act of 1932 as amended as the case may be, as the value of or, 77b See Section 123, supra note 79.

§ 130 

the property which was the subject of the gift and included in the gross estate bears to the value of the entire gross estate.78

Prior to the Act of 1934 the estates of nonresidents, regardless of citizenship, were taxed only with respect to property situated in the United States and the same provisions of the act applied to all nonresidents regardless of citizenship. Since the Act of 1934, however, the estates of nonresident citizens are taxed the same as the estates of residents, while the tax upon the estates of nonresident aliens is only imposed upon the transfer of the portion of the estate situated in the United States. No exemption is allowed the estates of nonresident aliens. 

Deductions, however, from the gross estate may be taken subject to certain limitations, for funeral expenses, administration expenses, claims against the estate, unpaid mortgages, losses, etc. Such deductions, however, are allowed only in the proportion which the value of the gross estate in the United States bears to the entire gross estate wherever situated. No deduction may be taken of any income taxes upon income received after the death of the decedent or of any estate, succession, legacy or inheritance taxes. It is immaterial whether the amounts to be deducted were incurred or expended within or without the United States. In the case of such decedent dying prior to the effective date of the Act of 1928 the deductions were limited to 10% of the gross estate in the United States. The deductions allowed the estates of such decedents for previously taxed property and on account of bequests, legacies, etc., for religious, charitable, scientific, public, etc., purposes, are, with two or three modifications, similar to the deductions allowed estates of resident decedents.

In order to obtain the deductions in case of a nonresident alien (or a nonresident citizen dying prior to the effective date of the Revenue Act of 1934) it is essential that the executor include in the return a statement of the gross value of the estate not situated within the United States.

PRELIMINARY AND FINAL RETURNS. 

It is the duty of every executor or administrator of every resident or citizen (or of a resident only, without regard to citizenship, if the decedent died prior to the Act of 1934) whose gross estate exceeds $40,000 in value at the date of death to file within two months after qualifying as such, on Treasury Department Revenue Service Form 704, a preliminary notice in duplicate with the Collector of Internal Revenue for the district in which the decedent was domiciled at the time of his death. Where there is doubt as to whether or not the gross value of the estate exceeds $40,000 notice should be filed as a precautionary measure in order to avoid the possibility of incurring penalties.

In the case of a nonresident citizen, the preliminary notice must be filed with the Collector in whose district the gross estate in the United States is situated or, if situated in more than one district or if no part of the gross estate is situated in the United States, it must be filed with the Collector for the Second District of New York or with such Collector as the Commissioner of Internal Revenue may designate.

In estates of nonresident aliens (or of nonresidents regardless of citizenship, if the decedent died prior to the enactment of the Act of 1934) notice on Treasury Department Revenue Service Form 705 is required to be filed if any part of the gross estate is situated, within the meaning of the statute, in the United States. This notice should be filed in duplicate with the Collector of Internal Revenue within whose district the gross estate was situated or, if in more than one district then with the Collector for the Second District of New York or such Collector as the Commissioner may designate. 

A return on Form 706 is required to be filed in the case of every resident or citizen (or resident without regard to citizenship, if the decedent died prior to the effective date of the Act of 1934) whose gross estate exceeded $40,000 in value at the date of death, except that if the decedent died (1) after September 8, 1916 and prior to 

February 26, 1926 or (2) after June 6, 1932 and prior to August 31, 1935 the return is required only if the

§ 131 

gross estate exceeded $50,000 in value at the date of death, and except that if the decedent died after February 26, 1926 and prior to June 6, 1932, the return is required only if the gross estate exceeded $100,000 in value at the date of death. The duty to file a return depends upon the value of the gross estate on the date of the decedent's death.

In the case of a resident, the return must be filed with the collector in whose district the decedent had his domicile at the time of death. In the case of a nonresident citizen the return must be filed with the collector in whose district the gross estate in the United States was situated, or, if situated in more than one district, or, if no part of the gross estate was situated in the United States, it must be filed with the Collector for the Second District of New York, or with such collector as the Commissioner may designate.

In the case of a nonresident alien (or nonresident, regardless of citizenship, if decedent died prior to the Act of 1934) the return must be filed where any part of the gross estate was situated, within the meaning of the statute, in the United States.

All returns on Form 706 must be filed in duplicate within fifteen months after the date of death, if the decedent died on or after August 31, 1935, and within one year after the date of death, if the decedent died before 

August 31, 1935.

When the last day for filing the return falls on a Sunday or on a legal holiday, the return must be filed not later than the day immediately following.

If for any reason it is impossible for the executor or administrator to file a reasonably complete return within the required period, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue may, upon application for good and sufficient cause, grant an extension of time for filing such return, such extension not to exceed, however, three months from the due date of the return if the decedent died on or after 

August 31, 1935, or six months from the due date if the decedent died before August 31, 1935. Before the expiration of the extension period the executor or administrator must file a return as complete as possible. Such return cannot thereafter be amended, although supple-

§ 301 

mental information may subsequently be filed that may result in a finally determined tax different from the amount shown as the tax by the executor upon his return. 

An extension of time for filing the return does not operate to extend the time for the payment of the tax.78a 

It is to be borne in mind that if there is more than one executor or administrator the return must be made jointly by all. Where an executor or administrator is unable to make a complete return as to any part of the gross estate, he is required to give all of the information he has as to such property, including a full description and the name of every person holding a legal or beneficial interest in the property. If no executor or administrator has been appointed, every person in actual or constructive possession of any property of the decedent is constituted by the statute an executor for the purpose of the tax and is required to make and file a return as provided by law. If for any reason the executor is unable to make a return the statute requires that every person holding a legal or beneficial interest in the property of the decedent, shall, upon notice from the collector, make a return as to such part of the gross estate. 

The act provides that the executor or administrator shall file with the Department any additional data which it may require for determining the amount of the tax due and a failure to comply with the Department's request for additional data renders the executor or administrator subject to a fine, not to exceed $500 and proceedings may be instituted in the Federal Court to obtain compliance with the request.

The instructions printed on the form for the return should be carefully followed. All documents and vouchers used in preparing the return should be retained by the executor or administrator so as to be available for inspection whenever required by the Internal Revenue 

Department. Duplicate copies of the will, if any, one of which must be certified, should be filed with the return, together with copies of such other documents as required under the instructions on Form 706 and the regulations properly applicable thereto and also any documents (in 78a As to the time for the payment of the tax see Section 132, infra.

§§ 131, 132  

duplicate) which the executor or administrator may desire to submit in explanation of any of the items appearing in the return.

In the case of a nonresident citizen who died after the date of the enactment of the Act of 1934, the executor is required to file with his return a copy of the inventory, the schedule of liabilities, claims against the estate and expenses of administration filed with the foreign court of probate jurisdiction, certified by a proper officer of such court as well as a copy of the return filed under the foreign inheritance, estate, legacy or succession tax Act, certified by proper official of the foreign tax department if the estate is subject to such foreign tax. 

132. PAYMENT OF TAX. 

The tax is due and must be paid within fifteen months from the date of death, if the decedent died on or after 

August 31, 1935, or within one year from the date of death if the decedent died before August 31, 1935, unless an extension of time for payment thereof has been granted by the commissioner. No discount is allowed for payment in advance of the due date. Interest on the amount of tax shown by the return is added if payment is not made on or before the due date. Interest in such cases is computed at the rate of 6% per annum, except that during any part of such period of time prior to August 31, 1935, interest is computed at the rate of 1% a month.

If, upon examination of the return and investigation of the estate it appears that more tax than the amount shown due by the return is properly payable, interest will accrue on the additional tax at the rate of 6% per annum from the date when the tax became due, viz., fifteen months after the date of death if decedent died on or after August 31, 1935, or one year from the date of death if the decedent died before August 31, 1935, until the date of assessment of such tax.

Where a return is made and the amount of tax shown due is paid within the required time, if upon investigation by a representative of the Department of Internal Revenue, an additional tax is found due, such additional

§ 303 

tax, with interest, must be paid within one month after notice and demand for same by the Collector, and if not paid within such period, such unpaid portion bears interest from the date of the notice and demand until payment is received by the Collector at the rate of 6% per annum, except that during any part of such period of time prior to August 31, 1935, interest accrues at the rate of 1% a month.

The act provides that the executor shall pay the entire tax, even though the gross estate may consist in part of property which will never come into the possession of the executor.78b If the executor before paying all the 

78b In Ely's Est., 28 D. & C. 663 (adjudication of Bok, J., in the Orphans' Court of Philadelphia County), the court decided that Federal estate tax payable by an executor, though greatly increased in amount by reason of the inclusion therein of assets held under a deed of trust having different beneficiaries than those in the will could not be recouped to the estate of the decedent from the assets held under the said deed except to the extent as specifically provided with respect to that portion of the corpus of the trust represented by policies of insurance under the specific provisions of Section 314b of the Revenue Act of 1926, and that a testamentary direction to pay all "Income, Estate, Succession, Transfer and Inheritance Taxes levied against'' testator's "estate or the devisees and legatees and beneficiaries of" his "estate and under'' his "will," refers only to taxes upon his testamentary estate and not to taxes imposed at his death by reason of assets in a revocable trust inter vivos. 

In Ostheimer's Est., 19 Erie 356, 30 D. & C. 120, the court held that the words "any transfer inheritance taxes' as used by the decedent in his will includes both state and Federal transfer taxes, since otherwise each legatee would not 'receive in full the full legacy bequeathed by the preceding paragraphs' as the will specifically provides.' 

In line with Ely's Est., supra, it was decided in Uber's Est., 29 D. & C. 

341, that where pursuant to an antenuptial agreement a man establishes a trust for his wife for life, the principal to be paid to him if she dies during his lifetime and to her if she survives him, the Federal estate tax due upon the trust fund at the death of the creator during his wife's lifetime should be paid by the residue of the creator's estate as if the widow had received the trust fund as a pecuniary legacy, it being settled law that the Federal estate tax is not to be apportioned among specific and money legacies but is to be borne by the residue; but not decided whether if there were something comparable to a residue in the trust estate, such residue should bear a share of the tax. 

It seems that if the beneficiary of a trust created during a decedent's lifetime is liable for the Federal estate tax due thereon upon the creator's death and the tax is paid by his executor, contribution could be enforced against a claim by the beneficiary of the trust against the estate as assignee of a beneficiary of the estate even though the former is not directly a beneficiary of the estate.

Relying on its two former decisions in Ely's Est. and Uber's Est., supra, the same doctrine was extended to estates over which the decedent exer- 11

$132 

estate tax pays in whole or in part any debt due by the decedent, or the decedent's estate, or distributes any portion of the estate, he is liable to the extent of such payment or distribution for so much of the estate tax as remains due and unpaid.

The amount of tax due and payable, whether or not disclosed by the return, is a lien for a period of ten years upon all property constituting the gross estate, whether or not it comes into the possession of the executor or administrator, except as follows: (a) If the tax is paid in full before the expiration of such period. (b) It is not a lien upon that portion of the gross estate which is used for the payment of charges against the estate and expenses of its administration as allowed by any court having jurisdiction thereof. (c) It is not a lien upon that portion of the gross estate which is transferred to a bona fide purchaser for value after payment of the full amount of tax determined by the commissioner, pursuant to a request of the executor for discharge from personal liability, but there is substituted a like lien upon the consideration received from such purchaser by the heirs, legatees, devisees or distributees. (d) It is not a lien upon such property as was received from the decedent as a transfer by trust, or otherwise, in contemplation of or intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after his death, or under which the decedent retained for his life or for any period not ascertainable without reference to his death, or for any period which does not in fact end before his death (1) the possession or enjoyment of, or the right to receive income from, the property, or (2) the right either alone or in conjunction with any person, to designate the per- cised a power of appointment charging the Federal tax caused by the existence of the appointed estate against the general residue of the decedent's individual estate. Snowden's Est., 29 D. & C. 581. Van Dusen,

The tax may be paid in cash, by check or, under certain conditions," in bonds or notes of the United States 79a bearing interest at a higher rate than 4% per annum, which bonds or notes have been owned by the decedent continually for at least six months prior to his death and which constitute a part of his estate at the time of his death. When payment is made in bonds or notes they will be received at par and accrued interest. 

Payment of the tax, of course, may be made partly in bonds or notes and partly in cash or by check. 

If the payment of the tax is made by an uncertified check it must be collectible at par, that is, for the full amount appearing on the face of the check without any deduction for exchange or other charges. If for any reason the check is dishonored when presented or, if the bank upon which it is drawn should refuse to pay it at par the collector, in the event that the drawer fails or refuses immediately to make the check good, together with any expense incurred by the collector on account of nonpayment of the said check at par, will proceed to collect the amount of tax due as if no check had been given for the same. 

133. INVESTIGATION OF RETURNS AND AP- PEALS FROM COMMISSIONER'S FIND- 

INGS. 

Investigation and audit of returns of Federal Estate

Tax are conducted by representatives of the Department 

79 See Department Circular 225. 

79a Issued under the provisions of the First or Second Liberty Loan 

Acts, as amended.

§ 133 

of Internal Revenue to determine the accuracy of the returns. 

When the investigation is made, the executor or administrator should coöperate in every way possible with the examining officer, in order that the tax liability of the estate may be correctly determined and the case finally closed. An examining officer in making his investigation inspects the records of the estate, sometimes interviews the legal representative and others who may have knowledge of the decedent's affairs, verifies the values of the various assets constituting the estate, verifies the deductions claimed, and takes such other steps as may be necessary to correctly determine the proper amount of tax due.

Upon completion of the investigation of the return by the Internal Revenue Agent in Charge a report is sent to the Miscellaneous Tax Unit, in Washington, for an independent and final audit of the return. Upon completion of the audit and the proposed determination of tax liability an official notice is issued to the executor (a) that the amount of the tax shown upon the return is accepted as correct, or (b) that an overassessment of tax is determined, or (c) that the assessment of a deficiency in tax is proposed.

In the case of a proposed deficiency the executor is given an opportunity to protest and be heard if he so desires. In such case, if the protest involves questions of fact so that the assistance of the local Internal Revenue officials is desirable, the deficiency notice directs the filing of a protest with the Internal Revenue Agent in Charge. In every other case of a proposed deficiency the notice directs the filing of a protest either in the field or in Washington, as the executor may prefer. The deficiency notice prescribes a reasonable time for the filing of a protest. If the executor elects to file his protest directly in Washington it is considered by the Miscellaneous Tax Unit and a hearing may be granted, provided the executor makes a request for a hearing in the protest. If no protest is filed within the prescribed time or within any period of extension the determination of a deficiency becomes final.

Protests must be filed in duplicate and must cover all

§ 307 

the items which the executor questions and be accompanied by a statement of all additional facts upon which the executor intends to rely. The protest may be supported by a brief. It must contain the information required by the commissioner. 7b Protests and accompanying statements of fact, if any, must be under oath. Where there is a hearing, if the executor does not appear in person, his representative who appears for him must present a properly executed Power of Attorney and must be enrolled to practice before the Treasury Department.

In all cases where a deficiency in respect of a tax (including penalties or other additions to the tax provided by law) is finally determined by the Commissioner a notice thereof is sent to the executor by registered mail, even though a jeopardy assessment may be made, and within ninety days (but not counting Sunday or a legal holiday in the District of Columbia as the ninetieth day) after the mailing of the registered letter notifying him of the final determination of a deficiency by the Commissioner the executor may file a petition with the Board of Tax Appeals for a redetermination of the deficiency, other than a deficiency resulting from the correction of a mathematical error appearing upon the return. If the notice of the deficiency is mailed prior to or within thirty days after the enactment of the Act of 1934, the period within which a petition may be filed with the Board is sixty days (not counting Sunday as the sixtieth day) after mailing of the notice.

Where the executor is satisfied with and acquiesces in the tentative or final determination of the whole or any part of the deficiency, the form of notice, which generally accompanies the letter of notification waiving the restrictions on the assessment and the collection of the tax, should be executed by the executor and returned to the commissioner in order to expedite assessment which stops the accrual of interest on the amount assessed until after notice and demand by the collector. 

The executor and the Commissioner, subject to the approval by the Secretary or the Under Secretary of the 

79b A copy of Treasury Mimeograph 4261, setting forth the information required, may be obtained from the local Collector of Internal Revenue.

§ 133 

Treasury, may enter into a closing agreement in writing relating to the tax liability as either tentatively or finally determined in order that the question of the tax may not be reopened.

A closing agreement is final and conclusive, except upon a showing of fraud or malfeasance or misrepresentation of a material fact.

Penalties 

In the case any statement in the preliminary notice or final return is knowingly false, the person making it is subject to a penalty not exceeding $5,000 or imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year, or both, and for a false or fraudulent return 50 per cent will be added to the amount of the tax. Any person required to file any notice or make a return who wilfully fails to do so at the time required is guilty of a misdemeanor, and upon conviction thereof may be fined an amount not to exceed $10,000 or imprisonment for not more than one year or both, together with the cost of prosecution. 

If the preliminary notice is not given or no return filed within the time prescribed the executor is subject to a penalty not exceeding $500.00. For failure to make and file the return within the time prescribed by the Commissioner, or within an extension of time granted by the Commissioner or the Collector 5% will be added to the tax if the failure is for not more than thirty days, with an additional 5% for each thirty days or fraction thereof during which failure continues, not to exceed 25% in the aggregate, except that if the last date allowed for filing the return is on or before August 30, 1935, 25% will be added to the tax and except that if the return is filed after the time allowed and it is shown that the failure to file within the time allowed was due to a reasonable cause and not to willful neglect, no such addition will be made to the tax. Refunds A claim for refund of estate tax for refund of interest or penalties erroneously or illegally collected should be made on the form prescribed by the Treasury Department and should be filed with the Collector of Internal

§  

309 Revenue. Forms for the filing of such claims may be obtained from the local collector. A claim for refund should set forth in detail and under oath each ground upon which a refund is claimed, and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis of the claim should be set forth. Any claim which does not comply with these requirements will not be considered for any purpose as a claim for refund. 

Claims for the refund of estate tax imposed by the Revenue Act of 1926 and the additional estate tax imposed by the Revenue Act of 1932, or the Revenue Act of 1932 as amended by the Revenue Act of 1934, must be filed within three years after the payment of the amount sought to be refunded. If, however, the tax was imposed by the estate tax title of any of the acts prior to the Revenue Act of 1926 the period within which the claim must be filed is four years after the payment of the tax.

If a petition was filed with the Board of Tax Appeals for the redetermination of a deficiency and the Board finds that the executor has made an overpayment of the tax, and further determines as part of its decision that any portion of the overpayment was made within three years (or within four years in a case of a tax imposed by an act prior to the Act of 1926) before the filing of the claim or the filing of the petition, whichever is earlier, the amount of such portion of the overpayment will be refunded. The portion of the overpayment made within such period will be refunded, even though the Board does not determine as part of its decision that the overpayment was so made, provided a hearing upon the petition was held by the Board prior to the expiration of thirty days after the date of the enactment of the Act of 1934. 

Upon the allowance of a claim for refund of any tax or penalty, unless the refund results from the allowance of a credit for payment of estate, inheritance, legacy or succession taxes the statute provides for the payment of interest upon the total amount of such refund at the rate of 6% per annum from the date such tax or penalty was paid to the date preceding the date of the refund by not more than thirty days. If a refund is based upon a claim for payment of estate, inheritance, legacy or succession

§133a  

taxes the refund will be made without interest, unless the overpayment was made prior to the enactment of the Act of 1932, in which case interest will be paid upon the amount of such overpayment at the rate of 6% per annum from the date of payment to the date of the en actment of the Act of 1932.

134. DUTY TO ACCOUNT. 

One of the principal duties of an executor or administrator is to make and file a true account of his administration. This is mandatory under the act,¹ and is also embodied in the oath and bond of the administrator. By the latter an administrator is required "to make or cause to be made a just and true statement of said administration at the expiration of six months from the date hereof, or when thereunto required by the orphans' court."

While this is true, yet there are cases where an account may be dispensed with' and the expense incident to the filing thereof, thus avoided, as where the entire estate is less than the funeral bill or the widow's exemption, or where by the will the executor is also the sole 3

In reducing the period from one year to six months, the Commissioners of 1915, in their report, said: "Formerly the term of one year was perhaps a convenient period for filing an account, but under modern conditions of rapid communication and transportation, it is no longer necessary or advisable. The majority of estates can now be settled by the end of six months, and it is often a great hardship to legatees and creditors to compel them to wait for a full year before their just claims can be satisfied. And where the estate is so complicated that a final account cannot be rendered at the end of six months, a partial account may be filed, debts paid or at least ascertained with some degree of certainty, and the will construed by the court at the audit of the account. 

66 'The Commissioners are of opinion that this shortening of the term will be of great advantage."

137. NATURE OF ACCOUNT FILED. 

Usually, of course, but one accounting is necessary and such would be termed the "First and Final Account.'

Where, however, other assets remain for future accounting and the account first filed is only partial, then, of course, it is properly termed a "First and Partial Account," and succeeding accounts, likewise, "Second and

Partial Account," etc. 

"A partial account of an executor, administrator, guardian or trustee, confirmed by the orphans' court, is only conclusive of what it contains. Whatever has thus been omitted from any previous account, whether debit or credit, so that it was not conidered or passed upon, can be settled in the final one. 999 17 Where the administration is joint, all the executors or administrators should join in the account as in many instances all are liable as principals¹s and the neglect or refusal of one is no relief to the other.

CHAPTER XXI. 

METHOD OF ACCOUNTING. 

138. FORM AND CONTENTS OF ACCOUNTS. 

The account 19 should contain as the first item on the debit side of the principal account the amount of the inventory and appraisement.20 If this amount is inserted as a gross sum a copy of the inventory and appraisement should be submitted at the audit.21 It is the better practice, therefore, unless the inventory is very voluminous to copy it in full as the first item of the account. Immediately following should appear all subsequent items received by the administrator, including, for instance, after discovered assets or gains 22 arising from the sale of items previously included in the inventory. 

It is important that every item of debit or credit should show the date of its receipt or disbursement, and unless this is done the accountant runs the risk of having the account restated at his own expense. Full details should, of course, be given as to each item for the benefit 19 Where one acts in the capacity of an executor, guardian or trustee, his duties are different in each capacity and there should be separate and distinct accounts for each. Dalrymple's Est., 7 Erie 18.

The account of the ancillary administrator of a nonresident decedent should be limited to matters which took place in Pennsylvania and relate to Pennsylvania assets only: it should not include payments made in the state of domicile. Hopkin's Est., 28 D. & C. 431. 

At the audit of an executor's account, the orphans' court refused to confirm the account and directed that it be returned to the clerk unaudited, where the writing admitted to probate by the register of wills did not conform to the statutory requirements incident to a will. The court must take judicial notice of the record, and cannot recognize the account of an executor where there is no will. Rufus's Est., 85 P. L. J. 319. 

20 The inventory should be made the basis of the account and if there is a discrepancy between the inventory and account the account will not be audited. Schaeffer's Est., 22 Sch. 278. 

21 Generally so required by Rule of Court. 

22 Where an administrator collects the full amount of a note belonging to the estate, he must account for the amount collected and not for the appraised value of the note. Halstead's Est., 17 Erie 57. 323

$138 

of the court or for any party who may desire to vouch the account.

When a widow takes assets as part of her allowance at more than the inventoried value, the increase should appear as a charge against the executor in his account, just as if he had sold them at that increase.23

Fiduciaries in accounting for the proceeds of a sale of real estate should charge themselves with the actual purchase price and take credit for all deductions therefrom, so that the account will show on its face just what they did without supplementary or explanatory statements. A mere statement of the net amount received in the general account, after deducting expenses of the sale, is improper and justifies an order by the auditing judge requiring a restatement of the account at the expense of the accountant.25

The credit side of the principal account should include credits for costs, expenses of administration,25a debts26 of the decedent that have been paid and an explanation of losses on the sale of any assets at less than the inventory value. While it is proper practice to take a general credit

If the entire estate is subject to a direct or collateral tax, credit therefor may be taken in the principal account. If, however, different portions of the estate are subject to varying amounts of tax chargeable to different persons, and this item is included, it should be adjusted against the different distributees in the schedule of distribution hereinafter referred to. In many instances it is better to carry the amount paid as a credit in distribution.

In the event of the sale by the accountant of any of the assets of the estate the transaction should appear in the account as a short entry and only the gain or loss, if any. should be carried out into the body of the account. 

Credit should be taken, of course, only for sums actually paid and not for claims unpaid, even if they are valid. Strictly speaking, this applies also to commissions and counsel fees, though very frequently the accountant may wait until after confirmation of his account before making actual payment. It is the better practice, where possible, to have the amount of commissions and counsel fees included in the account and paid over prior to the audit.

After these have been totaled there should be deducted therefrom, however, that portion of the income which was included as accrued income in the principal account, so that the total on the debit side of the income account will be a correct statement of the income actually received as such by the accountant.

Ordinarily, the credit items will be limited to the accountant's commission and possibly a state or county tax paid on the income.

The above remarks, of course, apply only to the personal estate of the decedent and no items as to real estate should be included in the account,30 except where by order of court, or for some other necessary reason, the accountant has been compelled to sell real estate or collect the rents in which event a separate real estate 30a account should be stated following in general the method hereinabove set forth.

At the end of the account there should be a recapitulation picking up the various totals and balances and carrying them into one grand total for distribution. This is required by the Rules of Court, especially of Philadelphia County, and is of great aid in the audit of the account.

139. ACCOUNTS UNDER $300. 

If the assets of the decedent are of a value less than $300 gross the statute provides a short method for the settlement of the account which will save the trouble and expense of an audit and combine in one proceeding the account, its confirmation and the discharge of the fiduciary. "When the personal estate of a decedent does not exceed the value of three hundred dollars, the executor or administrator may, after the expiration of one year after the date of granting the letters testamentary or of administration, present his petition 32 to the proper orphans' court, with an annexed account showing the administration and legal distribution of the estate, the statements in the petition and the account to be verified by the affidavit of such executor or administrator. There- . upon the court may, upon satisfactory proof or acknowledgment of notice to all parties known to be interested in said estates that said petition and account have been presented, order,35 at the end of thirty days from the date of filing the petition and account, the discharge of the executor or administrator and his sureties from future liability, without the expense of proceedings as in a formal account, unless during said period of thirty days exceptions be filed to the account." 36 140.

CHAPTER XXII. 

NOTICE OF ACCOUNTS. 

141. DUTY OF REGISTER. 

The duty of giving formal notice of the filing of an account is imposed on the register of wills. "Every register, with whom an account has been or shall be filed, shall transmit the same to the orphans' court of the respective county, at its next stated meeting, being not less than thirty days distant from the time of such filing, of all which he shall give notice to all persons concerned, in the following manner, viz., by an advertisement enumerating all the accounts to be presented at any one time to the said court, in at least two secular newspapers, if there be two, published in the respective county, or if there be but one newspaper published in such county, then in that one, or if there be none, then in one printed nearest to the said county, at least once a week during the four weeks immediately preceding the meeting of the court at which such account shall be presented, setting forth, in substance, that the accountants, naming them and the character in which they respectively act, have filed their accounts in the office of the said register, and that the same will be presented to the orphans' court for confirmation, at a certain time and place, mentioning the same; and also by setting up conspicuously in his office, and in at least six other of the most public places in the county, at least four weeks before the time appointed for the presentation of such accounts as aforesaid, fairly written or printed copies of such advertisement. The actual expenses of such advertisement, according to the usual rates of advertising in such newspapers, and the setting up of such notices, shall be divided among all the accounts presented at the same court, and the proper portion only shall be charged in any of the said accounts, and allowed to the register as the cost of such advertisement and notices.'' 39

of the Act of March 15, 1832, (P. L. 135), 1 Purd. 1125 (o-q). (Section

 142. SPECIAL NOTICE TO CREDITORS. 

Actual notice (as distinguished from that by formal advertisement) must be given all parties known to the accountant to be interested in the estate. To accomplish this it has been enacted that: "The several orphans' courts of this commonwealth shall by general rule provide that any person who, claiming to be interested in the estate of any decedent as creditor, legatee, next of kin or otherwise, has given written notice of his claim to the executor, administrator or trustee, or his attorney, shall be entitled to receive actual notice from said executor, administrator or trustee, or his attorney, of the filing of his account; or such rule of court may provide for the filing of such claims with, and the giving of notice by, the register of wills or the clerk of the orphans' court." 40 

(3 Sm. L. 296), and April 1, 1823, Sec. 1 (P. L. 286). The insertion of the word "secular" in line 8 covers the provision of the Act of April 15, 1867, (P. L. 86) 1 Purd. 1125, note (o). See also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 

20, Sec. 834.

It is well settled that notice by advertising as directed by law that an account has been filed and will be presented to the orphans' court for confirmation is notice to all parties in interest, creditors as well as beneficiaries; and such an account settled and confirmed in the orphans' court in the absence of fraud will be reviewed only for an error of law apparent on the face of the record or for new matter which has arisen since the decree.

Under the former practice it was held that when an executor of an insolvent estate gives the public notice to creditors required by the act, those who do not present their claims within twelve months after such notice, or upon the audit, cannot, upon application after decree nisi, be allowed to participate in the fund: Cowan's Est., 45 P. L. J. 53. It is the duty of an executor or administrator to notify creditors, whose claims have been presented and disputed, of the time and place of the audit:

The court will not open a duly filed and confirmed administration account on the petition of a next of kin and a creditor, who failed to give written notice of their claims to the accountant as required by Section 46, (c), of the Fiduciaries Act, 1917, P. L. 447, and who had notice of the filing of the account from one other than the accountant, on the ground that the administrator had not given them actual notice of the filing of the account.

Interested parties who request it, should have ample notice of the time and place of the application for the appointment of an auditor to distribute the balance on an administration account. Morthland's Est., 32 York 137. "Section 10 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, provides for advertisement by an administrator, fixing the manner in which this shall be done, and Section 49 (d) directs that claims not presented at the audit of an account filed shall be barred. In the first instance, no actual notice to the creditor is required, and in the second, only where the demand has already been presented to the personal representative before distribution, when so required by rules of court, Section 46 (c). The knowledge of the appointment of the administrator made, of course, only after the filing of an affidavit of death, is effective as to all parties, whether they have actual information of its contents or not.' Lorch's Est., 284 Pa. 500.

While notice of the claim should be given within the period of six months, yet if the creditor presents it later before distribution, no harm is done, and by this is meant distribution to third parties and not a mere reduction to possession by the accountant. 143. EFFECT OF FAILURE TO GIVE NOTICE. 

The notice as hereinbefore outlined is a matter of right to creditors and others in interest. It is also a prerequisite to the settlement of the estate, as the act further provides: "No account of an executor, administrator or guardian shall be confirmed and allowed by the orphans' court, unless it shall appear, at the presentation of such account, that notice of such presentation has been given, conformably to the directions of this act."'43

A petition for review of the adjudication of an executor's account will be granted, where it is undisputed that two creditors of whose claims the accountant had actual knowledge but no formal notice did not receive notice of the audit, and that the averment of the petition for distribution, supported by affidavit, that all creditors of whose claims the accountant had notice or knowledge had been notified was untrue; if the facts had been correctly stated in the petition for distribution, audit of the account would have been refused until the claimants had been given notice and opportunity to present their claims. Ford's Est., 16 D. & C. 531.

The right to file exceptions is only recognized inferentially by the statute" but is almost universally provided by rule of court 15 express or implied.10 45 Such exceptions to be of use, must be filed within the time limited by the rules of court or on special allowance by the court for cause shown, when they may be allowed nunc pro tunc. 

The right is only available to a party in interest.*7

Such exceptions 18 lie to any item in the account either because of failure to include assets or as against alleged wrongful disbursements and as to the latter to the fact of payment, the amount paid or the right to pay.

"The judges of the orphans' courts of this commonwealth, respectively, shall have power, and are hereby authorized, to establish, in their discretion, such rules and regulations as they may deem proper for the publication of advertisements of notices of the auditing of accounts of fiduciaries and shall have supervision of and regulate the cost of such publication in all such cases, as well by special order in particular cases, as by general rules.'' 58

AUDITS IN COUNTIES HAVING SEPARATE ORPHANS' COURTS. 

In such counties the duty of auditing accounts is placed upon the court itself, except under extraordinary circumstances. "In any county in which a separate orphans' court shall be established, all accounts filed in the office of the register of wills, or in the orphans' court by fiduciaries, shall be examined and audited by the court, without expense to the parties, except where all parties in interest in a pending proceeding shall nominate an auditor, whom the court may, in its discretion, appoint. 99 59 For the purpose of such audits it is usual for the court to meet monthly, or at least once in every term, usually on a fixed day in each month excepting the months of July and August. The matter is regulated entirely by rule of court.

The right of the parties to a hearing before an auditor, subject to the discretion of the court, is usually invoked for the purpose of relieving the court of the arduous duties incident to the hearing of extensive testimony where matters are in dispute requiring the production of a great mass of testimony, especially where the estate is insolvent or the creditors are extremely numerous. The appointment is on motion or by stipulation" of counsel. 

Exceptions may of course be filed before the auditor to his report and before the court to the actions of the auditor on consideration of the same, which exceptions are disposed of in the customary manner.¹ 149.

Because of the great volume of matters of fact and of law which may be passed upon and considered by the auditing judge in his adjudication, it is almost impossible to give a form for exceptions to the adjudication which would be in any way satisfactory. If the error complained of is the dismissal of a claim that error may be set forth in the exceptions by the creditor. Supreme Court Rule 58. Mallory's Est., 295 Pa. 406.

It is only for clear error in fact or law that the findings of an auditor in the orphans' court can be set aside. Hartzell's Est., 12 Leh. 343.

Exceptions to an auditor's report should be founded on the record, and no answer is required to them, nor are depositions usually taken in support of them.

It is not good practice to file exceptions to the report of an auditor which embody testimony sought to be produced to the auditor, on a rehearing. The proper method to secure a recommitment of the case to the auditor is by petition. Herring's Est., 21 North. 156, 11 D. & C. 59.

Grumbling's Appeal (Smith's Est.) 99 Super. 345.

157. PROCEDURE TO PROVE CLAIMS. 

Probably no other questions have caused greater litigation in the orphans' court than the presentation and proof of claims against a decedent's estate, either to property in the hands of the decedent alleged to belong to the claimant, claims to distributive shares or claims. for money due.

Lack of space prevents an exhaustive consideration of these cases, but a few of the latest decisions are here given as illustrative of general principles of practice. 

Aside from certain stringent rules of evidence hereafter referred to, the method of proof of claims is, of course, similar to that in effect in other courts and governed by the ordinary rules of evidence. The orphans' court is little bound by acts of assembly 10 and not at all by inflexible rules relating to pleadings. Frequently cases are tried at audits involving fundamental principles and property of great value without any pleadings at all, and the court has never felt compelled at any time to impale any person on technicalities." In this court 9 The findings of fact by an auditor as to a claim against a decedent's estate, approved by the orphans' court, is entitled to the same weight as the verdict of a jury. Schwoyer's Est., 288 Pa. 541. And see Kline's 

Est., 4 D. & C. 614. And see sec. 153, note 98, supra.

Where a person has a claim against an estate and presents same to administrator, and an auditor is appointed to make distribution, but the administrator does not present claim to auditor and the claimant has no notice of the audit, upon application to orphans' court the audit will be opened and if properly proven, claim will be allowed. Beard's Est., 3 Som. 85. 

10 The orphans' court has no authority to invade the province of common pleas in determining the validity of an attachment. It is not bound to take judicial notice of bankruptcy proceedings in the Federal Court but the same must be proven before it. Froess' Est., 11 Erie 319. 

11 Where one has his day in court, with knowledge that a matter is being disposed of in which he has a direct interest, and concerning which he has an opportunity to ascertain his right, he dare not remain silent without losing his chance. Gartner's Est., 94 Super. 45.

(a) Claims of Ownership. 

The orphans' court has full power to inquire into and determine all questions standing directly in the way of the conversion and distribution of the property of a decedent, if at testator's death the property is shown to have been in his possession, or if for any other reason it was presumptively his. In such case, the mere denial of his ownership, unsupported, will not oust the court of its jurisdiction, but the court may proceed with the ina certain asset in fact belongs to her brother is not in itself sufficient to raise a trust in his favor. Pleibel's Est., 20 D. & C. 389.

In order to sustain a decree of a resulting trust, the necessary facts such as the furnishing of the purchase money by the beneficiary must be alleged in the pleadings.

Compromises of doubtful rights and more especially family compromises are favored both in equity and in law. When made in good faith with full disclosures, family compromises may be sustained in equity on ground less than would be required among strangers.

When the Orphans' Court obtains jurisdiction of a subject, it takes cognizance and decides all matters necessary to a full, fair and final de termination of the whole matter. Loesch's Est., No. 2, 17 Erie 310. Rel'g on: Fitzgerald's Est., 49 Montg. 363; Crawford's Est., 12 Wash. 33;

The finding of an envelope in decedent's safe deposit box containing a sum of money and bearing the name of claimant was sufficient to establish a trust in her favor, where the claim was supported by declarations to various persons over a period of years that he (decedent) had provided for claimant in his safe deposit box. There is no prescribed form for the declaration of a trust.

Whether the trust is perfectly created will depend upon the circumstances of the case. If the facts show a clear intention to create a trust, effect will be given to the plan invoked, if the purpose is lawful and the settlor has done the necessary things to make his intention plain. Phillips'

In every valid gift a present title must vest in the donee, irrevocable in the ordinary case of a gift inter vivos, and must be accompanied by delivery.

The mere deposit of money belonging to a depositor in the depositor's and another's name, does not, after the depositor's death, entitle the survivor to have the money paid to him. It must be paid to the executor or administrator of the depositor's estate for distribution through the Orphans Court. DiCrosta's Est., 23 North 196, and see cases there cited.

Nor is such an attempted gift valid as against an enforceable contract to make a will. Culhane's Est. (Nos. 1 and 2), 19 Erie 303, 313.

Constructive or symbolic delivery of a bank book prior to death could not be invoked to establish a gift inter vivos, where a husband executed and delivered to his wife an order for "all my money' in a specified bank, his deposit in a savings bank, there being no evidence of actual delivery of the (Continued on page 358.) 

name, a resident of Canada and distant relative of depositor, makes no claim. Migut Est., 30 Luz. 38.

A deposit by one person of his own money, in the name of himself and another, standing alone, or with words permitting either or both to withdraw, is not sufficient to establish a gift inter vivos, and it is essential that there be a further expression of intention on the part of the donor. 

An essential element of a gift inter vivos is that the donee be given complete control of the subject-matter and the donor release his dominion. 

A deposit by one person of his own money, in his own name as trustee for another, standing alone, establishes a tentative trust, revocable at will, until the depositor dies or completes the gift in his lifetime by some un- (Continued on page 358.) 

future.

The intention was to make a gift and the transaction was complete. 

There was a complete equitable assignment of a savings account to claimant, where decedent a few days before her death delivered a check for the entire deposit and at the same time gave him the pass book. No seal to import a consideration was necessary to make it a gift inter vivos. 

Vance's Est., 80 P. L. J. 429, af'd in 106 Super. 467. "There was a presumption of a gift arising from endorsement and delivery of the check: McConville v. Ingham, 268 Pa. 507, Campbell's Est., 274 Pa. 546; Yeager's Est., 273 Pa. 359. 'Such a transaction is naturally (Continued on page 358.)

The law never presumes a gift. To constitute a valid gift there must have been the intent to give a delivery of the thing. The evidence must show that the donor intended to divest herself of the possession of the property, and it should be inconsistent with any other intention or purpose. 

Feeney's Est., 33 Lack. 72, rel'g on Flanagan v. Nash, 185 Pa. 41; Grady v. Sheehan, 256 Pa. 377.

Where a gift, inter vivos, is made of money or securities, the donor may reserve the right to demand and receive interest from the donee, without invalidating the gift.

A valid gift of principal may be made to one person, and of the interest thereon to another. Sharpe's Est. v. Davis, 25 Del. 524.

A valid gift of non-negotiable securities (postal savings certificates) may be made by delivery of them to the donee without assignment or endorsement in writing. This principle has been applied to notes, bonds, stocks and deposit certificates and life insurance policies. Diskin's Est., 80 P. L. 

J. 115, af'd in 105 super. 519.

To establish a gift inter vivos, there must be an actual delivery of the subject matter of the gift such as to vest a present title in the donee. 

Where manual delivery is not practicable, a transfer may be made by assignment or by other writing or token which will indicate a present intention to pass right of possession to the donee. 

Any gift made to become effective after the death of an intended donor is testamentary in character. Allen's Est., 16 Erie 314.

Where a gift by a husband to his wife is reasonable and not in fraud of creditors, equity sustains it as a provision for her to which the interpretation of a trust is not indispensable; but such gift must be established by clear and convincing proof, not only of the act of donation and delivery, but of her separate custody of it.

A resulting trust is one which arises where the legal estate in property is disposed of, conveyed or transferred, but the intent appears or is inferred from the terms of the disposition, or from accompanying facts and circumstances, that the beneficial interest is not to go to or be enjoyed with the legal title. In actions to recover against the estate of a decedent, the burden of proof is upon the claimant and his right to recover must be shown with definiteness and precision, especially where the claim could have been made against the decedent while he was living.

There is no burden upon the personal representative of a decedent to show that payments made to the decedent, not prima facie unlawful, were made pursuant to a contract or debt owing to the decedent. 

Voluntary payments by a corporation, properly authorized, are not recoverable if made under a claim of right. Donlevy's Est., 323 Pa. 173, af'g, 25 D. & C. 157. An oral agreement to give land as compensation for services to be rendered is enforceable only if it is followed by exclusive possession of the land and the making of improvements which cannot be adequately compensated in damages.

Where the contract is entire, and part is within the statute, it is unenforceable as a whole, and no action can be maintained to enforce the part which would not have been affected by the statute if it had been separate and distinct from the other part.

Contracts to devise realty and bequeath personalty, unless a contrary intention appears or the consideration for the devise of real property is distinct and severable from that for the bequest of personal property, are generally regarded by the court as entire, not severable, and unenforceable as to the part relating to personalty.

On exceptions to an adjudication in a decedent's estate, it appeared that the decedent, for several years prior to her death, was mentally infirm. 

The decedent's husband requested the claimant to take care of his wife and agreed to pay her. The decedent's husband predeceased her and his estate was insolvent. The claimant presented her claim for nursing the wife for a period of more than three years to the administratrices of the wife's estate but failed to aver that the decedent had employed her or that the services had been performed on the credit of her estate. 

In such circumstances, the wife's separate estate was not responsible for the payment of the claimant's services and the decree of the court below allowing the claim will be reversed. McGinnis's Est., 109 Super. 249.
