Since the passage of the Act of May 23, 1887, P. L. 158, competency is the rule, incompetency the exception. The disqualification depends not only on the fact of a witness being a surviving or remaining party, to the thing or contract in action, but of his having an interest adverse to the right of the deceased party. Heere v. Taylor Hose Co. No. 1, 99 Super. 561. 

To effect a disqualification of a party as a witness under the Act of May 23, 1887, P. L. 158, it must appear that the rights of the party dead have passed to the other party on the record who represents his interests. Wolfe v. Scott, 275 Pa. 343.

Under clause (e), section 5, of the Act of May 23, 1887, (P. L. 158) a surviving party to a transaction with a decedent is not disqualified from testifying as to any fact occurring before the death of the decedent and bearing on the transaction unless his interest is adverse to that of the decedent's estate.

A person who acted for the decedent as his agent in making a gift to another is not disqualified as a witness on the ground of interest adverse to that of the decedent.

Such rule is applicable even though the gift was to the children of the agent; the fact of close relationship affects merely the credibility of the witness. Weaver v. Welsh, 325 Pa. 571.

In determining the competency of a witness as against the objection that he has an interest adverse to that of a decedent represented on the record, where his rights will be materially affected by the success of either party he is to be deemed favorable to that side on which his personal interest preponderates. Schmidt's Est., 18 D. & C. 567. 

Merritt v. Blaine, 33 Lack. 60, citing Waugaman v. Henry, 75 Super. 94; 

King, Admr., v. King, 96 Super. 585; First National Bank of Bloomsburg v. Gerli, 225 Pa. 256; Dickson v. McGraw Bros., 151 Pa. 98; Horne & Co. 

Edmundson's Est., 259 Pa. 436.

Surviving husband, sisters, nieces, nephews as well as the wife of the v. Petty, 192 Pa. 32;

§ 157 

This provision of the law applies not only to actions in assumpsit, but also in trespass. In proving such a claim therefore, it is necessary that witnesses be produced other than the claimant and having no interest in the subject matter. To exclude a witness, however, on the ground of interest, it is necessary that he should have a vested interest, not in the question involved, but in the event of the suit. It must be an interest that the judgment in the cause would operate upon; for if by the event, he would neither acquire nor lose a right, nor incur a responsibility which the law recognizes, he is competent. Every other kind of interest goes only to credibility.18 Thus, it has been held that a stockholder of a cornephew, are incompetent witnesses to testify as to matters occurring prior to the death of decedent as they have an adverse interest to the right of a claimant as donee inter vivos as provided for under the Act of May 23, 1887 (P. L. 158), Sec. 5, Clause E. Gallagher v. Rogan, 53 Montg. 138, rel'g on King v. Zemmer, 315 Pa. 254.

An interested person is competent to testify to a fact or condition of facts existing after the death of a deceased party in interest, notwithstanding that such testimony may inferentially tend to show that the same state of facts existed, or that some other connected fact existed or occurred, prior to the decedent's death.

A witness who has read a lost writing, or otherwise has actual knowledge of it, and is able to testify giving his best recollection of its contents, is competent even though he cannot state the precise language of the writing. 

Lepper's Est., 106 Super. 123.

The plaintiffs' witnesses, viz: children of the decedent, who testified to matters that occurred before the death of the decedent and afterwards, not adverse to the estate, were competent witnesses. 

The defendant, who testified to matters adverse to the estate before the date of the decedent's death is not a competent witness to testify to anything which occurred before the death of the decedent. Mader v. Stemler, 39 Dauph. 71, 81.

Where one is authorized by another to act for her as an agent (the principal being disclosed) in employing an attorney on a contingent fee, the agent, after the principal's death, is a competent witness, under the Act of 

May 23, 1887, P. L. 158, for the attorney to prove the contract of employment. The agent's competency cannot be attacked because of a bare possibility that an action might be brought against her. 

Where the orphans' court finds as a fact, upon competent evidence, that a decedent had made, in her lifetime, a contract of employment with an attorney-at-law based on a contingent fee, such finding will not be reversed on appeal, in the absence of manifest error. Dillon's Est., 269 Pa. 234.

The adverse party may also be compelled to testify as if under cross-examination, as it is provided that: "In any civil proceeding, whether or not it be brought or defended by a person representing the interests of a deceased or lunatic assignor of any thing or contract in action, a party to the record or a person for whose immediate benefit such proceeding is prosecuted or defended, or any other person whose interest is adverse to the party calling him as a witness, may be compelled by the adverse party to testify as if under cross-examination, subject to the rules of evidence applicable to witnesses under cross-examination, and the adverse party calling such witnesses shall not be concluded by his testimony; but such person so cross-examined shall become thereby a fully competent witness for the other party as to all relevant matters, whether or not these matters were touched upon in his cross-examination; and also, where one of several plaintiffs or defendants, or the person for whose immediate benefit such proceeding is prosecuted or defended, or such other person having an adverse interest, is cross-examined under this section, his co-plaintiffs or co-defendants shall thereby become fully competent witnesses on their own behalf as to all relevant matters, whether or not these matters were touched upon in such cross-examination." 53

Where the judge, who made the order or decision heard and saw the witnesses, and came to his decision with that advantage, a subsequent judge will not disturb his findings. Fenton's Est., 14 Erie 141. "The auditing judge, who saw and heard the witnesses, and whose duty it was to find the facts, was best able to consider the scope and effect of the testimony (Phillips's Est., 295 Pa. 349; Belmont Laboratories, Inc., v. 

Heist, 300 Pa. 542), and he unequivocally found that decedent made an express agreement to pay the indebtedness. That finding, being amply supported by credible evidence and approved by the court in banc, will ordinarily be accepted by this court on appeal: Robb v. Stone, 296 Pa. 482; 

Thorndell v. Munn, 298 Pa. 1.'' Copeland's Estate, 313 Pa. 25.

Although it is the duty of the court in banc to review carefully such of the findings of fact of the chancellor as have been made the subject of exceptions, yet great weight is to be given to the chancellor's findings where they depend, in a large degree, on the credibility of witnesses whom he saw and whose testimony he is best able to weigh. Hasson's Estate, 110 Super. 23. 

The credibility of witnesses and the weight to be given their testimony, in view of their character, intelligence, and knowledge of the subject, are matters for determination by the judge who hears them, and his findings will not be disturbed except for a clear error. Ruetschlin's Est., 19 D. & C. 45.

Where a hearing judge refuses to believe the testimony of a witness, his conclusions as to credibility will not be disturbed unless his acts are biased, capricious, or unreasonable. Marley's Est., 29 D. & C. 245.

Where no exceptions are taken to the findings of fact of the auditing judge, the correctness of the findings of fact is admitted, and on appeal the question for the appellate court is whether the findings support the decree. 

Kane's Est., 121 Super. 117, aff'g 22 D. & C. 245.

It is within the discretion of the auditing judge to accept and rely upon the testimony of a witness who has previously given false and fraudulent evidence, the auditing judge being best qualified to form an opinion as to the reliability of such testimony. Celenza's Est., 16 D. & C. 473, aff'd in 

308 Pa. 186.

The appearance of the witnesses and their manner of testifying affords the hearing judge a better opportunity to determine their credibility than the judges on appeal. Kovacevich's Est., 309 Pa. 268.

Findings of fact of an auditing judge, like the verdict of a jury, will not be set aside except for errors clearly appearing, although another judge might have arrived at a different conclusion; the auditing judge, having seen and heard the witnesses, is far better qualified to determine their veracity, credibility and bias than is the court in banc. The construction of a will adopted by an auditing judge in the distribution of an estate becomes "the law of the case, " and will control subsequent distributions arising from the same fund or parts of the fund affected by the former adjudication. Charles's Est., 99 Super. 51.

Particularly is this true where the fund is turned over to trustees for the purpose of the will as construed by the auditing judge. 

Where it is asserted that the fund in question is not the same fund affected by the former adjudication, the burden of proving so, rests upon him who asserts it. Gould's Estate, 270 Pa. 535.

Only such facts and issues as have been judicially ascertained or determined, can be held res judicata in a subsequent litigation between the same parties over the same subject-matter. Bullitt's Est., 308 Pa. 413, rev'g 16 D. & C. 376. 

No objections to the items composing a fiduciary's account may be heard, where exceptant approved in writing a prior account made up of the same items. Large's Est., 21 D. & C. 531.

 159. AMENDMENT OF ADJUDICATION. 

Occasionally, however, errors of fact or law apparent on the face of the record, or ascertainable from facts admittedly occurring after the account has been filed, estate is quasi in rem and, however erroneous, stands unless reviewed in an appropriate proceeding. 

It is the duty of one asserting a right to share in a decedent's estate to make all his claims at the audit, stating them in alternative form if necessary, so that they may all be disposed of by the court in its order for distribution. 

Where an appellate court, modifying the order of distribution made by the orphans' court, has specifically directed how the awards of principal and interest shall be made, a beneficiary may not, by presenting a claim based on contentions not previously presented to either court, obtain an award embodying a modification or change of the appellate court's decision. 

Lockhart's Est., 17 D. & C. 620.

Where adjudications upon former accounts of trustees in the same estate go no further than to determine the validity of a trust for life, and do not confirm the validity of remainders to take effect after the death of the life tenant, such adjudications are not res judicata upon the audit of a subsequent account of the same trustees at which the validity of the exercise of a power of appointment creating the gifts in remainder is raised. Johnson's Estate, 1 D. & C. 420.

While a decision of the Superior Court on a question of the distribution of income under a will, may not be res adjudicata on a question of distributing the corpus of the estate, yet such construction, if applicable, and proper, will be adopted by the Supreme Court in distributing the principal. 

Harned's Estate, 273 Pa. 237.

A decree of the Orphans' Court, based upon an award of distribution pursuant thereto, no appeal having been taken and no review granted, is res adjudicata in so far as the rights of the parties and their privies are concerned, not merely as to the principal of the fund and accrued income, which was the subject of the decree, but also as to the income thereafter accruing on the fund in the hands of the trustees and included in a subsequent account. Chew's Estate, 1 D. & C. 79. "In order to make a matter res adjudicata the general rule is that there must be a concurrence of four conditions as follows: 1. Identity in the thing sued for. 2. Identity of the cause of action. 3. Identity of the persons and parties to the action. 4. Identity of the quality in the persons for or against whom the claim is made. Pennebaker v. Parker, 33 

Super. 458; Siegfried v. Boyd, 237 Pa. 55." "The proceeding in the orphans' court was against the heirs of decedent; the action here is against his administrators. A judgment against the heirs precludes a judgment against their representative. Under the law, therefore, there is identity of parties and of the quality in the persons against whom the claims were made. Dyer's Appeal, 3 Grant 326; Walthaur's 

Heirs v. Gossar, 32 Pa. 259; Taylor v. Cornelius, 60 Pa. 187." "Even though the causes of action or the subject matter may not be the same, nevertheless an estoppel results between the same parties in a different claim or demand as to matters in issue or points controverted and actually determined in the original suit. Trosell v. D. L. & W. R. R., 227

A decree of court construing a will is not res judicata as to a later proceeding where identically the same question is raised, but the parties are different. Freeman's Est., 280 Pa. 273.

Where a widow has filed an account as trustee and has been discharged, and a substituted trustee appointed, and afterwards the substituted trustee, under an order of the orphans' court, affirmed by the supreme court, sells real estate and files an account, all questions passed on by the supreme court in affirming the order to sell are res judicata on the adjudication of the substituted trustee's account, if the parties are the same. Bailey's Est., 287 Pa. 478.

The refusal of the Court of Common Pleas to allow the guardian of the widow, a weak-minded person, to take against the will is not such determination of the interest of said weak-minded person in said real estate as to be res adjudicata. Miller's Est., 47 Montg. 230, 17 D. & C. 127.

The filing of an account of the trustee of decedent accounting for rents is not res adjudicata as to the interest in real estate which the devisee took under the will of decedent. Miller's Est., 47 Montg. 230, 17 D. & C. 127.

An Orphans' Court adjudication of an account and the award of the balance on the assumption that the property was that of the decedent, is not res adjudicata of the question whether he held it in trust, and does not bar a bill in equity against the executors for an accounting on the basis of a trust. Colflesh v. Prov. Tr. Co., 27 Del. 152.

The binding effect of a former adjudication applies with the same strictness when the new cause of action, while not technically the same as the old, is nevetheless so related thereto that some matter essential to a recovery in the new proceeding was in fact determined in the earlier one. 

O'Connor v. O'Connor, 291 Pa. 175.

Decisions of law made in distributing one fund are not binding in a subsequent distribution of another fund, between the same parties, in the same estate; but the contrary rule prevails as to questions of fact. 

The rule as to the conclusiveness of the finding as to a question of fact, applies, where the cause of action in the second proceeding, while not technically the same, is nevertheless so related to the cause in the prior litigation that some matter of fact, the establishment of which is essential to the recovery in the second, was determined in the first. 

A finding by the adjudication of the account of an executor, covering personal property only, that a charge of nonsupport against a husband was unfounded, is res judicata of the same question in a subsequent proceeding in partition of real estate between the same parties in the same estate. 

Lease v. Ensminger, 5 Super. 329, overruled. Havir's Est., 283 Pa. 292.

Where a widow's claim for exemption is denied by the orphans court because of the fact that her marriage to the decedent is not established, but on appeal the superior court finds the fact of marriage in favor of appellant and reverses the decree, the decree of the superior court is res judicata of the fact of marriage when the widow claims her share as a

A petition to open the adjudication of an executor's account, so that a claim may be proved against the estate of a decedent, is not the proper remedy to enforce a claim arising out of a bond of indemnity given by decedent to claimant, when the liability upon the bond was contingent throughout the complete settlement of decedent's estate and did not become absolute until all assets of the estate had been duly accounted for and distributed.

Although Sec. 49 (d) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 does not refer to contingent claims, and under it a contingent claim need not be presented and could not be allowed if presented at the audit of the executors' account, nevertheless it is an act of limitation and repose which bars enforcement of such a claim against the estate, where it becomes absolute after the time for presenting claims against the estate has passed and the estate has been distributed, no assets remaining in the hands of the executors.

DISTRIBUTION. 

CHAPTER XXVIII. 

GENERAL RULES AS TO DISTRIBUTION. 

WHEN DISTRIBUTION MAY BE COMPELLED. 

The culmination of the duties of an executor or administrator is the distribution of the estate (after the payment of creditors, taxes, etc.) to the heirs or the beneficiaries under the will.

The former are as set forth in the Intestate Act of 

1917;¹ the latter as set forth in the will, as controlled by the Wills Act of 1917.2 

The executor or administrator has six months to settle the estate and "no executor or administrator shall be compelled to make distribution of the estate of his testator or intestate until six months be fully expired from the granting of the letters testamentary or of administration in the estate." 1 P. L. 429. 2 P. L. 403. 

Property of a decedent at the time of death, both real and personal, can only pass to heirs or legatees in one of two ways, namely: (1) under a last will and testament, (2) under the intestate laws. Any part of an estate that does not pass by last will and testament must be distributed under the intestate laws. Shupe's Est., 15 Erie 170. 

3 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 49, (a), which is a modification of Sec. 38 of the Act of February 24, 1834, (P. L. 70), 1 Purd. 1130, (c) (see also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 861), which related to administrators only. It was copied from Sec. 15 of the Act of April 19, 1794, (3 Sm. L. 143), except that under the Act of 1794 the year ran from the death of the intestate.

The period has now been reduced to six months. 

This also involved the repeal of the first part of Sec. 19 of the Act of 

March 29, 1832, (P. L. 190) 1 Purd. 1127 (z, a-c), providing for the appointment of auditors in insolvent estates "to settle and adjust the rates and proportions of the assets to and among the respective creditors, according to the order established by law," and the last part of Section 1 of the Act of April 13, 1840, (P. L. 319), 1 Purd. 1127 (d-g), providing 401

If there is any doubt of the ability of the respondent to pay, the petition should recite the sureties on his administration bond and join them as parties respondent. 

162. DISTRIBUTION WITHOUT AUDIT. 

Generally, however, recourse to this procedure is unnecessary and distribution follows administration in due course.5 In fact in many cases distribution is made without accounting or audit, as the law provides: "Executors or administrators may make distribution," and pay or deliver legacies, without the audit of their accounts, upon such security as may be satisfactory to for the appointment of auditors to make distribution on the application of any legatee, heir or other person interested. 

One who has a prima facie claim against the estate of a decedent is entitled to require an account by personal representatives. 

The orphans' court will not deny a creditor of a decedent the right to proceed to have his claim adjudicated in that court and relegate him to his common law action.

DISTRIBUTION BY EMPLOYER OF WAGES DUE DECEDENT. 

As a further aid to the simple settlement of small estates without expense where wages of the decedent are involved, the law provides: "It shall be lawful for any employer in this commonwealth at any time not less than thirty days after the death of his employee to pay all wages due to such deceased employee to the wife, children, father or mother, sister or brother (preference being given in the order named) of the deceased employee, without requiring letters testamentary or of administration to be issued upon the estate of said deceased employee, where such wages due do not exceed $15014 in amount. If such deceased employee shall not leave a wife or any of said relatives surviving him, then it shall be lawful for the employer in like manner to pay such wages to the creditors of the decedent, as follows: undertaker, physician, boardinghouse keeper, and nurse, each his or her pro rata share, upon affidavit of fact furnished. The payment of such wages as aforesaid shall be a full discharge and release to the employer from any further claim for such wages. 99 15 In such case the employer should secure from the claimant an affidavit¹ setting forth facts in sufficient detail to satisfy the requirements of the act.

A soldier in the late World War took out a War Risk Insurance Policy and named his mother as beneficiary therein. The soldier died intestate in 1918 and his mother, as beneficiary, received the installments of insurance until her death in 1931. The commuted balance due on the policy then became payable to the estate of the insured soldier. Held (1) That the heirs of the deceased soldier must be ascertained as of the date of his death. (2) That the mother, having survived the deceased soldier (the father being dead), has a vested interest in his estate, including the commuted value of the insurance, which she could dispose of by last will and testament, and (3) That, therefore, the balance for distribution should be awarded to the estate of the deceased mother rather than to the brothers and sisters of the deceased soldier. Podany Est., 31 Sch. 146.

The orphans' court is the proper tribunal to decide questions of fact as to alleged kinship with the decedent in a contest to determine who shall take the property of a decedent who dies without issue or known relatives. 

Where the property of a decedent, who dies without issue or known relatives, is awarded to the Commonwealth under section 1314 of the Fiscal 

Code, the Act of April 9, 1929, P. L. 343, and not in escheat proceedings under the Act of May 2, 1889, P. L. 66, the decree should conform to the Act of 1929; a direction in the decree that the proceeds of an estate be transmitted to the state treasurer of Pennsylvania in the nature of an escheat is improper and will be corrected on appeal. 

In a contest to determine who shall take the property of a decedent who dies without issue or known relatives, the Commonwealth stands in relation to the property of the decedent as one asserting a circumstantial right thereto.

The burden is upon those who claim kinship to a decedent who dies without issue or known relatives to prove their claim by a fair preponderance of trustworthy and satisfying evidence.

To defeat the claim of the Commonwealth the evidence must be so clear, precise and definite in quality and quantity as to satisfy the court below that the relationship claimed existed.

Where the claimants seek to establish kinship by means of birth, death, and marriage records from a foreign country, and affidavits as to family reputation, and the declarations as to relationship of deceased members of the family all coming from or near a particular place in the foreign country, satisfactory evidence must first be produced showing the place of origin, the town or place in the foreign country from which decedent's ancestors came and where kinship was created. 

Hearsay evidence is admissible to establish pedigree where (1) the declarations are made ante litem motam, (2) the declarant is dead, and (3) there is evidence dehors the declaration to connect the declarant with the family.

It is not necessary that the person who testifies as to the declaration be related to the person whose pedigree is under consideration but only that the declarant whose statements are given in evidence by the witness be so related.

Identity of names, religion and nativity alone are insufficient to evidence family connection.

Where a hearing judge refuses to believe the testimony of a witness, his conclusion as to credibility will not be disturbed unless his acts are biased, capricious or unreasonable.

In a contest in the orphans' court to determine who shall take the property of a decedent who dies without issue or known relatives, the court sits as a jury to weigh and consider the relevant testimony, and when a finding is made it is binding on this court unless there has been legal error in the course of its submission. Link's Est. (No. 1) 319 Pa. 513.

When the interests of distributees have been assigned ³° 39 39 At common law an heir expectant may not assign or transfer his expectancy during the ancestor's lifetime, but such a sale or transfer will be sustained in equity whenever good conscience so requires and it is founded upon a valuable consideration.

One claiming under assignment of an interest in the estate of a person then living must assume the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction and the adequacy of the consideration, no presumption thereof arising from the fact of assignment. 

A husband may make a valid transfer of property to his wife for an honest purpose and to secure or pay a just debt, as to any other creditor, but the transaction is to be carefully scrutinized and the indebtedness must be established by clear, full and unequivocal evidence, mere recitals in a writing being insufficient for that purpose. 

Recitals and statements contained in a written instrument are competent evidence against a party thereto as admissions of the facts recited, but they are not evidence against third parties who are strangers to the writing. Douglass' Est., 17 D. & C. 672.

Parol evidence is admissible to establish that a contract or assignment was obtained through fraud, and this is so although such evidence varies or contradicts the terms of the writing. 

Parol evidence held admissible to establish that written assignment, purporting to convey to the assignee a first and prior interest, to the extent of a stated amount, in the share of the assignor, as a residuary legatee, in a decedent's estate, had been obtained through fraud practiced on the assignor, who had believed that the transaction was only a loan to him in an amount less than the amount of the assignment, and written assignment held invalid. It is well settled that one may enter into a valid contract to dispose by will of his property, real or personal, in a particular way, and that such will is irrevocable and the contract will be specifically enforced. There are many examples of the recognition of this doctrine in this state and other states: Cawley's Est., 136 Pa. 628; Smith v. Tuit, 127 Pa. 341; 

Wright's Est., 155 Pa. 64; Shroyer v. Smith, 204 Pa. 310; Lewallen's

In Thompson on Wills, Section 28, the learned author says: "Mutual wills, that is, where two persons execute wills reciprocal in their provisions, but separate instruments, may or may not be revocable at the pleasure of either party, according to the circumstances and understanding upon which they were executed. To deprive either party of the right to revoke such mutual wills, it is necessary to prove such wills were executed in pursuance of a contract or a compact between the parties and that each is the consideration for the other.'' Culhane's Est. (No. 2), 19 Erie 313, quoting McGinley's

167. 

PETITIONS FOR DISTRIBUTION. 

In most of the counties having a separate orphans' court, it is provided by rule of court that a petition for distribution¹¹ shall be submitted at the audit and to the auditing judge.

In certain counties a regular printed form is furnished to be used where possible or modified to suit peculiar conditions.¹² It is advisable that such forms be secured from the clerk and accurately filled in.

It will be noted that the following features are usually essential: 

1. Name of decedent. 

2. Date of death. 

3. Testate or intestate. 

4. Date of probate and grant of letters. 

5. Names and status of heirs or legatees and nature of their interests. 

6. Averment of notice to all parties in interest. 

7. Statement as to liability to inheritance tax and facts as to payment. 

8. Names of unpaid creditors and status of their claims. 

9. Statement of any question involved requiring consideration by the court. 

10. Suggested method of distribution. 

11. Signature and affidavit by accountant.

It is generally necessary to submit to the court, with such petition: 

1. The original letters testamentary or of administration. 

2. Proof of publication of notice of grant of letters. 

3. Original receipt for inheritance taxes. 

41 Such a petition is only informative and is not conclusive of anything. 

It can be amended at any time. Levenight's Est. No. 2, 42 Lanc. 197.

44 If the decedent had been domiciled in this state distribution should be made in accordance with the laws of Pennsylvania, but if domiciled in a foreign country, succession to his property is regulated by the laws of the country of his domicile. Wayda's Est., 16 Del. 444.

In the distribution of the estate of a deceased citizen of Russia, the orphans' court will take judicial notice of the private rights of individuals domiciled in Russia arising under the laws of Pennsylvania, and will not concern itself with political problems arising from the severance of diplomatic relations and unrecognized governments. When the distribution is involved either in the number of distributees or the varying quantity of their interests or the fund is represented other than by cash5³ it is advisable to file a schedule of distribution.54

The preparation of such a schedule usually devolves upon counsel, though where the accountant is a trust company, the calculations involved should be performed 

53 Distribution in kind. See Sec. 165, supra. 

54 Where a decree of the orphans' court directs payments in accordance with a schedule of distribution, and the schedule does not include a certain claim made against the estate, the decree as against the claimant is a final decree and he must take his appeal within the statutory period of three months provided by the Acts of May 19, 1897, (P. L. 67) and March 

12, 1925, (P. L. 32).

In such case it is immaterial that the decree as to other matters was amended, inasmuch as subsequent proceedings could not extend the time for the claimant's appeal. Henry's Est., 290 Pa. 537.

A schedule of distribution is not necessary where the adjudication contains a definite award; it is merely a part of the adjudication and a convenience in a complicated estate. 

An order of the orphans' court, dismissing exceptions to an adjudication and confirming it absolutely, embodies by implied reference the award in the adjudication and becomes the final decree, from which an appeal may be taken. Whitmore's Est., 20 D. & C. 432.

A decree awarding a balance for distribution to those entitled thereto, without naming the parties or fixing their shares, and directing that counsel shall prepare a schedule of distribution to be approved by the auditing judge, is an interlocutory order not subject to appeal. 

There can be no final decree of the orphans' court distributing a balance of account until a schedule of distribution is approved by the court. 

A rule of the orphans' court fixing fifteen days as the limit of time for filing exceptions to an adjudication "irrespective of whether (the auditing judge) shall or shall not have directed the submission of a schedule of distribution,'' can have no effect on the right of appeal. Graham's Est., 294 

Pa. 493.

An appeal taken from the orphans' court before the schedule of distribution was filed and the adjudication confirmed absolutely, exhibits no final decree from which an appeal lies, and such an appeal will be dismissed. Levy's Est., 307 Pa. 522, cit'g: Graham's Est., 294 Pa. 493, 495; Hoyt's Est., 232 Pa. 189; Kaeir's Est., 264 Pa. 224. 

And see 

Brusstar's Est., 123 Super. 45; Maron's Est., 317 Pa. 476. And generally, Sec. 289, infra.

Where at the adjudication of an executor's account a schedule of distribution is submitted but not approved and no other schedule is presented, but in a subsequent account the executors take credit in distribution for a trust fund composed of specified assets and that account is confirmed absolutely, any defect caused by the failure to file a schedule of distribution with the first account is cured, and the trustees may properly file an account. Clay's Est., 25 D, & C, 257.

172. REFUNDING BONDS. 

The requirement of such bonds, as has been heretofore noted,62 has to a great extent been abrogated except when distribution is made without the protection of a decree of court.

An exception occurs however where the executor or administrator himself has received the fund only on the giving of such bond to his distributor. In such case it is provided: "Where any fiduciary has been required, or hereafter shall be required, upon the receipt of money, to give a refunding bond, it shall be lawful for such fiduciary, upon paying over such money to creditors, or to parties beneficially interested, to require, under the direction of the orphans' court having jurisdiction of his accounts, a bond, refunding receipt or other obligation from each person receiving such money, to indemnify such fiduciary to the amount such person may receive." 63

Such a situation arises quite frequently where the accountant has been compelled to give bond in order to secure delivery to him of corporate securities on the loss or destruction of the stock certificate or bond. In such case the matter should be brought clearly to the attention of the auditor or auditing judge so that the same protection from the distributee can be given to the accountant as he was compelled to give in securing the fund. 

62 See Sec. 163, supra. 

63 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 50, (a), which is Sec. 1 of the Act of April 13, 1859, (P. L. 604), 1 Purd. 1132 (m). (See also 

Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 868.) In their report on this section, the 

Commissioners of 1915 said: "The Act of June 10, 1881, P. L. 106, 1 Purd. 1132, note (m) amended the Act of 1859 by adding a clause authorizing a ward who had reached lawful age and was a married woman to give her own refunding bond. 

This is now omitted as unnecessary since the married women's acts. For the same reason, Sec. 4 of the Act of April 11, 1856, P. L. 315, 3 Purd. 

2454, authorizing a married woman entitled to a legacy or distributive share to give a refunding bond and to execute all other instruments and perform all other acts on payment to her of moneys so distributed, is recommended for repeal."

§ 172 

The refunding bond should be retained by the administrator as his protection in the event of any subsequent claims being made against the estate which would require its use.

Action on all refunding bonds is limited and controlled by the statute: "In all cases where refunding bonds shall be given upon the distribution of the estate of any decedent, no action or suit thereon shall be brought after the expiration of six years from the date of such bond: Provided, That where the creditors or other persons entitled to the protection of said bonds, shall be within the age of twenty-one years, non compos mentis, imprisoned, or from or without the United States of America, or where a creditor whose debt shall not mature within such period, shall file within the said period in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court where said distribution shall have been made, a copy or particular statement of any bond, covenant, debt or demand upon which his claim arises, then and in any such cases an action may be brought by the creditor at any time not exceeding two years from the coming of age, or removal of such disability of the creditor or other person entitled to the protection of said bonds, or the maturing of the debt or demand aforesaid." 65 

64 See Form No. 138, App., p. 166. 64 

65 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 50 (b), which is Sec. 1 of the Act of June 30, 1885, (P. L. 203), 1 Purd. 1132. See also Purd. 

Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 869.

The bond of a corporate surety, being usually in terms prescribed by it and being given for a consideration, is to be construed most strictly in favor of the obligee.

A "refunding bond,'' within the meaning of section 50 (b) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, requiring actions on such bonds to be instituted within 6 years, is one given to or for the protection of an executor or administrator who makes voluntary distribution before expiration of the time allowed for the presentation of creditors' claims; the term does not include a bond given by an executor to a single creditor, whose claim has already been presented, determined, and allowed, to induce the withdrawal of exceptions to an auditor's award and thus to effectuate a plan for assignment of the entire estate to a corporation whose obligations are to be issued to creditors of the estate. 

Interest commences to accrue on the bond of a corporate surety only from the date on which demand for payment was made, and not from the date on which the suit resulting in the surety's liability was instituted against the principal. Pyles v. Fidelity Etc. Co., 21 D. & C. 680.

It is proper for an accountant upon payment or delivery of a distributive share of an estate to any creditor, legatee or distributee to demand and receive as a prerequisite thereto, or concurrently therewith, a receipt and release" as record evidence of such payment and in discharge of his liability therefor. If the decedent owned real estate there should be prepared separately from this a release 7 of all real estate and the document should be acknowledged before a notary public for recording if necessary. 

All of the receipts and releases thus obtained from the distributees should be filed by the administratrix in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court under the term and number of the estate.

517) authorizes the entry of judgment, but where an appeal has been taken, must be read in conjunction with Section 6 of the Act of May 19, 1897, (P. L. 67). Therefore the appeal acts as a supersedeas. The effect of a supersedeas is not only to stay an execution on a definitive decree but to preserve the status in quo pending the determination of the appeal. Therefore, the act of appellant in changing this status by the entry of judgment is improper, and, notwithstanding an appeal has been taken, the court below retains the right concurrently with the appellate court to control the actions of the respective parties in so far as to preserve the status in quo of each as it was at the time the decree was made. New Brighton R. R. 

Co. v. Pittsburgh R. R. Co., 105 Pa. 13, and, therefore, striking off the judgment entered after appeal, was demanded under the circumstances."

THE FIVE HUNDRED DOLLAR EXEMPTION 176. RIGHT TO EXEMPTION, PROPERTY LIABLE. 

Greatly favored by the law, and properly so, is the right of a widow or children of a decedent to the exemption of $500. With but few exceptions 4 it is prior to 83 

82 Merten's Est., 14 Erie 240, 47 York 27. 84 The claim for the widow's exemption has the effect of a judgment at common law. Seller's Est., 82 Pa. 153. Under the rules adopted by the Orphans' Court of Philadelphia County the proper procedure 15 is as follows: 

A petition is filed with the clerk of the orphans' court. 

An advertisement is then inserted twice successively in the Legal Intelligencer and twice a week for two weeks in a daily newspaper published in Philadelphia. 

Fifteen days after the last appearance of the advertisement if no exceptions have been filed, upon the submission of proof of publication, the claim may be allowed, provided, however, that advertisement may be dispensed with if payment is not asked until the audit of the estate.15a 

If payment is not to be requested until the audit the prayer in the above petition and also the form of decree should be changed accordingly. It has become the practice, however, where the widow does not claim her exemption until the audit and cash is claimed to allow the same merely upon the oral request of her counsel at that time without the presentation of a petition. In such case the only advantage of a petition and decree is that it fixes the rights of the widow, so that the amount of the exemption will pass to her estate in the event of her death before the audit.

Where the exemption is selected in personal property other than money, the procedure is slightly different. A petition and appraisement is filed with the clerk.

In cases where it is necessary for the court to appoint appraisers the necessity for such action should be stated in the petition and the appointment and subsequent apof expenses out of the estate is new. See also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 474.

An exemption can be adjudicated only in the orphans' court and not by a writ of dower in the Common Pleas. Bridgeford v. Groh, 306 Pa. 572. 

Where an appraisement for a widow's exemption has been set aside because of an excessive overvaluation of the property, the costs will be directed to be paid out of the general estate. 

In such case, the costs should not be imposed on the exceptant, who is the successful party, nor upon the widow, who in good faith defended the appraisement. Morrison's Est., 11 D. & C. 447.

A widow, who has claimed her exemption in cash before the conversion of decedent's property, is entitled, under sections 12 (a) and (d) of the Fiduciaries Act, to have it afterwards set apart to her out of the proceeds of decedent's real and personal property if there was not sufficient cash in the estate. Sitkin's Est., 23 D. & C. 689.

Several fundamental differences between the allowance and the exemption will be noted, however. (1) The allowance is available for either spouse and is not confined to the widow or children as is the exemption. (2) It does not take precedence over the claims of creditors or taxes." (3) It is not available as against a valid will.48 by the Acts of April 1, 1909, (P. L. 87) 5 Purd. 6476 (v), and July 21, 1913, (P. L. 875) 5 Purd. 6478 (see also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 11), further amended so as to apply expressly to husband as well as wife, so as to be limited to cases of actual intestacy, and so as to make the estate of the surviving spouse absolute in real as well as personal property. 

In offering this section the Commissioners of 1915, in their report, said: "In accordance with their view that the interests of the surviving husband and wife should be the same, the Commissioners have made the provisions of the Act of April 1, 1909, apply equally to both cases. The special allowance of $5,000 where there is no issue, conferred upon the widow by this act, appears to have been favorably considered during the time it has been in operation, and no change in the amount is suggested. 

The Act of April 1, 1909, was most probably not intended by the legislature to apply to the case of a husband who should elect to take against the will of his wife (there being no issue), but this result followed logically from a consideration and comparison of the Acts of April 8, 1833, P. L. 

315, April 11, 1848, Section 11, P. L. 536, and May 4, 1855, Section 1, P. L. 430, as shown in Buckland's Estate, 239 Pa. 608; Moore's Estate, 50 Super. 76.

A result of the Act of 1909 in connection with prior legislation is that a married person having no issue whose estate amounts to $5,000 or less cannot make any testamentary disposition of his or her estate. The Commissioners recommend in this section that the special allowance of 1909 shall be made only in cases of actual intestacy, and not where the surviving spouse elects to take against the will of the deceased spouse.'

"The controlling distinction between the law relating to the $500 exemption and the $5,000 allowed to widows under the Act of 1917 is that the $5,000 worth of property, real or personal, vests in the widow at the death of her husband, and does not require any action on her part to secure the same."'

Under the Intestate Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 429, Section 2 (a), when a husband dies intestate leaving a widow, but no issue, the share to which the widow becomes entitled vests in her absolutely as an inheritance, and on the death of the widow, intestate, passes to her next of kin. 

In such case her next of kin are entitled to have $5,000 in value of the husband's estate appraised and set apart for their benefit, although no claim therefor was made by the widow in her lifetime. Nolan's Est., 68 

P. L. J. 588, 21 Lack. 239, 2 Erie 211, 9 Lehigh 57. 

And see Johnson's Est., 5 Erie 200, 37 York 106; Wigington's Est., 28 

Dauph. 317; Braum's Est., 88 Super. 109, aff'g 74 P. L. J. 217. And see id., 86 Super. 246, rev 'g 73 P. L. J. 344; Anderson v. Wilson, 46 Montg. 86.

190. PROCEDURE FOR CONFIRMATION OF AP- PRAISEMENT. 

As in the case of the $500 exemption the details of procedure are governed by rules of court, as the act pro vides: 

60 Intestate Act of 1917, (P. L. 429) Sec. 2 (b), which is founded on the Act of April 1, 1909, (P. L. 87) 5 Purd. 6476, as amended by the Act of July 21, 1913, (P. L. 875) 5 Purd. 6478 (see also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 

20 Sec. 12), further amended so as to provide for the appointment by the orphans' court of two appraisers, for the swearing and affirming of such appraisers, and for their compensation.

In proposing this clause, the Commissioners of 1915, in their report, said: "The Commissioners have concluded that the appraisement of the property chosen by the surviving spouse to be awarded under this act should be made by appraisers appointed by the court rather than by the appraisers of the "other personal estate, as is now the law. In many cases, where real estate is selected, the regular appraisers are not necessarily qualified to value it, and as the rights of the heirs are involved, it seems best that the appraisers should be formally appointed. 

"In this and other clauses of the act relating to this special allowance, the Commissioners have avoided any reference to the procedure under prior acts of assembly relating to the widow's exemption, which introduced a needless complication in the Act of April 1, 1909."' 

See Desmond's Est., 28 Dist. 231, 36 Lanc. 217, 8 Leh. 255.

The collateral heirs cannot control in their own interest the election of a spouse to take certain property for his or her special allowance of $5,000. 

No appeal is given from the report of the appraisers fixing the value of the property from which a spouse elects to take his or her special allowance, and in the absence of fraud or collusion or such clear undervaluation of the property as may suggest fraud or collusion, the valuation fixed by the appraisers will not be interfered with. 

The mere fact that one of two appraisers was a second cousin of the widow is not ground for setting the appraisement aside. Troutman's Est., 30 Dist. 708, rel'g on Vandevort's App., 43 Pa. 462. And see Craig's Est., 30 Dauph. 273. 

In the absence of fraud or collusion, the value placed upon real estate by appraisers, appointed by the court to set aside the $5,000 allowance of a surviving spouse, will not be interfered with, and no such fraud is shown where exceptant's witness differs but little in his valuation from that fixed by the appraisers. Roop's Est., 15 D. & C. 752.

An intending husband. knowing what he is doing, who freely executes an antenuptial agreement which declares that he has full knowledge of the property and estate of his deceased spouse, cannot, in the absence of fraud or overreaching, repudiate his agreement after her death, and claim that which, by the agreement, he declared he would not claim. 

Each antenuptial contest is in some respects unique. In each, all of the relevant facts must be grouped together, and, when so grouped and considered, the court must determine whether or not the party objecting has a just right to complain.

Antenuptial agreements are not inherently nor presumptively fraudulent. They require good faith, but fraud is not presumed in them any more than in other matters. There must be some evidence of gross disproportion or other fact from which fraud may be inferred before the onus changes.

§ 196 

such acts as would deprive the spouse of his or her rights under the Intestate Act.8 83 The law does not regard with disfavor an antenuptial contract especially where the parties to it are advanced in years and have separate estates. 

If there is no evidence of what took place at the execution of a written agreement, which one of the parties to it seeks to set aside, the law presumes that there was no designed concealment or imposition. 

If an antenuptial agreement was fairly and openly made, it is not necessary that it should be shown that the party afterwards seeking to set it aside, was told of the exact means of the other. It suffices that the latter should have known that the former was in comfortable circumstances. 

If an elderly woman marrying an elderly man is provided, after his death, with a comfortable support, she has no just cause of complaint. 

The true test of the adequacy of the consideration in an antenuptial agreement is whether the provision for the intended wife is sufficient to enable her to live comfortably after his death, in substantially the same way, as, under all the circumstances. she had previously lived. 

A complaining party's signature to an agreement which states that he knew its contents, is affirmative proof that he was not deceived when he signed it.

If one who signs a paper can read and write, and is under no duress when he signs it, the law presumes that, under such circumstances, it was signed with full knowledge of its contents. McCready's Est., 316 Pa. 246, aff 'g 82

An election by a widow to take against the will affects her interest and the result is as though there had been no will in so far as she is concerned. 

The Wills Act and the Intestate Act do not contemplate a one-half interest to the surviving spouse in what may be left after payment of amounts of annuities and legacies provided in the testator's will, but a one-half interest in the estate without deducting annuities or legacies, or amounts for specified purposes.

The widow's election destroys the provisions of the will made for her. 

Testator's intent, plan or scheme relating to her cannot be carried out, but that does not render inoperative the other provisions of the will; the intent must be observed as far as possible. Carter's Est., 5 Erie 235. 

As to the acceleration of interests in remainder, see Loew's Est., 291 Pa.

Where land is devised to an heir, subject to the payment of a legacy of one thousand dollars to another heir, the legacy is not affected by the election of the husband of the decedent to take against the will. The taking of one-third of the land under his election, under such circumstances, and the devisee of the land fails to pay the legacy, his interest in the land must be sold for the payment thereof. Janes' Est., 14 Erie 237.

Where a widow elects to take against a will, under which she is the beneficiary of a life interest in a trust estate, the remainder interests will be accelerated, even though not vested but contingent upon the remaindermen surviving the widow, if her life estate is a mere obstacle to possession by the remaindermen; but if it was used as a means of preserving the interests of some third person, other than the widow or remaindermen, the remainders will not be accelerated.

Where a testator bequeaths his estate in trust for his wife and daughter for life and upon the death of either to pay the entire income to the survivor, and provides that 1 year after the death of the wife, the daughter is to receive a certain share of the principal, if she survives, but, if she should die before then, it is to go to her son, and the widow elects to take against the will, the daughter is entitled to receive the share of principal 

1 year after the widow's election, for the testator's intention seems to have been that his daughter should come into possession of the share of principal 1 year after she began to be the sole recipient of the income rather than that that period was intended to mark her arrival at years of discretion. After the said election shall have been recorded in the office for the recording of deeds, as aforesaid, the said election, at the cost of the estate, shall be filed in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court and a record made of such filing by the said clerk.10 In cases where the decedent died possessed of personal property only, the election by a surviving spouse, or a certified copy of the final decree of any orphans' court in cases where there shall have been an election in accordance with clause (d) hereof, or a neglect or refusal to elect within the time prescribed by the order of the said court, shall, at the cost of the estate, be filed in the office of the clerk of the orphans' court, and a record made of such filing by the said clerk."'11

203. PROCEDURE WHERE BENEFICIARY CANNOT 

BE FOUND. 

Adequate provision is made where a person to whom any charge on land is payable cannot be found: "In all cases in which, under any proceeding in any orphans' court of this commonwealth, or by any last will and testament, or by the provisions of this act, any dower, legacy, recognizance or other charge shall have been imposed upon land, or any part thereof, and such charge is due and payable, and the person or persons to whom such payment is due cannot be found after diligent and reasonable search, it shall be lawful for the owner of the land charged to apply by petition 23 to the orphans' court of the county where said land is situated, or, in case said land is divided by a county line, to the orphans' court of the county where the mansion house may be situated, or, if there be no mansion house, in the county where the principal improvements may be, or, if there be no improvements, in either county, setting forth the circumstances of the case, the name or names of the person or persons to whom such payment is due or the fact that such names are unknown, and the time when such legacy or charge, or any part thereof, became due and payable, and a description of the land subject to the charge. Thereupon said court shall make an order directing such petitioner to give public notice 24 of the facts set forth in such petition, by publication once a week for four successive weeks in one or more newspapers published within or nearest to said county or within or nearest to each of said counties, requiring the person or persons to whom such legacy or charge, or any part thereof, is due and payable, or who wish to lay claim to the moneys as aforesaid, to appear in court on a day designated, not less than twenty days after the last publication of said notice, and show cause why the amount

§ 481 

DISTRIBUTION 205. PROCEDURE UPON PAYMENT, OR PRESUMP- TION OF PAYMENT, OF CHARGE. 

Substantially similar procedure is followed where the charge has actually been paid or, by lapse of time, payment is presumed: "In all cases in which, under any proceeding in any orphans' court of this commonwealth, or by any last will and testament, or by the provisions of this act, any dower, legacy, recognizance, or other charge shall have been imposed upon land, payable presently or at a future time, and such charge shall have been paid, or a period of twenty years shall have elapsed after the principal of such charge has become due and payable and no payment shall have been made within such period on account of such charge by the owner or owners of the land, and no sufficient satisfaction, release, acquittance or acknowledgment of payment thereof shall be of record in the county in which the land is situated, it shall be lawful for the orphans' court of said county, or, in case said land is divided by a county line, then the orphans' court of the county where the mansion house may be situated, or, if there be no mansion house, in the county where the principal improvements may be, or, if there be no improvements, in either county, to entertain a petition for the discharge of said land from the lien of said charge." 28 

28 Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. L. 447) Sec. 27, (b), 1 which is the first part of Sec. 1 of the Act of May 8, 1895, (P. L. 44) 4 Purd. 4047 (z, a-b), 6 Purd 7285 (see also Purd. Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 693), altered so as to apply only to charges enforceable in the orphans' court. The section formerly included encumbrances and charges enforceable in the common pleas.

This part of the section has been modified so as to include legacies and other charges, and thus supply Sec. 1 of the Act of June 8, 1893 (P. L. 356), 4 Purd. 4046 (x-y). The period has been made twenty years, which is the ordinary period for presumption of payment, instead of twenty-one years. 

The section in the Act of 1895 is very long and consists of one sentence. 

It is here subdivided for the sake of clearness.

The rule that after the lapse of twenty years debts of every kind are presumed to be paid is a rule of convenience and policy, resulting from a necessary regard for the peace and security of society, and also for the debtor, who should not be called upon to defend stale claims at a time when witnesses are dead and papers are lost or destroyed. 

This presumption does not bar the debt, it is merely a rule of evidence affecting the burden of proof.

Within twenty years the onus of proving payment lies on the debtor; after that time it devolves on the creditor to show the contrary by such

§ 205 

"Such petition shall be presented by the owner or owners of said land or any part thereof, shall be duly verified by affidavit, and shall set forth the facts and allege that said charge has been paid or that no payment of principal or interest has been made within said period of twenty years on account of said charge by the present owner or owners, or, so far as can be ascertained, by his or their predecessors in title, and shall state the names of all known parties interested in such charge, their places of residence, if known, and a description of the lands subject to the charge and sought to be released and discharged.'' 29 facts and circumstances as will satisfy the minds of the jury that there were other reasons for the delay of the prosecution of the claim than the alleged payment.

The presumption does not arise where there is affirmative proof beyond that furnished by the specialty itself that the debt has not been paid, nor where there are circumstances that sufficiently account for the delay of the creditor.

Where land was sold pursuant to directions contained in the owner's will subject to a dower charge during the lifetime of the testator's widow; and after the widow's decease the land was levied upon under executions on judgments against the then owner, the owner later having made an assignment for the benefit of his creditors, and the executions were stayed by the court in proceedings in the assigned estate and the real estate was sold under the order of the Court of Common Pleas and, twenty-three years after the death of the widow, the owner of the land presented a petition under the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, praying for the discharge of the land from the lien of the dower charge, and in the proceedings on the petition and answer averring non-payment of the dower charge and interest, there was no evidence to account for the delay in the prosecution of the claim on the dower charge, nor that it was owing within twenty years of the presentation of the petition; the court made an order discharging the lien of the dower charge. Kohler's Petition, 48 York 173.

Payment of a legacy charged upon land will be presumed, at the expiration of twenty years, if no demand for payment was made for twenty years after the legacy became payable.

A petition to discharge the lien of a legacy upon land, under Sec. 27 of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, (P. L. 447) can be granted only where petitioner shows payment of the legacy or such circumstances as give rise to a presumption of payment. Lightcap v. Swan, 13 D. & C. 737.

Where, on a petition under this section of the Fiduciaries Act, for the discharge of land from a dower fund, the weight of the evidence showed that the fund in question was paid to the parties thereto entitled more than twenty-eight years before the hearing of the case, and in the opinion of the court was sufficient to establish this fact, a decree discharging the land from the fund was entered. Harbold's Est., 34 York 149.

The devise of a "house," when referring to the dwelling house of the owner, has been held the equivalent to the word "messuage," and in the absence of some term or clause restrictive of its meaning, it is said to convey the lot on which the dwelling is situate together with the outbuildings customarily used by the owner as a part of the residence. 

The actual state of the property disposed of leads us to the conclusion that the intention of the testatrix at the time of making her will was not to separate it, and the words of a will should be construed so as to give effect not to their conventional meaning, but to the actual intent of the testator. CHAPTER XXXV. 

LEGACIES, LIFE INTERESTS AND ANNUITIES. 

GENERAL PROVISIONS. 

It is no part of this present work to consider in detail the subject of legacies and devises as set forth in the 

Wills Act 52 or the reported cases.

As a practical matter, however, in distribution, certain provisions of the law will be referred to in passing. 

In the absence of a contrary provision in the will: "If, after deducting the amount of debts of the testator and the expenses of administration, the residue shall not be sufficient to discharge all the pecuniary legacies bequeathed, an abatement shall be made, in proportion to the legacies so given." 53 

52 Of 1917, (P. L. 403).

When the estate of a testator is insufficient to pay both debts and legacies, it is the rule that general legacies abate proportionally to an amount sufficient to pay the debts. If the general legacies are exhausted before the debts are paid, then, the specific legacies abate and proportionally: 

Armstrong's App., 63 Pa. 312. Demonstrative legacies are specific bequests of personalty payable out of a particular fund set apart for that purpose: 

Grim's App., 89 Pa. 335. . . This section of the Act of 1834 is merely declaratory of the rule recognized at common law: Pennsylvania Company's 

App., 16 W. N. C. 170. The priority of some general legacies over others, however, is not to be presumed, but must be established either by the express language of the will or by a fair construction thereof: Waln's Est., 109 Pa. 479. Specific legacies charged on land are not abated pro tanto by a sale of part of the real estate: McDowell's Est., 3 Dist. 271. A testamentary charge of debts and legacies cannot effect the right of priority over legacies given to debts by this act: Blake's Est., 134 Pa. 240. A legacy charged with the payment of debts is general and abatable: Ingersoll's Est., 3 Dist. 399; Loomis' App., 10 Pa. 387.

Where an estate of a testator is insufficient to pay legacies in full, and also to provide for annuities to his only blood kin, and it appears from the will as a whole that his blood kin were the objects of his first consideration, the whole estate or so much of it as may be necessary will be set aside to pay the annuities. Elmore's Est., 292 Pa. 571, 490

In general, when personal property is bequeathed to any person for life, etc., the latter is allowed two alternatives, either receive it himself and give bond to protect the remaindermen or he may have a trustee appointed. 

If he takes possession of the assets and gives bond, he is in the position of debtor, for the amount involved, but if a trustee is appointed, the trustee's responsibility is only that of any other general trustee for all the parties in interest.

In the present case, however, the life tenant was the surviving executor and testamentary trustee of his father's estate and the award at the audit of that estate was made to him as surviving executor, conditioned upon his filing proper bond, the requirement of the bond being for additional protection to the remaindermen, he being also the life tenant. The effect of the father's will was to make him a trustee, and there is no legal objection to his acting in that capacity although himself a beneficiary. Therefore, his being named as a trustee by the testator takes the case out of the rule which places a life tenant in the position of a debtor to the remaindermen, and his liability is only that of an ordinary trustee. Griffith's Est., 16 

Wash. 56, 26 D. & C. 75.

§ 215 

 215. PROCEDURE TO ENFORCE PAYMENT LEGACIES, ETC., CHARGED ON LAND. 

OF To enforce the collection of legacies, etc., charged on land the procedure is similar to that for the sale of real estate for the payment of debts: "1. In all cases in which, by the provisions of any last will and testament, or by the provisions of this act, or by proceedings in the orphans' court in any county, any legacy or any money payable at a future period, or any money the interest on which is payable to any person, is or shall be hereafter charged upon, or payable out of real estate, it shall be lawful for the legatee or the person entitled to such money or interest to apply by petition" to the orphans' court having jurisdiction of the accounts of the fiduciary. On the presentation of such petition, the court, having caused due notice" to be given to such fiduciary, and the devisee or heir, as the case may be, and the present owner, of the real estate charged with such legacy, sum of money or interest, and to such persons interested in the estate or property as justice may require, may proceed according to equity to make a decrees directing such devisee, heir or owner to pay the amount of such legacy, sum of money or interest then due, within a time to be limited by such decree, and providing that in case such devisee, heir or owner shall fail to make payment within such time, the fiduciary, or a trustee to be appointed by said court, in its discretion, shall, after giving public notice of such sale, once a week for a period of three weeks before the day appointed therefor, by advertisement, in at least one newspaper published in the county if there be one, or, if there be none, then in an adjoining county, and by handbills posted at a conspicuous place on the real estate proposed to be sold," and in at least three of the most public places in the vicinity of such estate, make sale of said real estate or so much thereof as may be necessary, for the purpose of payment of such legacy, sum of money or interest. The proceeds of such sale shall be distributed, under the direction of said court, as in other cases of judicial sales, to the persons legally entitled to receive the same. In the

Where a testator bequeaths a farm to one son subject to a dower charge in a specified amount on which interest is to be paid annually to another son, the principal amount of the charge to be paid to said son's heirs upon his death, a subsequent grantee of such real estate is not personally liable for the dower charge or interest thereon, by reason of the Act of June 12, 1878, (P. L. 205) sec. 1, unless he has expressly assumed liability therefor, but payment of the principal amount of the charge and interest accruing thereon during the period the grantee has owned the land, may be enforced by execution against the land in accordance with the provisions of section 

25(a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, McFarlan's Est., 30 D. & C. 584, q. v.

A citation to executors to file an account is not the proper remedy to collect a pecuniary legacy charged on real estate where the account of the personal property has been confirmed absolutely, and there is no allegation and proof of fraud, and five years have elapsed since the final confirmation. 

The Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403, section 17, provides that pecuniary legacies shall be charged upon, and payable out of any real estate not specifically devised where the personal estate is insufficient for their payment, unless a contrary intent appears by the will, and sections 24 and 25 (of the Fiduciaries Act) provide the proper remedy for the collection of legacies charged on real estate. Goldsmith's Est., 25 North. 213.

Where, under Sec. 25 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, there is a proceeding to enforce the payment of a pecuniary bequest out of real estate, and the devisees have failed to pay and discharge its lien on the property, which accordingly was sold by a trustee appointed for that purpose, and where one of the devisees is indebted to the decedent in a larger amount than his share of the estate, the orphans' court has power, under said Sec. 25 and 

Sec. 9, clauses (e) and (n) of the Orphans' Court Act of 1917, to charge such indebtedness against the debtor's share of the proceeds. Hinterleiter's 

Est., 13 Leh. 144, and cases there cited.

A petition to sell real estate of a decedent for the payment of legacies will not be denied on the ground that no account of the estate has yet been filed, where the answer admits the filing of an inventory and appraisement which shows that the personalty will be insufficient to pay the pecuniary legacies. 

A devise of real estate in trust, contained in the residuary clause of decedent's will, is general rather than specific, although decedent owned only one piece of real estate, and the property so devised is subject to sale for the payment of pecuniary legacies.

Where a testator directed that a certain annuity be paid out of the income from a business, and upon the audit of the executors' account the business was awarded to a trustee for this sole purpose and all other assets were regularly awarded and distributed, and many years later, upon audit of the trustee's account, a claim for unpaid instalments of the annuity was refused as to instalments accruing when the business was operating at a loss on the ground that the annuity was payable solely out of the income from the business, and the adjudication was confirmed absolutely on this point and no appeal was taken, the representatives of the annuitant are without standing to seek, by an amended petition under section 25 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act, to charge real estate formerly owned by the decedent with payment of the annuity.

The inability of a trustee to pay a surcharge imposed upon him for failure to pay certain instalments of an annuity payable out of the income from a business, in no way enlarges the rights of the annuitant or enables him to proceed against other property of the donor of the annuity, his only right of action being against the trustee individually. Dahm's Est., 23 D. & C.

220. PROCEDURE FOR THE REDUCTION OF THE FUND SET APART. 

It sometimes occurs that by the death of one or more annuitants or great increase in the value of the corpus. of the fund, the latter will exceed in size that necessary for the proper protection of the parties, so that a portion can be released for the benefit of others in interest. 

In such case: "Upon the application of any person interested in any residuary estate, set apart as aforesaid, setting forth that, by reason of the decease of any such annuitant, or by the happening of any other event, the charge of any annuity or legacy as aforesaid has become extinguished, in fact or law, it shall be lawful for the said court, from time to time, after due notice and inquiry into the facts, to make an order and decree for the exoneration and discharge of such part or portion or so much of the real estate, securities and investments, so set apart and appropriated, as may appear to such court to be beyond the amount requisite or proper for the purpose of providing a sufficient continuing security for the payment of the remaining annuities and legacies. Every such order or decree shall have the same force and effect in respect to the real estate, securities and investments, therein and thereby exonerated and discharged, as is declared in clause (d) of this section, in respect to the residuary estate not specifically set apart and appropriated. An appeal from the entry of or refusal to enter such order judgment determining the amount which should be set aside to secure the payment of an annuity created by the will, the orphans' court having exclusive jurisdiction of the subject. Hirst's Est., 13 D. & C. 683.

Where a testator establishes trusts in which it is clearly set forth that certain annuities are to be paid monthly, the trustee should pay the same out of either principal or income available in its hands. 

In such a case, when the investments in the hands of the substituted trustee are of such a character that it is impossible for it to liquidate or borrow money on them, the Orphans' Court will order it to pay the annuitants all of the accumulated annuities as soon as available funds come into its hands. Janson's Est., 46 Lanc. 35.

223. DECREE ON CITATION TO ACCEPT OR RE- 

FUSE. "Upon the return and confirmation of such appraisement, the court shall issue its citation to the person or persons entitled to take such real estate on compliance with the terms of the will, to appear at a time fixed by said court to accept or refuse the same. If, upon the return of such citation, duly served, such person or persons shall appear and accept such real estate at the appraisement, and shall pay or secure the payment of the amount thereof at such time and upon such terms as shall be fixed by said court, then the court shall adjudge such real estate to such person or persons. If such person or persons shall fail or neglect to appear and accept such real estate at the appraisement or shall refuse to accept it, or, having accepted, shall fail to pay or secure the amount of such appraisement as aforesaid, then the court shall adjudge such real estate to the person or persons entitled thereto under the provisions of the will in the event of such real estate not being taken at the appraisement directed by the testator, or, if the will contains no provision for such event, then the court shall adjudge such real estate to the persons legally entitled thereto. 

Any such decree may be recorded in the deed book in the office for recording deeds of any county in which such real estate is situated, with the same effect as deeds are recorded, and shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantors' index under the name of the decedent, and in the grantees' index under the name or names of the person or persons accepting such real estate at the appraisement, or of the person or persons entitled thereto in the event of such real estate not being taken at the appraisement, or of the person or persons legally entitled thereto where the will contains no provision for a failure to take at the appraisement, as the case may be, and shall be registered in the survey bureau, or with the proper authorities empowered by law to keep a register of real estate, if any there be, in said county, and the charges for 

99 See Form No. 193, App., p. 215.

§ 223 

recording and registering shall be the same as are provided by law for similar services." 1

At the same time the draft of the decree of confirmation is submitted to the court as is set forth in the preceding paragraph, there may also be then submitted the decree for citation to accept or refuse. Assuming that the respondent desires to accept the real estate at its appraised value, thus ascertained, he should file his acceptance with the clerk of the court on or before the return day whereupon a decree will be entered awarding it to him, a certified copy of which should be recorded as above outlined. 

Of course if the respondent for any reason refuses to accept the said premises at their appraised value as aforesaid, because, for instance, in his opinion, the value thus fixed is more than the market value of the said premises, upon the certification of these facts to the court a decree will be entered similar to the foregoing but awarding and adjudging the property to the residuary devisee instead of to the respondent.

As to the effect of decrees under the procedure here involved, it has been enacted: "Whenever any orphans' court shall have heretofore made a decree adjudging real estate to certain persons, in any case mentioned and provided for in clauses (e) and (f) of this section, such decree shall be valid and available to vest in the person or persons to whom such real estate was adjudged, all the right, title and interest of the testator who had died, leaving a will wherein the right to accept such real estate was given. 995

CHAPTER XXXVII. 

GUARDIANS. 

NATURE OF GUARDIANSHIP. 

A minor being under our law incapable of holding and dealing in property in his own right is peculiarly within the protection of the orphans' court in its jurisdiction over his person and estate and the appointment of a guardian therefor and the control, removal and discharge of such guardian and the settlement of his accounts.8 

The father is the natural guardian or guardian by nature of his minor children, or if he be deceased or have deserted his family, the mother.10 Neither can act as such however, by appointment, under the statute.¹¹ Guardians of the person or estate may be appointed by will in certain cases 12 and also under decree of the orphans' court,13 and the latter may also under certain circumstances appoint guardians ad litem.¹*

Stat. Ann. Tit. 20, Sec. 1024). The Commissioners of 1915, in their report advocating this section said:

This is a new section, framed in part in accordance with the existing practice in many counties. The Commissioners regard it as always inadvisable and frequently dangerous to appoint the parent of a minor to be the guardian of its estate. Parents are too often tempted to regard the estate as virtually their own and use it for purposes which could not be approved by the court; or even when actuated by proper motives will not keep the accurate accounts of the estate which the minor on coming of age is entitled to receive. The consequence may be either an unfortunate and distressing litigation, or perhaps the condonation of an injustice.

Also, in Philadelphia County at least, the appointment of a guardian may be avoided, where the fund is too small for investment, and is not needed for maintenance, by a deposit in a saving fund account in the minor's own name.
