As to the residence of guardians, rarely indeed will one not residing in Pennsylvania be appointed guardian for a minor resident in this state and except for very special reasons the court will not appoint a person guardian who is not a resident of the county in which the appointment is to be made.42 This, of course, does not apply to a guardian ad litem, as very frequently the very nature of the case requiring the appointment necessitates one resident in the jurisdiction where the litigation is in progress as being most familiar therewith and in closer touch with the matter in controversy.

Where an accountant admits that he knew certain investments of trust funds were improper, but paid the losses incurred "out of his own pocket" for the consequences of the unlawful investment, that is all the law requires. 

It is where a loss occurs by reason of improper investment that a surcharge should be imposed to replace the amount lost. The accountant is, however, liable for a fair return on the money which should have been kept invested and was not.

A guardian will not be surcharged for investing in a $400 mortgage on a low class dwelling house which was appraised by a real estate expert at $1,500 and assessed for taxation at $1,300, and which was producing a monthly rental of $18, although it later proves to be of a substantially lower principal value.

The primary purpose of appointing a guardian for a minor is to preserve the latter's estate, protecting it even from the minor until he becomes of age, and then to turn it over to him, but the ward should not be allowed to continue in penury and want during minority to the end that he may have more when he becomes of age; on the contrary, the guardian should see that the ward receives not only necessaries to the preservation of health but education and training for the future, and recreation and enjoyment reasonable in view of his associations and the amount of the estate.59

CHAPTER XXXVIII. 

TRUSTEES. 

237. TESTAMENTARY TRUSTEES. 

The class of trustees which is by far the most numerous is embodied under this designation; that is, trustees by appointment under the will of a decedent.

It very frequently happens that a testator will desire a specific portion of his property or his residuary estate not to be distributed outright, but to be held in trust for some specific purpose, such as to pay the income to his wife for life, with ultimate distribution among his children or a trust for the benefit of his children during their minority, or in the form of a spendthrift trust to protect the beneficiaries against the claims of creditors. 

It is almost impossible to foresee any limit to which the forms of such trusts may adapt themselves, and therefore no attempt has been made to set them forth herein. 

Upon the audit of the executor's account the award of a specific fund or the residuary estate will be to the trustee as nominated in the will, and thereafter the trust fund must be administered by such trustee in accordance with the terms of the trust, and here also the rights, duties and liabilites of the trustee should be set forth clearly in the will itself, as otherwise they will be strictly limited by the statute.

When the same individual is an executor of a will and also a trustee of a fund arising out of the estate of the testator, and receives money in contemplation of law as a trustee, it is demandable of him in no other character.18 

18 When the same person is named as executor and also as trustee in a will by which certain trusts are created, he does not lose his distinctive character as executor and also as trustee, and when, in the course of the administration of the estate, the duties of the representative as an executor have been performed in administering the personal property, then his duties and responsibilities as a trustee begin, and it is proper practice to first file his account as executor and then by petition apply for a rule to show cause why the unadministered assets of the estate, subject to the several trusts mentioned in the will, should not be held by him in his capacity as trustee. 

An executor as such is primarily restricted in his administration to the personal estate of a decedent, and if also a trustee under the terms of the 547

§§ 237, 237a  

If such trustee be a resident of the state, even though not of the county, he need not enter security. "Any fiduciary appointed by any orphans' court of this commonwealth or by virtue of any last will and testament, probated within this commonwealth, may, if resident within this commonwealth, lawfully execute the duties of his trust, whether or not he is a resident of the county in which the trust was created, or in which the decedent had his domicile. "' 19

Such trustees have the usual duties of their office 20 as changed, modified or enlarged by the express terms of the will. If the latter be well drawn it will carefully define their rights and powers to conform not only to the nature of the estate but to the wishes of the testator and its terms should be carefully considered by the trustee in his every act in connection with the management of the estate.

When one deals with a trustee, or agent, it is his duty to look at the nature and extent of his authority. If an investigation or inquiry had been made by the mortgagor, or his agent, it could have been readily ascertained that Atkinson was without authority to receive this money, and that the record disclosed that the mortgage was held in the name of trustees. The equities do not favor a mortgagor who was so careless as to pay money without first assuring himself of the authority of the person to whom he made the payment. Corn Exchange N. B. & T. Co. v. Jones, 112 Super. 32.

60 The duties of an executor and trustee are separate and distinct. 

The executor must take charge and make an inventory of the personal estate, collect monies due the estate and pay the decedent's debts and obligations, and make distribution of the balance to the persons entitled thereto, whether heirs, legatees or trustees. Except when necessary to pay decedent's debts, he has nothing to do with the real estate unless so directed by the will. He is appointed by the testator and derives his authority to act from the will.

directions 8sa in the will or deed all the customary expenses of the trust should, of course, be charged against estate forming part of corpus of a trust to pay income to life beneficiaries are, in absence of specific provisions in the terms of the trust, properly chargeable to principal and not to income until the real estate is sold when there shall be a final adjustment between income and principal. The general rule that carrying charges of real estate are payable out of income does not apply to unproductive real estate in a trust to pay income. Such real estate is not a proper investment for such a trust as to the life beneficiaries, but its sale under present market conditions would be improper as to the remaindermen, entailing the sacrifice of an asset of great potential value.

Two of the three trustees under a will filed a petition praying that $10,000 of cash corpus in the trust be allocated to income in place of uncollected mortgage interest and that they be authorized to pay that amount to the widow for her maintenance. The estate amounted to upwards of $900,000, and under the terms of testator's will, the widow was entitled to the income from half of the estate until the year 1937. The estate was almost entirely invested in mortgages, many of which were in default in payment of interest, to a total amount of $22,000, in half of which the widow had a vested interest. The income received by the widow from the trust in the year prior to the application was $2,000. 

The third trustee admitted the facts alleged and joined in the prayer, as did all sui juris heirs and the guardian of a minor heir. A trustee and guardian ad litem appointed by the Court to represent all contingent interests reported after investigation that he favored the relief sought for. 

Held, that the dominant purpose of the trust as gathered from testator's will was to provide inter alia for the maintenance and support of his widow, which was prevented by the economic, financial and industrial depression of the past four years, for which emergency he had not provided. Decree granted, subject to assignment by the widow of her entire interest in the estate and also in a checking and savings account in a closed bank, as security. 243. EXTRAORDINARY DIVIDENDS, ETC. 

For many years, and much more frequently of late, a considerable portion of the assets of decedents' estates has consisted of shares of stock of corporations. By reason of merger or consolidation," or to distribute equitably among its stockholders unnecessary accumulations of profits in surplus or for any other reason deemed fitting by the corporation, extraordinary dividends either in cash or stock (or sometimes in securities in kind") are declared or opportunity given to subscribe to new issues. of stock and the like. 

A fiduciary receiving such extraordinary corporate distributions or rights and having before it the absolute necessity and duty not only of protecting the rights of 95 Rules determining the payment of commissions, attorneys' fees and other expenses out of principal and income are of little value except as applied to the particular facts in connection with which the rule has been enunciated. Whoever has benefited by the trust's administration should pay for it and in the present case the court determined that the attorney's fees should be equally divided between the parties, namely the life tenant and the remandermen, one-half from income and one-half from principal. 

Griffith Est., 16 Wash. 56, 26 D. & C. 75. "So far as deducting commissions from income affects life tenants unfairly, it is a rule of law that the income, and not the principal, of a trust fund must bear the expense of administering it-Butterbaugh's App., 98 Pa. 351; Crawford's Est., 256 Pa. 504. This rule just stated has an exception where unusual or extraordinary expenses are necessarily incurred, for instance, where expensive legal proceedings are necessary not only to collect the interest, but also to preserve the corpus of the estate from actual loss-Davidson's Est., 287 Pa. 354." First Nat. Bk., etc. v. Farmers' 

Trust Co. of Lancaster, 45 Lanc. 229. 

96 Daily's Est., 323 Pa. 42, af'g (but mod 'g) 24 D. & C. 628; Buist's 

Est., 297 Pa. 537, aff'g 12 D. & C. 159.

Where two corporations merge there is a coalescence of physical properties, accounts and assets, and once the rights of the stockholders of each corporation in those assets are determined and the new stock equitably distributed to them, the new stock with its consolidated surplus, as earnings or income, must be treated as any other stock in questions of apportionment. Neafie's Est., 25 D. & C. 608, af'd in 325 Pa. 561. 

97 Waterman's Est., 279 Pa. 491, rev'g. 3 D. & C. 442.

life tenants but of preserving the rights of remaindermen is faced with a difficult problem.

In its solution three rules have been evolved 98: the "Massachusetts" rule, that "all cash dividends are awarded to the life tenant, and all stock dividends to the remaindermen"; the "Kentucky" rule, that "a dividend, whether of stock or cash, goes to the person entitled to receive the income at the time the dividend is declared, without regard to the time when it was earned," and the "Pennsylvania" rule which may be briefly stated as an endeavor, regardless of difficulties involved, to keep intact for the remainderman the value of corpus as it actually existed at the decedent's death or the inception of the trust and to distribute all else as income to the life tenants." This frequently requires an apportionment or allocation of stock 100 and the like between corpus and in- come. 

98 Nirdlinger's Est., 290 Pa. 457, mod 'g. 8 D. & C. 595. 

99 First enunciated over eighty years ago in Earp's App., 28 Pa. 368, applied where stock was sold. 

100 Whatever remains after awarding to the trust estate so much of the proceeds of the property sold as will restore the principal to its original value, must go to the life tenant. Cassatt's Est., 105 Super. 14.

A capital gain in the assets of a corporation from the sale of securities, the increase in the value of which does not represent earnings of the issuing corporations, should be awarded to corpus and not to income. McCahan's 

Est., 18 D. & C. 171.

The legal rights of cumulative preferred stockholders are analogous to those of common stockholders, and dividends on cumulative preferred stock held in trust are, therefore, allocable to income if declared from earnings made subsequent to the creation of the trust, even though the dividends had accrued previously. Crozer's Est., 27 D. & C. 179, 26 Del. 328.

On the declaration of an extraordinary cash or stock dividend of a corporation, during the life tenancy of a trust estate, the rule is to give to the life tenant the income earned since the trust arose, but, at the same time, to preserve intact the corpus as it was at the date of the death of the testator. 

In the modification and change of the capital structure, as to newly issued stock and as to cash, the above stated rule prevails, and, in this case, the entire dividend was awarded to corpus. 

The fact that accrued dividends were due on the preferred stock does not alter the situation. Ormrod Est., 17 Leh. 82, 21 D. & C. 245.

The court, in apportioning the dividend actually received, must consider the whole of the surplus existing at the time the dividend was declared, and not merely so much thereof as was included in the dividend. Mallory's 

Est., 285 Pa. 186, rev'g 7 Erie 62; s. c. 5 Erie 277, 5 D. & C. 333. And under certain conditions gain on sale of capital assets may be included in calculating the apportionment. Chauncey's Est., 303 Pa. 441, aff'g 45 

Montg. 111.

"The value of a trust estate, where its income is paid to life tenants with remainder over, is determined as of the time the testator dies and is called intact value. 244. WASTING INVESTMENTS. 

"A person entitled to the use and income of property for life, or for a time otherwise limited, must provide for repairing the waste of the corpus which comes from its use or from lapse of time. Similarly, a trustee who holds property under directions to pay the income to one person or set of persons for a time must preserve the principal or corpus of the estate intact from the ordinary processes of waste, by deductions from income. This does not mean that the value of the principal fund must always be kept up out of income; that, in a trust estate or life estate, is usually changing, sometimes increasing and sometimes decreasing. Mere decrease in value should not be made up out of income, nor should increase in value be added to income. Loss of principal by unfortunate investment or by misappropriation of the actual corpus must ordinarily be borne by the principal. But whenever a payment to the trustee or life tenant of what is called income reduces the value of the investment, or whenever the value of the investment decreases from mere lapse of time, part of what is received as income should be added to the principal to repair the waste, unless the intention of the creator of the trust estate or the life estate was opposed." 37

In so enacting the jurisdiction of the common pleas was specifically saved "under existing laws in cases of trustees who have filed their accounts in such courts before the approval of this act, and cases of substituted testamentary trustees in the orphans' court of the county where the will is probated, as required by the act: 49 Such an account is exactly similar in form, with, of course, the necessary change in the heading, etc., as that "The first part of this clause is derived from Sec. 1 of the Act of May 

3, 1909, (P. L. 391) 6 Purd. 6565, altered so as to apply only to trustees who are within the scope of the present act, and to provide in what courts the accounts shall be filed. The remainder of the clause is new and is intended to take away the concurrent jurisdiction of courts of common pleas in cases of testamentary trusts in persons named in the will. This jurisdiction as to trusts nominatim was conferred by Sec. 15 of the Act of June 14, 1836, (P. L. 632) 4 Purd. 4880, upon the court of common pleas of the county where the trustee resided at the commencement of the trust, and was held to be concurrent in Brown's App., 12 Pa. 333, although as to trusts virtute officii the jurisdiction of the orphans' court is exclusive:

C. 39, 9 Phila. 14, it was remarked that the safest course was to invoke the aid of the orphans' court in all cases of testamentary trusts. The jurisdiction of the common pleas has been rarely exercised in recent years, and the late decision of the Supreme Court in Simpson's Est., 253 Pa. 217, rev'g 23 Dist. 750, brought the matter to the attention of the

COMBINATION OF TRUSTS. 

Frequently different persons or the same person by different instruments may provide for trusts having identical charitable purposes. As an aid to their efficient management it has been provided: "That whenever two or more trusts for charitable or benevolent purposes have been established, or shall hereafter be established, by the same donor or testator, or by separate donors or testators, and for any cause or reason the income from the trust estates set apart for the purposes of the trusts is insufficient or inadequate to carry out effectively and efficiently the purposes expressed by the donors of the trusts through separate administration of the trusts, and the charitable or benevolent purposes of the trusts are of a nature that they may be more effectively and efficiently carried out if the same are combined, the trustees of the trusts may, in their discretion, join in a petition to the orphans' court having jurisdiction over the accounts of any one of the trustees setting forth such facts, and the court being satisfied with the truth thereof, may order and empower said trustees to carry out the purposes of the trusts by combining the trusts in the manner and to the extent that such court shall approve, provided that such combination shall not be authorized where it would violate any specific provision to the contrary in the will or other instrument creating the trust."' 67 

67 Act of May 4, 1933 (P. L. 271) which took effect immediately.

CHAPTER XXXIX. 

MISCELLANEOUS RIGHTS, POWERS AND LIABILITIES OF FIDUCIARIES. 

247. RIGHT OF ELECTION, PROCEDURE. 

"Whenever, by the provisions of any last will and testament admitted to probate in any county of this commonwealth, any of the real estate of the testator is ordered or directed to be sold and the proceeds therefrom are bequeathed, or are payable or distributable, in whole or in part, to any minor or minors, or cestuis que trust, and it is the desire of all the legatees and beneficiaries interested in said proceeds to elect to take said real estate, in lieu of the several bequests or legacies or interests, it shall be lawful for the orphans' court having jurisdiction of the accounts of the executor of said will, upon the petitions of any fiduciary interested, to authorize and empower said fiduciary, on behalf of his ward or cestuis que trust, to enter into an election in writing, to take said real estate or part thereof in fee, in lieu of the legacy or legacies, interest or interests, bequeathed or payable or distributable as aforesaid, taking and being entitled to an estate in said real estate commensurate with the interest said minor or cestui que trust would have had in the fund derived from the sale of said real estate, if the same had been sold in accordance with the provisions of said will. Such election shall be duly acknowledged and recorded in the deed book in the office of the recorder of deeds for the county in which such real estate is situated, and shall be indexed by the recorder in the grantors' index under the name of the decedent, and in the grantees' index under the name of the ward or cestui que trust, the charges for recording to be the same as are provided by law for similar services, and shall then be filed in the office of the clerk of said orphans' court."' 69

248. VOTING OF CORPORATE STOCK. 

Where a corporation has been organized to carry on the business of a decedent**: "The stock of any such corporation issued to such fiduciaries shall be held by them for the same uses, trusts and persons as the estate and property were held before the organization of such corporation; they shall have the same right and power to vote such stock, subject to the same control by the court, as prescribed by Section 43 of this act regarding shares of stock belonging to the decedent; and they shall have the right to sell such stock under the direction of the court." 75

A petition for the right to sell such stock will be substantially similar to that set forth in the case of the sale of stock distributed in kind.

In voting such stock whether taken on the organization of a corporation after death or owned by the decedent during his lifetime, it is provided that: "Fiduciaries, whether appointed by last will and testament or by decree of the orphans' court, shall have the same right and power, either in person or by proxy, at all corporate meetings, to vote any and all shares of stock, held by them in a fiduciary capacity, in any corporation organized under the laws of this commonwealth, as the deceased, or legal owner thereof had in his lifetime. And where such stock is registered on the books of such corporation in the name of, or has passed by operation of law or by virtue of any last will and testament to more than two fiduciaries, and dispute shall arise among them, the said shares of stock shall be voted by a majority of such fiduciaries, and in such manner and for such purposes as such majority shall authorize, direct or desire the same to be voted. If the number of fiduciaries

Thereupon the court will enter a decree issuing the citation prayed for and upon answer being filed by the respective respondents the matter will be referred to a master to report to the court all the circumstances so that the court may form an opinion as to the manner in which such stock should be voted for the best interest of the parties beneficially interested therein, and enter a decree in accordance therewith. This decree, if no exceptions be filed thereto, or if exceptions are filed and should be subsequently dismissed, will thereafter be binding upon the fiduciaries until the further order of the court. 249.

FIDUCIARIES 250. POWER TO LEASE. 

As distinguished from selling or leasing on ground rent fiduciaries as part of their duty in the management of their trust are empowered to lease real estate so that it will be productive. In fact they would be open to surcharge for a neglect or failure to do so.

Long term leases and mining leases are, however, specifically governed by statutory enactment. As to the former the act provides: "Unless it be otherwise provided by the will, any testamentary trustee shall have power to make a lease of real estate included in the trust for a term not exceeding five years, and any guardian shall have power to make a lease of real estate belonging to his ward for a term not exreeding five years that shall expire before the minor, if living, would attain his majority. If any testamentary trustee or guardian shall deem it advisable to make such lease for a longer period than aforesaid, the orphans' court of the county wherein such real estate shall be situated, on the application of such trustee or guardian, being aided where necessary by the report of a master, may authorize such trustee or guardian to lease such real estate, on such terms and conditions, at such rental, and for such period, as shall appear just and equitable to said court, with the same force and effect as though said lease were made by the beneficial owner or owners and he or they were sui juris and owned the property in fee. In all cases where such application shall be approved by any orphans' court, the court may direct said trustee or guardian, before making such lease, to file his bond in said court, in such sum as the court shall direct, and with good and sufficient corporate security, or with two good and sufficient individual sureties, approved by said court, conditioned for the faithful application or payment by him of all rents to be received under said lease: Provided, That where such trustee or guardian shall be a corporation, duly authorized by law, the court may, in lieu of security as aforesaid, permit such corporation to enter its own bond without surety.' 995 3 Heretofore considered as to executors under Fiduciaries Act of 1917, (P. In recommending this clause, the Commissioners of 1915, in their report, said: "The changes are, to make the section include cases where sale is authorized or directed but no one is designated to make the sale, and cases where the sale is merely for the purpose of distribution. "So far as sales under testamentary powers are concerned, Sec. 19 of the Act of February 24, 1834, (P. L. 70) 1 Purd. 1122 (g-h), providing for payment of purchase money into court, is superseded by the Act of 1911, and is now recommended for repeal."'

This section of the Fiduciaries Act makes no change in the law as it previously existed with respect to the lien of general debts against a decedent's real estate where a discretionary power to sell is given as mentioned in the act.

It was not the intention of this section to change the course of devolution nor to break the current of descent by holding that a conversion took place from the moment of the testator's death, under a mere authority in the will to sell realty.

Nor did it intend to take away from general creditors the land as security for the payment of debts. It still remained such security and the lien of general debts attach thereto, but such debts will be discharged not only by judicial sale, but also by sale under the discretionary power of sale contained in the will. Davidson v. Bright, 267 Pa. 580.

On sale of testator's real estate by his executrix under power conferred by his will, such general lien (a claim in an equitable proceeding for a personal accounting, pending against a testator at the date of his death) would be divested by operation of Section 30 of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, which in terms relieves the purchaser from the necessity of looking to the proper application of the purchase money when the sale is made under a testamentary power. Copeland v. Hurovitz, 28 

Lack. 198.

While prior to the effective date of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, section 30, which provides that a purchaser from an executor takes real estate free and discharged of any obligation to see to the application of the purchase money, it was undoubtedly true that an executor under a will which did not effect a conversion could not give a clear title to the real estate since it had become charged with the lien of the decedent's debts, nevertheless if the conversion was actually effected by a sale by the executor, which was ratified and confirmed by all legatees and devisees by their acceptance of the proceeds, and there were in fact no unpaid creditors, the purchasers of such property have a good title. 

Even though an executor may not have given good title in conveying real estate of a decedent, nevertheless if the purchaser and his successors in title continue in possession of the premises after the sale, they may acquire good title by adverse possession. Brinkerhoff v. Martin, 28 D. & C. 227. 

When the purpose of a testamentary power of sale has been accomplished, it is well established law that the power fails. It is necessary, in the interpretation of the will, in each case to ascertain judicially from the will itself, precisely what purpose the testator had in mind when he created the

A recent Legislature, in an endeavor to make uniform with other states the rights and liabilities of innocent third parties in dealing with a fiduciary in various capacities, has now provided by Act of Assembly" that all persons dealing in any manner in good faith 18 with any fiduciary¹º are protected against all liability unless they have "actual knowledge that the fiduciary is committing a breach of his obligation" or have "knowledge of such facts that his action" in the premises "amounts to bad faith." 253. LIABILITY FOR INTEREST. 

Fiduciaries should in all cases distribute to the parties entitled as soon as it is legally practicable to do so and cash in hand of any substantial amount if such distribution be postponed for any considerable time for proper cause, should be invested in readily negotiable legal investments. Failure to observe this rule will result in surcharge of legal interest, as it is provided: "No executor or administrator shall be liable to pay interest but for the surplusage of the estate remaining in his hands or power when his accounts are or ought to be filed: Provided, That nothing herein contained shall be construed to exempt an executor or administrator from liability to pay interest, where he may have made use of the funds of the estate for his own purposes. 20 The cases are not uniform however as to when such interest will be charged." 21 

It is further provided: "The amount of interest to be paid in all cases by fiduciaries shall be determined by the orphans' court, under all the circumstances of the case, but shall not, in any instance, exceed the legal rate of interest for the time being." 22

2. THE CONSTITUTION 

Prior to 1873,5¹ there was no constitutional provision in Pennsylvania relating to the investment of trust funds. 

To stem the tide of legislation broadening the scope of legal investments it was provided in the Constitution of 

1873, as Article III, Section 22, as follows: 

"No act of the general assembly shall authorize the investment of trust funds by executors, administrators, guardians or other trustees, in the bonds or stocks 52 of 49 The Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, as amended by the Act of June 

29, 1923, P. L. 955, which provides that a fiduciary may invest in bonds of one or more individuals secured by mortgage on real estate in this Commonwealth, which may be either a single bond secured by a mortgage or one or more bonds of an issue of bonds secured by mortgage or deed of trust to a trustee for the benefit of all bondholders, is not mandatory or exclusive, but provides that the fiduciary may invest as indicated to escape liability. 

An investment in securities not of a class expressly authorized by the acts of assembly is not prohibited nor made unlawful. "The law, however, does not forbid or make unlawful an investment in securities not of a class expressly authorized by the acts of assembly; 

Darlington's Est., 245 Pa. 212, 217." Gibson's Est., 312 Pa. 359. 

50 Bok, J. in Carwithen's Est., 28 D. & C. 66, 73.

Where an investment is challenged, the burden of showing that it was legal and prudently made falls on the fiduciary. Grammes' Est., 16 Sch. 297. 

A trustee has no power to invest trust funds in the stocks or bonds of private corporations, and, if he does so, it must be at his own risk, even though acting in good faith and exercising sound discretion. Taylor's Est., 277 Pa. 518; Frazier's Est., 74 P. L. J. 517.

These acts were intended primarily to permit small amounts in estates to be invested in mortgages, though it may incidentally also permit a spread of risk of loss over several mortgages: it therefore applies to cases where interests in a single mortgage have been assigned to various cestuis que trustent as well as to general trust funds of mortgages. Blair v. Pa. Co., 24 D. & C. 490. 

Their purpose was to permit investment of odd amounts in mortgage securities, and at the same time to spread the risk of unwise selection by giving even a small estate an opportunity to own an interest in a number of mortgages. But the Act of 1925 did not fundamentally change the nature of the investment. An estate buying a participation in a trust fund of mortgages does not become the owner of any particular mortgage, but it does become the owner of an undivided interest in all the mortgages. 

Every gain or loss of principal is shared pro rata by all the participants. 

A participant is not entitled to receive back the amount invested, but is entitled to its pro rata share of the entire fund. A participant is not entitled to interest at any fixed rate, but to its pro rata share of all interest received by the fund." Manayunk Trust Co. No. 2, 21 D. & C. 405.

There was no principal of law which could be enforced against the operation of a pool prior to that date so long as there was no fraud or negligence in the formation and management of the pool. Harton's Est. (No. 1), 86 P. L. J. 13.

Where there is no suggestion that investments in a mortgage pool made by a trustee are not good, and that a loss is probable, a trustee who, under normal financial conditions, could, in a reasonable time, liquidate the investments and dispose of the mortgages will not, under an abnormal economic depression, be required to pay the fund in cash on termination of the trust, but will be permitted to give participating certificates instead, these participating certificates to show the interest of the beneficiary in the installment mortgage fund or pool.

A trust company which invested trust funds in participation in a mortgage pool, which is now closed, the participation having no present market value, will not be surcharged and compelled to assume the investment at its original cost, because such investment was authorized by the Act of April 

6, 1925, P. L. 152.

The Act of 1925 authorizes trust companies to invest its trust funds in mortgage pools, and in so doing is not unconstitutional by reason of its title failing to give notice that it deals with the subject of legal investments.

Nor will an individual cotrustee of the trust company be surcharged on the ground that the Act of 1925 authorized such investments by trust companies only, and not by individuals, where the trust company was the active trustee and actually made the investment, and the individual trustee was inactive. 

Such investment is also authorized by Sec. 41 (a) 1 of the Fiduciaries 

Act of 1917, as amended by the Act of April 26, 1929. Although the investment was made before the amendment of 1929, no loss was sustained until thereafter, and no surcharge can be imposed because the investment was legal when the loss was sustained and the trustee relieved from liability by Sec. 41 (a) 3 of the Fiduciaries Act. Iredell's Est., 51 Montg. 174.

(" A provision in an instrument creating a trust inter vivos, providing that the corpus is to be invested "in good interest-bearing securities, which may be readily converted into cash, "' does not make the trustee an insurer of the funds but only requires it to place the trust funds in such investments.

86 Taylor's Est., 277 Pa. 518, rel'g on Barker's Est., 159 Pa. 518. The act refers to "reasonable diligence. (Sec. 165, supra.) 

It is a trustee's duty, upon receiving investments made by his settlor, to inform himself immediately concerning the nature of each item and the outlook for the future and to use his best judgment, after obtaining adequate information, as to whether to sell it or keep it; if he does so, and repeats the process at reasonable intervals of time, he is not liable to surcharge for failing to guess correctly as to the future of the investment. Ingram's Est., 30 D. & C. 400.

While there is no absolute duty upon an executor to convert investments made by his decedent in nonlegal securities within six months after the grant of letters, he should not, unless especially authorized to do so, hold such investments beyond a reasonable period; if he does so and a loss occurs, he must be held liable for failure to exercise due care, unless he shows that his retention of the securities in question represents not a mere lack of attention but an honest exercise of judgment based upon actual consideration of existing conditions.

The rule that a fiduciary should convert nonlegal securities within a reasonable time is to be applied more liberally in the case of executors and administrators than in the case of trustees, and is to be more strictly applied where the rights of creditors are affected. 

A trustee will not be surcharged with loss resulting from the retention of nonlegal securities purchased by his testator where, after consultation and careful consideration, all parties concerned agreed that certain of the securities should be sold and that application be made for distribution of the balance in kind, under section 49 (e) 1 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, the proceedings being subsequently delayed due to pending litigation over the securities sold, but the account being filed and the request for distribution made promptly upon its termination, and especially where the securities were at all times subjected to the closest scrutiny, expert advice was had, and such sales were made as were deemed expedient. 

A determination by the orphans' court upon the audit of one account of a trustee that there has been no abuse of discretion in retaining nonlegal securities up to that time does not authorize a further delay in their conversion, but any such delay may be made the subject of inquiry upon the audit of a subsequent account. Mitchell's Est., 21 D. & C. 225.

The rule with regard to the duty of a trustee into whose hands investments made by the testator himself may come differs very greatly from that which governs him in making his own investments. In the latter case he becomes liable if he deviates from the line marked out by the law, should a loss arise. In the former case it is left to the discretion of the trustee, and if, in the honest and proper exercise of that discretion, he delays the realization, he may not be held liable for any loss arising from such delay. Courtright's Estate, 15 Erie 229.

A testamentary trustee who is given authority by the will to retain or invest in nonlegal securities, of types similar to those acquired by testator, is liable to a surcharge for loss sustained through the retention of such investments only for failure to study carefully the circumstances and conditions controlling the value of those securities, or, having made such a study, for failure to act intelligently with respect thereto. 

A greater latitude in the exercise of discretion is to be allowed a testa. mentary trustee permitted by the terms of the will to retain nonlegal investments, where the securities in respect of which a surcharge is sought have constituted part of the trust res for more than 25 years and have been retained, with profit to the trust estate, during prior periods of adverse economic conditions. 

In determining a trustee's liability to surcharge for retention of nonlegal securities, as permitted by the terms of the instrument creating the trust, the wishes of beneficiaries expressed to the trustee are to be disregarded except in so far as they communicated information upon which the trustee should have acted, since the latter is charged with the duty of interposing his own judgment between the trust estate and the beneficiaries. 

Dickinson's Est., 21 D. & C. 247, af'd in 318 Pa. 561.

Investments in stock or bonds are a means by which money is made to earn for itself money or income. The primary thought in both should be property value, then income.

In considering the sale of investments that have no open market, or bonds in a depressed market, or stock whose intrinsic value is established paying dividends equal to and above what would be a normal interest rate, reasonable latitude, according to the circumstances, must be allowed a fiduciary in the disposition of such property. 

The first essential thing for a fiduciary to consider is the safety of the principal even though it may sacrifice income. Brown's Est., 287 Pa. 499. 

A fiduciary cannot retain nonlegal securities indefinitely, and in case of loss he must show that he honestly exercised vigilance, discretion and judgment based on actual consideration of existing conditions. This applies equally to such securities taken by a guardian from an administrator.

Where a testator empowers his trustees to select whatever securities they choose from his estate to form trusts created by his will, authorizing them to select and retain nonlegal investments including stock of one of the trustees and of a corporation closely affiliated with it, and the trustees select and retain such stock and purchase additional shares thereof in the exercise of rights to subscribe, they will not be surcharged for a depreciation in the value of the investment, in the complete absence of proof of any failure by the trustees to study carefully the circumstances and conditions controlling the value of the investments or to act intelligently with respect thereto, or that the officers ought to have known that the investments were in a precarious siuation or of any other negligence, wilful default or lack of good faith.

Where a testator authorizes his trustees to retain or convert securities which he owns at the time of his death and then provides that, subject to that authorization, no one investment shall exceed a specified sum, the limitation on amount applies solely and exclusively to new investments and has no relation to securities already owned by the testator. Clay's Est., 25 D. & C. 257. 

Ordinarily a fiduciary has no right to retain, beyond a reasonable period, investments made by the decedent in unauthorized securities; unless spe- cially empowered to do so. 

When a trustee continues to possess such nonlegal investments after a time when he could properly dispose of them, and a loss occurs, he may be held liable for a failure of due care, unless he shows that his retention of the securities in question represents, not a mere lack of attention, but the honest exercise of judgment based upon actual consideration of existing conditions.

In considering the sale of investments that have no open market, reasonable latitude, according to the circumstances, must be allowed a fiduciary in the disposition of such property. 

The judgment of a fiduciary acting in good faith on considered circumstances, should have controlling effect as to the time of sale of the particular investment; the rule is, what would a prudent man ordinarily do if a similar situation confronted the disposition of his personal affairs?

97 In so holding the Court reaffirmed four primary rules as controlling: 

1. Where a trustee is clothed with discretionary powers as to investments and reinvestments, neither the state constitutional provision as to trust funds nor the rule as to legal investments applies. 

2. In determining whether a trustee should be surcharged with depreciation in value of securities in which he has invested the trust funds, the case must be judged as it appeared at the time of the investment. 

3. All that a court of equity requires from a trustee is common skill, common prudence and common caution, and he is not liable when he acts in good faith as others do with their own property. 

4. He will not be held personally liable for an honest exercise of a discretionary power in the absence of supine negligence or wilful default, nor for the result of an intervening world calamity beyond his power to foresee or prevent.

The general rule is that an estate must be maintained in such condition that cash legacies or other cash charges directed to be paid therefrom can be paid at the time designated, but future dispositions of money, whether under wills of testators or otherwise, must be subject to the ordinary vicissitudes of future payments, including economic or other business depressions. 

Where loss is sustained on an investment made by an executor or trustee acting in good faith, through no fault of the fiduciary but because of an extraordinary occurrence beyond the knowledge, skill and diligence of prudent business men, the executor or trustee is not liable therefor and may, upon distribution to a legatee, turn over the security invested in or reduce it to cash. "We understand there are ample assets in the residue from which this legacy may be paid in cash, but if this security were the only item, there is no question of the good faith of the executors and trustees in lending the money on first mortgage secured by real estate which though now depreciated in value as a result of the great economic depression, at the time of the investment was sound. It was a legal investment on ample security. While it is true the general rule is that for the payment of a cash legacy or other cash charge, the estate must remain in such condition that the money directed to be paid therefrom can be paid at the time designated, future dispositions of money, whether under wills of testators or otherwise, must be subject to the ordinary vicissitudes of future payments, including economic or other business depressions which affect everyone. Under such circumstances it is not necessary to comply with the general rule stated above, that an executor or trustee hold money in a strong box uninvested and undeposited in a bank. If the rule does require this, it is entirely too harsh; it is unreasonable to exact from a fiduciary, acting prudently, who suffers a loss because of an extraordinary economic disturbance, higher knowledge, skill and diligence than is expected of prudent business men. 

We therefore hold in such cases that where loss occurs through no fault of executors or trustees, acting in good faith, but because of an extraordinary occurrence precipitating loss upon the honest and diligent and ignorant and slothful alike, the executors and trustees are not required to make good the difference in value from their own pockets, but may turn over the security or reduce it to cash and turn it over to the beneficiary." Jones's

Under the former acts on which this was based fiduciaries might "invest in ground rents or other real estate, by leave of the proper court,' under proceedings as provided in the act. But in the nature of the transaction no security would be required in such case; for the property purchased stands good for the purposes of the trust, and is taken at the risk of it: which trust should appear in the title deed taken; but if a power of re-sale be given by the court, as in case of a temporary investment, or the ground rent be subject to redemption, when it is the paramount right of the tenant to redeem, then security should be taken at the time of the investment, in double the amount of principal; otherwise the deed should express that the purchase was allowed upon condition that the trustee, etc., should not sell or extinguish without first giving security under the act, to be approved by the court. An equal exchange would not be a case of exacting security. Under this act, it is the province of the court having jurisdiction of the trustees to authorize their investment of the trust funds, in real estate, whether situated in the same or any other county; and if the vendors hold the land in their own right, the court of the county where the land is situated has no jurisdiction to direct the sale and purchase. Under those acts, the orphans' court has power to authorize the exchange of real estate belonging to a decedent's estate, for other realty; but the power should be exercised with extreme caution, and to doubt is to deny.

But though a petition which combines with an application to sell real estate at private sale, a further application to be allowed to invest the purchase money in other real estate, is defective, the latter application may be treated as surplusage, and the petition be passed upon as if it were solely for the sale of the real estate: Graham's Est., 14 W. N. C. 31.

Preliminary objections to a bill to enforce contribution against a surety on the first of two indemnifying bonds given by a guardian appointed in another county of this commonwealth were overruled, where defendant resisted the claim, on the ground that a formal order of the orphans' court could not be set aside in a collateral proceeding, but the order being void was ineffective to cancel the first bond. 

An order of the orphans' court, authorizing the substitution of an indemnifying bond in a guardian's estate and the cancellation of the original bond, was null and void and of no effect, where the provisions of the act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, were not complied with. This would not relieve the co-surety of liability after a surcharge had been paid by the first surety. 

Compliance with the provisions of the statute was a prerequisite to the entry of any decree on the subject and without it the court had no jurisdiction of the cause, lacking any power to act in the premises. 

Decrees or judgments of the court which are or may become in whole or part ineffectual are to be classed as either void or voidable. A voidable decree is one where the court entering it had jurisdiction of the parties, the subject matter and the general power to act, but its effect could be avoided by a party in interest because of some irregularity. A void decree is no decree at all-its entry was entirely futile, and did not and could not have

The act provides for "notice to all parties interested," the better practice would therefore be to include such parties as respondents in the citation or have them join in the petition.

This citation should be made returnable not less than thirty days after the date of its issuance and thereafter after proper accounting by the guardian, unless some cause be shown to prevent, the court will discharge the surety from future liability upon the entry of a substituted surety in his place on the bond of the said guardian. 

265. PROTECTION OF SURETY. 

For the protection of a surety and also, incidentally, of any "other person interested in the trust" a fiduciary may be called on at any time for a statement of his investments and an accounting thereof if such statement show anything irregular. The procedure is thus detailed: "In case any surety or sureties, or the personal representatives of any deceased surety or sureties upon the bond of any fiduciary, or any person interested in the trust, shall apply to the fiduciary for a complete and detailed statement of the nature and character of the securities in which the trust funds are invested, and the said fiduciary shall fail for the space of ten days to furnish such statement, or if, such statement having been furnished, it shall appear to the said surety or sureties, or the representatives of said surety or sureties, or other person interested in said trust, that the funds in the hands of the said fiduciary are badly invested 51 so as to be likely to result in a loss to the trust, the said surety or sureties, or the representatives of said surety or sureties, or other person interested in the trust, may present a peany legal consequence. It may be attacked collaterally by anyone at any time and anywhere.

Defendant, a co-surety, resisting a claim for contribution on an indemnifying bond, could not invoke estoppel against plaintiff, where both were parties to the entry of an order whereby one bond was cancelled and another substituted therefor, in that the order was absolutely void for want of jurisdiction, and not merely voidable. The principle of estoppel could not be invoked to bring into being a judgment that never existed.

The Act of 1836 in its terms provides a complete system of procedure to enforce bonds of this nature and its requirements should be strictly followed. 

This act "does away with the necessity for any cautionary judgment, and provides for a direct action on the bond in the first instance, in which two judgments are secured; the first for the commonwealth in the amount of the obligation, and the second for the plaintiff in the original issue for the amount of his individual damages and costs. The judgment for the commonwealth remains for all future persons entitled to the benefit of the bond, who may proceed thereon by scire facias and have damages assessed in each case, but the plaintiff in the original action in which the judgments are given has his execution in like manner as may be had in the case of judgments in other personal actions. The plaintiff in such original action can no longer rely upon a mere general breach of the condition of the bond, such as the nonfiling of an inventory or an account, unless he can show a particular injury to himself caused by the breach. Upon the practice now established before any judgment can be had on the bond, a plaintiff must appear with a particular injury suffered, and if he maintains his suit to judgment, then he not only has his claim determined and reduced to judgment, but for the first time judgment is entered in the money to be tied up in a closed bank; if the accountant is to be relieved. from his definite liability as fixed by the orphans' court, it is for that court to grant it. Comm'th v. Wenger, 22 D. & C. 87.

CHAPTER XLII. 

NONRESIDENT AND FOREIGN FIDUCIARIES 267. APPOINTMENT 

CIARY. 

OF NONRESIDENT FIDU- 

It is mandatory upon every court within the state to recognize a fiduciary properly appointed and qualified by a register of wills or orphans' court of the county having jurisdiction of the fiduciary, as the act provides: "Any fiduciary appointed by any orphans' court of this commonwealth, or by virtue of any last will and testament, probated within this commonwealth, may, if resident within this commonwealth, lawfully execute the duties of his trust, whether or not he is a resident of the county in which the trust was created, or in which the decedent had his domicile."' 57

Where such fiduciary is not a resident of the commonwealth, however, his appointment is within the discretion of the court and the entry of security is mandatory under the further provision: "The court having jurisdiction may, in its discretion, appoint or refuse to appoint as trustee or guardian any person who is not a resident of this commonwealth, or a corporation of any state of the United States of America, other than Pennsylvania, duly authorized by its charter or by law to act as such fiduciary, and shall require in all cases of a nonresident of this commonwealth, or of such corporation, a bond, with sufficient sureties, conditioned for the faithful discharge of the duties of the trust; but the court may, in its discretion, permit such corporation to give its own bond without sureties."' 57

Tit. 20, Sec. 991), "confined to fiduciaries who are within the scope of the new act, altered in phraseology and extended to testamentary guardians and to corporations of other states. The clause as now worded is believed to express the meaning of the ambiguous language of the Act of 1871. See Plummer's Estate, 24 Dist. 542. The last sentence is new."

But a resident attorney-in-fact must be designated: "No such appointment shall be made of, nor shall letters testamentary be issued to, a corporation of another state, unless such corporation shall first file with the clerk of said court or with the register of wills, as the case may be, an appointment in writing of an attorney-in-fact, resident within the respective county, upon whom service of process and notices may be made." 57

A similar appointment must be filed in the office of the register of wills in the case of the grant of letters testamentary or of administration to any nonresident person or corporation.58

CHAPTER XLIII. 

DISCHARGE AND REMOVAL OF FIDUCIARIES. 

273. DISCHARGE OF FIDUCIARIES. 

Any fiduciary who has entirely completed the duties of his office may secure his discharge. This is advisable where security has been given. In other cases it is permissible though not always advisable, especially in the case of a resident executor, as the existence of afterdiscovered assets would require the raising of administration d. b. n. c. t. a. with its consequent expense. The act provides: 85 "Any fiduciary whose accounts shall have been settled and confirmed 84 and who shall have paid and transferred the remainder of the property in his hands to his successor in the administration or trust, if any, or to the persons legally entitled thereto, may, on petition, be discharged by the orphans' court having jurisdiction of his accounts from the duties of his appointment; and his sureties may be discharged from future liability with respect thereto: Provided. That in every case of the petition of a guardian for his discharge during the minority of his ward, it shall be the duty of the court to appoint some suitable person to appear and act for the ward in respect thereto."s7 

84 The confirmation of an executor's final account and of the auditor's report thereon does not operate as a discharge of the executor, who should, upon the completion of his duties, petition for his discharge, first giving notice to those whose interests may be affected thereby. 

In order for an executor to shift responsibility from his sureties as such to his sureties as trustee, upon transferring property to himself in the latter capacity, the transfer must be evidenced by some overt act or express election, and it seems that the entry of a decree directing the transfer is not, of itself, sufficient. Comth. v. Hughes, 25 D. & C. 210.

To justify the removal of trustee appointed by will there must be a clear necessity for interference to save the trust property; mere error or even breach of trust may not be sufficient, but there must be such misconduct as to show want of capacity or of fidelity putting the trust in jeopardy.

In determining whether testamentary trustees should be removed, the court will take into consideration the fact that one only of numerous beneficiaries wishes the removal while all the others oppose it or remain neutral. Bailey's Est., 13 D. & C. 455, af'd in 306 Pa. 334.

A trustee will not be removed at the mere whim or caprice of the beneficiary; a substantial reason therefor must appear before such fiduciary will be removed. Hughes' Est. (No. 1), 319 Pa. 321.

A substantial reason therefor must exist before the court will remove a trustee, who enjoyed the confidence of the person who created the trust. 

In a doubtful situation a mere error as to legal duties is not a breach of trust warranting dismissal of the trustee. 

Active antagonism of the beneficiaries of an estate or their representatives toward the trustee is not sufficient to require the removal of the trustee unless provoked by the latter and likely to jeopardize the estate. 

The retention of income as a separate fund for the purpose of meeting exigencies which might arise and which might otherwise necessitate a depletion of the principal does not constitute unlawful accumulation.

A testamentary trustee who fails to acquire the corpus of the trust for more than two years after testator's death, and then only on demand of the parties in interest, and who makes a precarious and improvident investment without any examination of the security afforded and entirely on reliance upon the advice of others, is guilty of such supine negligence and wilful default in the management of the trust as to require his removal. Reik's Est., 18 D. & C. 252.

 276. PROCEDURE FOR REMOVAL OF FIDU- CIARIES. 

The usual course of procedure is by citation, and for this the method is outlined in detail: ⁹a "Whenever it shall be made to appear to the orphans' court having jurisdiction of the accounts of any fiduciary, on the oath or affirmation of any person interested, that there exists any one or more of the grounds for removal of such fiduciary enumerated in the last preceding clause of this section, such court may issue a citation to such fiduciary, requiring him to appear on a day certain, to answer the charge so preferred, and may make all such necessary rules and orders as the said court may deem proper for bringing the matter complained of to a hearing. If, on such hearing, the said court shall be satisfied of the truth of the matters charged, it may remove such executor or administrator and vacate the letters testamentary or of administration or remove such guardian or trustee, as aforesaid, and direct the issuance of new letters testamentary or of administration, or appoint a new guardian or trustee, and make such orders for the security of the trust property 10 and for the delivery of such property and the books, accounts, papers and moneys belonging or relating to the trust to the successor of such fiduciary as the circumstances of the case may require." 99 11 which applies only to Philadelphia, modified so as to conform to the decision in Neafie's Estate, 199 Pa. 307.

This combination has been made in order to avoid unnecessary repetitions. The following clauses deal with the procedure common to all the cases above enumerated.

CHAPTER XLIV. 

JURISDICTION AND POWERS. 

GENERAL SCOPE OF JURISDICTION. 

It has been impracticable heretofore to treat logically of all the various matters of practice and procedure incidental or collateral to the management of estates by fiduciaries. Such, however, all fall within the jurisdiction of the orphans' court where the estate of a minor or decedent is involved, or the settlement of trusts inter vivos.19 

Such jurisdiction while limited 20 is appellate, inciden- 

19 See sec. 281, infra, notes 56-61. 

20 The orphans' court is a tribunal of limited jurisdiction, and has no power to make an order striking off satisfaction entered on a mortgage. 

Cutter's Est., 286 Pa. 505, rev'g 7 Erie 253.

When a claimant voluntarily appears in the orphans' court and presents its claim thereby admitting jurisdiction of the court and its claim is decided adversely, it cannot subsequently question the jurisdiction of the court. 

Tuttle's Est. (No. 2), 19 Erie 251. 

The orphans' court applies equitable principles and, where it has jurisdiction of the fund and of all the parties involved, has the power by subrogation to make a decree of reimbursement. Boles' Est., 316 Pa. 179. 

See also Keiper's Est., 44 Lanc. 285, 21 D. & C. 639.

A petition by a creditor of a decedent, holding as collateral for his debt certain stock certificates in the decedent's name, to show cause why the executrix should not perfect petitioner's title to the stock, will be dismissed if the petitioner is a nonresident and the securities are not within the jurisdiction of the court and the petitioner refuses to deposit the stock or its proceeds within the Commonwealth and to submit himself to the court's jurisdiction. Krause's Est., 24 D. & C. 711.

Where the conservator of a bank, pursuant to instructions from the comptroller of the currency, under a claim of right, sets off a deposit in the bank of the funds of a decedent's estate, against notes given by the decedent and notes given by the administrator as additional security, the orphans' court does not have jurisdiction to pass on the legality of that action and order it to be rescinded, nor can it make any order on the bank to pay over any of its funds to the administrator. Where a state court has taken jurisdiction in a proper case of the subject matter there involved prior to the filing of a petition in bankruptcy, it has complete and effective power to determine finally all rights and title in and to such property.

Where the orphans' court has once acquired control of property, the jurisdiction of all other courts, though concurrent, is subject thereto. 

Controversies, not strictly or properly part of the proceedings in bankruptcy, but independent suits brought by the trustee in bankruptcy to assert a title to money or property as assets of the bankrupt against strangers to those proceedings, should not come within the jurisdiction of the federal courts. McCahan's Estate, 312 Pa. 515.

A federal court had jurisdiction of a bill in equity against a trust company for an accounting as well as damages, where defendant was administrator of the estate of plaintiff's father. The bill alleged that the trust company had fraudulently obtained a release of liability and then while acting as administrator failed to sell securities held as collateral to secure a loan made by defendant to her father until their current price was less than the loan. This taking of jurisdiction would not be an improper interference with the functions of the orphans' court, which had fully administered the estate except this item, as the bill was not directed against defendant in its representative capacity. Showers v. Franklin Trust Company, 82 P. L. J. 17.

An orphans' court may not, at the instance of the purchaser of real estate, comprising part of a trust res, at a sale held pursuant to a decree of the court of common pleas, set aside the sale and order the trustee to return the down money, on the ground that the common pleas lacked jurisdiction of the subject matter and that its decree was therefore void. 

An orphans' court is a court of limited jurisdiction concurrent with that of the court of common pleas, and has no power to vacate or set aside a decree made by the latter court because it lacked jurisdiction. Roseberry's 

Est., 32 Sch. 334.

When the pendency of a suit in one court is relied on to defeat a second suit in another court of concurrent jurisdiction, the identity of the parties, of the case made and of the relief sought, should be such that if the first suit had been decided, it could be pleaded in bar as a former adjudication. "The question before the orphans' court now is whether plaintiff can maintain this suit in the orphans' court while an action concerning the same subject matter and between the same parties is pending and undetermined in the Court of Common Pleas.

This being a matter concerning the estate of a minor and his right for an accounting from the administrator of the minor's deceased guardian, the orphans' court has jurisdiction under secs. (a) and (d) of Sec. 9, of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363. 

That the ward could not have brought an action against the guardian in Common Pleas Court during his lifetime and because of that fact that the Common Pleas Court may not now have jurisdiction to hear and determine a suit brought by the ward against the administrator of his deceased guardian, is a matter wholly for the determination of the Common Pleas Court and we will not presume to pass upon that question. 

At the hearing on the petition it was urged on behalf of the guardian that all proceedings should be stayed in the Orphans' Court until the question of jurisdiction in the Common Pleas Court is finally determined. With this we cannot agree. It is our duty to require the filing of an account by the guardian's administrator and to pass upon the claim of the ward against the deceased guardian's estate. What may afterwards be done in the matter relative to the jurisdiction of the Common Pleas Court should further action be necessary, is a question wholly for that court. The action was originally instituted in the Common Pleas Court for the purpose of preserving a lien against the deceased guardian's real estate, under the provisions of Sec. 15 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 6, 1917, P. L. 447,

$279 

the estate,25 which may also be made by recourse to the common pleas.26

The original jurisdiction of the orphans' court is now based on one of four fundamental facts, that is, the death of a person, the minority of a ward, the creation of a trust by deed inter vivos, and the adoption of one person by another. In the case of a decedent the jurisdiction attaches at the moment of death, subject only to such matters as may be purely within the scope of the jurisdiction and power of the register of wills. 

To those not versed in Pennsylvania law, the name of the court may seem peculiar. Its name is derived from the "Court of the Orphans," which in the seventeenth century was an institution of the City of London and by the emigrants from that city to Pennsylvania, was founded in this state in 1682.27 as amended by the Act of June 7, 1919, P. L. 412. The very purpose of that act is to secure and preserve a lien upon decedent's real estate in the Common Pleas Court, while the settlement of the estate is pending in the 

Orphans' Court. 

It is a familiar principle of law that two suits between the same parties, upon the same cause in action, in the same court or in different courts, will not be tolerated. See Doyle's Est., 291 Pa. 763. But two or more courts may, under certain conditions, have concurrent jurisdiction of the same parties and the same subject-matter at the same time.” Poniatowski's 

Est., 16 Erie 401. 

25 See Chapter 16, supra, Secs. 92-97. 

26 Where the bill shows that the subject matter was not in the decedent at the time of her death proceedings for its recovery must be had in the court of common pleas and not in the orphans' court. Miller v. Miller, 19 

North. 400.

Proceedings against an executor in the Common Pleas bars a similar action in the orphans' court. Henderson's Est., 29 D. & C. 1.

Where a public official has deposited trust funds in bank and appropriated them to his own use for the purchase of real estate, being at that time in default with the trust funds in his care it was held: That the equity powers of the orphans' court are sufficient to allow the adjudication by the orphans' court of the matters involved. However, when the same question has been raised by bill in equity in the common pleas, the orphans' court will await the determination of the questions by the common pleas, before entering a definite decree. Cutter's Est., 7 Erie 166, 253.

"The Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, controls this case. Section 3 of that act reads: 'Whenever by reason of sickness, absence, interest, or other cause a judge of a court of common pleas in a judicial district having no orphans' court, may be unable to sit in any matter depending on the orphans' court of such district it shall be lawful for said judge to call upon any judge to preside in and determine such matter.' Venango County has no separate orphans' court and is within this class. "The act reads 'unable to sit in any matter.' A challenge to the qualifications of any judge is such an issue as will bring the judge within the meaning of 'unable to sit in any matter,' and it is therefore within the scope of the act. The fact that the judge was not called in to pass on the main question involved, but only a subsidiary point, the decision of which had no bearing on the substantive question involved, will not take the question out of the apparent scope of the act. There is no conflict between this act and its predecessors which affects the matter before us. The Act of 1917 enlarges, as to orphans' courts, the causes for which change of the hearing judge may be had, and would seem to embrace any reason. Moreover, it specifically permits the calling in of any judge in the Commonwealth." Crawford's Est., 307 Pa. 102.

L. 81, denominated the orphans' court "a Court of Record"; section 2 of the Act of March 29, 1832, P. L. 363, sec. 1, provides that in every county of the Commonwealth there shall continue to exist, as heretofore, a court of record (the orphans' court). "It is a clear principle in the construction of statutes, that the jurisdiction of a court of record cannot be taken away, but by express negative words': Kline v. Wood, 9 S. & R. 294, 298. 

As to the import of the phrase "actions at law," in Bouvier's Law "action "" Dictionary is defined in practice as: "" formal demand of one's rights from another person, made and insisted on in a court of justice. In Bartley's Estate, 20 Pa. C. C. 451, 452 [7 Dist. 36], action is held to be: "" a word whose generally accepted meaning seems to be identical with its technical significance, to wit, a proceeding in a court, whether of equity or law." In this case Judge Ashman says: "A proceeding in the orphans' court is therefore undoubtedly an action." In Jacoby v. Shafer, 105 Pa. 610, an action is said to include "all the formal proceedings prescribed by law for adjudicating and enforcing a right, or denying an unfounded claim or demand."

In Painter v. Henderson, 7 Pa. 48, the orphans' court is said to be a court of record at common law, as declared by the statute, and in Brinker v. Brinker, 7 Pa. 53, 55, Mr. Chief Justice Gibson says: "But although the orphans' court has been called a court of equity, in respect to the few subjects within its jurisdiction, the ancillary powers of such a court have not been given to it. It is a special tribunal for specific cases; and its resemblance to a court of equity consists in its practice of proceeding by petition and answer. Sando, P. J. in Jones' Est., 28 D.

As a general rule it is within the sound discretion of the orphans' court to set aside its own orders. Huff's Est., 299 Pa. 200-203.

The decree of the orphans' court and a deed made in pursuance thereof may be attacked collaterally in the common pleas if fraud accomplished the procurement of either or both. Rubinsky v. Kosh, 24 Sch. 378. 

Since the action of the Orphans' Court in awarding the premises to the husband of original owner on account of his spouse's allowance of $5,000, carries with it a finding of the intestacy of the original owner, the decree in that court is conclusive and not subject to collateral attack in the 

Court of Common Pleas. MacBeth v. Woodfill, 14 Wash. 66. 

The orphans' court has exclusive jurisdiction over all things pertaining to the settlement and distribution of estates. 

A court of equity cannot vacate the appointment of a guardian made by the orphans' court nor remove an administrator, nor vacate an order for the private sale of real estate by a guardian, nor set aside such sale.

The jurisdiction of the orphans' court being entirely statutory," it is essential that it be clearly defined as the 

37 Power v. Grogan, 232 Pa. 387; Spear's Est., 26 Del. 371. "There are many matters which arise in the settlement of an estate wherein the orphans' court has been held to possess no jurisdiction. Thus it may not appoint a 'receiver': Power v. Grogan, 232 Pa. 387; has no power to make an order striking off a satisfaction entered on a mortgage; has no power to ascertain and order distribution of profits of a corporation even where organized by executors under authority of the orphans' court: 

Goetz's Est., (No. 1) 236 Pa. 630; has no power to remove directors of a charitable corporation organized at the direction of a will: Watson's

In Schnepf's Estate, 20 Dist. R. 517, affirmed in 48 Pa. Superior Ct. 580, a petition was filed by an administrator to restrain the transfer of stock which decedent in his lifetime had transferred to respondent. A question arose as to whether the assignment was made as collateral for a loan, or to the respondent as a trustee for decedent. It was ruled by this court, and affirmed above, that the orphans' court had no jurisdiction over the controversy. Freihofer's Est., 25 D. & C. 547. 

The orphans' court within the sphere of its jurisdiction is a court of equity. Lonergan's Est., 303 Pa. 142; in that in the exercise of its limited jurisdiction conferred entirely by statute it applies the rules and principles of equity. Douglas's Est., 303 Pa. 227; Lamparter's Est., 15 D. & 

C. 639, 42 Lanc. 377; Mallory's Est., 285 Pa. 186; Crawford's Est., 12 

Wash. 33; Main's Est., 322 Pa. 243; Freihofer's Est., 25 D. & C. 547, q. v.; William's Est., 236 Pa. 259; Cutler's Est., 225 Pa. 167.

The orphans' court within the scope of its jurisdiction is a court of equity, and will not only grant a rehearing on behalf of a residuary legatee who had no notice of the original hearing on exceptions to the executrix's account, but will vacate an order awarding property included in said account to the decedent's niece on the basis of said hearing when the testimony produced thereat, in the light of evidence at the rehearing, shows that at attempted survivorship account was opened between the decedent and the niece for the very purpose of defeating an irrevocable reciprocal will agreement between the decedent and her husband who had bequeathed her the subject matter of said account on the strength thereof; especially when the decedent expressed hearty approval of the disposition provided for in said agreement at the time it was made, and after accepting the husband's property pursuant thereto, opened the account in an attempt to deprive his niece of her one-half interest in the residue of the property under the agreement and give it all to a niece of her own who was entitled to the other half interest thereunder. Culhane's Est. (No. 2), 19 Erie 313.

The jurisdiction of the orphans' court is limited to the estate of which the testator died seized. Kubitza's Est., 12 D. & C. 71. "The orphans' court has no jurisdiction of cases arising between a legatee and a stranger to the estate." Commonwealth v. York Trust Co., 41 York 125. 

Where a contest was between a stakeholder and two adverse sets of claimants, and the fund never was in the orphans' court, that court had no jurisdiction. Kunsman's Est., 21 North. 335, 11 D. & C. 783.

There is no such thing in the orphans' court as a case stated. Yost's
