Where an administrator claims to receive a debt due to the estate of a decedent, he must proceed by action in the common pleas and not by citation in the orphans' court. Strohm's Est., 13 D. & C. 436.

Where it appears from the petition for a citation upon one in possession of real estate to file an account of rents as testamentary trustee, and from the will upon which the petition is based, that both the petitioner and the respondent claim to be owners of the property, their respective claims being dependent upon the construction of the will, the petition will be dismissed on the ground of want of jurisdiction in the orphans' court, and the parties remitted to their remedy in the court of common pleas. Krull's Est., 6 D. & C. 21. 

Under section 40 (d) of the Act of June 15, 1923, P. L. 809, and section 

803, Article VIII, of the Act of May 15, 1933, P. L. 565, the court of common pleas was given exclusive jurisdiction to determine, upon audit of the account of the secretary of banking, in possession of a trust company, whether the beneficiary of a trust is entitled to priority of payment out of a mortgage pool fund on the ground that the trustee acted illegally in making an investment in the mortgage fund after the beneficiary became of age. 

The Act of June 15, 1923, P. L. 809, as amended by the Act of May 5, 1927, P. L. 762, presented a complete system for the winding up of banking institutions and for the establishment of claims. 

The Department of Banking Code of May 15, 1933, P. L. 565, now provides a comprehensive scheme for the liquidation of closed banks. Stopp's 

Est., 122 Super. 47.

The orphans' court may exercise the powers of equity to enforce obedience to its decrees only within its restricted, statutory jurisdiction. 

Where the property was never in the control of the orphans' court, no jurisdiction over it or its possessor can be asserted if the latter holds under a claim of right, asserts ownership, and is not a fiduciary. 

The orphans' court has no jurisdiction to compel a third person, not associated with the administration of an estate, to pay over money or property in her possession to the estate where the money or property was not in the possession of his representative. Under these circumstances the personal representative must seek his remedy by action at law or in equity. 

Even where such property was within the possession of the decedent at the time of his death, or subsequently was in the hands of the personal representative, the orphans' court must certify an issue to the common pleas, where the third person presently in possession claims it by right of ownership and a substantial dispute as to title exists. McGovern's Est., 322 'Pa. 379. 

When the testimony shows that the money claimed by the estate was not in possession of decedent at the time of his death and has never been in the hands of administrator, and is not included in the inventory, the Orphans' Court will certify the question of ownership of the money to the 

Court of Common Pleas for trial by jury. Bartlett's Est., 19 Erie 409.

Where petition prays that orphans' court ascertain extent of trust estate, and require administratrix of deceased trustee to convey to substituted trustee personal assets of such estate, petition taking form of bill in equity,

Orphans' Court is a court of equity only in the sense that in the exercise of its limited jurisdiction it employs the principles of equity. Mains'

An orphans' court has jurisdiction to direct a third party to pay over to a fiduciary money in the former's possession which belonged to the decedent at the time of his death, unless there is a substantial dispute of fact as to the ownership of the fund at that time, in which case the issue must be determined by a jury.

An order will be entered by the orphans' court directing the payment to an administrator of the proceeds of a savings account received by respondent subsequent to the decedent's death, decedent having given respondent the passbook and a power of attorney to make withdrawals; under such circumstances, the account was presumptively an asset of the estate at the time of decedent's death, the transaction being merely the creation of an agency, and the burden rests upon respondent to show the transfer to him of a present irrevocable title, in order to establish a valid gift inter vivos. 

Disken's Est., 21 D. & C. 38, 48 York 95.

The orphan's court does not have jurisdiction to enforce the payment to an administrator of a sum of money delivered by the decedent to one who claims the money as a gift and, therefore, in the distribution of the estate such a claim cannot be set off against the distributee's share. "The jurisdiction of the orphans' court is limited to the estate of which the testator died seized. With respect to such estate, it has full jurisdiction; but this marks its ultimate limit, whether a specific article of property belongs to the estate, is a question standing in limine; if it does not, the administrator is not acocuntable therefor, and it is beyond the power of the court to control it in any way or charge liability on anyone in connection therewith. Presumably every item of property an administrator has included in his inventory belongs to the estate, and for all such he must account: Cutler's Est., 225 Pa. 167; Cooper's Est., 263 Pa. 37"; 

Sprenkle's Est., 46 York 169.

"There remains to be considered section 9 (e) of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, and section 13 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447. Burton's Est., 116 Super. 249.

Mr. Chief Justice Frazer said: 'Appellants' suggestion that the orphans' court has jurisdiction to grant the relief prayed for, seems to be based upon the erroneous theory that the court named, because of its aspect as a court of equity can proceed upon the broad jurisdictional powers of a court of that class. Such is not the sense of our decisions. As we said in Willard's App., 65 Pa. 265, 267-8: “When it is said that the orphans' court is a court of equity, all that is meant is that, in the exercise of its limited jurisdiction conferred entirely by statute, it applies the rules and principles of equity. . . . It is a special tribunal for specific cases. It would, perhaps, be a very convenient practice immediately upon the death of a decedent to have all possible questions which might arise upon the construction of a will, and in the settlement and distribution of his estate, settled by a decree of the orphans' court in limine, and by way of anticipation and by an appeal to the Supreme Court from such a decree, have a final and conclusive determination of the subject. It would certainly save counsel a great deal of responsibility in giving advice. But the acts of assembly which confer jurisdiction on the orphans' court may be searched in vain for any such power. That decision was followed in Sharples's Estate, 305 Pa. 12. Those decisions are conclusive.' Birkel's Est., 25 North. 191.

 A prime purpose of the Declaratory Judgments Act is to render practical help in ending controversies which threaten litigation but have not reached a stage where other relief is immediately available, or where, under the attending facts, established forms of action will not immediately afford the relief required. 282. RULES OF COURT. 

From a practical standpoint, probably no other attribute of the orphans' court is greater than its right to make rules whereby the practice and procedure is amplified and detailed in a manner impracticable to the legis lature: 

"The several orphans' courts shall have full power and authority to make, from time to time, such rules for regulating the practice thereof, respectively, and for expediting the determination of suits, causes and proceedings therein, as in their discretion they shall judge necessary 

76 Cryan's Est., 301 Pa. 386; Dempsey's Est., 288 Pa. 458; List's 

Est., 283 Pa. 255; Myers' Est., 10 D. & C. 291.

As in the case of a petition by an executor for a judicial determination of his right, under the will of the decedent, to convey certain of her real estate would not terminate the uncertainty and where another established remedy is available, to wit, assumpsit for purchase money under the contract of sale, which was the procedure in Crozer et al. v. Green, 298 Pa. 438, in which the question involved was whether the executors under the will could convey a good marketable title to real estate, Loughlin's Est., 103 Super. 409. 

A petition for a declaratory judgment to determine whether an interest under a will is vested, subject to being divested by the birth of issue to other beneficiaries, or contingent upon survivorship, will be dismissed, where it appears that the question will arise on the audit of the account of testamentary trustees at the death of life tenants, to whom, within the contemplation of the law, children may be born in the future, and the only reasons assigned in support of the petition are that it is necessary to know in settling inheritance taxes upon the estate of the deceased beneficiary whether or not it will be entitled to share in the distribution, and that it would be more convenient for the executors of such beneficiary to have an immediate adjudication of the point. Straus's Est., 16 D. & C. 231, af'd in 307 Pa. 454. 

77 Cryan's Est., 301 Pa. 386; Morris v. Morris, 13 D. & C. 634.

§§ 282,283  

or proper for the exercise of the powers hereby conferred or which may hereafter be conferred: Provided, That such rules shall not be inconsistent with the constitution and laws of this commonwealth."' 78 

In many counties this right has been freely used, especially where the business of the court is excessive in amount, and in many instances a system of rules has been built up from time to time only less important than the acts of assembly themselves. 

Needless to say that in every case such rules should be consulted and followed explicitly in all matters of practice and procedure. No step of the way should be taken without the aid of both the statutes and rules of court.

This provision is sufficiently broad in its terms to cover any proceeding which may be brought, though of course, accounts, audits, motions and arguments will only be considered at stated periods as provided in the rules of court. 

The former act limited the power to granting citations and rules to show cause. Under the present enactment, however, the scope is broadened "to administer the business of the court." This, in itself, discloses the legislative intent to encourage and sanction all proper proceedings in vacation.

Where any court arbitrarily refuses to act except in cases of great emergency, it would seem to be a substantial denial of justice and an entirely unwarranted delay to citizens entitled to immediate relief. 

286. INJUNCTIONS. 

The close analogy between practice in the orphans' court and in equity is well illustrated by the specific jurisdiction given to enjoin prejudicial acts: 

"The said courts shall have power to prevent, by orders in the nature of writs of injunction, acts contrary to law or equity, prejudicial to property over which they shall have jurisdiction: Provided, That security may be required as in other cases of writs of injunction. 99 89

Under the authority of this section, the court may grant in chambers a petition for leave to pay a legacy of $100 to the father of a minor as its natural guardian. Storer's Estate, 28 Dist. 215.

By section 16 of the orphans' court act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, 373, that tribunal has power to prevent, by orders in the nature of writs of injunction, acts contrary to law or equity, prejudicial to property over which it has jurisdiction.

Even aside from any statute, the power of the orphans' court, as respects matters within its jurisdiction, is only limited by the necessities of the case and by its duty to administer equity in accordance with established rules. Heinz's Est., 313 Pa. 6.

§ 286 

This act gives the orphans' court chancery powers, so far as injunction is concerned, in regard to property over which it has jurisdiction; and the court has power to restrain the sale and transfer of assets of a decedent's estate by anyone having possession thereof, and as an incident thereto, the power to order that property admitted to belong to a decedent's estate, in the hands of one not an executor, administrator, guardian or trustee, shall be surrenderd for administration."⁰

Under this act an injunction will be granted against an executor or testamentary trustee upon satisfactory proof of such actual or threatened misconduct as will render the property in his charge likely to suffer loss or be jeopardized by its further continuance under his control and management.⁹¹

The court may restrain the personal representative from wasting or mismanaging the estate,92 and may at the suit of the executor enjoin a depositary from paying the funds deposited to distributees until the determination of a petition for a review of the account." It may direct the satisfaction of a mortgage which has been paid, and restrain a sale of the mortgaged property under a judgment on the bond. Where the goods of a decedent are 94

TRANSLATIONS. 

It frequently becomes necessary in the administration of an estate or in its distribution, to introduce as part of the record a document in other than the English language. In such case, it is provided: "Any person who shall offer any written or printed instrument to be filed in any orphans' court or in the office of the clerk of any orphans' court, which instrument shall be in any other than the English language, shall furnish at his own expense, to the clerk of such court, a sworn translation in English of such instrument thus offered, and the clerk shall attach or cause to be attached such translation to the original and file both the original and the translation of record in his office in all cases where filing is now or hereafter may be required by law, but in all cases where recording is now, or hereafter may be, required, both the original and the translation in 

English shall be recorded. Such clerk shall not file or mark filed, record or mark recorded, any written or printed instrument in violation of this clause, nor shall any paper filed or recorded in violation of this clause be notice to any person in any legal proceeding whatever, nor be received or considered in evidence in any proceeding at law or in equity.""

Such translation should be made ordinarily by the official court interpreter or by one skilled in foreign languages and known to the court as such.

On appeal from a decree refusing a petition by a substituted trustee for an order on the original trustee to turn over the trust fund and authorizing the original trustee to deliver to the petitioner the assets of the trust estate in kind, the appellate court considered the point that title to the property purchased by the original trustee had been taken in its name without any fiduciary designation, although such point was not brought to the attention of the court below nor argued before it, where it appeared that the facts necessary to sustain the point were contained in the petition and answer which constituted the record, that the question was one of law on the allegations of these pleadings and that the point raised was covered in the statement of questions involved and comprehended within the assignments of error. Fenelli's Est., 323 Pa. 49.

The rule that a question cannot be raised on appeal because it was not brought before the lower court until the oral argument, and because there was no asisgnment of error as to the specific point, is not applicable to a question whether an appellant was a trustee or not under a will, where it appears that he filed an account as trustee, but at the oral argument below claimed that he was not in fact a trustee, that the court considered the question, and that it was involved in the decree, which was assigned as error. 

Even if such question was not presented in the court below, it is the duty of the appellate court under the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, to pass upon it, as the act provides that in all cases of appeal from the definitive sentence or decree of the orphans' court, it is the duty of the appellate court to "hear, try and determine the same as to right and justice may belong, and decree according to equity thereof." 

Under the act, the appellate court is bound to consider a question not raised below, which is basic, and goes to the merits of the decree as made.

Unless sufficient data is given to justify a reversal, the supreme court will assume that the judgment or decree appealed from is justified by the law and the facts in the case. Baughman's Est., 281 Pa. 23.

On appeal from a decree of the orphans' court admitting a will for probate, the question for the appellate court is whether there is evidence to support the findings of fact and whether the findings support the decree. 

In cases of this character, the findings of the chancellor, supported by the court in banc, must be considered just as binding on the appellate court as the verdict of a jury. 

Under section 22 (b) of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, on appeal from a definitive sentence or decree of the orphans' court, in determining right, justice and equity and decreeing accordingly, the appellate court will accept the findings of fact of the lower court as conclusively binding on it where there is testimony to support them. 

In order to establish that the court below capriciously disbelieved the witnesses and that its decision was prejudiced, biased and prejudged, such facts must clearly appear from the record. 

To constitute capricious disbelief there must be a wilful, deliberate disbelief of an apparently trustworthy witness, whose testimony one of ordinary intelligence could not possibly challenge or entertain the slightest doubt as to its truth. Pusey 's Est., 321 Pa. 248.

On an appeal from a decree of the orphans' court dismissing an appeal from the register of wills, the findings of fact by the trial judge, where supported by competent evidence, must be accepted as conclusive by the appellate court. Carmello's Est., 289 Pa. 554. 

Where an executor, on appeal, complains of the refusal of the court to permit him to prove a receipt and release of one of the residuaries and claims that such rejection would have affected awards to residuary legatees under the rule laid down in Hertzler's Est., 192 Pa. 531, the appellate court, in sending the case back to the orphans' court, will direct that the lower court shall consider and give effect to the release, under the broad equitable principles which govern appeals from the orphans' court, as recognized by the Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 363), Sec. 22b. Constable's 

Est., 299 Pa. 509 and 515.

PREFACE 

In conformity with the plans announced at the time the Third Edition was published, there is presented to the profession this Cumulative Supplement thereto.

It purports to include all the Acts of Assembly relating to matters under the jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court finally passed and approved during the years 1938 to 1943 inclusive and all cases reported up to and including November 22, 1943, so as to bring down to that date all matters included in the original bound volumes of the Third Edition. 

Appropriate references are given to the standard Orphans' 

Court Rules promulgated by the Supreme Court as effective the first Monday of July, 1943.

As heretofore, it is planned to issue cumulative supplements biennially after each session of the Legislature. R. M. REMICK. 

December 31, 1943.

COPYRIGHT, 1943 BY GEO. T. BISEL CO.

CHAPTER III. 

PROBATE OF WILLS. 

12. PRODUCTION OF THE WILL. 

The purpose of the act.63 

63 The purpose of section 16 (a) of the Register of Wills Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 415, providing that the probate of a will shall be conclusive as to all property devised or bequeathed thereby, unless an appeal is taken within two years, and of section 16 (b) of the same act, providing that the last will of a decedent may be offered for probate at any time, provided that if it shall not have been offered for probate within three years from testator's death it shall be void as against a bona fide conveyance or mortgage of decedent's real estate duly recorded before the date of the offering of the will for probate, is to make marketable the property of a decedent passing under his probated will, or by conveyance from his heirs or transfer by his administrators; it is not intended to prohibit, after the expiration of two years, an appeal from the probate of the superseded will and the probate of the subsequent will where there has been no conveyance and only the rights of legatees are involved. 

Hetzel's Est., 37 D. & C. 440, 87 P. L. J. 499.

It is presumed that when a testator executes a paper purporting to be a will and prepared at his direction, it is valid, though not read to or by him at the time he executes it. Wetzel v. Edwards, 340 Pa. 121.

While the hearing judge on appeal from the register may in his discretion dispose in limine of the question of sufficiency of the proof of a will's execution, such practice, because it may involve a piecemeal hearing of the case, is not to be encouraged or approved. Drew's Est., 32 D. & C. 297.

Held, that the validity of a paper offered for probate, as a will, depends upon its compliance with the provisions of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403. Grankuskie's Est., 40 Lack. 94, 53 York 56. Alterations.

The validity of interlineations and apparent alterations appearing on a will is a question of probate and not of distribution.

Where a will has been probated with pencil marks thereon, the only remedy left for parties interested who contend that the pencil marks are not a part of the will is to appeal from the judicial act of the register of wills in admitting it to probate in that form.

Section 20, of the Wills Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403 (nuncupative wills excepted) provides that alterations of a will must be made by some other will or codicil in writing, or other writing declaring the same, executed and approved in the same manner as the execution of the will, that is by proving the alterations by two or more competent witnesses.

When a will is offered to the register of wills for probate having therein apparent changes or interlineations, it is the duty of the register at the time of the probate to inquire whether or not the changes and interlineations apparent on the will were made before or after the execution of the will. Laucks' Will, 57 York 86. 

Alterations and interlineations added by testator to will after having executed it and having discussed changes with attorney who drafted it, constitute merely memoranda for provisions of contemplated new will and do not operate as revocation. Knox's Est., 55 Montg. 210.

Where a will of a decedent was found in a safe in her home, an inference arose that the drawing of a line through a portion of her will was the act of the testatrix. The facts disclosed that there was such canceling or obliterating", within the meaning of the act, of the bequest to the decedent's son as to eliminate his participation in the residuary estate as if the portion canceled or obliterated had never been written. Lindeman's Est., 141 Super. 225; Guth's 

Est., 19 Leh. 351.

Where a testator wrote, with lead pencil, on, in and about a clause of his will words clearly indicating his intention to revoke the clause, adding a date subsequent to the date of the will and his signature, and this pencil writing was probated as a codicil to his will, from which probate no appeal was taken, it

§ 

he 's ill he on ៩ អន n, to on n- was held that the validity of the pencil writing was judicially determined and could not be impeached on the distribution of the estate, and that the clause over and into which it was written was revoked thereby. 

It is presumed that any alteration, interlineation or change appearing in a will was made prior to the execution of the will or the codicil, or the final act necessary to make such will effective. Thomas Est. (No. 3), 53 York 25; Guth's 

Est., 19 Leh. 351.

In the absence of evidence to the contrary, the presumption is that an addition to the will was made after the signature of the testatrix had been placed on the paper. 

Alterations to existing wills which attempt to substitute or to name additional legatees must be executed in strict compliance with sections 2, 20a, 20b of the 

Wills Act. 

Additions to existing wills by writing of the testatrix either in the body or margin of the will are in effect "codicils" and will be ordinarily ineffective because the formality of signing at the end as required by section 2 of the Wills 

Act has been omitted. Guth's Est., 19 Leh. 351.

Where a testator has signed his will on the first page and it is properly witnessed, the second page which contains three interlineations, none of which are properly executed, will not be considered as a part of the will. Barnes' Est., 24 Erie 219. 

An appeal to the orphans' court from the probate of a writing by the register of wills with certain insertions and interlineations was dismissed, where the evidence of the two witnesses to the will and of the son fixed the date and their testimony was credible and there was no evidence to the contrary, the will having been found sealed and among decedent's papers. Vey's Est., 87 P. L. J. 237. Revocation.

An unsigned statement written on the margin of a will in such a manner as not to touch any of the words thereof, stating "this will to be destroyed' and giving the date, is not an effective revocation thereof, since it is not a codicil or other writing executed in the manner required for the execution of a will, or a burning, canceling, obliterating or destroying, which, under section 20 (a) of the Wills Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403, are the only proper methods for revoking a will. 

In order to revoke a will by some other will or codicil in writing, or other writing declaring the same, it must be executed and proved in the same manner as a will. After the solemn execution of a will, it must remain in effect unless revoked by one of the modes designated in the act. Williams's Est., 1 Fay. 186, 86 P. L. J. 533, 34 D. & C. 411 af'd in 336 Pa. 235.

Partial revocation by cancellation was sustained on a question of distribution. 

Probate of the document as altered had no bearing on the matter. Crawshaw's 

Est., 6 Sch. Reg. 388.

Whether certain marginal notations upon a will have effected a revocation of a portion thereof is a matter exclusively within the original jurisdiction of the register of wills as a matter of probate. Rockett's Est., 48 D. & C. 6. Codicils. 

A codicil which makes a complete disposition of the testator's entire estate amounts to a revocation of the will to which it refers, and it is not necessary that there be an express clause of revocation. Ball v. Ball, 56 Montg. 68. 

In the absence of a contrary intention, a duly executed codicil operates as a republication of the original will, so as to make it speak as of the date of the codicil; and it not only operates as a new adoption of the prior will to which it refers, but also as a revocation of an intermediate will. Knecht's Est., 341 Pa. 292.

The doctrine, omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta, cannot be applied to establish compliance with Section 3 of the Wills Act, requiring proof of the circumstances of execution of wills by mark, by two or more competent witnesses. Drew's Est., 32 D. & C. 297. 

The law does not require wills to be read by or in the hearing of attesting witnesses; the proof of the signature or mark of testator by attesting witnesses imports competency, but when the burden has been shifted to a confidential adviser, the value of the credible testimony of attesting witnesses depends not only on their opinion that testator was of sound and disposing mind and memory, but also on their opportunity to detect incompetency and fraud. Schwartz's Est., 88 P. L. J. 295, af'd in 340 Pa. 170.

A will is sufficiently executed when the testator signs his name by mark and the two witnesses sign at the foot of each page in his presence and in the presence of each other. Morris' Est., 21 Wash. 120.

A will was held to be invalid, where there was no evidence who wrote decedent's name and the words "His Mark" at the end of the alleged will, the papers having been found in decedent's room with no explanation as to how they came to be there or who put them there. Kostovik's Est., 87 P. L. J. 134. 

The will of a testator unable to sign his name, executed by his mark or cross, under the provisions of Section 3 of the Wills Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403, is properly proven by the oaths or affirmations of two or more competent witnesses who do not necessarily have to be the subscribing witnesses. Each witness must separately depose to all facts necessary to complete the chain of evidence so that no link in it may depend on the credibility of but one. Marcus' Est., 34 Berks 105.

Where a present interest is vested, the fact that the actual enjoyment or payment of the money is postponed until after the death of the donor does not make the instrument testamentary.

A will must be ambulatory and capable of revocation at any time before the decedent's death. Lewis's Est., 139 Super. 83; Simun Est., 152 Super. 603.

An issue on the fraudulent substitution of a page in a testamentary instrument should not be granted unless the contestant satisfies the court that the ends of justice call for a verdict against the instrument or unless the court is so uncertain on this point that it could conscionably sustain a finding either way.

84 A paper to be accepted as a will must be not only testamentary in form but it must be signed by a decedent with a testamentary intent. 

In a will contest, in which it appeared that the decedent wrote a letter shortly before his death saying "in case of my death without having made a will it is my wish and desire that all moneys' from a named source "be paid to" X, it was held, under all the circumstances of the case, that the letter could properly be admitted to probate as a will. Wenz's Est., 345 Pa. 393. 

An instrument which constitutes a legal declaration of a person's intention directed to be performed after his death is a will. 

The execution of a carbon copy of a testamentary instrument and leaving the face copy unsigned does not make the signed instrument less effective for the purpose for which the testator intended it. 

Where the testamentary character of an instrument is apparent on its face, it is the duty of a court to give it effect as a will. Zell's Est., 329 Pa. 312. 

A written declaration of money due held not testamentary. Alfieri v. Dinio, 20 West. 126.

A jury's finding as to animus testandi is conclusive, and should not be disturbed by the hearing judge.

Where the validity of the will is disputed the right of the contestants to a trial by jury depends on the strength of their evidence and to determine that, the Orphans' Court must hear and weigh the proofs as a whole, and in so far as the testimony of the proponent of the will is not inherently unreasonable or improbable the judge may consider it in weighing the evidence. 

Even though contestant's evidence, standing alone, would be sufficient to justify an issue devisavit vel non, it will not be awarded if proponent's evidence is so strong as to make clear the fact that, in conscience, a chancellor could not sustain a verdict against the will.

Where a substantial dispute exists on a material point of fact concerning the status of an alleged will, and the evidence is of such weight as to support a verdict on either side, the court is bound to grant an issue devisavit vel non. 

If the testimony, however, is such that, after a fair trial, the court would feel constrained to set aside any verdict against a will as contrary to the manifest weight of the evidence, it cannot be said that a dispute has arisen, such as is necessary to require the granting of an issue to the common pleas. A will is invalid where it appears that it was executed as a direct result of a partial insanity or monomania under which the testator was laboring at the very time the will was made, that the testator's delusion was the moving cause of the disposition, and that if it had not existed the will would have been different; and this is so although the general capacity of the testator is unimpeached. 

A delusion which will render invalid a will executed as the direct result of it is an insane belief or a mere figment of the imagination a belief in the existence of something which does not exist and which no rational person, in the absence of evidence, would believe to exist. Leedom Est., 347 Pa. 180.

Where one indicates a general understanding of the disposition he desires to make of his property or estate such person has testamentary capacity. 

One who knows and understands the disposition he chooses to make of his estate is competent to make a will, though he may be incompetent to transact business, for less capacity is required to make a will than is usually required for ordinary business transactions.

Neither old age nor its infirmties, including untidy habits, partial loss of memory, inability to recognize acquaintances, incoherent speech, will deprive a person of the right to dispose of his own property, and mere feebleness of intellect or memory, whether natural or due to old age, sickness or other cause, is not itself sufficient to invalidate a will.

Where the evidence shows that the testator was addicted to the use of intoxicating liquors and was frequently under its influence, such evidence is insufficient to establish incapacity to make a will where the scrivener swore that when he received instructions for the will and when it was executed, testator was perfectly sober. Wonn v. McConnon, 1 Sch. Reg. 54.

Evidence that testator was judicially declared a lunatic without lucid intervals and that he was committed to a hospital for the insane, is prima facie evidence but not conclusive of a lack of testamentary capacity. 

Delusions will not destroy testamentary capacity unless they dictate or substantially affect the provisions of the will. Duncan's Contested Will, 147 Super. 133. 

The capacity of testator at the time of execution of the will is decisive. 

Olshefski's Est., 337 Pa. 420 rev'g 14 Northumb. 106.

Evidence of forgetfulness, characteristic of old age, or delusions irrelevant to the disposition of the property, do not preclude testamentary capacity. 

Sassaman Est., 36 North. 348.

Mere feebleness of intellect or weakness of memory due to old age, sickness, drunkenness, or other cause, is not of itself sufficient to invalidate a will. 

Confer's Est., 2 Cam. 106.

On an appeal from the probate of decedent's will, evidence was presented showing that he had been partially paralyzed by a "stroke," that he was forgetful and could not remember names of relatives, etc. However, by applying the usual test of testamentary capacity as fixed by a long line of decisions, the contestant showed nothing to indicate that the decedent did not understand the nature of the act he was performing in executing the will, or that he did not know what property he had, or the persons who were the natural objects of his bounty and whom he wished to benefit. Morris's Est., 21 Wash. 120.

As to sufficient averments of incapacity, see Schaffer's Est., 47 Dauph. 194. 

Exceptions to a decree of the orphans' court dismissing an appeal from the probate of a writing as the will of decedent and refusing an issue devisavit vel non were dismissed, where from reliable evidence there was no time prior to the signing of the will, at the time of the signing, and until her death that testatrix was not competent and capable of making her will. Racy's Est., 87 P. L. J. 209. 

28 Brennan's Est., 312 Pa. 335.

In order to constitute undue influence sufficient to void a will, there must be imprisonment of the body or mind, fraud, or threats, or misrepresentation, or circumvention, or inordinate flattery, or physical or moral coercion, to such a degree as to prejudice the mind of the testator, to destroy his free agency and to operate as a present restraint upon him in the making of the will. Shuey v. Shuey, 340 Pa. 27; Royer's Est., 339 Pa. 423; Olshefski's Est., 337 Pa. 420, rev'g 14 Northumb. 106; Wetzel v. Edwards, 340 Pa. 121; Sassaman Est., 36 

North. 348; Geho's Est., 33 Berks 43 af'd in 340 Pa. 412; Mohler's Est., 343 

Pa. 299; Buck's Est., 53 Dauph. 412.

There is no public policy condemning the receipt of a bequest by one who stood in a fiduciary relationship to the giver. Mohler's Est., 343 Pa. 299.

Where a will is properly executed in every particular, a presumption of testamentary capacity and lack of undue influence arises, compelling evidence to upset the will, unless it appears that the testator for some time prior to its execution was mentally incapable of transacting business, in which event the burden of proof is on the proponent of the will. Cressman Est., 346 Pa. 400.

The fact that the will in question was executed on February 2, 1940 and the decedent did not attempt to change it during the months intervening between that date and the date of her death on December 25, 1940, militates against the idea of undue influence. Buck's Est., 53 Dauph. 412.

A will attacked on grounds of testamentary incapacity and undue influence will be admitted to probate where contestant presents no testimony of a weakened mental condition of the testatrix at the time of the making of the will, excepting as such condition may be inferred from isolated occurrences and the general condition of the testatrix during the six years immediately preceding her death.

Nor will avail testimony that testatrix was at times bewildered on the street and did not immediately recognize her friends.

Mere solicitation on the part of a beneficiary is not enough to establish undue 2

§ 30 

influence; nor are slight circumstances which might tend to create suspicion. 

Robins' Est., 7 Northumb. 181.

The declarations of a testator have no force in establishing the substantive fact of undue influence. Geho's Est., 33 Berks 43, af'd in 340 Pa. 412.

Kindly care and solicitous attention do not amount to undue influence. 

Olshefski's Est., 337 Pa. 420 rev'g 14 Northumb. 106.

It was not undue influence when a legatee persuaded the testator not to raise her legacy but, instead, to increase the legacies to contestant's children. Morris' 

Est., 21 Wash. 120.

The averments of the petition are insufficient where there is no allegation that the undue influence procured the execution of the will, or that respondent made these statements. Hintz's Est., 31 Berks 323.

Details of facts and circumstances must be given. Schaffer's Est., 47 Dauph. 194. 

An issue devisavit vel non was refused, where there was not sufficient evidence to sustain petitioner's averments of improper influence on the part of either of the parties so charged or by any other person, and the failure to produce evidence of mental incapacity and undue influence was manifest. Racy's Est., 87 P. L. J. 209. 

If there is nothing in the evidence to support a finding that the beneficiary drew the will or suggested that it be drawn or that she be named beneficiary, a presumption of undue influence, theretofore existing due to the confidential relationship between the testatrix and the beneficiary, would be overcome. Wonn v. McConnon, 2 Sch. Reg. 54.

Where a petition on appeal from probate on the ground of undue influence alleges in substance that the decedent's mind was imprisoned in false and fraudulent representations, with the effect that the execution of the will and codicil were not the acts of the decedent but of another person, the charges will warrant the granting of an issue, and the respondent will be required to file an answer. 

Hintz's Est., 32 Berks 85. 

28a Confidential relation appears when the circumstances make it certain the parties do not deal on equal terms, but on the one side there is an overmastering influence, or, on the other, weakness, dependence or trust, justifiably reposed. 

Wetzel v. Edwards, 340 Pa. 121.

Where there was not a confidential relationship as a conclusion of law, and the evidence does not establish one, it cannot be held that there was any confidential relationship between the decedent and the residuary legatee. Buck's Est., 53 

Dauph. 412.

When a legatee, a stranger to the blood and in a confidential relation to the testatrix, whose mental and physical faculties are seriously impaired, receives the bulk of her estate to the practical exclusion of the natural objects of her bounty, there arises a presumption of undue influence brought to bear on testatrix, and the burden of proof rests on the beneficiary to overthrow this presumption.

A confidential relationship existed between petitioner and testatrix, where she handled all financial transactions, was the medium through whom testatrix conducted or attempted to conduct her correspondence, slept in the same room and was able to choose for testatrix her doctor, her lawyer, and the witnesses to the purported will.

An issue devisavit vel non was denied, when to sustain a verdict in favor of the will now proposed as a substitute for the probated will, credibility must be imputed where there is none at any of the vital turning points of the case and the good reputation of the scrivener necessary to exonerate the beneficiary, has been lost, must be assumed to exist. Schwartz's Est., 88 P. L. J. 295, in 340 Pa. 170. which af'd

A man may, however, be mentally so disabled as to have no earning capacity and yet be competent to make a will. Where the draftsman of the will is an attorney and acquainted with the testator and his opinion of capacity is supported by the subscribing witnesses, it makes a case for proponent which requires strong evidence to overcome. McBride's Est., 6 Cam. 116.

Where undue influence and incompetency do not appear, and the relation between the parties is not one ordinarily known as confidential in law, the evidence to sustain a confidential relation must be certain; it cannot arise from suspicion or from infrequent or unrelated acts. Minnick v. Johnstone, 342 Pa. 17. 

Where the charge is that undue influence has been exerted on a strong and free mind, nothing short of direct, clear and convincing proof of fraud or coercion will avail. Cressman Est., 346 Pa. 400.

In a proceeding to set aside the probate of a will, in which it appeared that the will had been prepared for decedent, a weak-minded person, by proponent, not of her own blood, without any request from her to do so, and that, although the will embodied the dominent thought of decedent's weakened mentality, the desire to be buried beside her husband, the proponent was made the sole beneficiary of her estate, it was held that on the testimony of proponent and of the witnesses called by him, when considered with the testimony as to the decedent's mental condition, the probate of the will should have been revoked. Where the evidence showed trips and visits from home made by decedent and a beneficiary in his will, but there was nothing but unveritable and unbelievable and unsupported testimony to prove there were any improper relations between them on these visits, the court refused to vacate the probate of a will. The presumption of undue influence does not arise from such conduct. Wright's Est., 91 P. L. J. 401, 57 York 117.

To set aside a will on the ground of undue influence, where the decedent's testamentary capacity is admitted or established, the evidence must be clear and strong; mere opinions or suspicions or belief not founded on facts testified to will not be sufficient. Royer's Est., 339 Pa. 423; Cressman Est., 346 Pa. 400.

As to facts held insufficient to set aside a gift inter vivos by a mother to her daughter, see Montgomery Trust Co. v. Griscom, 27 Del. 437.

In a proceeding upon an issue as to the validity of a will awarded by the orphans' court on the questions of forgery and undue influence, the evidence was insufficient as a matter of law to establish that testator was unduly influenced by the fifteen-year-old girl beneficiary of all his property or by her father, who was named executor. Angeluzzi v. Perotti, 330 Pa. 322. 

38 In order to constitute undue influence sufficient to void a will, there must be imprisonment of the body or mind, fraud or threats, or misrepresentations, or circumvention, or inordinate flattery, or physical or moral coercion, to such a degree as to prejudice the mind of the testator, to destroy his free agency, and to operate as a present restraint upon him in the making of the will. At the trial of an issue to determine the validity of a will, the judge sits as a chancellor; the evidence is addressed quite as much to him as to the jury, and he cannot permit the jury to do what he, as a chancellor, would not do. 

Where the trial judge feels that the ends of justice call for a verdict against the will, or he is so uncertain on this point that he could in good conscience support a finding either way on one or more of the controlling issues involved, the question should be submitted to a jury, and unless, on re-examination after verdict, the evidence proves insufficient to support their finding, that conclusion should stand, even though its effect be to set aside the will. Campbell v. Campbell, 146 Super. 58.

On a petition for the awarding of an issue d. v. n., it is the duty of the hearing judge, after weighing the evidence impartially, to refuse to present the question to the jury, unless he feels the ends of justice call for a verdict against the will, or he is so uncertain on this point that he could conscientiously sustain a finding either way on one or more of the controlling issues involved. Cressman 

Est., 346 Pa. 400.

The function of a judge of an orphans' court in hearing a will contest is to determine whether the testimony reveals the presence of a substantial dispute upon a material matter of fact: if the verdict of a jury either sustaining or setting aside the will could not be sustained, the grant of an issue to a jury would obviously be a useless formality, and under such circumstances the judge is required to sustain or set aside the will, as the case may be. 

Where, upon an appeal from the probate of a will charging forgery, a substantial dispute upon a material matter of fact exists, the case must be submitted to the jury, even though contestants produce expert testimony to the effect that the signature is a forgery and proponent's expert testifies merely that he is unable to determine whether the signature is genuine or forged. Zolyan's Est., 44 D. & C. 81. 

A new trial will not be granted where there is no material basis for holding that a trial judge abused the discretion lodged in him in the examination of witnesses as to their interest in the case. Wonn v. McConnon, 2 Sch. Reg. 54. 

44a The orphans' court sitting in banc to pass upon motions for new trial and judgment n. o. v. following a jury trial in an issue devisavit vel non under the Act of July 1, 1937, P. L. 2665, does so in a dual capacity: first, to sit with the trial judge to hear and dispose of the motions and to direct proper judgment to be entered on the verdict; and second, to apply the law to the facts found and enter an appropriate definitive decree. Plott's Est., 33 D. &. C. 490, af'd in 335 Pa. 81. 

45 See Morgan's Est., 90 P. L. J. 55 (s. c. 146 Super. 79).

In reviewing a judgment non obstante veredicto in favor of the proponents of a will, following the verdict of a jury on an issue devisavit vel non, the question for the appellate court to decide is not whether it would have reached the same result had it been acting as chancellor, but rather whether a judicial mind, on due consideration of the evidence as a whole, could reasonably have reached the conclusion of the chancellor. Shuey v. Shuey, 340 Pa. 27. 

On appeal from a decree of the orphans' court, admitting a will to probate or refusing to do so, the question before the appellate court is whether there is evidence to support the decree. Schwartz's Est., 340 Pa. 170, af'g 88 P. L. J. 295.

47 In the trial of an issue devisavit vel non before a jury, the subscribing witnesses to the alleged will are deemed the court's witnesses and may be freely examined and cross examined by both parties, without either one being bound by any adverse testimony given by such witnesses. 

The attendance of the subscribing witnesses at the trial should be required by the court, if necessary, upon the request of proponent or contestant. 

Unless the subscribing witnesses are deceased or their absence from the jurisdiction satisfactorily established, decedent's signature to a will may not properly be proved, in the trial of an issue devisavit vel non, by opinion testimony. 

Plotts' Est., 335 Pa. 81, af'g 33 D. & C. 490.

Subscribing witnesses are not regarded as ordinary witnesses, but rather as witnesses of the court. Szmahl's Est., 335 Pa. 89; Orlady's Est., 336 Pa. 369.

The testimony of handwriting experts that a will offered for probate is a forgery, corroborated by probative facts and circumstances, admissible under ordinary rules of evidence, may be sufficient to overcome the testimony of those claiming to be subscribing witnesses to the questioned document and to support a finding of forgery. 

In such case, it is sufficient if the corroborative evidence is the most nearly positive and direct evidence which the nature of the case will admit. Young Est., 347 Pa. 457.

Where the subscribing witnesses testify the sufficiency of the execution is properly raised. Orlady's Est., 336 Pa. 369. 

48 Where a will is properly executed, a presumption of testamentary capacity and lack of undue influence arises, and the contestants must adduce compelling evidence to upset the will, since the law favors its validity. Olshefski's Est., 337 Pa. 420 rev'g 14 Northumb. 106.

In the absence of evidence to the contrary, a presumption that the testatrix was mentally competent is raised where the court has before it, as part of record, the proof of execution of the will by the subscribing witnesses before the Register of Wills, although at the time of the trial such witnesses are unavailable. Wonn v. McConnon, 2 Sch. Reg. 54.

In a will contest, involving the testamentary capacity of one who had been judicially declared a lunatic, it was not error for the trial judge to refuse to charge that the burden was on the proponents to establish testamentary capacity by evidence of a most exceptional kind and character. Duncan's Contested Will, 147 Super. 133. 

49 The burden of proving lack of testamentary capacity is upon the one who contests the probate of a will. Sassaman Est., 36 North. 348; Trump's Est., 47 Dauph. 433.

The burden of showing that decedent was suffering from an insane delusion at the time he executed his will and that it controlled his violation and destroyed his freedom of action in disposing of his estate is on the contestant. Leedom 

Est., 347 Pa. 180.

Where the testimony before the court establishes a prima facie case of the execution of a will, the burden of showing that it was not executed shifts to the contestants. Davis's Est., 1 Sch. Reg. 211.

Burden of proving execution and validity of a will is met by offering in evidence register of wills' record of probate proceedings. And where contestants fail to produce evidence that raises doubt as to genuineness of signature to a will, appeal from decree of register admitting will to probate cannot be sustained. 

Thus where contestants attempted to prove forgery of signature of testator by claiming that one having no interest in the estate had allegedly said he had put the signature upon the will, but who called by contestants, denied such statement, but knowing the handwriting, verified decedent's signature. Kelpsh's 

Est., 34 Luz. 433.

On appeal from the register's order probating a will, the proponent may stand upon the decree of probate as sufficient to sustain the will unless testimony is produced by either party or at the instance of the court, but if such testimony

§ 31 

is produced the probate is not to be accorded any evidential value except by agreement of the parties; where no testimony whatever is offered, the probate stands as a binding judicial decision 'in rem. Szmahl's Est., 325 Pa. 89.

In the trial of an issue devisavit vel non before a jury in the orphans' court, as well as in appeals from probate to the orphans' court, the proponent's burden of proving a prima facie case is satisfied by the introduction in evidence of the probate record, and the contestant must then offer proof to overcome the prima facie case thereby established. Plott's Est., 335 Pa. 81, af'g 33 D. & C. 490.

Where a will has been probated the burden of proof is cast upon the contestant. 

Harrison's Est., 6 Som. 372.

Where a person has testamentary capacity but is so weak, physically or mentally, as to be susceptible to undue influence and a substantial part of his estate is left to one occupying a confidential relation to him, the burden is upon the latter to show that no improper influence controlled the making of the will. 

Schwartz's Est., 340 Pa. 170, af'g 88 P. L. J. 295.

But in a case where the decedent's testamentary capacity is conceded and there is no evidence of weakened intellect, the burden is upon those asserting undue influence to prove it even where the bulk of the estate is left to one occupying a confidential relation. Buechley's Est., 5 Northumb. 221.

Where the proponents offer the record of probate of a will in evidence, and no evidence is adduced assailing the validity of the execution of the will, its execution is established; and the mere fact that a scintilla of evidence is adduced to show undue influence will not necessitate any additional proof of execution. 

Where a will has been duly admitted to probate, and a subsequent appeal is taken on the ground of undue influence, the question of undue influence must be supported by testimony taken de novo without according any evidential value to the probate record; but as to execution and testamentary capacity, the probate record remains conclusive. Geho's Est., 33 Berks 43 af'd in 340 Pa. 412.

Where the testatrix has testamentary capacity, the burden of proving undue influence is on the contestant. Buck's Est., 53 Dauph. 412.

An appeal from the probate of a writing as the will of her brother on the ground of mental incompetency and the undue influence over decedent by the beneficiaries named therein was dismissed, where the burden of evidence did not sustain the charge of meretricious relations and there was no credible evidence that decedent's will was imprisoned or that his freedom was controlled by anyone, but that he was a man of ability and possessed of full mental capacity. Wright's 

Est., 91 P. L. J. 401, 57 York 117.

A person, who either prepares a will, or under whose advice it is written, or who is in a confidential relation to the testator, and who receives a substantial legacy thereunder, has the burden of proving testamentary capacity and showing that the testator acted with full knowledge of his estate and that the transaction was fair and conscionable. Baranowski's Est., 43 Lack. 87.

The effect of a prior adjudication of testator's incompetency to care for his property is to cast upon the proponent of the will the burden of showing capacity at the time of making and executing the will, and where this burden is met to the satisfaction of the court, the will is entitled to probate. Mohler's Est., 343 Pa. 299. 

Where there is evidence in the record which supports the finding on which an order denying probate to a paper was based, it is immaterial who offered the evidence or had the burden of proof. Trevaskis' Est., 345 Pa. 525. 

50 An appeal from an advisory judgment of the Court of Common Pleas on a feigned issue awarded by the orphans' court must be quashed without prejudice to the right to take an appeal after the entry of a final decree in the orphans' court.

Where the issue awarded concerns the status of an alleged will or testamentary writing, or the decision of a fact upon which the jurisdiction of the orphans' court depends, the judgment entered on the verdict in the court of common pleas, so long as it stands undisturbed, is binding on the orphans' court. 

In all other cases of feigned issues, the judgment does not bind the orphans' court; it is merely advisory. Rothermel v. Rothermel, 345 Pa. 139. 

53 Where a case is submitted to a jury upon clearly insufficient evidence, it is the duty of the appellate court to reverse. Olshefski's Est., 337 Pa. 420 rev'g 

14 Northumb. 106.

For a detailed statement of the circumstances under which a new trial will not be granted on an issue d. v. n. See Zolyan's Est. (No. 2), 46 D. & C. 74.

Declarations of testator tending to show undue influence or mental weakness must be supported by other evidence. Confer's Est., 2 Cam. 106; Freeman's 

Est., 43 Lack. 65.

Opinion evidence of experts, standing alone, was held to be insufficient to sustain a finding of forgery in the face of direct and credible evidence of disinterested subscribing witnesses who testified they saw the testator sign his name. 

In a will contest alleging fraud, undue influence and forgery, it was held that contestant's evidence was insufficient to require the granting of an issue devisavit vel non. 

Porter's Est., 341 Pa. 476.

Where the proponent of a will who testified in a will contest before the Orphans' Court died before trial of the issue granted in the Common Pleas Court, it was not error to permit defendants in the issue to have read in evidence a portion of his testimony with the understanding that plaintiff be permitted to offer any other parts of that testimony in explanation of that offered by defendants.

Where the issue was the date of the will offered for probate, there being an erasure on the paper where the date appeared, and the proponent was the executor and a beneficiary under the will, a statement made by the proponent, now dead, to the effect that he had in his possession a will "made" by the testatrix a year before the date appearing on the will as offered, was a declaration against interest and admissible as substantive evidence of the actual date of the will; its effect was not limited to impeaching the credibility of proponent's testimony. 

Where the plaintiff offered in evidence without objection testimony of oral declarations made by testatrix subsequent to the date of the alleged will and several months before her death, testimony of declarations made by her in the days just before her death was admissible in rebuttal. Berks Co. Tr. Co. v. 

Boyer, 30 Berks 225.

In an issue devisavit vel non, declarations of the decedent before or after the date of will are admissible to corroborate direct proof of its execution. McAlarney v. Ziegler, 33 Luz. 361.

After weighing the evidence, in the trial of an issue, the court may refuse to submit the issues to the jury, and he should refuse, unless he feels the ends of justice call for a verdict against the will or he is so uncertain on the point that he could not conscientiously sustain the finding either way. 

Expert opinions that testator was incompetent cannot prevail against positive statements of witnesses, who were present when the will was made, to the effect that testator knew what she was doing and was mentally competent to transact business. Wonn v. McConnon, 2 Sch. Reg. 54.

The weight of opinion evidence depends upon the cogency of the reasons given. 

Expert testimony, whether given by physicians or others, is of no value when opposed to established facts. 

A variance in a signature is not necessarily proof of its being a forgery. Dissimilitude may be occasioned by a variety of circumstances, by the state of health and spirits of the writer, by the material, by his position, or his hurry or care. 

Davis' Est., 1 Sch. Reg. 211. 

A testator's unjust prejudices against others have no relation to his testamentary capacity and an opinion by a doctor based principally upon the converse assumption is entitled to little weight.

An expert witness' expression of opinion does not restrict the court's exercise of judgment, and it is for the court to determine the weight to be given to the opinion of the expert. Mohler's Est., 343 Pa. 299.

On the trial of an issue devisavit vel non, in which the one specific question of fact was whether or not the names of certain legatees were written in the will, which was holographic, prior to itse execution and attestation, it was not error to admit on behalf of the proponents testimony by experts as to the genuineness of the handwriting in the will.

It was not an abuse of discretion for the trial judge to exclude expert evidence on handwriting on behalf of defendants offered in sur-rebuttal on the ground

§§ 31-33  

that the evidence proposed, was a part of defendants' case in chief and not in sur-rebuttal. Campbell v. Campbell, 146 Super. 58. 

Evidence that a proponent has not only advised the preparation of but has actually prepared, a will of an illiterate decedent to whom he stated that it was only a scrap of paper and under which he is to receive a substantial legacy, is sufficient to warrant the grant of an issue devisavit vel non to test decedent's testamentary capacity. Baranowski's Est., 43 Lack. 87. 

Where a will has been written by a lawyer without interference by any one, inference is that it was properly made by one of testamentary capacity, and such inference to be overcome only by clear, definite and weighty facts irreconcileable with possession of testamentary capacity. Baynack's Est., 36 Luz. 121.

An appeal from the probate by the register of wills of an alleged last will and testament of decedent was sustained and his order was vacated by the orphans' court, where the testimony fell far short of sustaining the validity of the probated writing. The act of assembly must be strictly followed and the evidence of each of two witnesses must be complete as to what took place and that everything was done that is required by law.

Evidence was insufficient to prove a signature by testator's mark, where there were three persons who subscribed their names as witnesses to the probated paper, but the evidence of no two of them was in agreement on the proof; nor was there any evidence to explain why decedent did not write her name at the end of the will, and it was not contended she was prevented by the extremity of her last sickness from doing so.

In a contested probate of an alleged will, a witness was incompetent under the Act of May 23, 1887, P. L. 158, where, if the will was valid, she would have taken the largest part of the estate. The exception to the general rule applies where both parties to the controversy claim by devolution or devise and not where one claims by devolution and the other by devise under the will. Polinchuk's Est., 90 P. L. J. 579. 

Where, on the trial of an issue to determine whether or not the signature on the alleged will of a decedent was the genuine signature of the decedent, a witness's "guessing" and "supposing" the date in question was not prejudicial to contestants. Bridy's Est., 339 Pa. 70.

LETTERS TESTAMENTARY. 

32. RIGHT TO LETTERS, Competency of executor.56 RENUNCIATION. 

56 An objection that an executor was not qualified to act as such because of an interest adverse to that of the estate was properly overruled, where it appeared that no petition for removal of the executor and no objections were made until after the executor had administered the estate and filed its final account, and that the estate had not suffered any prejudice. Purman's Est., 334 Pa. 238.

Where there is antagonism between parties otherwise entitled a disinterested person will be appointed. Huffman's Est., 3 Mon. 19.

While an executor or administrator should resign if he finds it necessary to press a personal claim against his decedent's estate, his claim will not be dismissed because of his failure to do so, where he was only one of three executors and where the proof of his claim was sufficient, both as to character and weight, to sustain it, even assuming that a confidential relationship existed between him and his decedent. Rosenthal's Est., 35 D. & C. 117, aff'd in 335 Pa. 49. 33.

35. ANCILLARY LETTERS. 

Necessity for ancillary letters.70 

Procedure when ancillary letters have been granted in other jurisdictions and estate is insolvent.70a 

Procedure here where ancillary letters were not granted elsewhere t, and executrix here has sold foreign real estate.7ob 

Normal distribution under ancillary letters.70c 

70 The personal assets of a decedent resident in a foreign state may not be removed from this state by the domiciliary fiduciary, but will be administered here by an ancillary fiduciary so that creditors and others in interest may not be driven to another state for satisfaction of their claims; from the ancillary, to the domiciliary fiduciary will pass only the balance of assets not so consumed. 

Gates' Est., 31 Berks 316.

A nonresident may properly take out letters of administration in Pennsylvania for the purpose of instituting a wrongful death action in accordance with Pa. 

R. C. P. 2202 and 2206 without having first taken out letters in the State of domicile, even though decedent left no other property in Pennsylvania. Pearson v. Conover, 47 D. & C. 387. 

70a Domiciliary administration of insolvent decedent's estate in Pennsylvania, with ancillary administrations in New York and Delaware. Partial account filed

§§ 35, 36  

in Pennsylvania of Pennsylvania assets, before assets in ancillary jurisdictions administered. Claims of all creditors in all jurisdictions admitted. Question raised whether entire balance for distribution should be awarded back to executors pending complete liquidation of assets in all jurisdictions, or whether partial distribution should be awarded presently, and if so, whether only to Pennsylvania creditors or also to foreign creditors. Held, partial distribution awarded to Pennsylvania and foreign creditors.

In so holding the court laid down the following rules: 

1. Where the entire estate is insolvent, the court of the domiciliary administration will as far as possible marshal the assets there so as to secure to all creditors a pro rata percentage. 

2. The court of the domiciliary administration having before it all claims of all creditors in all jurisdictions, a present award of a pro rata percentage to all creditors will maintain equality. 

3. The rule applied in solvent estates where Pennsylvania is the ancillary juris diction, that local creditors will be paid out of local assets and the balance remitted to the domiciliary jurisdiction, is to protect Pennsylvania creditors by avoiding the necessity of their going to a foreign jurisdiction; it is not designed to prefer local creditors and is no solution to achieve equality in an insolvent estate. 

4. The actual award of partial distribution to foreign creditors will not be suspended on the grounds that an ancillary jurisdiction might order distribution to its local creditors out of assets there, ahead of Pennsylvania creditors. Equality among all creditors cannot be accomplished unless each jurisdiction bases compu tation of allowable percentage on claims of all creditors, not solely on claims of its local creditors, and it is not to be supposed that if Pennsylvania marshals the assets there, the other jurisdictions will not do likewise. Maxwell's Est., 55 Montg. 154. 

70b The disposition of the proceeds of an insolvent resident decedent's real estate in Virginia sold by executrix in compliance with law of Virginia and in her capacities as executrix and as sole beneficiary, is governed by the law of Virginia.

The duties of an executrix to creditors are greater than to herself as sole beneficiary, and she should have raised ancillary administration in Virginia and should have accounted there for proceeds of sale of decedent's real estate. 

Whether proceeds of sale of Virginia real estate, held by executrix but not accounted for, are held by her as executrix or as sole beneficiary, is of no con sequence, as under Virginia law, which controls, the proceeds are subject to the lien of decedent's debts in either case.

Although no ancillary administration raised in Virginia, and proceeds of sale of Virginia real estate not accounted for in Pennsylvania, the proceeds are within the reach of the orphans' court by virtue of filing of executrix's account and admission that she holds proceeds. Being under duty as executrix to possess herself of proceeds for benefit of creditors, her possession will be regarded as in capacity as executrix and she will be surcharged for failure to account. Fox's 

Est., 55 Montg. 110. 

70c The general rule is that an orphans' court is an ancillary administration, where there are no local creditors or where all local creditors have been paid, should direct the balance to be paid to the administrator of the domicile. However, this rule is not absolute or inflexible. The court may exercise its discretion to distribute directly to the foreign legatee or creditor is an ancillary administration if, in the circumstances, it deems such distribution proper. Mamato's Est., 90 P. L. J. 74.

49. JURISDICTION IN GENERAL. 

Procedure before the register.45

Effect of refusal by register to revoke letters.45a 

45 Where it appeared that decedent's wife had executed a renunciation of her right to letters of administration in favor of a trust company, and that no credible evidence in support of the allegation of her petition that the renunciation was secured by misrepresentation was produced before the register of wills at the hearing had upon the petition, it was held that the register's refusal to revoke the letters of administration would not be disturbed. 

On appeal from a decree of the register of wills it is to be presumed that both the register's findings of fact and conclusions of law are correct. 

The findings of the register at the conclusion of a hearing upon a petition to revoke letters of administration have the force of a jury verdict and, upon appeal, can be set aside only when clearly against the weight of the evidence. 

After an administrator has performed all its duties and has filed an account, which is awaiting audit, no useful purpose can be served by revocation of the letters of administration. Bechtold's Est., 57 Montg. 295, 55 York 105. 

45a A decision of the register of wills refusing revocation of letters of admin. istration, applied for on the ground that the administrator is not in fact the husband of decedent as represented by him, is not conclusive upon distribution in the orphans' court of the issue of the relationship between the administrator and decedent.

Under the Register of Wills Act of 1917, which authorizes the register to revoke letters granted by him to persons who are not the next of kin, such power is merely permissive. Boytor's Est., 130 Super. 591.

An administrator is not only a trustee for the benefit of creditors but for the widow and children of the decedent.

It was not an abuse of discretion for the court below to revoke letters of administration, granted upon the petition of a judgment creditor of the decedent, where it appeared that the petition for the appointment of the administrator stated that the address of the widow and children of decedent was unknown although the administrator and the judgment creditor knew that the widow was represented by counsel and gave no notice to counsel nor made any request for the client's address; that the administrator failed to advertise the grant of letters, that the administrator failed to comply with a rule of court requiring the widow or children to be notified of the right to an exemption; and that the administrator failed to prepare and file an inventory within thirty days from the grant of the administration. CHAPTER IX. 

METHOD OF PROCEDURE. 

THE PRESUMPTION OF DEATH. 

At end of seven years." 68 

Procedure not exclusive." 70 

68 Where a person has been absent and unheard of for seven years, the presumption of continuance of life ceases at the end of that period. Meadville &c. 

Ass'n. v. Haskell, 40 D. & C. 145; Federal Land Bank v. Haskell, 24 Erie 140.

The presumption of death as used in the Act is an inference as to the existence of one fact not certainly known; it is a belief on incomplete proof; it is a presumption of law, not one of fact.

The presumption of death contemplated by the act is raised by the absence of a person from his domicile unheard of for seven or more years. Absence in this connection means that the person is not at the place of his domicile and that his actual residence is unknown. Wesner's Est., 7 Sch. Reg. 103, af'd in 139 

Super. 314. 

70 The Act of April 27, 1927, P. L. 425, amending the Fiduciaries Act of 

June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, does not provide an exclusive procedure for determining whether death of an individual is to be presumed from unexplained absence, but the common-law rules upon that subject are still applicable in cases arising in the courts of common pleas. Meadville &c. Ass'n. v. Haskell, 40 D. & C. 145. 

55. PROCEDURE FOR ORIGINAL LETTERS. 

Right of action.74 

74 The right to institute proceedings to have a person declared a presumed decedent is limited to those designated in Section 6a of the Fiduciaries Act. 

The provisions of the Fiduciaries Act relating to presumed decedents do not distinguish between an explained and an unexplained absence. 

The Act only provides for a decree of presumption of death; it does not call for a finding of death as a fact. Wesner's Est., 7 Sch. Reg. 103, af'd in 139 

Super. 314.

Sec. 6(a) of the Fiduciaries Act has now been amended by the Act of August 5, 1941, (P. L. 826), which has added the proviso "That in any case in which the total value of the estate of the presumed decedent, whether real or personal, is not in excess of five hundred dollars ($500), no master shall be appointed and no advertisement shall be necessary as may be required by any of the provisions of this section, and the said court in such case shall have the right to declare such presumed decedent legally dead upon the basis of such evidence and testimony as it may require to be produced before it by the said petitioner.''

1 Of a legatee: 

Where several promissory notes made by two of testator's sons payable to the testator were found among testator's possessions, and no further facts appear to explain their existence, the accounting executor properly deducted the amount

of the notes from the two sons' distributive shares under the will, it appearing that the notes were recoverable at the time of the testator's death, and were not disputed when the inventory and appraisement were made. 

Although it is a well-established rule that the Statute of Limitations is not tolled by the death of either party to a transaction, nevertheless where a debt owed by a legatee is recoverable by a testator at the time of his death, the debt may properly be deducted from the legacy even at a date when the Statute would be a bar to a suit on the debt, the Statute merely barring the remedy and not destroying the obligation. Confer's Est., 33 Berks 64.

Petitioner, after a contest over decedent's will having been appointed executor thereof, was entitled to receive a check for the funeral benefits due a deceased member of a labor union. 39a Where, after the sale by an administrator c. t. a. of certain shares of stock, appraised as of no value, at public auction for $100, and payment of the consideration, but before delivery of the certificates, an offer of $550 is received for the same stock, but the offer is withdrawn before the administrator has been authorized to accept it, the administrator's petition for a citation to show cause why he should not sell to the second bidder must be refused. 42 An executor is not liable for loss to the estate resulting merely from a mistake of law or from an error of judgment.

In the determination of what is business judgment, too much stress must not be laid on retrospection. 

Failure of an executor to first foreclose on mortgages held by a decedent and to purchase the properties upon which they were secured and then sell the real estate, as against liquidation of the mortgages at public sale, did not under the circumstances in this case, indicate failure to exercise sound business judgment or lack of prudence on the part of the executor so as to require that the executor be surcharged for loss on the mortgages. Martin's Est., 135 Super. 136.

Where testatrix's net estate at the time of her death was insufficient to pay all pecuniary legacies in full, and the principal assets consisted of shares of high-grade bank stock, the market value of which had declined sharply and which shares the executor in the exercise of common skill, caution and prudence retained for more than one year after the date of testatrix's death, and thereafter the legatees, all of whom were sui juris, acquiesced in their continued retention, it was held, under all the circumstances present, that the executor should not be surcharged, at the instance of the legatees, for an eventual loss on the sale of the shares of stock. Shipley's Est. (No. 1), 337 Pa. 571.

An exception to a decree of distribution in the orphans' court that specified stocks had depreciated in value and that accountant be surcharged with the loss resulting from the failure to liquidate them within a reasonable time after the death of decedent, was dismissed, where executrix was not careless or negligent and under the existing circumstances personal property in her hands should have been held rather than sold at a sacrifice. 

It is not required of fiduciaries that they be endowed with superior and exceptional judgment in the performance of their duties. Mistakes in judgment when made by executors or administrators using ordinary care and ability and after due consideration of the questions involved will not render them liable for unfortunate results. Hughes's Est., 87 P. L. J. 1.

An executor properly performs his duty when he makes prompt sale of the assets of the estate, and cannot justly be charged with fraud or gross carelessness in the sale of the assets at their inventory value in the absence of any evidence that the prices obtained were not the fair market value at the time of the sale. 

McLean's Est., 333 Pa. 293. 

44 Where an administratrix sells assets of an estate at private sale the burden is on her to show that the price obtained was the market value of the article sold. 

It is the duty of an administrator to use such diligence as a man of ordinary prudence would exercise in his own affairs. Weaver's Est., 46 Lanc. 374.

An exception relating to a credit claimed for a loss on a sale of certain stock was dismissed where it appeared that the stock was sold to the highest bidder at a public sale, of which due notice was given, and there was no evidence of collusion. Matter's Est., 49 Dauph. 437. 

There is no requirement in Pennsylvania that a vendue list be filed following the sale of personal property of a decedent by auction. Roderick's Est., 3 Fay. 93.
