Where a bill in equity alleges that defendant was the survivor of six children who jointly held title to a parcel of real estate, and where plaintiff as administratrix of one of the deceased children sought to have defendant account for the rents received, it was held, under all the circumstances, that an accounting would not be ordered.

Since plaintiff sued as administratrix of a deceased child, since ordinarily an administrator has nothing to do with the rents and profits of real estate, and since there was no evidence that the personal estate was insufficient to pay the debts of the decedent, the relief sought by the plaintiff should be denied. 71aa A real estate broker's right to a commission for procuring a purchaser of property owned by an estate may be defeated by the fiduciary's duty to reject such purchaser if a better offer be received for the property before title has passed. 

A person dealing with a trustee is required to know the extent of his powers.

Clark v. Provident Trust Co., 329 Pa. 421. 

This situation has been ameliorated by the Act of July 2, 1941, (P. L. 227), which adds a proviso to clause (p) of Sec. 9 of the Orphans' Court Act of 1917, (P. L. 363) as amended, which reads as follows: "That nothing in the foregoing shall be construed to relieve executors, administrators or trustees who have entered into an agreement of sale of real estate of a decedent or any other real estate held in trust in good faith, and who prior to the time fixed for settlement thereunder have received a higher offer for such real estate, from the payment of real estate broker or broker's commissions to the broker who had procured such agreement of sale, and in the event that more than one real estate broker is entitled to commissions for said agreements of sale, then such commissions shall be equally divided between or among such real estate brokers: Provided further, That the total aggregate commissions paid shall in no event exceed five per cent of the gross consideration of the final sale." 

Where a fiduciary, after it has entered into an agreement for the sale of real estate, accepts a higher offer, the respective share of the commissions to which each broker is entitled is determined by the Act of July 2, 1941, P. L. 227; there is no duty on the part of the second purchaser or his broker to secure an agreement with the first broker for a division of the fec. 

On the acceptance of a higher offer, the obligation is on the fiduciary to reimburse the first vendee with whom it has contracted for necessary expense incurred. Alexanian v. Fidelity &c. Co., 152 Super. 23. 

The orphans' court dismissed a petition for a division of the broker's commission for the sale of real estate, where petitioners did not represent the original bidder who made the written agreement of sale. They represent a second and unsuccessful bidder whose competition forced the original bidder to increase, her offer in order to secure the property. 

The provisions of the act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, as amended, did not apply. Prior to the enactment of this act a real estate broker's commission could be defeated by the fiduciary's duty to reject the original purchaser if a better offer was received. Straight Mortgage Pool, 90 P. L. J. 603, 45 D. & C. 695. 

71b An unexecuted contract of sale under a testamentary power must always be understood to be subject to the supervision of the Orphans' Court, and so long as title has not been conveyed, possession delivered or expenditures made, the contract may be cancelled in favor of an offer more advantageous to the estate. Barbey's Est., 33 Berks 238.

A power of sale given in a will, if not limited to public or private sale, includes the power to sell at either public or private sale. 

In the exercise of a power of sale given in a will, specific personal notice to or assent by the parties interested under the will is not essential to a valid sale unless the will requires such notice; however, it would seem that such notice will, if given, avoid subsequent adverse reactions. 

The Orphans' Court has power to review, set aside and, if necessary, to order a resale of real estate under a testamentary power, for gross inadequacy of price. 

But in the exercise of this power a distinction must be drawn between agreements to sell and consummated sales. 

In agreements of sale where the price is inadequate the performance of the contract will be restrained.

In consummated sales the proper procedure, in the absence of fraud, is to make demand for surcharge at the audit of the account,

# $ 45 

or f ion Fraud vitiates a sale whether consummated or not but mere inadequacy of price is not fraud; there must be at least gross inadequacy of price to create even an inference of fraud. Fritz's Est., 7 Schuyl. Reg. 271. 

71d Apple's Est., 46 Lanc. 81, 31 D. & C. 445, 52 York 18. (Vol. I, p. 169.)

Inadequacy of price, no matter how shocking, is not sufficient to invalidate an executed contract. Hardner's Est., 21 Erie 14.

A trustee must dispose of trust property upon the most advantageous terms which it is possible for him to secure for the benefit of the estate which he represents. Good v. Capital Bank &c., 47 Dauph. 414; Clark v. Prov. Tr. Co., 329 Pa. 421.

Exception to executors' account, questioning adequacy of price received by accountants for real estate sold, was dismissed when the court, from its own knowledge and from facts represented by counsel at the audit, although without a hearing, found that the price was fair and adequate. Heckman's Est., 57

Montg. 310. 

While there is no percentage laid down as a minimum advance justifying the setting aside of a sale of real estate in favor of a second sale, in a transaction involving a price between $5,000 and $6,000, the increase should be at least 10% to warrant consideration.

The orphans' court has power to set aside an unexecuted sale of real estate under its decree, on grounds of inadequacy of price, as well as to compel executors' to make a sale. Moore's Est. (No. 2), 57 Montg. 384. 

71e The refusal of an auditing judge to surcharge an executor and trustee for failure to sell certain real estate will not be disturbed upon exceptions where there is ample evidence that the property in question was not saleable during the period he had title to it and that he had done everything that could be done to effect a sale. Conrad's Est., 32 D. & C. 677. 

71f Now authorized by the Act of July 3, 1941, (P. L. 254), Sec. 2, which added a new clause (e) to Sec. 28 of the Fiduciaries Act which reads as follows: "" (e) In all cases wherein testators shall have devised their real estate or their personal estate or any part thereof to their executors to be sold, or shall have authorized or directed such executors to sell and convey such real estate or personal estate, or shall have directed such real estate or personal estate to be sold without naming or declaring who shall sell the same, if such real estate or personal estate is sold at private sale under the directions contained in said instrument or under the authority of this act, the orphans' court having jurisdiction over such sale shall have the power to authorize and approve the sale of such real estate and personal estate or any part thereof to the executor of said will or any one of them under such terms and conditions and after such reasonable notice to legatees, heirs and other parties in interest as it may direct, and where the purchaser is the.sole executor the court may make an order directing its clerk to execute a deed for said real estate to such purchaser who shall give security and shall account for the amount of said purchase money in the settlement of his accounts to said court.' "" 

71g Where a power to sell real estate is vested in two executors, one of whom desires while the other refuses to sell, the orphans' court may, upos petition of the executor desiring to sell, and if to the best interests of the beneficiaries of the proceeds, order the real estate sold. Moore's Est. (No. 1), 57 Montg. 380. 

71h The usual procedure for one executor who desires to sell real estate, where his coexecutor refuses, to bring the issue before the orphans' court, is to file a petition for a citation on his coexecutor to show cause why the court should not order the sale. Where, however, as here, the executor desiring to sell, prepared his petition and served a copy of it on his coexecutrix on July 16th, with notice that the petition would be filed and a hearing requested in the orphans' court at the next session thereof, on August 1st, the respondent coexecutrix had due notice, full knowledge and ample time to prepare to present her side of the case. 

Under these circumstances, and as the prospective purchaser demanded possession of the real estate by August 15th, the coexecutrix's technical objections to the procedure, being obviously only for delay and to forestall the sale, will be over ruled. Moore's Est. (No. 1), 57 Montg. 380.

83 11 10 90 72 Under the provisions of section 9 of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, the orphans' court has exclusive jurisdiction to compel specific execution of a contract made by a decedent to purchase real estate. 

When the orphans' court has obtained jurisdiction over a subject matter it should apply the rules and principles of equity and dispose of an incidental question of reformation of a contract. Mellinger's Est., 334 Pa. 180, rev'g 46

73 Preliminary objections to a petition for specific performance of an oral contract to devise realty for want of jurisdiction in the orphans' court and the bar of the statute of frauds were dismissed, with leave to answer to the merits without prejudice to the right to raise the defense of the statute in that pleading.

The orphans' court has jurisdiction, under section 18, of the fiduciaries act of 

June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, to decree specific performance of an oral contract to devise real estate. It is a re-enactment of the act of February 24, 1834, P. L. 73. 

Preliminary objections is not the proper procedure to raise the bar of the statute of frauds, where respondents contended that in order to satisfy the statute the testamentary writing should have been executed contemporaneously with the contract to devise. This defense must be raised by an answer. Kuhn's 

Est., 89 P. L. J. 309. 

83 In an action based on an alleged oral contract to devise real estate, a will made soon after the alleged contract was evidence, in connection with other evidence, to show a written memorandum of the oral contract and a definite description of the real estate. 

One may enter into a valid oral or written contract to dispose by will of his property, real or personal, in a particular way, and such will is irrevocable, and the contract will be specifically enforced.

A contract to devise real estate to another must be established not only by clear and satisfactory evidence, but also by such as is direct, positive, definite and unambiguous. Where such evidence was found to be sufficient, a decree for specific performance of the contract to devise the real estate was entered. Eppley's 

Petn., Emig's Est., 53 York 153, 37 D. & C. 123.

Specific performance of a decédent's parol contract to convey real estate is not a matter of right, and will be decreed only if enforcement of the contract appears equitable under all of the facts of the case. 

Where the grant of a petition is within the discretion of the orphans' court, the application must be supported by testimony that the transaction upon which the petition was based was fair and conscionable; relief will not be granted on petition and answer where the averments admitted are too meager to enable the court to determine that question. 

The grant of an application for specific performance of a decedent's parol contract to convey real estate is dependent upon the value and condition of the property involved and the nature and character of the services alleged to constitute the consideration, and the petition will therefore be referred to the auditing judge for consideration and decision. Ewing's Est., 41 D. & C. 44.

1 See Marks v. Morrison, 55 York 29, 41 D. & C. 669. 

2 An exception to an adjudication in which it is averred that an allowance made from the estate of a husband for the cost of funeral expenses and a tombstone for his wife, whom he predeceased, is improper, will be dismissed where the husband's will specifically directs the payment of the cost of tombstones and burial expenses for himself and wife. Patterson's Est., 47 Lanc. 269. (Subject discussed in "Fiduciary Review" of February 1942.)

Where a decedent's executor, with the approval of decedent's children, engages an undertaker, and it subsequently develops that all decedent's property was held in an estate by the entireties with his feeble-minded wife, the wife's guardian will, upon petition filed by the undertaker and decedent's children, be required to pay the undertaker's bill. By making arrangements for the funeral of her spouse a widow binds the decedent's estate for payment of reasonable expenses, but if she herself agrees to pay the bill which she definitely contracted, she is liable under the terms of such contract as under any other legal contract she might enter into, and she may be reimbursed for the money she expended, provided that the funeral contracted by her is suitable to the station in life of the decedent and not disproportionate to the size of the estate. Campton v. Janesofski, 16 Northumb. 25.

A surviving husband or widow first has the right of control of the place and manner of burial of the decedent.

Bair v. Dorris, 147 Super. 52.

94. TIME FOR PAYMENT OF DEBTS. 

Primary fund for payment of debts.13 

13 The personal estate is the primary fuad for the payment of a decedent's debts.

Lien creditors may have recourse to decedent's personal estate as the primary fund for their whole demand in the first instance, and subsequently to the land itself, although, where a creditor is a mortgagee, demand can be made that the land shall first be exhausted by a sale under the mortgage. Updegrave's Est., 4 

Sch. Reg. 9.

Where testator specifically bequeathed certain personal property to a legatee, and where real estate was generally devised in the residuary clause of the will, it was held that the executor would be enjoined from selling the personal property for the payment of debts until he had first sold all the real estate not specifically devised. 

As between specific legacies or devises of personal property and realty respectively, and personalty and realty not specifically bequeathed or devised, the latter are presumably liable for the payment of decedent's debts. Posey's Est., 59 

Montg. 186.

On the death of a husband or wife, the primary fund for the payment of their joint indebtedness secured by a mortgage on property owned by them as tenants by the entirety is, in so far as the estate of the deceased spouse is concerned, the mortgaged property, and, in the absence of a showing that it is insufficient to discharge the indebtedness, the mortgagee must look to it for payment, for to permit him to proceed against the deceased spouse's estate would be inequitable to the other creditors and heirs who have no claim to the mortgaged premises. Jeffrey's Est., 1 Fay. 53, 34 D. & C. 186.

Where decedent's personal estate insufficient to pay debts a creditor claiming on bond accompanying mortgage can participate therein only to extent his debt exceeds the value of his real estate security. Failure to obtain a lien on decedent's real estate within one year bars participation in surplus proceeds of sale of real estate for payment of debts.

A decedent's personal estate is always the primary fund for the payment of debts. Although in executors' account they took credit for payment of preferred and general debts out of proceeds of real estate sold for payment of debts, the court will transfer those credits to principal of personal estate because they should have been paid out of personal estate as far as it reached. Johnson's 

Est., 55 Montg. 314.

A testamentary direction to pay debts does not of itself work an equitable conversion or operate to charge the debts on real estate specifically devised. 

Hackett's Est., 44 D. & C. 593.

88 94, 95 

Where a husband and wife have executed a joint and several note, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, it must be presumed that the proceeds went to both equally.

In Miller Lumber & Coal Company, Appellant, v. Berkheimer, Admrx., et al., 342 Pa. 329, the court held that the doctrine of marshalling of assets only applied where both funds are in the hands of a common debtor of both creditors or where the fund not taken is one which in equity is primarily liable, and hence the foundation upon which the reasoning in Jeffrey's Estate, 34 D. & C. 186, rests was destroyed. Rex's Est., 58 Montg. 437, 46 D. & C. 443; 11 Som. 184.

Act construed.37 

36 A judgment on a note given by the decedent was entered after his death and the lien revived successively. At the time of the second revival, more than five years had elapsed since the previous one.

102. PUBLIC NOTICE OF SALE. 

Effect of such notice.85 

85 Where sale of a decedent's real estate for the payment of debts is advertised for a certain hour without reference to standard or daylight time, where between the first insertion of the advertisement and the day of sale daylight saving time is established for churches and business houses in the borough in which decedent's property is located, where the property is sold at the designated hour according to daylight saving time, where a bidder arrived at the place of sale at the designated hour according to standard time and after the property had been sold for $480, and was willing to pay at least $800 therefor, and where a reputable real estate company places in escrow the sum of $400 as a down payment in support of an $800 bid, a resale of the property will be ordered. 

The successful bidder at a public sale of a decedent's real estate for the payment of his debts is in the position of one making an offer to the court which it may or may not accept in its discretion, for it is the court's duty to see that a fair value is received for a decedent's real estate, so that if the bid is not adequate a resale must be ordered.

Where real estate has been sold at public sale for payment of a decedent's debts, and a resale is subsequently ordered because the high bid at the first sale is deemed inadequate, the down money paid by the successful bidder at the first sale must be returned to him and he must be reimbursed for expenses incurred in the expectation of becoming the purchaser. Yost's Est., 14 Northumb. 

400, 40 D. & C. 208. 

107. PROCEDURE TO EFFECT A PRIVATE SALE. 

Requisites of procedure."

Despite any defects in procedure private sales for debts heretofore made have been validated.99a

The court will, upon her petition, permit an executrix to sell the real estate at private sale if the consideration is fair and better than could be obtained at public sale, even though the will confers no authority to convert the real estate. 

The Act of 7 June 1917, P. L. 447, section 16, merely requires the court to receive a higher offer for real estate to be sold privately for decedent's debts, and not to decline a proposed sale for a fair price and a better price than could be obtained at public sale, on the ground that a better price might be obtained at a later date. Leinbach's Est., 33 Berks 191.

35 The death of a party plaintiff does not abate an action which survives the deceased, and where defendant makes no objection to proceeding in the case, and the same is tried on its merits and a judgment entered against the defendant and in favor of the deceased plaintiff's estate, such judgment is valid and will be sustained, provided no execution may issue thereon until a proper legal repre sentative appears of record and directs its execution. Klemstine v. Allen, 2 Cam. 162.

The right of action of a settlor as a donor to secure performance by the trustee of the right which she had reserved in her deed of trust survived.

60 A petition and rule by the surviving defendants in an action in the common pleas court for leave to substitute the executrix of a deceased defendant, as a party defendant, was discharged, where she had filed her first and final account and distribution had been made by the orphans' court. The proper procedure for substitution of parties is now by scire facias. 

The objection that the executrix could not be substituted as a party defendant for the reason that more than a year had elapsed since the death of decedent and the decree of distribution of the orphans' court made prior to the filing of the petition, was overruled. Nor did plaintiff have the exclusive right of substitution. 

Legislation has now changed the practice.

The Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, for the substitution of an executor or administrator of a deceased defendant, prescribes a complete and exclusive method of procedure which must be followed to the exclusion of any method authorized pursuant to common law or prior to the enactment of the act. 

The courts are consistently applying equitable principles in all such situations in order to prevent an injustice being done. The plaintiff, by a joint suit, prevented the use of a sci. fa. to bring in a party already on the record; and merely because he refused to apply for a substitution, justice should not permit one of the defendants to profit thereby to the detriment of another who may be entitled to a contribution.

A proceeding for the substitution of parties to actions is not an effort to establish a lien against property or to have execution upon assets in the hands of the executrix. These objections would have to come after a judgment, at which time it would be proper to bring up such objections as "written notice," so that the executrix could not be heard to say that no written notice of claim was filed with the executrix and since a final account had been audited and distribution made, there can be no proceedings against the executrix. Tallarico v. 

Autenreith, 89 P. L. J. 333, 55 York 27. 

62 A nonresident executor of a decedent who resided outside of this Commonwealth may not be made a party defendant in an action pending in a court of this state, by the service upon it of a writ of scire facias by publication, where such executor has qualified and is acting under the laws of another state. 

Section 35(h) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, does not authorize service by publication of the writ of scire facias upon a foreign fiduciary; its purpose is to prescribe the method of service of the writ upon an executor or administrator appointed and qualified in the state of Pennsylvania, who resides outside the county of the pending litigation, or who has removed from the Commonwealth and resides in some other state. Giampalo v. Taylor, 335 Pa. 121. 

The proper procedure for substituting as defendant in pending litigation a nonresident personal representative of a deceased party is that set forth in section 35 (h) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, including service by publication; service upon the personal representative's surety in accordance with the procedure outlined in section 37 of the act, dealing with the service of original process in suits against estates the representatives of which do not reside in the county having jurisdiction of their accounts, is defective. 

While a nonresident defendant may not question the court's jurisdiction over her by a petition under the Act of March 5, 1925, P. L. 23, after trial, the special remedy provided by that act being confined to preliminary proceedings, nevertheless, where the court in fact had no jurisdiction over defendant and the lack of jurisdiction has not been waived, such a petition will be treated as a motion to strike off the verdict or finding against the defendant and will be granted. Helfstein v. Milikowsky, 39 D. & C. 258.

Executors or administrators may not settle or compromise claims against a decedent's estate where, from a legal standpoint, the claims have no legal basis. 

An administrator was surcharged with the amount he paid on compromised claims for room, board and nursing for the decedent furnished by her niece without a contract for payment and while the family relation existed between the claimants and the decedent. Duncan's Est., 54 York 83.

Where exceptions to an account had been filed, and where an agreement of compromise and settlement had been executed on behalf of certain exceptants, by their attorneys, and where certain of the exceptants were not satisfied with the agreement and demanded a hearing on the merits, it was held, under all the circumstances, that the attorneys had no authority to compromise their client's claims, and that a hearing on the merits would be held. 

An attorney, merely by his relation as such to his client, has no authority to compromise his client's substantive rights. 

Where there are a number of exceptants, those that agree to a settlement are bound thereby, but those who are not parties are not bound, regardless of whether they are in the majority or minority of the total number of persons interested, and regardless of the number that are for or against the settlement. DeQueiroz's 

Est., 59 Montg. 98.

Insurance. 

Proceeds of insurance policies paid to estate of deceased beneficiary are not subject to tax. Buechley's Est., 3 Sch. Reg. 70.

The proceeds of policies of life insurance payable otherwise than to the estate of the insured, and whether paid directly by the insurer to beneficiaries named in the policies, or to a trustee designated therein, and held, managed, and distributed by such trustee to or for the benefit of such persons or classes of persons under such plan and in such statutes as may have been prescribed by the insured under agreement with such trustee, shall not be included in imposing any tax under this section.

To come within this statute exempting the proceeds of life insurance policies from the inheritance tax law, the proceeds of such policies must be payable "otherwise than to the estate of the deceased' and such proceeds must be payable to either of two designated classes: (1) "directly by the insurer to beneficiaries named in the policies, or (2) to a trustee designated therein." Section 1 of the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762, adding to Section 48 of the

$123 

Fiduciaries Act of 1917, does not apply to the normal Pennsylvania transfer inheritance tax but only deals with the federal estate tax and the additional Pennsylvania transfer inheritance tax on account of credits allowed by the Federal Government. Reed's Est., 58 Montg. 148, 45 D. & C. 628.

An assessment of additional transfer inheritance tax against the insolvent estate of the donee of a power of appointment, in the amount of the 80% federal credit allowed, is improper where the donee exercised the power without blending the appointed estate with her own, and where the appointee paid inheritance tax on the appointed estate in an amount exceeding the federal credit. 

The Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, supplementing the inheritance tax Act of 

June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, and providing for additional transfer tax imposed as estate tax, does not create a new class of taxable property. There is no basis for tax under either act unless there is in fact a transfer of property. 

The person to whom property is appointed under a power of appointment cannot be obliged to pay additional estate tax under the Act of May 7, 1927, P. L. 859, when he has already paid transfer tax under the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, in excess of the 80% credit allowed by the federal law. Davis' Est., 57 Montg. 237.

Even though there is no accounting before it, an orphans' court has jurisdiction under the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762, to prorate taxes between those who take an estate created by will or under the intestate laws and beneficiaries under insurance trusts or policies, upon petition by the fiduciaries who have paid the tax, and citation to the parties allegedly liable for contribution; but it does not have jurisdiction in such a summary proceeding to compel the parties cited to pay any amount which it may find to be due, section 48.1 of the act being unconstitutional insofar as it attempts to confer such jurisdiction. 

A testamentary direction "that all estate, inheritance and transfer taxes of every kind and character assessed against my estate or any interest therein, passing hereunder" be paid from testator's residuary estate and considered as administration expenses, sufficiently expresses an intention that taxes due upon life insurance policies in a trust created by testator are to be borne by his residuary estate to defeat the right to proration under the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762; and this is especially so where the beneficiaries of the trust are testator's wife and children. Crooks' Est., 36 D. & C. 58.

Payments of federal estate taxes out of their personal funds, by persons who are liable individually and as executors for such payments, made with the intention of discharging the liability of the estate as well as their personal responsibility, are payments by a "person acting in a fiduciary capacity'' within the meaning of the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762, providing for the proration of such payments "among the persons interested in the estate to whom such property is or may be transferred or to whom any benefit accrues. 

The purpose of the Act of 1937 was to achieve equality of contribution and to relieve distributees of inequalities which might result from imposition of the federal estate tax.

The Act of 1937 contemplates proration of interest upon deficiency assessments of federal estate tax and notice to this effect is given by the title. 

The Act of 1937 contemplates proration of the total federal estate tax payments made by the fiduciary, including payment in part by credits for payment of state inheritance taxes. Mellon Est., 347 Pa. 520. (Reviewed in "Fiduciary 

Review" of August 1943.)

83 Domicile is the determining factor in establishing the right of a state to impose inheritance taxes upon the decedent's estate. "Domicile" means more than "residence." It imports residence and a fixed intention to remain there.

Continuous residence for a long period of time in a given locality raises the presumption that there was the intent to remain and become domiciled there. 

Declarations of the party himself, where he can have no object or inducement to deceive those to whom such declarations are made, are the best evidence of his intention to make his actual residence his permanent residence also. But where acts unaccompanied by declarations concur with long-continued residence, they furnish as satisfactory evidence of intention as the express declarations of the party to that effect. Miller's Est., 20 Erie 248, 87 P. L. J. 16.

There is perhaps no one criterion of domicile apart from residence, which has been accorded more weight than the exercise of suffrage rights. McKinnon 

Est., 20 Erie 87, 52 York 42; Miller's Est., 20 Erie 248, 87 P. L. J. 16.

Provision is now made by the Act of Aug. 5, 1941, (P. L. 815), which, effective immediately, amends the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, by adding Sec. 43, which reads as follows: 

"Section 43. Where the Department of Revenue claims that a decedent was domiciled in this State at the time of his death, and the taxing authorities of another state or states make a similar claim with respect to their state or states, and the facts are such as to give rise to a reasonable doubt as to the domicile of the decedent, the department may, with the approval of the Department of Justice, enter into a written agreement with such taxing officials and with the personal representatives that a certain sum shall be accepted in full payment of the tax imposed by this act and the supplement thereto: Provided, That said agreement also fixes the amount to be paid to such other state or states in full payment of the death taxes thereof. Full power and authority is hereby conferred upon the Such personal representatives to enter into the agreement provided for herein. agreement shall finally and conclusively fix and determine the amount of tax imposed by this act and the supplement thereto, without regard to any other provision of the laws of this State. In the event the aggregate amount payable under such agreement to the states involved is less than the maximum credit allowable to the estate against the United States estate tax imposed with respect

thereto, the personal representatives forthwith shall also pay to the department 80 much of the difference between such aggregate amount and the amount of such credit as the amount payable to the department under the agreement bears to such aggregate amount. A copy of any such agreement shall be filed in the office of the proper register of wills, and any existing appraisement shall be deemed modified according to said agreement. In the event no appraisement has been made and filed prior to said agreement, the Department of Revenue shall direct an appraisement to be made and filed in the office of the proper register of wills in accordance with said agreement."'

88 Where a decedent leaves tangible property in Pennsylvania, it is subject to the inheritance tax laws of the commonwealth, notwithstanding the fact that she was a non-resident.

Tangible property is defined as that which may be felt or touched; it must necessarily be corporeal and may be either real or personal. 

Intangible property, on the other hand, is incorporeal; it comprises evidence or indicia of ownership or title such as deeds, bonds, and corporate stocks. Me 

Kinnon Est., 20 Erie 87, 52 York 42.

Upon appeal with regard to eleven promissory notes without interest given by a beneficiary, barred by the statute of limitations, where testator's will charged all loans and advancements against their respective interests, it was held that the notes represented an asset of the estate and were properly appraised. 

Advancements to a beneficiary made during the lifetime of decedent should not be appraised as estate assets for Pennsylvania transfer tax purposes. An advancement is a pure and irrevocable gift made by a parent in his lifetime his child on account of such child's share of the estate after the parent's decease. 

Barbey's Est., (No. 2), 34 Berks 155.

94 A tax is levied by the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, where property is transferred by a resident by deed, grant, bargain, sale or gift, intended to take effect in possession or enjoyment at or after death of the grantor, vendor or donor. 

The tax is due whether the deed is revocable or irrevocable, provided the power of revocation was not exercised, the only material difference between the two classes of instruments being that the transfer by a revocable deed is as of the date of the death of the settlor and by an irrevocable deed as of the date of its execution.

The fact that money was placed in a revocable trust by two donors, the income to be paid to one of them for life, and upon her decease the principal was subject to appointment by the other donor, did not affect the taxability of the trust fund, where the trust was not revoked and the power of appointment was exercised. 

Where a trust was created by the deed of two persons, the court traced the fund subject to tax to the respective donors in order to determine what proportion of the fund passed to lineals and what proportion passed to collaterals or strangers of the respective donors. 

A transfer inheritance is an excise tax on the privilege of inheriting property or receiving it by virtue of transfers of the kind specified in the statute; it is measured by the clear value of the estate which is transferred; it is paid by the legatees, donees or grantees in the proportions allocated to their respective inheritance or gift, or is deducted from their interests by the administrator, executor or trustees who control the property subject to the tax. 95 Whether or not such transfer was made in contemplation of death is a question of fact. There is no irrebutable presumption in favor of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania that a transfer of real or personal property of a person who died within one year from such transfer, was made in contemplation of death. 

To hold otherwise would be to ignore the language of the Act of June 22. 

1931, P. L. 690, when it says, "unless shown to the contrary." Case's Est., 26 

North. 285.

But such presumption is rebutted by evidence that decedent was in sound and vigorous condition, that he had recently undertaken great responsibilities which would require expenditure of time and energy for many years, and that the impelling motive for the transfers was apparently a desire to be relieved of responsibilities in order to devote his time to the new enterprises and a desire to benefit his family. Baker's Est., 39 D. & C. 405.

In order to rebut the presumption of the provisions of the Act of June 22, 1931, P. L. 690, Sec. (1c) that a gift, if made within one year from the date of the death of the decedent, was made in contemplation of death and therefore is subject to transfer inheritance tax, it is necessary to produce positive proofs that it was not made in contemplation of death. The gift must have been a bona fide and unconditioned transfer, fully consummated, and absolute and exclusive possession taken by the transferee. Haverstick's Est., 46 Lanc. 441.

An amount appraised for inheritance tax purposes, where the taxable amount is deposited in a joint account in the names of decedent and another person not her husband is not subject to inheritance tax to the extent of one-half of the amount of such joint account as against the estate of the one first dying.

The Act of July 14, 1936, P. L. 44, amending the Transfer Inheritance Tax Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, taxes the accrual to a surviving joint tenant of the interest of a deceased joint tenant, even though there may be no transfer of title at the time of death.

Acts of assembly are not to be lightly set aside as invalid because unconstitutional; courts ought not set themselves up as a supervisory body over the legislature, nor be alert to discover some flaw that can be magnified by refined reasoning into a conflict with fundamental law. 

The Act of July 14, 1936, P. L. 44, is not unconstitutional in that it imposes a tax upon a species of property, title to which may be traced back to a point prior to its enactment: it is not retroactive insofar as it applies to joint tenancies in existence at the time of its passage, since it taxes not the property itself, but the accruals which do not come into existence until the death of the joint tenant.

The subject matter of the Act of July 14, 1936, P. L. 44, is clearly expressed in its title which contains a reference to the general subject matter: even though to th

TO 2 The import of the word "transfer" as used in the acts signifies an extinguishment of the interest of a joint tenant when it accrues by death to a surviving joint tenant. When the interest accrues, it is taxable.

L. 521, as amended by the Act of 1936, P. L. 44, except when such joint tenants are husband and wife. Flanagan's Est., 86 P. L. J. 425, 33 D. &

In the appraisement of a decedent's estate to fix the transfer inheritance tax the appraisers correctly followed the Act of 1936, P. L. 44, which requires them to divide "the value of the whole property by the number of joint tenants in existence immediately preceding the death of the deceased joint tenant. This procedure applies to estates not held by the entireties. 

The legislature had power to pass the Act of 1936, P. L. 44, imposing the tax regardless of when the joint tenancy was created. Death gives rise to the accrual of the survivorship. It is this event and not the creation of the trust which controls. Flanagan's Est., 86 P. L. J. 493, 52 York 90.

L. 44, providing that, on death of a joint tenant, accrual to the survivor of the right to ownership or possession and enjoyment of property held or deposited in a bank under a joint tenancy shall be deemed a transfer and subject to transfer inheritance tax, is constitutional and applies irrespective of the amounts contributed by the respective joint tenants. The written assignment of an interest purporting to take effect immediately is sufficient to indicate a present intention to pass right of possession to the donee and constitutes constructive delivery.

An executor or administrator is a proper party to appeal from an excessive appraisement of personal property of a decedent's estate for transfer inheritance tax purposes, and he may also appeal from such an appraisement of real estate if he has been given jurisdiction over it. Noel's Est., 42 D. & C. 614.

On appeal from an appraisement of property for transfer tax under the Act of 1919, as amended, the trial is de novo and the court has the power to reduce or to increase the assessment.

On appeal from the order of the lower court entered in such proceeding, the question is whether the finding of the lower court is supported by competent evidence. McLure App., 347 Pa. 481.

A rule to set aside a rule should never be granted. 

A rule to show cause why an appraisement should not be set aside should not be granted even if it appears that no notice of the appraisement was given to the administratrix of the estate. The statute provides that all matters in dispute shall be decided upon an appeal, and that course must be followed. Updegrove's 

Est., 27 North. 197.

Where an inheritance tax appraiser fixes the clear value of an estate and no appeal is taken from such appraisal, it becomes final and cannot subsequently be challenged at the audit in the orphans' court. Haid Est., 347 Pa. 159.

It has become a well established practice in York County, Pennsylvania, to file directly in the orphans' court appeals from the appraisement of property of a decedent for inheritance taxation; and in view of this practice having been followed for more than thirty years, and in the absence of any statute prescribing the procedure, this practice was approved. 

The mere fact that the practice mentioned does not furnish the Commonwealth tar

$125 with prompt notice of the appeal, is not an insuperable objection to the procedure. 

An executor does not have the right to appeal from an appraisement for inheritance taxation of property in which the executor, as such, has no interest. 

An appeal taken from the appraisement for inheritance taxation in which and in the bond there are indications that the appeal was taken by the executors, but where the appeal and the bond were signed by the persons who were the executors and also the owners of the property appraised as individuals, was amended so as to be the appeal of the persons owning the property, and not that of the executors.

The commonwealth is not entitled to collect a transfer inheritance tax on assets of which the decedent did not die seized, and which were mistakenly included in the appraisement.

Laches in an equitable doctrine to be applied only against a plaintiff or one seeking affirmative relief, and cannot in any sense be applied against a defendant for failing to speed up an action against him. 

Laches may be imputed to the commonwealth as well as to an individual; but not for failure to move for disposition of an appeal from an appraisement of inheritance taxation where there is no claim or evidence to show that the appellant has been put to any disadvantage, or was prejudiced in any manner by reason of the death or disappearance of parties or witnesses or by reason of any change in the circumstances or conditions since the appeal was filed. Schaszberger's Est., 52 York 109, 34 D. & C. 367.

While as a general rule a transfer inheritance tax appraisement made by the Commonwealth is conclusive as to valuations, deductions and all other incidents thereof after the expiration of the period for appeal, nevertheless where a portion of the estate is left in trust for a direct heir for life with power of appointment, and the life tenant appoints a life estate following her death to her husband, a collateral heir as to the donor of the power, the Commonwealth may properly, upon the death of the life tenant, reassess and reappraise the trust as then constituted and impose a tax at eight percent upon the value of the life estate appointed to the donee's husband, it having been obviously impossible at the time of the original appraisement to determine whether such tax would be due. Duling's 

Est., 45 D. & C. 182.

On an appeal to the Orphans' Court from valuations for inheritance tax, the proceeding is analogous to appeals from the action of the county commissioners sitting as a board of revision. In such instances the taxing authorities make out a prima facie case by the introduction in evidence of the appraisement.

Under the Act of 1919, P. L. 521, the State Inheritance Tax Appraiser is directed to make a "fair and conscionable appraisement" which means that the appraisement must reflect the fair market value of the property as of the date of death.

The sale price of real estate six months after the death of the testator is not conclusive as to the fair market value of the real estate as of the date of death where the evidence shows a general improvement in economic conditions and increased tempo of real estate activity following the death of decedent. Deily's 

Est., 19 Leh. 401.

Where evidence produced on hearing disclosed that a decedent who died in 1934, had purchased real estate in 1923, and thereafter entered into an oral contract to sell the same said real estate is subject to appraisement for inheritance tax purposes only for the balance due on account of the purchase price, which testimony, in this case, disclosed to be the sum of $320.00. Rauch's Est., 48 Lanc. 5.

Where, on appeal to the orphans' court from the appraisement of two parcels of real estate for inheritance tax at $11,000 cach, appellant's evidence is of values of $7,700 and $7,000 respectively, and the Commonwealth's evidence is of values of $8,500 and $8,000, respectively, the unfairness of the appraisement is established and its prima facie effect is overcome. As the testimony of appellant's and of Commonwealth's experts is of equal weight, the difference being

$125 

 EX 

slight, the fair basis of valuation is the application of a rule ordinarily to be condemned, namely, the average of the two estimates. 

The procedure on appeal to the orphans' court from the appraisement of property for inheritance tax purposes, under the transfer inheritance tax Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, § 13, as amended, is analogous to an appeal from a board of revision of taxes. The proceedings in the orphans' court are de novo; a prima facie case is made out by the Commonwealth, by introducing the ap praisement; the burden of proof is then on appellant to show the appraisement to be unfair; and, where all the evidence is conflicting, the court must revalue the property according to the market value established, with due regard to the weight of the evidence. Porter's Est., 56 Montg. 59.

Federal decisions dealing with appraisements of property under the federal estate and gift tax laws are binding in the application of those laws but do not prevent the authorities, required to apply the state transfer tax law, from attributing to an agreement providing for an option on the part of a third person to purchase stock owned by the decedent at a stated price less probative force in the valuation inquiry than is accorded such agreements by the federal courts in ap plying the federal law. McLure App., 347 Pa. 481.

49 Under section 16 of the Act of 1919, as amended, it is the duty of the executor to deduct and pay the tax. McLure App., 347 Pa. 481.

The inheritance tax Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, is not objectionable as rendering a deceased joint tenant's estate, or his executor, liable for tax on the joint estate, which is not a part of decedent's estate and never in the executor's possession. The whole theory of that act is that liability for the tax is upon the property transferred, or upon the person receiving it. 

An executor or administrator is chargeable only with tax he is required to deduct from a distributive share. Cochrane's Est., 56 Montg. 389 af'd in 342 Pa. 108. 

49a An inheritance tax is ultimately payable by the legatee or out of the property or estate passing to him, unless the will clearly indicates, either expressly or by implication, that the legacy was given free of the tax. 

The residue of an estate, in the absence of language showing a contrary intention, means the estate remaining after satisfaction of charges, debts, and particular legacies and devises, and the withdrawal of specific gifts made in codicils. 

In this case, it was held, construing all of the instruments executed by testatrix together, that a direction to pay "direct inheritance tax'' from the proceeds of the conversion of the residuary estate related exclusively to the residuary estate, and did not refer to a specific devise or bequest made by a codicil. Rettew's Est., 142 Super. 335.

Where, as part of the settlement of a will contest, the parties agree that title to certain of decedent's real estate shall be conveyed to his widow "free of any encumbrances not in existence at the time of" decedent's death "or imposed by law, to the same force and effect as though title thereto had been in the" widow's individual name "prior to the death of the decedent," the widow is not to be charged with any portion of the Pennsylvania inheritance and Federal estate taxes assessed against such real estate. Williams' Est., 45 D. & C. 207.

Where a paragraph in a will, containing a single sentence, not divided into separate sentences by periods or similar formal or informal punctuations, bequeaths a legacy to a person which is to revert to the residue of the estate if she predeceases testator and in that event bequeaths a smaller legacy to her son, free and clear of collateral inheritance tax, the phrase at the end of the paragraph, "free, and clear of collateral inheritance tax," applied to either of the provisions in the paragraph. Wood's Est., 48 Lanc. 389.

Unless the will, deed, grant or gift expressly provide otherwise, the transfer tax is ultimately payable by the legatee, grantee or donee, or out of the property or estate passing to him. Wheeler's Est., 25 Erie 113.

It is the transfer of property that is taxed and the tax is payable by the transferee, if he accepts it. Town Est., 25 Erie 210.

The fact that a testator specifically provides that pecuniary legacies shall be subject to the payment of Pennsylvania inheritance tax but that the tax on specific legacies shall be paid out of the residuary estate does not indicate an intention that the pecuniary legacies are to be exempted from any apportionment of the Federal estate tax. Harvey's Est., 47 D. & C. 12. 

50 Uber's Est., 29 D. & C. 341, af'd in 330 Pa. 417. 

Testamentary direction that executors' pay inheritance tax, where executor also appointed trustee, is not sufficient to impose duty on fiduciary as executor, to pay tax on future estate otherwise not due until estate vests in possession of remainderman, when fiduciary functioning as trustee. Swift's Est. (No. 1), 54 Montg. 147.

Where will gave all legacies free of inheritance tax, directing payment of tax out of residue, credit for entire tax on remainders of legacies given in trust will not be allowed out of remainder or trust of one-third the residue, the other two-thirds of the residue having been given absolutely and distributed on executor's account. Credit allowed for all tax due on residuary remainder, and for one-third tax now paid for remainders of legacies given in trust, but trustee must bear other two-thirds of tax individually, having failed to reserve amount to cover future tax before distributing two-thirds the residue. Swift's Est. (No. 2), 54 Montg. 154.

As to when the tax on an annuity is payable by the annuitant and not out of the general estate, see Hick's Est., 3 Blair 41, 39 D. & C. 351.

Where the will of a decedent provides that all legacies herein are to be free of tax, all inheritance taxes in the estate must be paid out of the residuary estate and the full amount of each legacy be paid to the several legatees without deduction. Lamberton 's Est., 20 Erie 339.

But this does not apply to the tax on jointly held property. Such tax must be paid by the survivor. Lamberton's Est., 23 Erie 1, 55 York 29, 33.

Where the will directed that all "inheritance, legacy, succession, or similar duties or taxes shall be paid out of my residuary estate," it was held that inheritance taxes due on a trust inter vivos were not payable by the estate, but must be borne by the trust. Crooks' Estate, 36 D. & C. 58, and Ely's Estate, 28 D. & C. 663, distinguished. Reed's Est., 58 Montg. 148, 45 D. & C. 628.

When the only fund out of which testatrix directs the transfer, inheritance, succession and estate taxes on all the legacies and devises in her will to be paid, in order that the said legacies may be paid in full," is residuary estate of which there is none and therefore the bequest as to the payment of these taxes falls and is ineffectual, since there is no direction in the will to pay these taxes out of any other fund and each legacy or devise must pay its part of said taxes. 

Curtze's Est., 25 Erie 48.

Where a will directs that all taxes be paid out of the corpus of the residuary estate, and a portion of the residuary estate is placed in trust, the life tenant being given a power of appointment over the remainder, additional transfer inheritance taxes due upon the death of the life tenant because of her appointment of a life interest, succeeding hers, to an appointee standing in the position of a collateral heir as to the donor of the power, are to be paid from the corpus of the trust. Duling's Est., 45 D. & C. 182.

Inheritance tax becomes due and payable at the end of one year from the death of the decedent, at which time the Commonwealth has the right to proceed to enforce collection, and the right of the Commonwealth, cannot be frustrated because of the existence of disputed or contingent claims against the estate which have not been paid.

Where delay in the payment of inheritance tax was due in part to the honest belief of the executors that contingent liabilities are proper deductions and to the hope that the primary debtor might become able to pay the obligations within a reasonable time, and partly because of the long continued illness of counsel for the estate, it was held that interest from one year after the decedent's death must be reduced from 12 per cent to 6 per cent. 

The burden rests on the taxpayer to prove that the property subject to inheritance tax yielded less than the statutory interest rate, and in the absence of such proof the statutory rate must be charged. 

Inheritance tax is really not a tax in the ordinary meaning of the word, but

§ 126 

rather a distributive share of the estate which the State claims for itself, and, therefore, the Act of April 7th, 1870, P. L. 57, which provides that where a debtor shall suffer any claim due the Commonwealth to remain unpaid for a period of sixty days, there shall be paid by said debtor a commission of 5 per cent to the counsel or attorney of the Commonwealth, which shall be in addition to other penalties or interest, does not apply to inheritance taxes. Harlacker's Est., 54 

York 74. 

Where the life beneficiary of a trust under testator's will died on February 13, 1938, the trustees filed their appraisement of the remainder on June 18, 1938, the Commonwealth filed its appraisement of the remainder on March 2, 1939, the trustees paid tax upon the remainder on March 11, 1939, based on their own appraisement, the Commonwealth reduced its appraisement on March 14, 1939, the trustees paid the balance due under the Commonwealth's reduced appraise ment on November 13, 1939, and the remaindermen came into actual possession immediately upon the life beneficiary's death; held that interest on the total tax was due at the rate of 6% from February 13, 1938, the date of the life beneficiary's death, to March 11, 1939, the date of the first payment on account, and at the rate of 12% from March 11, 1939, to November 13, 1939, on the balance. 

Under § 3 of the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, inheritance tax upon future interests need not be paid, at the legatees's election, until he comes into actual possession. 

Where neither accounting nor litigation cause delay, a remainderman comes into actual possession within § 3 of the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, immediately upon the termination of the preceding estate. 

Under § 3 of the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, inheritance tax on future interests is payable, and interest begins to run from the date the legatee thereof comes into actual possession; and the tax is to be calculated, without regard to actual possession, on the value of the interest as of the date of the termination of the preceding estate.

The provisions of § 38 of the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, under which interest begins to run one year after the decedent's death, have no relation to payments of tax upon future interests deferred under § 3. 

The provisions of § 38 of the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, with respect to rate of interest upon overdue inheritance tax, do apply to tax on future interests under § 3.

Failure of the Commonwealth to appraise the remainder estate and settle the tax promptly constitutes an "unavoidable cause of delay" under § 38 of the Act of June 20, 1919, P. L. 521, as amended, so that interest shall run at the rate of 6% only. Morgan's Est., 57 Montg. 178, 55 York 50, 41 D. & C. 360.

The Act of July 2, 1937 (P. L. 2762), providing for the proration of Pennsylvania and Federal estate taxes by the orphans' court among the persons interested in a decedent's estate to whom property is or may be transferred or to whom any benefit accrues, for payment of such taxes by the fiduciary, and for reimbursement to the fiduciary by order of the orphans' court directing the fiduciary to charge the prorated amounts against the persons against whom the tax has been so prorated, in so far as he is in possession of property or interests of such persons against whom such charge may be made, and summarily directing pro effe Sto 276 the all est ex

§ 91 

De 1 hat! eat! mer P.I 116 Com ing all other persons against whom the tax has been so prorated, or who are in possession of property or interests of such persons, to make payment of such PL prorated amounts to such fiduciary, applies to estate taxes accrued before the effective date of the Act. So applied the Act is constitutional since it provides only a procedure for collection of the taxes, and does not disturb vested rights. 

Stockler's Est. (No. 1), 30 Berks 149. 

In a proceeding to prorate estate taxes under the Act of July 2, 1937 (P. L. 

2762), where the taxable estate includes proceeds of life insurance, the exemp tion of $40,000 (of insurance payable to beneficiaries other than the estate of the insured) allowed by the Federal Revenue Act of 1926 will be allocated to all insurance proceeds, and not to any specific insurance. 

Under the Federal Revenue Act of 1926, Sec. 314 (b), if any part of the gross estate consists of proceeds of insurance policies on the decedent's life, receivable by a fiduciary other than the executor, the executor may recover from the beneficiary such portion of the total tax paid on the estate as the proceeds, in excess of $40,000 of such policies bear to the net estate. Stockler's Est. (No. 2), 30 Berks 156.

A testator has the power to direct the apportionment of his estate and property in trust created inter vivos. 

Where deeds of trust which have been executed by testator at a time when revocable trusts were subject to federal estate tax on the settlor's estate, required the trustee to pay out of the trust fund all "costs, charges and expenses of said trust estate," and the will showed that testator intended to benefit his wife and daughter, it was held that the trust deeds provided for apportionment of the tax.

The Act of July 2, 1937 (P. L. 2762), which provides for the proration, except in a case where the testator otherwise provides in his will, of any estate tax paid by a fiduciary, among the persons interested in the estate to whom such property is transferred, applied to proceedings existing at the effective date of the Act, and is applicable to proceedings in the orphans' court, in which the adju dication had not been made at the effective date of the Act. 

Such interpretation of the statute does not take away vested rights in violation of constitutional limitations. Jeffrey's Est., 333 Pa. 15, af'g 32 D. & C. 5; 

Elliott's Est., 58 Montg. 114.

Even though there is no accounting before it, an orphans' court has jurisdiction under the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762, to prorate taxes between those who take an estate created by will or under the intestate laws and beneficiaries under insurance trusts or policies, upon petition by the fiduciaries who have paid the tax, and citation to the parties allegedly liable for contribution; but it does not have jurisdiction in such a summary proceeding to compel the parties cited to pay any amount which it may find to be due, section 48.1 of the act being unconstitutional insofar as it attempts to confer such jurisdiction. 

A testamentary direction "that all estate, inheritance and transfer taxes of every kind and character assessed against my estate or any interest therein, passing hereunder' be paid from testator's residuary estate and considered as administration expenses, sufficiently expresses an intention that taxes due upon life insurance policies in a trust created by testator are to be borne by his residuary estate to defeat the right to proration under the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762; and this is especially so where the beneficiaries of the trust are testator's wife and children. Crooks' Est., 36 D. & C. 58.

The federal estate tax imposed on the estate of a decedent who exercised a power of appointment over part of a trust under the will of another, will be prorated, under the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762, and the trustee of that trust, who has submitted to the jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court for the purpose of proration, will be directed to pay to decedent's executor out of the part of the corpus in his hands which passes under the power and charge to the persons taking under the exercise of the power, such proportion of the total tax as the value of the property so passing bears to the total net taxable estate. 

Clapp's Est., 56 Montg. 16.

A provision in a deed of trust inter vivos, that any inheritance or succession taxes due upon the passing of the trust estate be paid from corpus so that the life estates shall be enjoyed "free from deduction for any such taxes," means only that there shall be no direct deduction for such taxes from income: the corpus

§§ 132, 133a12  

of the trust must bear its proportionate share of the tax assessed upon the settlor's with estate, in accordance with the Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762, amending the for 

Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, even though as a result of the alti charge upon principal a diminution of income may indirectly result. Mc- 19, Laughlin's Est., 39 D. & C. 573.

The Act of July 2, 1937, P. L. 2762 (which is constitutional) requires apportionment of Federal estate taxes between pecuniary and residuary legatees unless the testator directs otherwise in his will.

The fact that a testator specifically provides that pecuniary legacies shall be subject to the payment of Pennsylvania inheritance tax but that the tax on specific legacies shall be paid out of the residuary estate does not indicate an intention that the pecuniary legacies are to be exempted from any apportionment of the Federal estate tax. Harvey's Est., 47 D. & C. 12.

On appeal from an assessment for personal property tax under the Act of 

June 22, 1935 (P. L. 414), at the rate prescribed by the Act on three-quarters of the total value of the taxable property of an estate, three of the four trustees of which resided in this state and the fourth was a corporation domiciled in another state, it was held that the ownership, holding or possession of the trust company was not within the provisions of the statute, where it appeared that the property was identified as trust property and was located and administered as a unit at its trust domicile in another state, that the decedent's will clearly indicated an intention that the trust be administered in that other state, that the trust property was intangible property, consisting mainly of the capital stock of a company established in the other state all of which belonged to testator and which by his will he provided should be conserved for purposes there stated, that the will conferred on the trustees extensive powers for the investment of trust funds in aid of the company, and that none of the duties of the trustees was performed in this state.

Under the Act of 1935, there is no provision for dividing trust property among resident and nonresident trustees for purposes of the tax. Dorrance's Est., 333 

Pa. 162.

14a Proceedings in the orphans' court are equitable in character. 

Laches may be asserted as a bar to the right to force the personal representative to account.

Where more than fifty years had elapsed from the death of the testator to the petition for an accounting and almost fifty years had elapsed from the death of a remainderman, and the evidence of the existence of property had become slight and direct proof of other surrounding circumstances showing family settlement was difficult, it was held that the surviving husband of the deceased remainderman was precluded by laches from compelling the life tenant and executrix to account.

A family settlement may be presumed on the failure to account, acquiesced in over a long period of time.

Family settlements are preferred by the law. 

Where such settlements exist or are presumed to exist, an accounting is unnecessary. Cannon's Est., 330 Pa. 513.

While delay on the part of a beneficiary of an estate in demanding an accounting may bar his right thereto if circumstances have intervened which make an accounting difficult to render or inequitable, mere lapse of time alone is not sufficient to destroy the statutory duty to account imposed by section 46(a) of the 

Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 447), and preliminary objections to a petition for a citation to show cause why an inventory and account should not be filed, upon the sole ground that over 25 years have elapsed since decedent's death, must be dismissed with leave to respondents to file an answer disclosing what circumstances, if any, render it inequitable to compel the accounting at such a late date. Darragh's Est., 35 D. & C. 364.

A claim against a decedent's estate based upon promissory notes under seal accompanying a mortgage may be sufficiently stated to entitle the claimant to demand an accounting, even though all the detailed items which enter into the calculation of the deficiency upon the notes may not be given. 

A petition to require an administrator to file an account will not be dismissed upon preliminary objections on the ground of laches because not presented until nine or ten years after decedent's death, in the absence of a showing of actual prejudice resulting from the delay. Joyce's Est., 35 D. & C. 406.

A creditor has a right to demand that an account be filed, unless the right is lost by laches, for until an account has been filed it is not determinable whether the creditor may or may not recover. Wetzel's Est., 58 Montg. 281.

The question of laches does not depend, as does the statute of limitations upon the fact that a certain definite time has elapsed since the cause of action accrued, but whether, under the circumstances of the particular case, plaintiff is chargeable with want of due diligence in failing to institute or prosecute his proceeding. 

Where the delay has made difficult the doing of justice because of death, by reason of which the facts have become obscure, a court will refuse equitable relief. 

A decree for an accounting should be denied where it clearly appears that the party secking it has, by his laches, rendered it impossible for the court to do full justice to both parties, whether the infirmity of the case consists in the death of a party, loss of evidence or other cause.

Section 21 of the Intestate Act indicates an intent to compel persons who have an interest in the estate of an intestate, to lay legal claim thereto within This section of the Act affords some standard as to the diligence seven years. of the petitioner in the case at bar. Schadt's Est., 20 Leh. 41.

Where parties in interest execute and deliver to an executor a release in full settlement, satisfaction and payment of all moneys due, owing and payable to them in the estate of a decedent and four years later petition the orphans' court for a citation to file an account to which they subsequently filed exceptions, Held, the account will be confirmed. In such case the exceptants are guilty of culpable negligence and laches. The petitioners should have insisted upon the filing of an account in the first instance. Phalm's Est., 46 Lanc. 355.

While so much of the rule of Stitzel's Estate, 221 Pa. 227, as renders a summary surcharge by the orphans' court under such circumstances unwarranted, is equally applicable in an insolvent estate, that part of the rule which would deprive the orphans' court of authority to impose a surcharge even after notice to accountants and a hearing, unless exceptions are filed, is distinguishable in the ordinary insolvent estate before a separate orphans' court under Sec. 47(b) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917. Colton's Est., 56 Montg. 76, 38 D. & C. 123.

The cost of a tombstone not being a proper charge in an insolvent decedent's estate, where credit for such a payment is claimed in an executor's account, the auditing judge has the authority and the duty on his own motion to disallow the credit and surcharge accountant, although no creditor objects, and although no notice was given to accountant or hearing had. Stitzel's Est., 221 Pa. 227, distinguished. Krewson's Est., 56 Montg. 87, 37 D. & C. 555.

Where the validity of a complete gift inter vivos is challenged, the primary burden of establishing its invalidity ordinarily rests on the challenger. 

The factors which bring into operation the rule that the donee of a challenged gift is required to show that it was the free, voluntary and intelligent act of the donor are fraud, confidential relation, weakness of mind not otherwise incapable and gross deception.

A confidential relation will be deemed to exist whenever the relative position of the parties is such that the one has power and means to take advantage of, or exercise undue influence over, the other. 

As between parent and child, the existence of a confidential relationship is a question of fact to be determined from the evidence.

$157 157 

A gift between persons in a confidential relationship will be condemned, even in the absence of actual fraud, or of mental incapacity on the part of the donor, unless there is full and satisfactory proof that it was the free and intelligent act of the donor, fully explained to him, and done with a knowledge of its conse quences. Lochinger v. Hanlon, 348 Pa. 29.

Clear, satisfactory and convincing evidence of a gift is established where decedent, at the time she executed notes, delivered them to a third party with instructions to deliver them to the payee after her death, at which time at least two of the notes were by the terms thereof made payable, and where after the execution of the notes the donor or maker thereof never exercised any dominion over the same.

19 The mere allegation of a gift, donatio mortis causa, will not oust the jurisdiction of the orphans' court to hear proof and determine preliminarily whether a substantial dispute of ownership of property, real or personal, exists.

An exception to an executor's account filed for the reason that the executor had p failed to account for Fourteen Hundred Dollars, which sum was given to a third person by the decedent in his lifetime for the purpose of safe keeping together with directions to dispose of it after his death as the third party sees fit will be dismissed upon proof of the creation of a trust inter vivos. Nagorski's Est., 20 Erie 317. inter 20 Where a bank depositor endorses the signature card of a savings account, in which he has made frequent deposits and withdrawals, a statement that he is placing the account in trust for his brother, but continues to make deposits and withdrawals, apparently without informing the brother of the trust or delivering the pass book to him, and thereafter dies intestate, the beneficiary having predeceased him, the bank deposit belongs not to the estate of the beneficiary, but to the estate of the depositor, first, because, the trust being a tentative one during the life of the depositor, the beneficiary had no estate which passes to his personal representatives upon his death and, secondly, because the death of the beneficiary effected a termination of the trust. Collopy's Est., 33 D. & C. 169.

Where an owner of a bank account signs a new deposit application card which recites that he and another are the joint owners of the money on deposit or to be deposited therein and that the survivor shall be the absolute owner of the deposit balance as surviving joint tenant, the signed application card represents a prima facie complete gift inter vivos by the owner to the other. Lochinger v. 

Hanlon, 348 Pa. 29.

A deposit in a savings fund account in the name of the depositor in trust for a named beneficiary constitutes a tentative trust which is revocable during the life of the depositor or by his will, but if not so revoked, becomes the property of the beneficiary upon the depositor's death. Cardoni, Gdn., v. Cardoni, 43 Lack 

141; Gorgas' Est., 147 Super. 319.

Where each of two depositors has a savings fund account in his own name in trust for the other, and, after the death of one, the survivor transfers the account which was in trust for her to the account in her own name in trust for the decedent, the deposit is unimpressed with any trust and is to be distributed to the heirs of the survivor rather than to the heirs of the predeceased beneficiary, and this is especially so where the survivor's will bequeaths the residue of her estate to the deceased beneficiary conditioned upon his surviving her, thus negativing the idea that she intended his heirs to benefit. Snyder's Est., 33 D. & C. 25. 

Where a sum is deposited by one person in his own name as trustee for an other, the general rule is that if the depositor dies first the balance on deposit becomes the property of the named beneficiary, but in the event of the prior death of the beneficiary his interest in the estate ceases and the fund becomes the absolute property of the depositor free from the trust. 

Since it is an inherent incident of a tentative trust that the beneficiary must survive the settlor before title to the fund can vest in him, unless the gift is completed in the depositor's lifetime by some unequivocal act or declaration, where one who has deposited money in a savings account in his own name as trustee for another dies in a common disaster with the beneficiary, under cir cumstances giving rise to no presumption of survivorship, the balance of the deposit passes to the personal representatives of the depositor rather than to those of the beneficiary. McWilliams' Est., 38 D. & C. 93.

Where a joint bank account is awarded by the Supreme Court to the surviving party and it is not a part of the estate, but is the property of the survivor and should not be included in the inventory of the decedent's estate. There should be no criticism of an executor when he litigates a debatable question as to the ownership of the property and two judges of the Superior Court dissent from the opinion of the majority awarding a fund to a claimant. Culhane's Est. (No. 3), 22 Erie 62.

The mere act of a person in changing an account in a savings bank to the name of the depositor "in trust" for another does not establish an irrevocable trust, but rather a tentative one.

Nor does the delivery of the passbook, under such circumstances, in itself, make

Where a deposit is made in trust for a minor and the depositor dies, the depositary would be protected, under sections 902 and 904 of the Banking Code of May 15, 1933, P. In the absence of a contractual relation between an attorney and a decedent, the estate is not liable for counsel fees for services rendered decedent during his lifetime, even though, the said services were highly commendable and tended to preserve the estate. Harvey's Est., 3 Northumb. 243.

When one person is rendering service to another which he is under no legal obligation to perform, and the party receiving the benefit makes an express promise that the service shall be paid for, and upon the faith of that promise the services are continued, there is a sufficient consideration to support the promise to pay for all the services, past as well as future. 

The measure of damages for a breach of an agreement to will real property in consideration for services rendered is the value of the services performed on faith of the contract and not the value of the property promised. 

In such case, it is incumbent upon the plaintiff merely to show the existence of an agreement to pay him for the services rendered, the nature and extent thereof, and that they were accepted; the value thereof is for the determination of the jury. Szusta v. Krawiec, 144 Super. 530. See also Hays v. Rose, 2 Beav. 208. 

Ordinarily an implied promise exists to pay for services rendered and accepted, and the burden is on the person denying liability to show no debt was, in fact, intended. 

In such a case a claim for board, lodging and nursing, less a credit for rent, will be sustained where the evidence shows the deceased lived with the claimants during such time and that the services were rendered although no demand was made for payment during the lifetime of the decedent. Where decedent and her sister had agreed with each other each to pay $300 per month to their mother, the claimant, for life, in consideration of the claimant's election to take under the will of their father, claimant's husband, whose will bequeathed the residue of a $3,000,000 estate to them equally and provided that if claimant should elect to take against the will the bequests otherwise given them should go elsewhere, it was held that the agreement was binding and that claimant was entitled to $300 per month for life out of decedent's estate, notwithstanding that claimant's election to take under her husband's will preceded the agreement. Woolsey's Est., 57 Montg. 102.
