The presumption of periodical payments is not applicable where a contract provides for payment at one specified time for services rendered. Fondelier v. 

Riddle, 152 Super. 586; Bemis v. Van Pelt, 139 Super. 282.

Where a considerable time elapses after the rendering of services without demand for compensation, it is presumed they were paid for at the time they were rendered or that the services were rendered without expectation of payment from motives of benevolence or affection, this presumption is greatly strengthened as between relatives. Anderson's Est., 23 Erie 387.

The presumption that wages for personal services rendered to a decedent, such as in the present case, are presumed to have been paid at stated periods may be rebutted by affirmative proof.

Where the presumption of payment has been rebutted, the burden of showing that the plaintiff had been paid in full then shifts to the defendant. Morrison v. 

Stone, Exr., 141 Super. 237.

Where a claim is presented against a decedent's estate for services to the decedent such as those rendered by plaintiffs in this case, ordinarily, there is a strong presumption that the services were paid for from time to time while they continued.

Where the existence of an express contract is in issue, the rebuttal of the presumption may be said to depend upon the accepted existence of the contract. 

Bemis v. Van Pelt, 139 Super. 282.

A claim for services against the estate of a decedent must be direct and positive; a presumption arises that payment was made in decedent's lifetime. The presumption is not rebutted especially where the claimant was a tenant of decedent and decedent's books show no income charged or received. Ingram's Est., 47 Lanc. 21. 

The quality of proof in claims against a decedent's estate which are usually paid at regular intervals, such as rent, is very high and the presumption that they were paid when due can be overcome only by clear, precise, indubitable proof. 

Bilaitis v. Nevereski, 42 Lack. 133. 

On a claim against the decedent's estate for domestic services rendered by the claimant to the decedent, there is a strong presumption of periodical payment which must be rebutted by direct proof, and it cannot be overcome by loose declarations of the decedent; and the presumption is strengthened by the fact that the decedent was a person who had cash available for payment. Est., 53 York 6.

Or had the reputation of paying obligations as they became due. Bechdel's Est., 344 Pa. 139.

Whether an estate would be liable for an injury caused by an executor's negligence in the course of carrying on a business which the will directed the executor to continue, was not decided. Clauson v. Stull, 331 Pa. 101. 

36a As a general rule a transfer of stock in a bank or other corporation after its closing or suspension, will not relieve the transfer of his statutory liability for its debts. The superadded liability of a shareholder does not cease upon the death of the stockholder; this on the theory that the stockholder's liability is contractual in nature and survives against his estate. 

The relationship of stockholder with its attendant liabilities is not forced upon the heir of the stockholder by the statute of descent and distribution. Such statute only operates to vest in him such rights and titles in the stock as to enable him to become a stockholder if he so desires. Shaffer's Est., 20 Leh. 117. 44c In order for a surviving party to be competent under the Act of 1891 to testify to any relevant matter occurring before the death of the other party, the subject matter of the proposed contradicting evidence must be something that occurred between the surviving party and another living and competent person who has testified against the surviving party at the trial, or something that occurred in the presence or hearing of such other living and competent person who has already been adversely called. The surviving party is then competent as to those matters only to which such witness has testified. Volkwein v. Volkwein, 146 Super. 265; Starkey's Est., 48 Lanc. 291.

It was held that the only benefit the claimant derived from the will was the recognition of the indebtedness and that it did not change her status when she sought to recover as a creditor, nor relieve her from the restrictions of the act as to proof. Tolling the statute. 

As to facts incident to tolling the statute, see Jordan Est., 25 Erie 202.

The voluntary filing of an account in the orphans' court by executors of the estate of a decedent tolls the statute of limitations as to all claims not barred on the date the account was filed, even though the statutory period may have expired at the time of audit and distribution. Brown Est., 152 Super. 252; Hendricks' 

Est., 9 Sch. Reg. 200.

In order that the statute of limitations may be tolled, there must be a clear, distinct and unequivocal acknowledgment of the debt as an existing obligation, consistent with a promise to pay on demand; an expression of a desire, intention or hope of ability to pay in the future is not sufficient. 

The fact that a statement relied upon to toll the statute was made before the statute had run does not change the measure of proof. 

When a decedent, a few days prior to his death, positively acknowledged his indebtedness on an account and promised to pay the same the Statute of Limitations is tolled. Weaver's Est., 25 Erie 246.

A letter written in response to a request for payment of the balance of a subscription to a hospital, in which decedent stated "I realize the necessity of your having funds; and can only state at this time that I will do the best I can at the earliest possible moment," was held not to be sufficient to toll the statute of limitations. Fix's Est., 140 Super. 60, rev'g 53 York 13.

The statute of limitations against the claim of receiver of an insolvent national bank based on an assessment by the comptroller of currency on shares of stock of the bank began to run on the date designated in the notice to the stockholders for payment thereof; and the filing of a petition in the orphans' court for a citation on the executor of a deceased stockholder to file his account tolled the statute. 67 Where no action is taken to collect a debt due on a specialty until twenty years has elapsed, a legal presumption arises, from delay itself, that the debt has been paid; the obligee must then show that payment was not made. 

Where there is a long delay, a presumption of fact of payment of a sealed instrument may arise in a period less than twenty years if there is a factual basis to support it other than the delay. 

No fixed rule of substantive law or evidence can be laid down as to the scope, quality or quantity of the additional circumstances necessary to support the presumption of payment arising from a delay of less than twenty years; each case depends upon its individual circumstances. 

Where the enforcement of a claim on a specialty has been delayed for a long time, any circumstance which shows conduct on the part of the obligee inconsistent with the existence of the debt as a valid claim, with the delay, support the inference that the obligation has been paid; and this is especially so where the claim is against a decedent's estate. Conrad's Est., 333 Pa. 561. 

Where a father who is indebted to his daughters dies, and it is shown that during his lifetime he made certain payments to the daughters, such proof raises the presumption that the payments were on account of the debts, and the burden of proving that they were gifts is upon the daughters. 

The rule that "a check offered in evidence raises a presumption that it was given by the maker either in payment of a debt or that cash was given at the time" means the former when the maker was indebted to the payee, and the latter when no cash indebtedness existed. Bass' Est., 35 D. & C. 300.

The presumption of payment arising from lapse of time does not work an extinguishment of the debt, nor does it require a new promise or its equivalent to revive it.

It is a presumption merely of fact, which makes it incumbent upon the creditor to prove, by preponderance of the evidence, that the debt was not actually paid. 

The burden of proof of the creditor may be sustained by direct testimony as to nonpayment, or by proof of circumstances tending to negative the likelihood of the claim having been satisfied and explaining the delay of the creditor in attempting to enforce it.

Evidence that the debtor, within the twenty-year period prior to suit, made an unqualified acknowledgment that the debt was still due and unpaid, and that the debtor for years had been in need of money, was held sufficient to sustain a finding that a judgment note had not been paid within the period of approximately twenty-six years between the time when it was payable and when it was presented at the audit of the account of the debtor's executors. Grenet's Est., 332 Pa. 111. 1 A claim against the estate of a decedent who gave a judgment note to his wife will not be allowed if more than twenty years has elapsed from the date of his death. In such a case the legal presumption of payment will not be rebutted, even though the note itself is produced, unless competent testimony is offered to prove an admission of liability by the debtor within the twenty-year period. Shenk's Est., 46 Lanc. 681.

The presumption of payment from the lapse of time is applicable to the Commonwealth just as are other legal rules and presumptions. 

The presumption of payment of debts unclaimed and unrecognized for twenty years is a strong one, and the evidence to rebut it must be satisfactory and convincing, especially where suit is not brought until after the death of the debtor.

A seal on a note imports consideration, and, therefore, want of consideration is no defense to an action on a sealed instrument.

There is a distinction between want and failure of consideration; want of consideration embraces transactions of instances where none was intended to pass, while failure of consideration implies that a valuable consideration, moving from the obligee to the obligor, was contemplated. 

The defense of want of consideration to a sealed instrument would contradict the terms of the instrument, while failure of consideration does not contradict the terms of the instrument, but shows that the consideration contemplated was never received. Murphy Est., 54 York 65.

It is well settled that a seal imports consideration. This is more than a mere presumption; the seal takes the place of proof of consideration and in the absence of fraud makes the promise enforceable without it. The defense of want of consideration is not available in an action on a sealed instrument. 

Where a transaction is explainable upon either of two different theories, one of which is consistent with good faith and fair dealing and the other involves fraud and deception, the explanation consistent with honesty and legality will be accepted unless the evidence clearly preponderates in favor of the illegal aspect of the transaction. Spence's Est., 22 Erie 41.

Evidence that a mortgagor conveyed the mortgaged premises, that thereafter the grantees made all payments of interest for a period of over 20 years, and that a mortgage extension agreement was entered into between the grantees and the mortgagee, is not sufficient to sustain a finding that the mortgagee had abandoned its claim against the mortgagor, where the mortgagee presents a claim against the mortgagor's estate for payment of the principal within 20 years after its maturity.

76a The doctrine of "the law of the case" is that, when an appellate court has considered and decided a question submitted to it upon appeal, it will not, upon a subsequent appeal on another phase of the same case, reverse its previous ruling even though convinced that it was erroneous.

The rule of "the law of the case" is one largely of convenience and public policy, and it must be accommodated to the needs of justice by the discriminating exercise of judicial power.

Where a prior decision is palpably erroneous, it is competent for the court, not as a matter of right but of grace, to correct it upon a second review where no wrong or injustice will result thereby, where no rights of property have become vested, where no change has been made in the status of the parties in reliance upon the former ruling, and where, following the decision on a former appeal, the court in another case has laid down a different rule, either expressly or by necessary implication, overruling the previous decision. Reamer's Est., 331 Pa. 117. 

An erroneous ruling of law by an orphans' court in dealing with the distribution of a portion of an estate becomes the law of the case for a subsequent distribution of a part of the same fund, if, at the time of both adjudications, the same question is raised, the parties are the same, and there is no appeal from the first adjudication.

Where the law of the case has been laid down and there is present every factor necessary to establish res judicata, the law must be followed even though it is in error. 

When determining whether an erroneous principle of distribution directed in a prior adjudication must be followed in a subsequent adjudication, the test is whether the fund is a different one, not whether it is a different distribution. 

If the question was passed upon at the time of the first adjudication, there was no appeal, the parties were the same, and the fund accounted for a part of the same fund, the error is irremediable. Talone's Est., 58 Montg. 62.

Colladay's Est., 333 Pa. 218, af'g 33 D. & C. 597. 

Where a petition for review has been held insufficient, it may not be amended after the period of limitation so as to introduce new matter or new additional grounds. 

Under Rule 15 of the Supreme Court Equity Rules, bill of revivor and replications (except as to the last, where new matter has been averred in the answer), shall not be filed in equity; and new matter may not be introduced by replication.

Freedom from liability depends upon the filing of an account.¹ 10 6a The Court is without authority to order the payment of a legacy until such time as the final account shall be filed and properly audited. Kreider's Est., 21

7a Under section 49 (b) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, a creditor of a decedent, who does not within six months after the granting and advertisement of letters testamentary give notice to the executor of his claims, cannot assert a personal liability against the executor who distributes the estate without an audit.

The use of the words "without the audit of their accounts" in the first part of section 49 (b) identifies the class of fiduciaries who elect to distribute at their own risk as distinguished from the class distributing "after audit and confirmation," and necessarily includes those who file no account as well as those who file accounts that are not audited and confirmed. 

No creditor who has failed to present his claim within the six months' period can receive anything out of funds distributed (1) because the first part of the section is a positive declaration that distribution shall be "without liability' to such creditors, and (2) because the second part of the section makes the decree conclusive as to the fund then before the court. Ray's Est., 345 Pa. 210. (Reviewed in "Fiduciary Review" of June, 1942.) 

9 A creditor's failure to give notice of his claim to the personal representative of the decedent, within six months of the grant and advertisement of letters testamentary, does not bar his claim, but protects the fiduciary against personal liability for risk-distribution made meanwhile.

Ray's Estate, 345 Pa. 210, goes no further than to hold that a fiduciary who has made risk-distribution is under no personal liability to a dilatory creditor for so doing. It does not hold that such a creditor cannot require that an account be filed.

L. 1037, is intended to enable the orphans' court, as in the case of a declaratory judgment, to decide a question when there exists an actual controversy between contending parties as to the propriety of retaining securities received in kind by a fiduciary, or where antagonistic claims are present between the parties which indicate imminent and inevitable litigation; it is not intended to provide for the rendition of purely advisory opinions, and, if so construed, would be unconstitutional. 

The orphans' court is without power to advise the guardian of a minor who has, at his own request, received distribution in kind from a decedent's estate under section 49 (e) 1 of the Fiduciaries Act, upon the propriety of retaining certain of the securities which are not legal investments for trust funds, where there exists no controversy nor the ripening seeds of one, the guardian's petition for advice under section 49 (e) 2 of the Fiduciaries Act, as amended, being assented to, not only by the minor, but by her father, mother, and stepfather, and where the obvious purpose of the petition is to secure insurance or protection to the fiduciary. Lee's Est., 40 D. & C. 194, 47 Lanc. 429, af'd in 342 Pa. 567. 166.

31a While it is ordinarily better practice to award appointed estates to the personal representatives of the appointor instead of directly to the appointee in order that the effect of the appointment with relation to the liability of the appointed estate for debts and legacies and for Federal estate tax under the Act of July 2, 1937 (P. A petition to review an adjudication of a trustee's account filed within three years of its confirmation will be granted where it appears that testator gave part of his residuary estate to an individual and a corporation as trustee, to pay the income to his daughter for life and upon her death to such persons as the daughter might appoint, that the daughter by will blended her individual estate with that of the appointive one, that the auditing judge awarded the fund in question to the trustees named in the daughter's will to whom distribution was made, the individual trustee being the same person as the individual trustee under the father's will and there being insufficient assets in the daughter's estate, after payment of all her debts and taxes, to pay in full all the legacies given by her will; had the auditing judge observed that there was a blending of the two estates he would have directed that sufficient funds be awarded from the father's estate to insure payment of all the daughter's debts, taxes, and legacies, and would have awarded only the balance then remaining for the purpose of the trust under the will of the daughter, a nonresident. 31b Now covered by Act of May 28, 1943, No. 334, which provides:

Section 1. Any power of appointment over real or personal property which is exercisable by deed, by will, by deed or will, or otherwise, whether general or special, other than a power in trust which is imperative, is releasable either with or without consideration, by written instrument, signed by the person possessing the power and delivered as hereinafter provided. 

Section 2. A power which is releasable may be released either absolutely or conditionally, and may also be released with respect to the whole or any part of the property subject to such power, and may also be released in such manner as to reduce or limit the persons or objects or classes of persons or objects in whose favor such power would otherwise be exercisable. No release of a power shall be deemed to make imperative a power which was not imperative prior to such release, unless the instrument of release expressly so provides. 

Section 3. Such release may be delivered to any of the following: (a) Any person specified for such purpose in the instrument creating the power; (b) Any trustee of the property to which the power relates; (c) Any person other than the person possessing the power who could be adversely affected by an exercise of the power; (d) The recorder of deeds of the county in which the person possessing the power resides or has a place of business, or in which the deed, will or other instrument creating the power is recorded or filed. 

Section 4. This act shall apply to releases heretofore and hereafter delivered.

Where a valid marriage is proved, the law presumes that it continues until the death of one of the parties (actual or presumptive after seven years) or a divorce is shown. Madison v. Lewis, 151 Super. 138. 

The burden is on one who claims as an heir of a decedent's estate to prove his relationship to the decedent, apart, primarily, from any question of claimant's legitimacy. 

Where kinship to the decedent is established by the claimant, it is not incumbent upon him to go further to prove his legitimacy; it is for those who contest his claim to disprove his legitimacy, and that by proof that is clear, direct, satisfactory, and irrefragable.

The presumption of legitimacy is in reality the presumption of the fact and of the validity of the marriage of the child's parents, once parentage is established. Mays' Est., 141 Super. 479.

The orphans' court is the proper tribunal to decide questions of fact as to alleged kinship with a decedent in a contest to determine who shall take the property of the decedent who dies without issue or known relatives.

Where a claim to participate in distribution of a decedent's estate is challenged the burden is on the claimant to establish his right. 

Church records of a marriage in Ireland and certificates and affidavits in support thereof, are admissible to show relationship, in proof of a claim to participate in the distribution of the estate of a decedent who had been born in Ireland where the place of origin, the town or place in Ireland from which the decedent came and the place where the kinship was created between the decedent and claimants' ancestor are conceded. 

Discrepancies in the spelling of Christian or family names will not operate to affect the probative value of affidavits and certificates from a foreign land, offered to show relationship.

The rights of existing or subsequent creditors of the settlor of an inter vivos trust in which the settlor retains all the advantageous attributes of property in the fund constituting the trust, except for the payment of an annuity out of income, cannot be defeated by the insertion of a spendthrift trust provision.

Where the settlor of an inter vivos trust retains beneficial incidents of the ownership of the property, including a general power of testimentary appointment sin himself, an assignment by him to his creditors of his interest in the trust is valid and not only transfers whatever interest he has but also extinguishes his general power of appointment.

If a person attempts to create a spendthrift trust for his own benefit, he may, while solvent, voluntarily transfer his interest to certain creditors, although the terms of the trust contain an express restraint against his voluntary alienation. 

Mogridge's Est., 342 Pa. 308.

Acquiescence and laches bar objection to the payment of income to the assignee of a life beneficiary under a spendthrift trust. Drinkhouse's Est., 33 D. & C. 712. 

The sale or assignment of an expectancy is not valid at law but may be enforced in a court of equity whenever good conscience seems to require it, but not otherwise.

When a mere expectancy or hope of receiving an interest or estate is the subject of a contract of assignment, no property passes; if, when the res comes into existence, the assignee invokes the aid of a court of equity to obtain the subject of the assignment, he must disclose a transaction that is not uncon scionable or inequitable. Norris's Est., 329 Pa. 483.

A son of decedent, who had previously executed, together with other children, an assignment to their father of all interest in their mother's estate, excepted to certain credits for funeral expenses, etc., on the ground that they were properly payable by the father, who survived the decedent. And it was sought to avoid the effect of the assignment on the grounds that it was executed on Sunday, was executed under a mistake of fact, there was no consideration, there was no delivery, and the assignment was personal to the father and revocable on his death the assignment was upheld. De Haven's Est., 33 Berks 81.

Where a testatrix gives all of her estate to a trustee and directs that it pay the income to a named beneficiary for life, and further provides that if the income should prove insufficient for her maintenance and support part of the prin cipal may be contributed by the trustee in its discretion, a general assignment by the beneficiary of future income is invalid as the testatrix impliedly restricted its use for her support and maintenance even though the trust is not specifically a spendthrift trust. Shenk's Est., 47 Lanc. 93, 54 York 50, 9 Som. 381; 8. c. 

47 Lanc. 249.

No special form and no particular language is necessary to create an equitable assignment. It is sufficient that the assignor express an intention to make an immediate transfer of his right to the assignee, and the transfer is supported by consideration.

In the absence of fraud, a debtor, though insolvent, may assign assets to a creditor as security for an antecedent debt even though the effect of the assignment will be to prefer that creditor. Hilliard Est., 28 North. 14.

Where a will, after making provision for bequests of absolute interests in the estate of the decedent, further provides that the interest of any beneficiary shall not be subject nor liable to any attachment, execution or other legal process on the part of any creditor of the beneficiary, the legacies are immune from attachment in the hands of the executors or in transit to the legatees. 

Such provisions protecting a legacy while it is in the hands of the executors is valid and effective even though a legatee whose interest is sought to be attached is one of the executors. 

Such rule is applicable even though there is no express provision in the will against assignment of the interest of a legatee. 

Where a testator's intention to restrict a gift is clear, it must be given effect, if possible, and only such interest, as limited, will pass. 

The property of a testator becomes the property of a devisee or legatee only so far as it is made such by the will, and then with such control, incidents of ownership, and liability to creditors as are therein given to it. Holmesburg 

B. & L. Ass'n v. Badger, 144 Super. 65, rel'g on Goe's Est., 146 Pa. 431.

By execution attachments two creditors of decedent's insolvent estate acquired priority over his general creditors, where the administrator of his deceased wife's estate, then under administration, was summoned as garnishee. His death did not abate the attachment process, and there could be no marshalling of assets for pro rata distribution with the general creditors. 

The legal rights of the parties were not disturbed by the death of the judgment debtor, except that his estate came into the orphans' court for distribution, unchanged as to its liability. The rights of the attaching creditors were fixed, only the method of collection was changed by the shift to a different forum for distribution. 

The effect of an attachment execution under the act of 1843, P. L. 233, Sec. 10, as amended by the Act of 1849 (P. L. 619), Sec. 11, under which acts the attachments were issued, is the same as under the Act of 1836 (P. L. 755). Evan's

An attachment execution under the Act of June 16, 1836 (P. L. 755), is concluded and ended where the attaching creditor takes judgment against the gar nishee, is paid the amount of the judgment and satisfies the judgment of record. 

Where a judgment creditor of a life tenant of a trust, who also owns a remainder interest therein, issues an attachment execution upon the trustees and obtains a judgment against them which is subsequently satisfied of record, and thereafter, the beneficiary having died, his executors receive his remainder interest in the trust, the judgment creditor, is not entitled to priority in distribution of the assets of the beneficiary's estate, but only to share pro rata with other creditors. Where a garnishee is an administrator or executor and judgment is entered against him, it cannot be entered against him de bonis propriis. Merchants N. B. v. Davis, 4 Sch. Reg. 148.

Where a banking institution, which with the beneficiary and another is the trustee of a spendthrift trust, credits income collected by it to the beneficiary in a bank account in her own name, funds so credited lose their immunity from attachment just as if they had been paid over to the beneficiary and deposited in another institution. Provident Tr. Co. v. Gordon, 41 D. & C. 188.

A vested interest in a decedent's estate is the subject of an attachment execution; a contingent interest is not.

The effect of an attachment of a vested interest in a decedent's estate is to transfer to the attaching creditor the rights of the defendant in the decedent's estate.

The court of common pleas has the power, in an attachment execution proceeding, to determine whether the interest of the defendant in a decedent's estate is vested or contingent.

In a case of doubt as to whether or not an interest in a decedent's estate is vested in the debtor, the court of common pleas would refuse to permit an attachment of such an interest and would direct the creditor to await the determination of the question by the orphans' court. 

Where a vested interest in a decedent's estate is attached, and the executor does not admit that there are sufficient funds of the debtor in his hands to pay the claim, judgment should be entered in favor of the plaintiff and against the garnishee, in the representative capacity of the latter, in the amount of the claim against defendant, to the extent that the same may become payable, after due determination of the orphans' court, out of the share or interest of defendant in the estate of the decedent.

The orphans' court has the exclusive jurisdiction to ascertain the amount of the estates of decedents and to order their distribution among those entitled, creditors as well as legatees and distributees. Overbrook, &c. Ass'n. v. Wilson, 333 Pa. 449.

On an execution attachment, summoning the executrix of her deceased husband as garnishee, it was held that she could not set off unmatured obligations of a legatee to the testator against the amount of a legacy.

40a Where a testator provided by his will that any advancements made to any legatees should be deducted from their distributive shares, and one of the executors named in the will is a legatee and son of the testator, and the remaining legatees, daughters of the testator, file their petition in Orphans' Court alleging, inter alia, the failure of the executors to file a correct inventory of the estate and their refusal to permit inspection of testator's books and papers by the legatees, the court will grant a hearing on the petition and the answer denying the allegations of the petition. § 166 

It is a basic principle in the distribution of a decedent's estate, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the parent intends to make an equal distribution among his children and, if during the lifetime of the decedent, property is transferred to one child, it is presumed that the transfer was made in anticipation of the amount that the child would likely receive from the estate of the decedent and as a repayment thereof; and if the decedent dies intestate these prepayments are considered advancements; however, if the decèdent dies testate, the payments are considered as satisfactions pro tanto of the legacies to the payee. 

As between a loan, a gift and an advancement, there is a rebuttable presumption in favor of an advancement, because of its tendency to equality. 

Interest is not chargeable upon an advancement during the lifetime of the decedent; although, for the sake of equality, interest will be charged from one year after the decedent's death to the time of distribution, unless the will or other circumstances require otherwise. Beard's Est., 56 York 161.

Where a testator lends money to A and his right of recovery on the loan is barred by the Statute of Limitations before his death, the amount of the loan will not be deducted from a specific legacy bequeathed by testator to A. Bendel's 

Est., 33 Berks 175.

The presumption of advance satisfaction of a legacy is akin to the doctrine of advancements in cases of intestacy and to the doctrine of ademption of specific legacies. 

The presumption of advance satisfaction of a legacy may be invoked by and for the benefit of a grandchild, the child of a deceased child of a testator, the testator being in loco parentis to such grandchild. Glessner's Est., 57 Montg. 78.

Whether money advanced by a decedent in his lifetime to those who may take as his heirs or legatees, is to be treated as a debt or an advancement, is always a question of intention.

Entries made by the donor in a family book or account are admissible to show advancement. 

Lapse of time does not affect an advancement, whereas a debt can be set off against a legacy only if subsisting and recoverable at the time of the death. 

An advancement is an irrevocable gift, without expectation of repayment except in the way of deduction. Thus a repayment repels the idea of an advancement. 

Money expended in the education of a child is presumed to be in discharge of a parental duty and not an advancement. Ruch Est., 19 Leh. 12. 

As to right of executors to make advancements see Koons' Est., 34 Berks 199.

Where one fails to perform a contract to bequeath to another all of his property in consideration of support and services during his lifetime, the court may not upon a claim for support at the settlement of the estate of the promissor, fix the value of the support and services in the absence of evidence to show the fair market value of the contract. Schartner's Est., 29 Del. 401.

Where decedent during his lifetime entered into an antenuptial agreement with his proposed second wife, by the terms of which each agreed not to claim any part of the estate of the other except the "amount" given to the one by the other in his will, and decedent agreed to, and did, pay to his intended wife a specified amount in money and securities; it was held that the decedent in the antenuptial agreement impliedly covenanted to make a will and in that will to give the woman who was to become his wife some "amount" but that this covenant was unenforceable for lack of definiteness, even though the widow was bound by her release of all her interest in the estate of decedent. 

A promise is unenforceable unless the nature and extent of the obligation is certain. 

Damages are not recoverable for breach of contract where there is no evidence to afford a sufficient basis for their assessment reasonable certainty. Friese's 

Est., 336 Pa. 241.

The measure of damages for breach of an agreement to will property in consideration of services to be rendered is the value of the services performed on the faith of the contract, and not the value of the real and personal property promised. 

Where the contract or agreement between the parties was that the services so rendered the decedent at his request should be compensated for by a money legacy definite in amount, or capable of being ascertained, that sum may be recovered if the decedent fails to provide for the legacy agreed upon. 

Where plaintiffs averred that decedent, in consideration of plaintiff's taking care of him during the balance of his life, preparing his meals and doing his house work, agreed to give to plaintiffs at the time of his death certain real estate and "some money besides," and that this agreement was not kept, plaintiffs properly brought their action against decedent's estate for the reasonable value of their services. Bemis v. Van Pelt, 129 Super. 282. 

40c Webb's Est., 29 Del. 200. 

40d Sec Act of Aug. 5, 1941, (P. L. 816), Moore v. Prudential &c. Co., 342 Pa. 

40e The doctrine of subrogation can be invoked only for the protection of one 570.

§§ 166-168  

who has paid the debt of another because he had made himself legally liable in connection therewith. 

Where it appeared that the husband of a decedent, whom she had made her executor, elected to take against the will; and that out of his personal funds he paid certain legacies, receiving releases, not assignments, from the legatees, and also paid the direct and collateral inheritance taxes; it was held that the husband, in paying the legacies charged on the real estate which descended to collateral heirs, and in paying the inheritance taxes was a volunteer, and his heirs were not entitled to reimbursement out of the proceeds of the real estate. Beck v. Beiter, 146 Super. 114.

Residence of widow in another county is not in itself sufficient to bar her right of exemption. Smollensky's Est., 1 Sch. Reg. 10. 

The exemption provision in section 12(a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, is not a statute of distribution, and the exemption is not an inheritance; it is wholly a gratuity, based upon the existence of the family relationship at the time of decedent's death.

Title to the exempted property and the right to claim it does not vest upon the husband's death, and the widow's right to the property attaches only upon her claiming it.

The right of the widow or of a child is determined with reference to the date the claim is made and not as of the date of death of the decedent. 

Where decedent's wife at the time of his death was on her death bed and died ten weeks later without having claimed her widow's exemption, and during the whole of the period by which she survived her husband she was inarticulate and incapable, both physically and mentally, of claiming the statutory benefit, failure of the widow to assert her claim did not constitute a forfeiture nor a waiver thereof. 

The mere fact that decedent was survived by the mentally incompetent widow, on whose behalf the right was not asserted and who died shortly after her hus band, did not defeat the claim of a daughter of decedent, who had formed a part of the family and who presented her claim within a reasonable time after the death of her father.

Section 12(a) of the Act of 1917 is to be construed to make effective its policy. Bell's Est., 139 Super. 11, rev'g 34 D. & C. 200.

Under the Act 7 June 1917, P. L. 447, section 12(a) allowing a widow to "retain or claim" of the property of the estate to the value of $500.00, the widow's right is personal and may be exercised by her alone or may be waived by her voluntary failure to "retain or claim" the exception; but should marriage or death intervene before retention or claim, or should retention or claim be too long deferred, the right is lost. Lutz's Est., 33 Berks 101.

Where the widow of a decedent whose only substantial assets were certain adjusted service bonds promises an undertaker that if he will give the decedent a funeral out of proportion to the decedent's estate, and much above the county and Federal allowance therefor, she will see that he is paid out of the bonds, and pursuant thereto executes an application to the Treasury Department for the payment of certain of the bonds to the undertaker, the promise and subsequent direction constitute a waiver of her right to her widow's exemption insofar as it may conflict with payment of the funeral bill, and she is estopped from re- taining so much of the proceeds of the bonds, set aside to her as her exemption, as is required for such payment. Fuller's Est., 37 D. & C. 252.

The guardian of a minor child of a decedent cannot secure the $500 exemption for such child where the decedent leaves a widow to survive him who has not forfeited her rights. Walston's Est., 27 North. 47.

A widow of a man domiciled in Pennsylvania and residing in Ohio at the time of his death is not entitled to an exemption under the 12th Section of the Fidu ciaries Act of 1917 (P. L. 447), where a year's allowance under a statute of the state of Ohio had been allowed and paid. She forfeited her right to a claim for an exemption in the state of Pennsylvania. 

The only amount that a widow can have from a Pennsylvania estate in any

181. PROCEDURE WHERE ESTATE DOES NOT EXCEED $500. 

Act of 1931 construed.¹ 19 The act is now effective whether or not letters have been issued or a will probated.¹ºº 

19 Section 12 (f) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, (P. L. 447), as amended by the Act of May 12, 1931 (P. L. 116), providing a procedure by which the personal estate of a decedent may be set aside to his widow on account of her exemption without appraisement, was intended to provide a means of avoiding the expense, delay and inconvenience of administration on the estates of intestates valued at less than $500, and procedure under that section cannot be taken after letters of administration have been issued and the administratrix has entered her bond and taken legal possession of the assets of the estate.

CHAPTER XXXIV. 

DESIGNATION OF CURTILAGE. 

210. PROCEDURE, APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONERS. 

Curtilage defined.42 

42 In a testamentary disposition, the word "house" is synonymous with messuage, and conveys all that falls within the designation of curtilage. 

In the absence of testamentary limitation of curtilage resort must be had to supporting oral testimony.

Evidence is only admitted dehors the will, from necessity, to explain that which would otherwise have had no operation. 

Curtilage of a building includes only such land, belonging to the same owner, as is reasonably needed for the general purpose of the structure, or which the owner has in some way manifested his intent to treat as appurtenant. 

A report and return of Commissioners appointed under the provisions of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, Sec. 34, "to designate the boundaries of the curtilage or lot appertaining to the dwelling house" which is based upon facts designating the use of the premises by the owner, and his intent that certain land apurtenant to the dwelling house be included as part of the curtilage, will be confirmed. 

Kutz's Est., 31 Berks 35.

56 The intention of the testator determines whether a legacy is specific or demonstrative.

Legacies bear interest from the time they are payable, and this time is to be ascertained from the intention of the testator.

Where a testator directs a sale of his real estate and the payment of certain legacies from the proceeds, an intention is indicated that the legacies should not bear interest until they are payable, to wit, the date when the sale is effective.

57 Where an antenuptial agreement provides that if the wife survives the husband she is to receive a certain sum "at or before the audit upon the first account rendered by the executor', she is entitled to interest on that sum only from the date of audit: the fact that the husband's will acknowledges liability under the agreement and directs the payment thereof does not change the status of the widow as creditor to that of legatee within the meaning of section 21 of the 

Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447.

Even though a testamentary acknowledgment of liability to testator's widow under an antenuptial agreement were construed to render her a pecuniary legatee, she would be entitled to interest on the sum due her only from the date of audit if the agreement specifically provides that the sum be paid at that time, for such provision constitutes the expression of a "contrary intention" within the meaning of section 21 of the Fiduciaries Act, providing that interest on a pecuniary legacy to a widow runs from the date of testator's death "unless a contrary intention appears by the will." Brown's Est., 36 D. & C. 426, af'd in 340 Pa. 350.

[Interest on all pecuniary legacies, whether bequeathed directly or in trust, shall, unless a contrary intention appear by the will, begin to run from the expiration of one year from the death of the testator; except that, if the account of the executor be filed and confirmed and distribution awarded before the end of such year, then interest on such legacies shall run from the date of the award.] Unless otherwise provided in the will, on all pecuniary legacies, whether bequeathed directly or in trust, interest at the legal rate or at the rate earned by the particular estate out of which such legacies are payable, whichever shall be less, shall begin to run at the expiration of one year from the death of the testator; except that, if the account of the executor be filed and confirmed and distribution awarded before the end of such year, then interest thereon shall run at such rate from the date of the award, and on all pecuniary legacies payable at a future period or upon contingencies or under other circumstances by which the payment and satisfaction of such legacies may be postponed or may not take place until a distant period after the death of such testator, interest at such rate, shall begin to run from the time when such legacy becomes payable: Provided, That where a pecuniary legacy is bequeathed to or for the use of the widow of the testator, or any child or descendant of the testator, or any person toward whom the testator in his lifetime stood in loco parentis, or for the maintenance of any person, interest at the legal rate shall, unless a contrary intention appear by the will, begin to run from the date of the death of the testator. 

Interest on legacy given by will of testatrix who died in 1930, but not paid until 1940, when funds first became available from sale of real estate, awarded from one year after death at 1%, the rate earned by estate, and not at 6%. 

Although testatrix died before Act of June 24, 1939, P. L. 714, which amended

Sec. 21 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, the rate of interest on a pecuniary legacy payable one year after testatrix's death in 1930 is that provided by the amendment and not that provided theretofore, as the statutes constitute rules of distribution and do not confer vested rights to the legatee. Loughlin's Est., 57 Montg. 243, 41 D. & C. 678.

Pecuniary legacies, expressly postponed by testator until after sale of real estate, do not become due until that time, and interest. does not accrue thereon, under Sec. 21 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, as amended, until that time. Cross' 

Est., 57 Montg. 148, 41 D. & C. 250. 213.

214. LIFE ESTATES, ETC.,-PROTECTION OF REMAINDERS. 

Procedure under the Act.67

Effect of power of consumption.67a 

67 Where a will gives the remainder of an estate to a wife, and after her death or remarriage to the testator's children, Section 23 of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917 governs, and such estate will be turned over to the widow, upon her filing a bond, or a trustee will be appointed.

§ 21415 

An administrator c. t. a., d. b. n. should not be appointed. Strock Est., 18 ridon 

Leh. 46.

The law does not require that successive life tenants give security nor that a trustee to hold the life estates, be appointed for them when the life tenants are constituted the sole judge of what use they shall make of the property and also have the right of consumption of both principal and interest. Law Est., 23 

Erie 59.

The relation of such a life tenant to the remaindermen is that of debtor for the fund named, and she is responsible to them only for the value of the estate at the date of distribution, and not for any increase in the value of the fund thereafter. 

Where a life tenant takes over personal property to use the same during his lifetime, pursuant to a will, the result is in effect to make the sum thus received a part of his individual estate. 

A life tenant who takes possession of the assets without giving bond is not a trustee for the remaindermen, but is a debtor to them the same as if he had given a bond.

The Act of May 17, 1871, P. L. 269, which requires a life tenant to give a bond, does not apply to a life tenant having the power of consumption of principal. 

Where an estate is bequeathed to the legatee for life with remainders over, the rights of the life tenant and remaindermen are fixed by the decree of distribution and the failure to make distribution is immaterial. Powell's Est., 340 

Pa. 404. And see Seaman's Est., 19 Leh. 420.

In determining the net estate for which a life tenant is obliged to account to those entitled in remainder, moneys advanced by the life tenant, or commissions owing to him as executor, must be deducted. 

Where a life tenant takes over the property for his life use, it becomes to all intents and purposes his own, and he becomes a debtor to the remaindermen for the value of the property so taken. 

The failure of the life tenant to enter the bond required does not affect the rights of the remaindermen. Gillett's Est., 130 Super. 309. (See reviews of this and other cases pertinent to this subject in "Fiduciary Review" of February and April, 1943.)

An executor's account of a life tenant's estate, when called for audit in the orphans' court, could not be confirmed absolutely, and was returned to the files and marked "not audited," where it remained to be determined preliminarily whether the account, designating the deceased life tenant as trustee, was properly filed, and whether the estate was subject to debts created by her under the terms of an agreement filed at the audit of her deceased husband's estate, the distribution having been made to her in trust to be by her held under the terms of the will *** without requiring her to give bond or security for the faithful performance of the trust. 

The only effect of the agreement filed at the audit of the executors' account was that the widow should not be required to give bond, something she was not obligated to do under the will or by act of assembly. 

While section 23 of the fiduciaries act of 1917 provides for a bond by the life tenant who elects to take personalty, it has been held that, where said life tenant has the power of consumption under the will, section 1 of the act of 1871, P. L. 

269, does not apply, and section 23 of the fiduciaries act of 1917 is practically a re-enactment of the former act. 

The agreement to distribute to her as trustee, followed by the decree in that form, did not impose any new liability upon her, because the balance was to be taken and held by her in trust for the purposes specified in the will, and under this she had power of consumption and was the sole judge of the necessity of using the corpus. The distribution to her in trust did not in any way change the relationship between her and the remaindermen. col rife, The contention that distribution should be made to the remaindermen, without any deductions for debts incurred by the life tenant, was rejected, where under the will the widow had the power of consumption and could obligate the life estate. 

Claims of creditors should be presented at the audit. Flannery's Est., 90 P. L. J. the Residuary legatees as remaindermen could not claim as creditors and the estate AT 89.

DISTRIBUTION 

of the widow was not liable for losses to real and personal property due to general economic conditions, where testator gave the residue and remainder of his estate to his wife, "for and during the term of her life," with power to manage and control the property absolutely, and without security. She was not only trustee for herself during her life but necessarily trustee for the remaindermen as well, although not named as such, and there was no occasion to invoke the 23rd section of the fiduciaries act of 1917. 

The widow had a beneficial interest for life and not a legal life estate, where #5 testator's property was given to his wife for life with powers to manage and control it if unconverted, and it passed by his direction in his will after her death, instead of its value at his death. DuPuy's Est., 90 P. L. J. 505.

The liability of the life tenant to the remaindermen is the same whether or not a bond was entered by her. 

The extent of the widow's liability to the remaindermen should be determined as of the date she came into possession of the corpus with the right to enjoy the income therefrom. Since she filed no account, it must be as of the date of the death of the decedent. Baker's Est., 54 Dauph. 39.

The purpose of security is to guarantee the corpus to remain intact. This is not contemplated or required where there is a power of consumption. Waters' Est., 28 North. 85. 

215. PROCEDURE TO ENFORCE PAYMENT OF LEGACIES, ETC., CHARGED ON LAND. 

Method of procedure."¹ 

Application of the Act.75 

71 Where a testator directs his daughter, to whom he has devised specific real estate and also the income from a share of the residue of his estate and a contingent interest in the corpus thereof, to pay certain annuities from "her share of my estate," the annuities are charged upon the real estate, and if not paid the annuitants may properly petition for an order requiring payment and, in default thereof, for the sale of the property. 

Where one clause of a will charges specifically-devised real estate with the payment of certain annuities, another clause authorizing the mortgaging of real estate not specifically devised to pay legacies does not apply to the annuities. 

Boyle's Est., 37 D. & C. 479.

By the Act of May 27, 1943, No. 321, Sec. 25(a) of the Fiduciaries Act there are added to those who may apply for relief "the executor of the last will and testament of any decedent, or the administrator cum testamento annexo, or the administrator de bonis non cum testamento annexo of the said last will and testament." 

75 See Shaffer's Est., 3 Northumb. 363; Shipe's Est., 4 Northumb. 296.

Where a testator bequeaths his farm to his sons but provides that his daughters are to be allowed to live thereon so long as they remain single and that they are to have a good comfortable living out of the farm," and that this shall be a charge upon the land, the charge so created runs with the land. 

Since a testamentary charge of "a good comfortable living" upon land is indeterminate both as to time and substance, it is not rendered unenforcable by the Act of April 27, 1855, P. L. 368, sec. 7, because not enforced for a period of over 

21 years, for the statute does not begin to run until the legacy is payable, and such a legacy is continuously payable during the life of the beneficiary. 

A bequest of "a good and comfortable living" is to be measured by the station, habits, and tastes of the testator and the beneficiary. 

The proper forum in which to enforce a testamentary charge upon land is the orphans' court having jurisdiction of the testator's estate. Norris' Petn., 44 D. & C. 297. 

Where a testator leaves all his property to his widow with a proviso that, if there should be sufficient for the widow's support for the balance of her life "and to spare," certain specific legacies are to be paid to others, and at the time of

$$ 215-219 

the widow's death over eight years later the real estate remains intact, it must be presumed that the testator's estate was sufficient to support the widow for life and to spare,' " and the land is therefore charged with the specific legacies; it is immaterial that the widow may have paid her husband's debts and funeral expenses or that the real estate may be subject to her own debts and funeral expenses if she made no claim for reimbursement from her husband's estate and no creditor is making claim against her estate. Reynolds' Est., 43 D. & C. 160. 

218. DECREE ESTABLISHING FUND, AND DISCHARGING RE- MAINING ESTATE. 

Method of procedure.85 

85 Where a testator directs his executors to set aside out of his estate a sum sufficient to produce a net income of approximately $1,200 annually and to pay it over in quarterly instalments to named beneficiaries, but makes no provision for the payment of taxes, the fund to be set aside must be sufficiently great to produce the stipulated income after payment of personal property taxes at the rate imposed at the time of testator's death, but it must bear its proportionate share of the transfer inheritance tax.

Where a testator directs his executors to set aside in trust a sum sufficient to produce a net income of approximately $1200 annually it seems that the amount of $32,500 would, under present conditions, be a just and equitable sum for the purpose. Hick's Est., 3 Blair 41, 39 D. & C. 351. 20 While an auditing judge, in setting aside a sum sufficient to yield an income to pay annuities established by a decedent's will, may, upon request or of his own motion, preserve to the residuary legatees, whose bequests may have been reduced by such a capitalization, a contingent right to share in the excess income or principal, should actual experience demonstrate the excess to have been unnecessary to produce the specified annuity, if this is not done, the amount so fixed p must be regarded as a judicial determination of the matter submitted to the court, which, when confirmed absolutely and unappealed from, is to be regarded as irrevocably fixed and binding upon all parties and their privies. 

Years of experience have demonstrated the wisdom of fixing the capitalization of an annuity on a basis of three percent as a sum sufficient to make certain beyond all contingencies the payment specified, and where distribution is ordered upon the basis of such a capitalization, those entitled to the remainder of the sum set aside to secure payment of the annuities, rather than the residuary legatees, are entitled to the entire corpus of the sum so set aside even though in fact a lesser sum would have been sufficient. Henson's Est., 36 D. & C. 109.

226. TESTAMENTARY GUARDIANS. 

Right to appoint." 18 18 Testatrix by her will gave to a minor grandson $500 and appointed her son, the father of the minor, "as his guardian without bond to hold and invest said money for the benefit of my said grandson during his minority."

That the estate vested in the grandson and that its administration must be given to a guardian to be appointed by the Orphans' Court. 

The Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403, section 8, as amended by Act of May 13, 1925, P. L. 689, gives the right to the surviving parent to appoint a testamentary guardian for the minor, who has authority over both the person and the estate. 

The Act nowhere grants appointing powers to a grandparent though the right exists to appoint a trustee over an estate bequeathed or devised to a grandchild. 

Such appointment must, however, pertain to a trust in fact and not to a guardianship of the person or estate of the minor. The present gift being to the grandson vested title in him and the bequest erected a guardianship and not an active trust. Klein's Est., 32 Berks 172, 54 York 42, 38 D. & C. 632.

6 The purpose of appointing a guardian and trustee ad litem is to allow the judge to remain judicial and to place the burden of investigation and claim on another: the guardian's duty is to be a reasonable litigant, asserting only what is arguable, and he will not be interfered with by the judge unless he is clearly taking the wrong position, in which case the remedy is to appoint another guardian. 

At the audit of an account in the orphans' court, whether executor's or trustee's, a guardian ad litem for minors, or a trustee ad litem for unborn persons is not a necessary party, the direction for the appointment of such person in Section 59 (k) of the Fiduciaries Act, as amended, being under such circumstances directory rather than mandatory, and a decree of confirmation is not void as to minors and persons unborn who were not represented, but the court should be solicitous to see that there is someone to speak for minors and unborn persons: Under some circumstances, they may be represented by other parties who have like interests. Steel's Est., 32 D. & C. 55.

It is the duty of a guardian ad litem vigorously to defend every legal right possessed by the persons whom he represents: he has no authority to surrender without consideration any right or property which is theirs regardless of his natural sympathy for other parties in interest, and his agreement to do so is a nullity. Mark's Est., 38 D. & C. 489. 

8 No account will be audited until guardian is appointed for minor and unborn children, etc., not otherwise represented. Simon's Est., 23 Erie 212.

Where testamentary trustees are directed to "expend" income for benefit of weak-minded beneficiary it is their duty to expend the income themselves, in their absolute discretion. Where a testatrix gives a sum to a trustee whom she directs to use the income or any part of the principal, as he may deem fit, for the benefit of testatrix's brother, the fact that the trustee does not see fit to distribute any part of the income during the beneficiary's lifetime does not render its accumulation unlawful. On a motion to take off a compulsory nonsuit, entered in an action in trespass brought against a trust company, trustee of a certain estate, to recover damages for injuries alleged to have been sustained by the plaintiff due to the defendant's negligence, it was held that the estate cannot be held liable for the negligent acts of the trustee, and that, therefore, the nonsuit was properly entered.

63a Those who deal with trustees are presumed to do so with notice of the legal limitation of their power; and when they go outside of this, they do so at their own risk.

A trustee can properly exercise such powers and only such powers as (a) are conferred upon him in specific words by the terms of the trust, or (b) are necessary or appropriate to carry out the purposes of the trust and are not forbidden by the terms of the trust. 

An express power to join in the execution of a renewal mortgage does not necessarily include authority to a trustee to execute the bond. 

Where personal and real property was transferred to a trustee as security for the performance of an agreement by the settlor and the trust agreement authorized the trustee to execute a new mortgage on the real estate in order to pay off an existing mortgage, it was held, under the circumstances, that the trust agreement did not authorize the trustee to execute a mortgage bond and make the trust assets other than the mortgaged premises liable for the payment of such bond. 

Hartje's Est., 345 Pa. 570.

Whether an obligor who signed a bond as trustee is individually liable thereon depends upon the intent of the parties at the time the bond was executed. 

The facts that a trust company signs a bond accompanying a mortgage as trustee and not individually, that the warrant of attorney authorizes confession of judgment against it only in its trust capacity and not in its individual capacity, and that wherever it is referred to in the bond it is designated as trustee under an identified agreement, indicate that it was the intention of the parties to the bond at the time of its execution that the trust company should be liable only as trustee and not in its individual capacity.

It seems that the Act of June 24, 1939, P. L. 871, providing that where a fiduciary signs as such and discloses the estate or trust for which he contracts he shall not be personally liable unless the instrument contains an express provision to the contrary, is unconstitutional insofar as section 4 thereof provides that it shall apply to instruments executed before its enactment. 

Where title to property is registered in the name of a trustee for a disclosed trust, the trustee's tax liability is limited to the trust estate. Phila. Sav. Fd. Soc. v. Comm'th Tr. Co., 90 P. L. J. 47, 44 D. & C. 98.

The individual trustees of a Massachusetts trust who, with authority, execute in the name of the trust by its trustees, a bond and mortgage which names the trust as obligor and mortgagor, and which does not contain any express or clearly implied personal covenant of the trustees, are not personally liable as obligors to an obligee who knows that the other party to the transactions is a Massachusetts trust.

The trustees of a Massachusetts trust may adopt a name for business purposes. 

Knowledge by a person that he is dealing with a Massachusetts trust and that neither the shareholders nor trustees of such an association are ordinarily per-

240241 

sonally liable for its debts is legally equivalent to an express agreement by the creditor that he will not attempt to hold the shareholders or trustees personally liable for the obligation that the trustees entered into. 

Business trusts of the character known as Massachusetts trusts are not against public policy. Penna. Co. v. Wallace, 346 Pa. 532. 

63b Act of June 24, 1939 (P. L. 871) which provides: 

Section 1. Where an instrument contains, or a person adds to his signature thereto, words indicating that he contracts or signs in his capacity as fiduciary, and such words disclose the estate or trust for which he so contracts or signs,, he shall not be personally liable on the instrument uness it contains an express provision that he shall be personally liable, and in the absence of such a provision, any action on the instrument shall be brought against such person only in his fiduciary capacity, or against his successor in such capacity, and execution upon any judgment obtained in any such action shall be had only against the assets and property in the hands and possession of such person or his successor, as fiduciary, and not against his own assets or property. 

Section 2. (a) The word "instrument," as used in this act, shall include every agreement, note, bond, mortgage, extension of mortgage, warrant of attorney, and every other instrument in writing of any kind. 

(b) The word "person, as used in this act, shall include a corporation, partnership, association, bank, bank and trust company, trust company, title insurance company, and national banking association, as well as a natural person. (c) The word "fiduciary," as used in this act, shall include an executor, administrator, guardian, committee, receiver, trustee, assignee for the benefit of creditors, and any person acting in any similar capacity. (d) The singular shall include the plural and the masculine shall include the feminine and neuter.

Section 3. If any provision of this act shall be held to be invalid or unconstitutional, by any court of final jurisdiction, as applied to any particular instrument or group of instruments, the Legislature hereby declares its intent to be that such provision shall thereupon become inoperative and inapplicable as to such instrument or group of instruments, but shall remain operative and applicable as to all other instruments. 

Section 4. This act shall become effective immediately upon its final enactment; and it shall apply to all instruments executed either before or after such final enactment: Provided, however, That it shall not be applicable in any action instituted prior to July 1, 1939, on an instrument executed prior to such final enactment.

Clyde's Est., 329 Pa. 552. 

Where a corporate trustee improperly invests trust funds in mortgage certificates in such a manner that the relation is merely that of banker and depositor, with the mortgage pool as security for the repayment of the deposits, it necessarily follows that, in the liquidation of the bank, no interest is payable upon the certificates after the trustee's insolvency; under such circumstances the life tenant should receive the income from the entire estate, including the income on any of the funds received on account of the defaulted certificates, pending completion of the salvage operation, and upon such completion the proceeds must be allocated between income and principal on the formula of 

Nirdlinger's Estate (No. 2), 327 Pa. 171.

Where certain proceeds of the salvage operation upon certain defaulted certificates in a trust estate are improperly distributed as income, the trustee may, upon completion of the salvage operation, recoup itself concerning such overpayment from future income. 

Where the assets of a trust estate include certain defaulted securities as to which the salvage operation has not been completed, the court may refuse finally to discharge the trustee, upon its petition, until the salvage operation shall have been completed and accounted for. Haugh's Est., 33 D. & C. 202. 

Where mortgages held by a trust estate have been foreclosed and the properties covered by them have been bought in by the trustees, the net rents from the properties, that is, gross rents, less taxes, insurance, repairs and other carrying charges, should be paid to life tenants during the time the properties remained unsold and are held by the trustees. The net rents to be paid to life tenants are the amounts received from each individual property; the properties taken over by foreclosure, productive of : income, and those which are not, are not to be considered together in determining the amount distributable to life tenants. 

Ordinary current expenses as well as extraordinary expenses incurred in connection with unproductive property are payable out of principal, unless it is otherwise provided by the terms of the trust, even though the trust estate includes other property from which an income is derived. 

The carrying charges on unproductive property can be advanced out of principal, and these advances can be recouped when the properties are sold. 

Where an overpayment has been made to the life tenants, the trustees can recoup the amount thereof from income in their hands. Nirdlinger's Est., 331

Pa. 135. 

The question whether carrying charges on unproductive real estate, part of a decedent's estate, shall be paid out of income or principal, or divided betweenthe two, must be determined in each case, when it arises, according to the equities as between recipients of income and those entitled to principal. 

The determination of this question is for the court of first instance in the exercise of a sound discretion, and its decision will be reviewed on appeal only where there has been a palpable abuse of discretion. 

Nirdlinger's Estate, 331 Pa. 135, distinguished. 

Levy's Est., 333 Pa. 440, mod 'g 34 D. & C. 312, where it was held by a divided court: 

Where a testamentary trustee retains unproductive real estate during a period of depression following the testator's death and eventually sells it for more than the appraised value, the carrying charges during the period of retention are to be charged against principal rather than against income, especially if the 1

life tenant is the primary object of the testator's bounty; nor is it material whether the will effected an equitable conversion. 

A life tenant is not estopped from having the carrying charges on unproductive real estate charged against principal rather than against income because she requested that the property be retained, where, in advising delay, she acted wisely and was solicitous not only for her own position but also for succeeding interests, and where the record further fails to show that her action definitely influenced the action of the trustee. 

Under Levy's Estate, 333 Pa. 440, question whether charges of carrying unproductive trust real estate are to be paid out of income or principal is to be determined by orphans' court in exercise of its discretion and according to the equities in the particular case. 

When the gross income of a trust is about $150,000 and the total cost of carrying unproductive real estate therein is $47,000, of which 95% is for maintaining testator's residence, which is to be sold when its value can be realized, and where life beneficiaries are testator's widow and descendants, the primary objects of his bounty, whom he maintained during his lifetime by payments exceeding the income from the trust, the equities are all in favor of income and the carrying charges of the unproductive real estate must be charged against principal of the trust. Stotesbury's Est., 56 Montg. 296.

The estate of a life tenant is entitled to all of the net rents from real estate derived from foreclosed mortgages to the date of the death of the life tenant and no further; carrying charges on unproductive real estate, with each property considered as a separate unit, must be borne by principal. Myers' Trust, 35 D. & C. 492. 

Apportionment is a discretionary matter and should be refused where practical difficulties make it impossible or it is inequitable and will result in frustrating the settlor's purpose.

Where a trustee forecloses a mortgage, buys the property covered at the foreclosure sale, and thereafter sells it, while the life tenant is living, the net proceeds of the sale must be apportioned between the life tenant and remainderman. 

Where a testamentary trust containing a spendthrift provision as to the life tenant provided for the payment of the principal to the remainderman at the death of the life tenant, and at that time the trustee held certain parcels of real estate and small undivided fractional interests in other parcels of real estate acquired as a result of the foreclosure of mortgages, and also held other mortgages and participation certificates which were in default and it appeared that the liquidation of these investments by the trustee would take a long time and unduly extend the life of the trust after its real purpose had been accomplished, it was held that the rule of apportionment should not be applied and that all of the property should go to the remainderman. Spear's Est., 333 Pa. 199, af'g 

26 Del. 371.

A life tenant is not barred by laches from seeking the transfer of carrying charges upon unproductive real estate from income to principal because she had not specifically complained to the trustees about such charges over a period of years, although she had received notice thereof, where she had complained about the diminution of her income and where both the life tenant and the remainderman are living, the trust continues, and there is nothing to prevent determination of their respective rights.

Participating interests in mortgages are not to be distinguished and differentiated from ordinary mortgage investments in the application of the rules relating to the allocation of carrying charges on unproductive or underproductive real estate. 

Where a mortgage against which participating interests have been issued is foreclosed, and the real estate so acquired is operated at a net loss, the portion of that loss chargeable against participating interests held by a trust should be borne by principal rather than by income, where the testator's primary purpose was to afford the life tenant a periodical and regular income. 

The fact that a trust is subject to spendthrift provisions does not prevent an advancement from principal to carry unproductive or underproductive real estate. 

Where real estate owned by a decedent at the time of his death is sold nine years thereafter for less than the deficit in the carrying charges in the meantime, and the testator's primary purpose was to assure a regular income to the life 13

tenant, his daughter, the deficit in carrying charges should be charged against principal to the extent of the amount realized from the sale of the property, but the balance will be charged against income, for to do otherwise would unduly prejudice the remainderman.

Carrying charges on unimproved lots owned by decedent must be borne by principal rather than by income where the life tenant is the primary object of testator's bounty.

Where a trustee's account is filed in order to obtain determination of the proper allocation of carrying charges on unproductive or underproductive real estate, the costs thereof should be apportioned equally between principal and income, since the accounting was for the equal benefit of life tenant and remainder-

Mc- 

Hugh's Est., 55 Montg. 206.

Any enhancement in the value of unproductive real estate owned by a decedent at the time of his death and left in trust belongs to principal: the theory of apportionment adopted by section 241 of the American Law Institute Restatement of Trusts is not accepted in Pennsylvania. 

In every instance where the question of allocation of carrying charges of unproductive real estate owned by a decedent and left in trust arises, the problem is for the sound discretion of the court of first instance: if the land is actually sold, the allocation made by the court becomes final; if the land is unsold, the allocation is a temporary expedient and must be regarded as an advance by principal.

Where a decedent leaves a considerable quantity of unproductive real estate, the existence of which is not discovered until almost five years after his death, at which time a portion of it is sold for a price far in excess of its fair value at the time of decedent's death, taxes paid upon such property should be charged to principal, and taxes and carrying charges on the remaining real estate should also be charged to principal as an advance, where otherwise the life tenants will receive little or no income and it may become necessary to sacrifice the real estate for unpaid taxes and other carrying charges. Mark's Est., 38 D. & C. 489. 

Where the original corpus of a trust inter vivos consists of a single piece of real estate which is subsequently sold, the consideration being partly cash and partly a purchase money mortgage, and, default having subsequently occurred in payment of interest upon the mortgage, the trustees accept a deed to the property and a cash payment in satisfaction, and thereafter the real estate so reacquired is unproductive, its status if that of property acquired in liquidation of a foreclosed mortgage rather than decedent-owned real estate, and apportionment of carrying charges is therefore to be made under the rules and formula of 

Nirdlinger's Estate, 331 Pa. 135, rather than under those of Levy's Estate, 333 

Pa. 440. Cope's Trust, 38 D. & C. 327.

The orphans' court will not, at the audit of a trustee's account, determine the proper allocation as between principal and income of carrying charges upon unproductive or underproductive real estate held by the trustees either as mortgagees in possession or pending liquidation following foreclosure, where the real estate has not yet been sold; the purpose of such an accounting is solely to verify actual receipts and disbursements, and questions of allocation must await completion of the salvage operation. Romberger's Est., 39 D. & C. 604.

The mere confirmation of a trustee's account showing that deficiencies of the carrying charges of foreclosed properties, as to which salvage operations have not been completed, were paid out of income, without the auditing judge being requested or required to approve the same, is not res adjudicata on the question of proper allocation at the audit of a subsequent account. Scott's Trust, 40 D. & C. 227. 

Where testamentary trust includes decedent-owned unproductive real estate, the deficit of carrying charges over rents received is properly allocable to principal, temporarily, subject to reimbursement from possible future net income and final apportionment after real estate is sold.
