Although in Levy's Estate, 333 Pa. 440, the real estate was unproductive in sense that it produced no gross income whatever, the rule of that case is equally applicable where gross income was produced, as long as gross income was less than the carrying charges.

The nature of unproductive real estate, and whether unproductive because inherently incapable of producing any income, or because carrying charges exceed gross income which the real estate is capable of earning, is not conclusive against allocating the deficit temporarily to principal. In either case the net result to the income beneficiaries is the same. 

In considering the equities, so as to determine the proper allocation of carrying charges of unproductive real estate, the court may consider that the real estate is potentially productive, as against inherently unproductive, and constitutes an equity in favor of remaindermen.

That a $15,000 mortgage secured on unproductive real estate at decedent's death has been reduced to $5000, by payments out of principal of the trust thereafter, does not constitute an equity in favor of remaindermen as the net. worth of the trust remains unchanged thereby. 

That the income beneficiaries are decedent's children, the primary objects of her bounty gives rise to equities in their favor sufficient to outweigh equities favoring the remaindermen, and to warrant allocation of carrying charges of unproductive real estate to principal. Fischer's Est., 57 Montg. 135.

Where a corporate fiduciary is trustee both of a trust inter vivos and of a testamentary trust created by the settlor, and there is doubt whether the fiduciary has properly allocated between the two trusts certain securities received in the course of salvage of an obligation owned in part by the testamentary trust and in part by the trust inter vivos, the orphans' court having jurisdiction over the trust inter vivos will not, as a practical matter, although it has jurisdiction to do so, surcharge the trustee before it for failure to obtain a sufficient portion of the proceeds of the salvage operation, at a time when audit of the testamentary trust is pending before another orphans' court; but it will direct the fiduciary to present a claim for any deficit to the other court and will recommit the account of the trust inter vivos to the auditing judge pending determination of the other proceeding. Keasbey's Est., 40 D. & C. 300; s. c. 342 Pa. 439.

In determining the allocation between income and principal of the proceeds realized upon salvaging operations in dealing with foreclosed real estate, the income rate to be considered is the income return from trust investments that is current at the time of apportionment. 

Nirdlinger's Estate No. 2, 327 Pa. 171, does not decide that 4% is necessarily the current rate for trust investments that is to be used as a constant factor in all salvage calculations. The case enunciates the principle that the rate to be used is the current rate for trust investments, presumably at the time the question is being considered in any particular case. Osborne's Est., 59 Montg. 55.

Where the settlor of a trust authorized monthly payments to his widow for life and additional payments to the widow out of principal "at any time on her request," in such amounts "as in the judgment of said trustee shall be advisable and necessary," stating it to be his intention that "broad discretionary powers be vested in the trustee and that the terms of this trust be given a liberal interpretation so that the beneficiaries herein named shall receive not only the bare necessities but shall also be provided with the better things in life," it was held that under the terms of the trust, when construed in the broad way settlor obviously intended, a formal request by the widow was not an indispensable prerequisite to the making of additional payments to the widow and that in the circumstances disclosed by the record trustee's payment of taxes and insurance on the widow's individual estate and widow's hospital and medical expenses, after the widow allegedly became insane, was not so clearly not advisable and necessary" as to form the basis for a surcharge; hence, that a claim for surcharge because of alleged unauthorized disbursements was properly denied. 7a It is a rule of property that all dividends from coal leasing and coal mining companies representing net income without deductions for depletion or depreciation are to be paid to life tenants, and are not to be apportioned between life tenants and remaindermen.

In apportionment cases, the rights of the parties must be determined in the light of the intent of the creator of the trust when it is possible to ascertain his purpose from the instrument creating the trust and the surrounding circumstances. 

The action of the directors of a corporation in discontinuing the maintenance of a depletion fund does not require resort to apportionment. 

The acts of a testator during his lifetime as an officer and director of the corporation in creating and maintaining a depletion account and paying dividends only after deductions for such account are not such "surrounding circumstances as require the rule of property to be set aside and the dividends declared after his death without deduction for the depletion fund to be apportioned. 

The acts of the testator in serving as an officer and director of the corporation during his lifetime must be considered as separate and apart from his individual acts in personal affairs.

8 It is the intact value of a trust estate at the inception of the trust which must be preserved for the remainderman and a trustee cannot at will write down or up the value of stock held in trust and thereby change the intact value. 15 A dividend, declared to be in a specified amount, which takes the form of a promissory note payable at the option of the company in its preferred stock, is to all intents and purposes a stock dividend.

Ordinary dividends are those paid at more or less customary rates and uniform interval. 

Where extraordinary dividends are declared and paid on shares of stock left by a decedent in trust, they must be distributed by adding to the corpus a sufficient portion to keep intact the value of the shares as they existed at the time the trust was created, and allotting the balance to those entitled to the income of the trust estate.

The intact value existing at the time of the creation of the trust may be added to by "capital increases" or diminished by "capital losses" sustained by the corporation. 

Operating losses incurred in the course of the regular business of a corporation, although large, resulting merely from unfavorable business conditions extending over a period of years, are not capital losses so as to require the fixing of a new intact value as of a time subsequent to the creation of the trust. Lueder's 

Est., 337 Pa. 155. 

16 Where extraordinary dividends are declared and paid on shares of stock left by a decedent in trust, all that the remaindermen are entitled to is that there be retained in the corpus a sufficient portion of the dividend to keep intact the value of the shares as they existed at the time the trust was created. 

Where a stockholder creates a trust of his stock in a corporation which, in addition to its capital, has accumulated surplus profits, the accumulated surplus is, in a sense, thereby capitalized as far as the trust is concerned, and when an extraordinary dividend is later declared out of such surplus the dividend must be awarded to the corpus of the trust in order that the value of the latter should not be reduced from what it was when the trust was created. 

Where profits are earned by the corporation after the creation of the trust, and an extraordinary dividend is declared in an amount not greater than such profits, the dividend belongs to the life tenants, and it is immaterial whether the medium in which it is paid consists of cash or other property, or, if the latter, whether the particular assets distributed were or were not in the portfolio of the company at the time of decedent's death.

244. WASTING INVESTMENTS. 

Stock in a "wasting asset" corporation.41a

Income represented by royalties.43 

41a Testamentary direction to trustees to treat stock dividends and proceeds of sale of stock rights as principal and not as income does not indicate testator's intent to favor life beneficiaries over remaindermen in general, so as to control allocation of extraordinary cash dividend to principal of trust. 

Relationship of parent and child between testator and life beneficiary of trust does not give rise to presumption of intent to favor life beneficiary over remaindermen; but does, in absence of express provisions, warrant leaning toward child as usually the primary object of testator's bounty. 

Allocation of extraordinary cash dividend on shares of corporate stock owned by testator at death and now in corpus of testamentary trust, resulting from sale of land owned by corporation at testator's death, is to be determined by same rules as though testator had died seized of the land. 

A corporation authorized to buy and sell land, and to exploit surface and sub-surface thereof, is a "wasting asset' corporation insofar as it leases coal lands on royalty basis, and dividends paid, whether derived from current royalties. or from depletion reserves, are allocable to life beneficiaries of trust as income; no question of intact value is involved. Insofar as corporation deals in land, by purchase and sale, it is not a "wasting asset" corporation, and dividends paid out of proceeds of sale are allocable to life beneficiaries only to extent that they represent profits on the sale; the intact value of the land at the inception of the trust must be maintained.

An extraordinary cash dividend paid by corporation out of proceeds of sale of land at profit will be allocated entirely to income of trust although the total dividend paid exceeded the actual net profit on the sale, where the corporation also conducts a "wasting asset' class of business and preserves no distinction in its accounting between the different classes of business, and where the intact value of the land sold is maintained, and the only possible source of the deficiency of net profits is the depletion reserve of the corporation as a "wasting asset' corporation. That the corporation's stock was valued at less after payment of the dividend than at inception of the trust has no bearing. Pardee's Est., 56 

Montg. 229 af'd in 343 Pa. 79. 

43 Exceptions by a life tenant to a decree of distribution in the orphans' court, treating royalties from a lease of coal and the sale of unmentioned timber as principal, were dismissed, where there was no open mine on the real estate at the time of testator's death, and the lease, from which the royalties in question were received, was made by the trustees, there being no specific power in the will to lease the coal, but the trustees considered the power of sale as including the authority to lease.

The rule in Pennsylvania is that a life beneficiary is entitled to the royalties from a mine opened in the lifetime of the testator, and, if the executors were empowered to lease the coal, as well as sell it, the same rule prevails. 

Royalties received from a lease of coal, which contemplated its removal before the expiration of the term, was equivalent to a sale, and became a part of the

59a The indebtedness of a beneficiary of the trust was properly paid from the funds for distribution, upon request of the trustee, even though individual creditors had not presented their respective claims, where it was admitted that the indebtedness was owing, that it had been incurred on behalf of the beneficiary, and that it had not previously been paid by the trustee, as he was authorized to do, only because he had before been without funds. 59b Where a person dies testate and by the provisions of his will gives his widow a life estate with the remainder over to his children, share and share alike, and the life tenant dies, but previous to her death but after the death of the testator one of the children dies, the interest of such deceased child in the remainder estate of the original testator should be distributed to the administrator of such deceased child and not distributed directly to the estate of his mother, the life tenant, who is his sole heir, he having died intestate, unmarried and without children.

It is very frequently a matter of discretion with the Orphans' Court as to whether the distribution should be made directly to the sole heir-at-law of a deceased remainderman.

Where the record does not show any accounting by the administrator of the estate of such deceased child, and does not show that there are no creditors or claimants against the estate of such deceased child, the orphans' court should exercise its discretion by directing that the distributive share of such deceased child in the remainder estate be distributed to his estate and not to his heir-at-law.

Where it appeared that a testator made a bequest in trust for his son, to pay the income to the son during his life and thereafter the principal to those specified, provided that if the trustee should at any time during his lifetime believe that the son would make good use of the money and that it would be to his interest to have the same, the trustee might in her discretion pay the principal sum over to the son and terminate the trust; and that during the infancy of the son the principal of the trust had been paid over to a guardian of the son; it was held, under all the circumstances, that the evidence did not establish that the trustee abused his discretion in terminating the trust.

If a testator who creates a trust has a definite purpose in mind the trust cannot be terminated until the purpose has been accomplished. Boyd's Est., 46 Lanc. 605. 

Where a trust is created by deed which contains no power to revoke or to amend, the trust may not be terminated or amended unless all who are or who may be interested in the trust property agree. 

The requisite consent of all who are or may be interested means that their combined interests must be quivalent to an absolute title which cannot be defeated or divested by the happening of any future event.

A contingent interest in such trust cannot be extinguished without the consent of the possessor of such interest by the mere agreement of the other parties to the trust. Donnan's Trust Est., 339 Pa. 43.

Where will creates trust of residue for beneficiary for life, with remainder to charitable uses to be designated by named co-trustee, and he predeceases beneficiary without having designated any charities, there is an intestacy as to the remainder. 

As the life beneficiary is also testatrix's sole next of kin, she thereupon has a vested interest in the remainder, and as the purpose of the trust has failed,

it will be terminated on her request and the entire income and principal will be awarded to her, absolutely. Farrell's Est., 56 Montg. 186, 38 D. & C. 238.

Where the settlor created a trust inter vivos to pay the income to himself and his wife, as successive life beneficiaries, and to distribute the corpus as provided in his will, already executed, and where the trust deed did not reserve to the settlor the power to revoke, but expressly provided that the trust should in no way be subject to the control of or to anticipation by the settlor or his wife, it was held that the trust could not be terminated by the settlor, and that it made no difference whether or not the trustee and all persons who might be beneficially interested consented to the termination of the trust. 

A deed of trust which reserves to the settlor no power to revoke cannot be revoked by any action of the settlor alone. 

While ordinarily a trust may be terminated by consent of all persons interested, a trust of which the settlor is a life beneficiary, with spendthrift trust restrictions, cannot be so terminated. Markley's Trust, 57 Montg. 183.

will terminate the trust and make the daughter the sole and absolute beneficiary of the asset. Miller's Est., 33 Berks 89.

A trust of residue of testator's estate to pay income and principal, if necessary, to wife, for life, for support of herself and minor children, with remainder to children, will be terminated where the life beneficiary has assigned her interest to her children, the remaindermen. A voluntary trust for the benefit of the maker for a fixed period of five years but not for his protection is revocable notwithstanding the failure to reserve a right to revoke. Rigg's Trust, 4 Sch. Reg. 143.

The action of a court in refusing to terminate a spendthrift trust created by a woman for her own benefit for life, with the right to dispose of the corpus by will at a time when it was paying her a living income, against her contention that she had the right to recover her own property despite the fact that she had deliberately made the trust irrevocable, does not prevent, by the doctrine of res judicata, the consideration of a later petition to terminate the trust on the theory that it has totally failed of its purpose, where the income therefrom has shrunk to such an extent that unless the settlor is able to recover the corpus she will have to be supported by private or governmental charity. 

A settlor who places his own property in trust for his own benefit with a spendthrift clause is a ward of the court, which has discretion to terminate the trust where it has totally failed of its purpose and where the result would otherwise be to drive the beneficiary and settlor to charity. Where the settlor is the sole beneficiary of a trust and is not under an incapacity he can compel the termination of the trust, although the purposes of the trust have not been accomplished.

If all the parties who are or may be beneficially interested in a trust are in existence and sui juris, if there is no ultimate purpose of any kind requiring its continuance, and if all the beneficiaries consent, a court of equity will decree its termination. 

If the purpose of the settlor in establishing the trust has not been fully accomplished, and if the settlor is deceased, the trust cannot be terminated even though all the beneficiaries desire that it should be. 

The interest of a trustee in his commissions does not militate against the termination of a trust. Bowers' Trust Est., 346 Pa. 85.

CHAPTER XXXIX. 

MISCELLANEOUS RIGHTS, POWERS AND LIABILITIES OF FIDUCIARIES. 

247. RIGHT OF ELECTION,-PROCEDURE. 

Procedure under the Act.69 

69 It seems, that an executor has no standing to object to a petition filed by a testamentary guardian for a minor beneficiary under Section 32(a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 447), asking authorization to elect to take real estate in lieu of the proceeds of any sale thereof, and certainly he should not file an answer pleading conclusions in general terms, though it might be proper for him to make known to the court any facts which he may have that bear upon the application. 

An orphans' court will authorize the testamentary guardian for a minor beneficiary to enter into an election in writing pursuant to Section 32 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 447), to take certain real estate in lieu of the proceeds of any sale thereof, even though the decedent expressly directed that the real estate be sold, where it remains unconverted because the guardian objected to a sale thereof contemplated by the executor, and a master appointed to take testimony found the property to be worth in excess of the proposed sale price and likely to increase in value, to be in fair condition, and to have a favorable rental history, and this is especially so where the minor himself, who is 18 years of age, joins in the petition. Piccinini's Est., 32 D. & C. 481. 

Where a testatrix directs the conversion of her estate into cash and orders distribution of the proceeds to her children, her real estate comes into the hands of her executor as personal estate under the testamentary conversion. The law does not recognize partition of personal estate nor partition of real estate on the petition of one vested with the converted interest. The executor, therefore, has no standing to file a petition for a writ of partition. Those entitled to the proceeds of the converted real estate, may, however, exercise by unanimity, a right to reconvert and to take and hold as real estate. This right is now available to minors and to the guardians of estates of minors, in accordance with Section 

32(a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917 P. L. 447. Kemp's Est., 34 Berks 

299; 56 York 119.

Where, following the death of a testatrix, the beneficiary of certain trusts and conveyances created or made during her lifetime is ordered to restore the subjects thereof to her estate on the ground that they were obtained by undue influence, but fails to do so, a legacy in his favor must be applied in reduction of the amount owing the estate, as must any commission payable to him as coexecutor of the estate. McCalla's Est., 33 D. & C. 643.

Where it appeared that there was no gross nor wilful misconduct on the part of the executors, and that what they had been doing was sufficiently dealt with by the surcharges imposed, it was held that they were entitled to commissions. 

Long's Est., 143 Super. 176.

A fiduciary should not be deprived of commissions, the filing of the account being delayed for a long period because of economic conditions beyond his control, nor because of failing to file an inventory within thirty days of grant of letters. Cassel Est., 18 Leh. 123. 

Where a Pennsylvania orphans' court surcharges a National banking institution, which is in process of liquidation, for breach of duty as a trustee, and at the same time allows its trustee's commissions, the commissions must be set off against the surcharge. Kerr's Est., 41 D. & C. 209.

Where, heretofore, no allowance had been made to any trustee for the management of the trust and it was admitted that the present accountant had discharged its duties with fidelity, the accountant was held to be entitled to commissions at the rate of 5% upon the corpus, which is the amount invested in the pool plus the balance of investments of the trust, regardless of the ultimate outcome of the liquidation. Sanderson's Est., 51 Dauph. 146.

An exception to an auditor's report will be sustained where he has allowed commissions to administrators on surcharges on amounts due by them to the estate and for which they have not accounted. Ritter's Est., 3 Northumb. 325.

Where one of three executors successfully defends a codicil in which he is named as a beneficiary and also successfully maintains a written option to purchase certain of decedent's stock, but apart from such litigation acts normally as executor and participates in administration of the estate to the fullest extent, he will not be denied all commissions, but they will be disallowed only upon the funds coming into the estate through the exercise of the option. Rosenthal's Est., 41 D. & C. 292. 

Compensation denied where trustee guilty of gross negligence in purchasing investment from itself when in default. Lewis' Est.; 16 Northumb. 163.

Where a trustee is guilty of wrongful conduct, neither grossly negligent nor wilful, and where no substantial loss to the trust has resulted, it rests within the discretion of the auditing judge to grant or refuse compensation.

A trustee is not entitled to commissions upon the cash dividends received and distributed upon shares of stock originally received by the trustee as stock dividends and which it wrongfully retained in its principal account although they should have been distributed as income. Card's Est. (No. 2), 337 Pa. 82.

The right of a trustee appointed by the court to liquidate a mortgage against which undivided participating interests had been issued by the corporate mortgagee which had subsequently become insolvent, to ordinary commissions and counsel fees for its services, is in no way affected by the fact that certain of the participating interests are owned by trust estates of which the corporate mortgagee had been trustee and that the beneficiaries of those estates have already been charged with counsel fees and commissions by the successor trustees thereof. Security Trust Co. of Pottstown's Acct., 32 D. & C. 113, 54 Montg. 182.

Where the sole executor of a decedent's estate is a lawyer, he may be allowed of reasonable compensation, in addition to his commissions as executor, for such services as a lawyer would have been called upon to perform had the executor in not been a lawyer.

Where, in addition to performing the routine legal services necessary to the settlement of a decedent's estate, the executor, who is a lawyer, performs certain extraordinary services in connection with the liquidation of real estate, he will be allowed as a counsel fee, in addition to his commissions as executor, in the absence of any expert testimony as to the value of his services, the amount fixed by the county fee bill as a minimum for the routine services, plus an amount representing fair compensation for the extraordinary services. Lutz's Est., 40

Hughes's Est., 87 P. L. J. 1. Wade's Est., 343 Pa. 520.

Buttorff's Est., 329 Pa. 561.

An executor is not entitled to commissions on advancements, which he is merely required to throw into hotchpot for adjustment of the shares, except by agreement of the parties in interest. Lutz's Est., 40 D. & C. 611, 8 Sch. Reg. 65.

An administrator c. t. a. who takes charge of the real estate of the decedent under direction in will to sell the real estate, and proceeds to administer the same by managing and operating it, is entitled to compensation, in addition to the usual commissions received from income during the period of administration, even though he effected no sale thereof, by reason of the election by the residuary legatee to take the real estate unconverted. 

The power of sale rendered him accountable for the real estate to a certain extent and brought him within the jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court. Mishkin's Est., 47 Lanc. 389.

The widow of a decedent, his administratrix, is entitled to a compensation in the amount of three per cent commission on real estate sold. Sober's Est., 7 Northumb. 145.

It is duty of faithful executor when the other fails in duty or when estate is in jeopardy, to bring matters to attention of Court by proceeding for removal of the one failing. In such case unearned commissions may revert to estate, or to a successor. A fortiori where a co-executor, deceased, had participated until administration was complete and petition for distribution executed.

One executor taking more commissions than his share has burden of proving his right.

93 Where the executors of the will are also named as trustees, they are entitled to but one commission on principal for functioning in both capacities, but the commission is properly allowable upon the accounting as executors, and there is no necessity to postpone payment until termination of the trust. 

Where accountant-trustee had also been coexecutor of decedent's estate, and where as coexecutor accountant had received a 22% commission on principal and the other coexecutor had likewise received a similar commission, and where accountant administered the trust for over 22 years as trustee, it was held, under all the circumstances, that the accountant should be allowed a commission of 22% on principal as compensation for administering the trust. Sower's Est., 58 Montg. 427, 46 D. & C. 378.

While in the ordinary estate this rule of law is strictly enforced, it does not however preclude the payment of additional compensation to the trustee into whose hands the property passes where a large amount of additional services are required to be rendered in caring for, preserving and distributing the estate. 

The rule in all cases is compensation for the responsibility incurred and the service and labor performed.

Compensation should be fair and just, taking into consideration the character of the services rendered, the responsibility incurred and the zeal and fidelity with which the trust has been carried out. Baldwin's Est., 24 Erie 112.

98 Where commissions are allowed to a trustee upon the basis of a percentage of the total assets administered, the percentage is properly calculated upon the value of the corpus at the time it reaches the accountant's hands rather than upon its value at the time of distribution, unless exceptional circumstances require some different method, and a shrinkage in the value of the assets during administration by a little more than 20 per cent does not constitute such an exceptional circumstance. Smith's Est., 35 D. & C. 383.

Where a testator's estate included an interest in the estate of another decedent, estimated at $2500 for appraisement purposes, and it subsequently appeared that the interest had a true value of $6600, the executor was not limited to a commission of 5% of the appraisement but could claim 5% of the true value of the assets as received by him for administration, since the basis of computation may be increased or diminished in the case of exceptional circumstances. Peck's Est., 33 Berks 245, 42 D. & C. 47.

Executor's commission is properly charged against inventory value of corporate shares owned by decedent, notwithstanding a part of their value may be attributable to the corporation's claim against decedent upon a note given for a loan of assets to decedent, and it makes no difference whether or not decedent held these assets at his death.

Executor's commission is not properly charged upon the full value of securities pledged to brokers to secure advances to decedent, but only upon the equity decedent had therein. League's Est., 57 Montg. 15, 39 D. & C. 620. 

2 A real estate broker's right to a commission for procuring a purchaser of property owned by an estate may be defeated by the fiduciary's duty to reject such purchaser if a better offer be received for the property before title has passed. 

A trustee has the duty to dispose of trust property upon the most advantageous terms which it is possible for him to secure for the benefit of the estate which he represents. 

A person dealing with a trustee is required to know the extent of his powers. 

Clark v. Provident Trust Co., 329 Pa. 421.

Trustees may properly employ expert real estate agents to collect rentals and manage multiple-tenant buildings of special character requiring skilled and competent service such as a fiduciary would normally be unable to render. Romberger's Est., 39 D. & C. 604.

Where trustee at the request of exceptant, a settlor and beneficiary, procures a purchaser for real estate representing the corpus of the trust estate, and where the original trust agreement contains no provision concerning such sale, and where, at the settlement for the sale of the realty, the trustee, with the knowledge of the exceptant, is paid a commission for acting as broker, the exceptant, at the accounting of the trustee several years later, may not rightfully object to the crediting of the trustee with its broker's commission; the trustee is entitled to an additional commission for such extra service. 

In such case an extra commission of four per cent of the value of the realty sold is not unreasonable. Steed's Trust Est., 56 Montg. 275, 40 D. & C. 1.

250. POWER TO LEASE. 

Leases for over five years." 

5 Section 31 of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, giving a testamentary trustee power to make a lease on real estate for five years or longer by leave of court, does not apply to real estate acquired by such a trustee in a mortgage salvage operation.

Where a trustee holds a mortgage in which beneficial interests are owed by several trusts, it is bound to do all that is prudent to save the investment for all, and may therefore enter into a long-term lease for the property although one of the trusts has terminated. 

Even if a fiduciary exceeded its powers in leasing trust property for a long term, the only result thereof would be that the lease would be void and not to require the trustee to make good the investment. Beutel's Est., 45 D. & C. 418, af'd in 347 Pa. 237.

252. UNIFORM FIDUCIARIES ACT OF 1923. 

Actual knowledge of breach of trust.19 

19a Under section 9 of the Uniform Fiduciaries Act of May 31, 1923, P. L. 

468, where a fiduciary deposits in a bank to his personal credit checks payable to his principal and endorsed, with authority, by him, the bank is not, bound to inquire whether the fiduciary is committing thereby a breach of his obligation as fiduciary, and is authorized to pay the amount of the deposit upon the personal check of the fiduciary, without being liable to the principal, unless the bank receives the deposit or pays the check with actual knowledge of a breach of trust by the fiduciary or with knowledge of such facts that its action in receiving the deposit or paying the check amounts to bad faith.

Where an attorney representing both the executor of an estate and a claimant against the estate receives payment of the claim from the executor and remits only a part of the money to the claimant, and the claimant fails to take any action for a period of three years during which time the attorney died, the claimant has no right of recourse against the executor. Hertwig's Est., 33 Berks 40. 

26a Where coexecutors of an estate are represented by independent counsel, the aggregate amount allowed as counsel fee to both should not exceed what would be paid if only one counsel represented both executors. McCalla's Est., 33 D. & C. 643. 

The same rule applies in the case of co-trustees. Hirst's Est., 58 Montg. 324. 

Ordinarily the proper time to ask for an allowance of counsel fees for a guardian's counsel is at the audit of the account; while the guardian may properly pay reasonable fees for legal services necessitated from time to time during the progress of the guardianship, the responsibility of determining the propriety and amount of such fees rests upon him, and if counsel believes them to be inadequate he may accept them without prejudice to claim an additional sum at the audit. 

The orphans' court will not, save under exceptional circumstances, grant a petition by a substituted guardian to award its counsel a fee for services consisting of procuring the appointment of the substituted guardian, collecting amount of surcharge from the former guardian, and securing an order for the payment of allowance for the minor's education and support. Linker's Est., 37 D. & C. 717. 

The right of an executor or administrator to the services of an attorney and the allowance of reasonable compensation therefor has always been recognized at common law; and though the attorney has no claim against the decedent's estate, it is to the advantage of the estate and parties in interest that the executor or administrator be allowed to pay a reasonable attorney's fee out of the estate. 

Peck's Est., 33 Berks 245, 42 D. & C. 47.

An executor is not bound to defend his testator's will and if he undertakes to do so it must be as agent and in the interest and at the expense of those expecting to be benefited by his action, and he cannot charge the expense of a contest to the estate he represents, unless the estate is benefited by the proceedings. 

In such case, the good faith of an executor is not important; the question is are those ultimately shown to be entitled to the estate benefited. 

The exception to such rule where a trustee accepts a trust and undertakes to carry out its provisions was held not to be applicable to this case. 

The question of interest on the amount of the surcharge against the executor is primarily a matter for the court below, and where the question is not raised nor presented in that court it will not be considered on appeal. Fetter Est., 151 

Super. 32.

A life tenant has no authority to bind the corpus of a trust for the payment of legal services rendered to it, and the act of the trustee in disbursing all of the income to the life tenant is an implied waiver of any claim for liability on the part of the life tenant for reimbursement to the trustee for legal services. Niccolls' Est., 6 Fay. 1. 

27 A counsel fee of $16,250 was allowed in decedent's estate inventoried at $541,350.47 where the administration was conducted under the guidance of counsel in a skillful and proper way and resulted in advantage to the estate. Hughes's 

Est., 87 P. L. J. 1.

In an estate of over three-quarter million dollars, the decedent having had a life estate in the entire income of her deceased husband's estate, the attorney having received no compensation for attending the audit of the account in that estate, the contention there being that the increases in the value of the assets belonged to the present estate as income, the other contention being as to the fee for services rendered in connection with the federal estate tax on the corporate stock, a counsel fee of $8,500 was allowed in addition to one of $7,500 shown in the account. Shimer Est., 18 Leh. 77.

A reasonable counsel fee for services in stating and filing the account of a guardian for a minor and appearing at the audit is assessable as an expense and properly allowable, even though the guardian has misapplied the entire estate. 

Wilczinski's Est., 40 D. & C. 179.

A counsel fee of $300 representing approximately 5% of the gross value of an

§ 254 

estate composed in part of mortgage participation certificates valued at $2001.43 on its face seems excessive. Stillwagen's Est., 19 Leh. 407, 56 York 65.

Where, upon exception to the fee of counsel for a testamentary trustee, the testimony, the record, and matters within judicial notice, disclosed that services sufficiently extensive to warrant a fee of $2,000 had been performed, a fee in that amount was held not excessive.

In passing upon the propriety of an attorney fee to counsel for a testamentary trustee, the court will take judicial notice of the performance of legal services which were within its own personal observation in proceedings before it, for which the fee accrued. McHugh's Est., 57 Montg. 299. 

While ordinarily $5,000 would be the proper attorney's fee in a gross estate of $366,000, the extraordinary services rendered justify a fee of $7,500. Eckel's 

Est., 56 Montg. 120, 37 D. & C. 383, 88 P. L. J. 321.

Where each of a number of cotrustees engages his own counsel, compensation should be allowed each counsel for the fair value of his services rendered, in proportion to those rendered by other counsel employed by one or more of the other fiduciaries. Hirst's Est., 58 Montg. 324. 27a Where a will expresses testator's desire that his executor employ a designated attorney and fixes the compensation the attorney is to receive for his services, and the executor does employ the attorney named for the settlement of the estate, the attorney is bound by the limitations of the will in the absence of evidence of extraordinary services, and the executor must be surcharged to the extent that the credit claimed in his account for attorney's fee exceeds the amount fixed in the will. Alderfer's Est., 56 Montg. 172. 

28 Where a fiduciary received and disbursed rentals of $35,564.58 over a period of four years, she will not be surcharged for having paid counsel fees of $2,249.79 in view of the fact that the estate was much involved and accountant was inclined to draw heavily upon the legal resources of her attorneys. Strickler's Est., 5 Fay. 194. When there is nothing complicated or unusual in the administration of an estate the usual and customary fees allowed are 5% for executor's commission and 22% for attorney's fees. Stafford's Est., 24 Erie 189, af'd in 152 Super. 551. 

29 It is the duty of a trustee to defend the trust and preserve its assets, and he has the right to defend it by counsel whose fee is a proper charge against the trust. 

Where the efforts of an attorney asking compensation from the trust fund merely parallel and incidentally supplement the actions of the trustees or his attorney, and no special need for them is shown, they cannot be compensated for out of the fund.

Where it appeared that the settlor of a trust, who was entitled to the entire income therefrom during her lifetime and who was, also, a co-trustee, attempted to revoke or cancel the trust; that revocation of the trust was opposed by counsel for the trustees, the settlor being represented by her own individual counsel; and that petitioner, who represented some of the remaindermen, joined in successfully opposing termination of the trust, but not at the request of the trustees nor could it be said that but for his efforts the fund would have been improperly handled by the trustees or the court; it was held on appeal that petitioner was not entitled to a counsel fee out of the trust fund. 

The fact that trustees' counsel did not prepare a separate brief and did not make an oral argument in addition to that made by petitioner on the appeal did not show dereliction of duty by the trustees. Smaltz' Tr. Est., 142 Super. 463. 

Where an attorney who represents the remaindermen in an estate, the actual payment of the corpus of which is deferred pending the death of another, is engaged in litigation to protect their interests against one claiming against the whole fund and, after the litigation has been unsuccessfully concluded and trustees have been appointed for the life tenants, presents his claim for services requesting the Court to order an allowance from the corpus of each trust estate, Held, (1) the claim should have been presented when the trust res was within the control of the Court for distribution; (2) the attorney has a general or "retaining" lien against his clients and not a "charging" lien against the trust estates. 

An attorney's general or "retaining" lien is the right to refuse to surrender

$217 

FIDUCIARIES 

43 2 documents, papers, etc., belonging to his client, whereas a "charging" lien is the right to be paid out of the fund which he has been instrumental in recovering for his client. Tomlinson's Est., 47 Lanc. 261, 54 York 115.

Fees of attorneys for parties interested in a decedent's estate are payable out of the estate only where the attorneys' efforts have increased the amount of. the estate, or where they have preserved it from dissipation; and not where the efforts have been beneficial merely to a group within the estate by changing the order of distribution. Chauncey's Est., 57 Montg. 33.

Successful exceptants in an Orphans' Court audit are ordinarily not allowed counsel fees from the fund, although by their efforts others may also have been benefited. Where, however, the audit is upon the account of a bank as trustee of a trust mortgage pool, consisting of bonds secured by mortgages on real estate and real estate taken on mortgage foreclosures, to a total value of more than $9,000,000., and exceptions are filed by beneficiaries in individual trusts holding interests in the pool, to certain investments and to management, an unusual situation is presented. The work of the attorneys for exceptants consisted of examination of the account of 2800 pages, and analysing investments made, liquidated or held in the trust, which was an extensive and unusually burdensome labor. 

They not only presented for view and determination alleged errors on the part of the accountant but, by favorably passing on the great majority of the investments made and still held, gave assurances that the great bulk of the estate was intact and the funds well secured. In such circumstances it would seem entirely unreasonable and inequitable to place upon a few excepting participants full responsibility for such extensive and valuable services. Decree entered for $2,000 counsel fee. Reading Trust Co. Mtge. Pool Ser. "A," 36 Berks 19.

Where counsel representing the residuary beneficiary, who, by citation, compelled the executors to file an account, has also acted as a de facto trustee ad litem for a life beneficiary who was mentally ill, though not judicially determined to be weak-minded, a fee was allowed him from the estate. Heckman's Est., 57 

Montg. 310.

While, as a general rule, each litigant must pay his own counsel for services in connection with the audit of a decedent's estate, a deviation from the general rule may be permitted in exceptional cases, in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances surrounding them, where the services rendered in securing an accounting and audit benefited all interested parties and were of assistance to the court. Grossman's Est., 39 D. & C. 553.

Where a trustee is in a genuine quandary as to the action it should take in respect to forcing payment of dividends upon certain stock constituting a portion of the trust res, and is under a duty to protect the interests not only of the life tenant but also of the remaindermen, it has a right to employ counsel to advise it, and such counsel will be awarded a reasonable fee from the trust estate. 

Wanamaker's Trust 38 D. & C. 347, af'd in 340 Pa. 419.

The orphans' court has discretion to award attorney's fees out of principal or income of a trust, or to apportion them, and where no account has been filed in a trust for over 30 years, will award the fees out of principal. 

That the allowance of attorneys' fees out of principal of a trust will diminishi the estate, is not a ground for a valid objection. 

The trustee's failure to file triennial accounts, where such accounts have not been demanded is not a ground for disallowing fees to the trustee's attorneys. 

The Fiduciaries Act of 1917, Sec. 46 (h), authorizes trustees to file triennial accounts, but is not mandatory. Stinson's Est., 56 Montg. 102, but see 143 Super. 512. 

The allowance of a counsel fee to counsel for the accountant in opposing exceptions was affirmed on appeal, no abuse of discretion having been shown. 

Jones' Est., 344 Pa. 100.

Even though the attorney fee should under the circumstances be paid by the estate of the deceased executor, it will be allowed out of the estate of the original decedent when the former's estate is insolvent and the attorney has rendered services which have been of assistance in straightening out the complicated state into which the original estate has been thrown through improper management. Deighton's Est., 25 Erie 50.

The fact that services performed by an attorney, in the course of his repre-

$ 254 

sentation of a client who has an interest in a trust estate, are valuable and incidentally benefit the other cestuis, does not entitle him to receive a counsel fee out of the estate.

In order to justify the payment of a counsel fee out of a trust estate to an attorney who did not represent the trustee, it must appear that the services for which a fee is claimed were necessary and that they created or saved the fund out of which payment is asked. Beard's Est., 56 York 161. erro 30 Where the executor had retained the same counsel to represent the estate of and the executor's individual rights as a legatee, the fee allowed such counsel out of the estate was reduced to an amount commensurate with the services performed for the estate.

An executor is not entitled to take credit for counsel fees expended in resisting exceptions to his account where he is also a legatee and the exceptions principally affect his rights as a legatee. Glessner's Est., 57 Montg. 78, 40 D. & C. 271.

Where an agreement between a trustee and the beneficiaries of the trust estate in provided that the trustee should charge a commission in a specified percentage onom the income arising from the trust, which expressly included the payment of counsel fees, it was held that the fee of counsel for the trustee could not be charged to the principal of the trust estate. 

Attorney's fees for services rendered for the personal benefit of a trustee are not chargeable to an estate. Stinson's Est., 143 Super. 512, mod'g & af'g 56 

Montg. 102, 253.

Monies expended by a trustee in the defense of litigation caused by the trustee's wrongful act are not chargeable to the trust property even though the litigation benefits the cestui que trust. Lessig v. Nat. Bk. of Pottstown, 342 Pa. 209. 

31 Heyl's Est., 29 D. & C. 672, af'd in 331 Pa. 202.

No allowance out of the fund may be decreed at this time to counsel for exceptants. Where the fund is in the hands of the court and in no jeopardy, and an exceptant is merely protecting his own interest, he will ordinarily not be allowed counsel fees, although through his efforts others may also be benefited. 

Reading Tr. Co. Mtge. Pool Series "A," 36 Berks 1.

The fees of attorneys for a party in interest in a decedent's estate, who successfully appealed to the Supreme Court from the orphans' court's decree of distribution, whereby an annuity to another party in interest was reduced from $3,000 to $1,000, are not properly payable out of the estate, and exceptions to a schedule of distribution which include such fees, will be sustained. Chauncey's 

Est., 57 Montg. 33.

The counsel fee awarded to a guardian ad litem for minors should be paid out of the income due such minors rather than out of income generally. Rosenthal's 

Est., 41 D. & C. 292.

The fees of attorneys for a party in interest in a decedent's estate, who successfully appealed to the Supreme Court from the orphans' court's decree of distribution, whereby absolute awards were changed to awards in trust for lives of those distributees, then to others including appellants, are not properly payable out of the estate, and exceptions to a schedule of distribution because such fees are not included will be dismissed. an Fees of attorneys for parties interested in a decedent's estate are payable out of the estate only where the attorney's efforts have increased the amount of the estate, or where they have preserved it from dissipation; and not where the efforts have been beneficial merely to a group within the estate by changing the order of distribution. Biddle's Est., 57 Montg. 4, 54 York 187.

Where many persons have a common interest in a trust property or fund, and one of them, for the benefit of all, at his own cost and expense, brings suit for its preservation or administration, the court of equity in which suit is brought will order plaintiff to be reimbursed his costs and expenses, including counsel fees, from the property of the trust, or order those benefited to contribute proportionately toward that expense. 

Except in the exceptional circumstances stated in the foregoing rule the litigant is responsible for the fees of counsel employed. Wilbur's Est., 334 Pa. 45.

Foreclosure, will not be disturbed upon exceptions in the absence of a showing of manifest error. Dickel's Est., 32 D. & C. 44.

The amount of fees to be allowed to counsel is a matter peculiarly within the discretion of the court of first instance. Harton's Est., 331 Pa. 507;

It is highly improper for an auditing judge on his own motion and without any Opportunity to present proofs as to the services performed to disallow claimed redits in an account for commissions on collections by the accountant and additional counsel fees. Newhall's App., 346 Pa. 519. 

33a The Court of Common Pleas does not have jurisdiction in a claim or counterlaim by an attorney-at-law based on services rendered by him to an executor in the administration of a decedent's estate in the Orphans' Court of the same 

County. Stegemann v. Lowell, 48 Lanc. 197, 56 York 85.

A claim by an attorney-at-law against an executor or administrator for legal ervices rendered to such person in his fiduciary capacity is properly made in the Orphans' Court and not in the Court of Common Pleas. 

A suit brought by an attorney-at-law against a legatee of an estate for legal ervices rendered to such person in his individual capacity is properly brought in the Court of Common Pleas, and not the Orphans' Court. 

Since it may be possible for the plaintiff to have rendered services to the particular heirs which would entitle him to compensation from them as individuals, and at the same time to have rendered services to an executor of the state that might entitle him to compensation from the executor in a fiduciary tapacity, it cannot be held, as a matter of law, that the plaintiff may not bring an action in the Common Pleas Court and an action in the Orphans' Court at the same time. Reed v. Greenawalt, 54 Dauph. 180. 

35 An attorney is not deprived of a reasonable counsel fee for necessary strictly legal services rendered the estate, such as probating the will, preparing and filing the inventory, adjusting State and Federal taxes, and filing and auditing the account, because he is also a fiduciary. Dickel's Est., 32 D. & C. 44.

Where a testator appointed an attorney as one of his executors, he probably did 30 in order to avoid extra expense to the estate by reason of legal fees, and the executor was bound not to employ another attorney unless reasonably necessary in the administration of the estate. Peck's Est., 33 Berks 245, 42 D. & C. 47.

A fiduciary who is a lawyer is entitled to employ counsel to perform services for his trust, and is entitled to reasonable counsel fees for such services. 

A fiduciary who is a lawyer is entitled to payment for legal services rendered the trust by himself in addition to his services as fiduciary. Niccolls' Est., 6 Fay 1. 1. -5.

Common skill, prudence and caution.40 38 The loyalty which a trustee owes to his beneficiaries is the basic factor or trust relationship; once a trust is accepted it must be administered solely inh the interest of the beneficiaries.

A trustee may not profit at the expense of the beneficiaries nor assert any adverse interest in the trust property. 

A trustee cannot at the same time be trustee of the same property under twc different trusts for different beneficiaries, whose interests are conflicting. 

A trustee of a mortgage securing an issue of bonds which takes title to the mortgaged property holds such title on behalf of the bondholders and not for the benefit of the prior owner. Where a trustee of a mortgage which is in default enters into possession of the mortgaged premises without foreclosing the mortgage he is trustee for the mortgage debtor only to the extent that he has the duties of a provident owner and is required to account to him for the management of the property. 

Where a trustee for bondholders of a first mortgage subsequently takes juniorb mortgages for its own benefit and thereafter makes payments to itself on account of the principal and interest due upon the junior mortgages, while the first mortgage remains unpaid in part, such payments are improper. 

Where a trustee of a mortgage which it should foresee is likely to fall into default is in possession of interest which has been earned by a fund held by the trustee as a portion of the trust res it has a duty to retain such interest for the benefit of its cestuis que trustent and not to pay it over to the mortgage debtor.

Where a trustee, by his own misconduct, makes the procurement of funds necessary, which he then advances to himself as trustee, he cannot claim priority in order to recoup himself for such loans. Commonwealth Tr. Co.. Case, 331 

Pa. 569.

The fact that the trustee undertook the task of acting as rental agent for the mortgagor and received from him a commission on rentals so collected, and that the trustee then applied the balance to payment of interest on the principal amount of the mortgage and distributed it as income to the participating estates, on which the trustee likewise took commissions as compensation for its services as trustee, so long as there was no default, did not constitute a violation of the rule against a trustee obtaining a bonus or commission from dealing with specific trust property. Harton's Est., 331 Pa. 507, rev'g 86 P. L. J. 18.

The principle that a trustee must administer the trust solely in the interest of the beneficiaries and must not deal with trust property for the benefit of himself was held not to be applicable, under the peculiar circumstances in this case, where it appeared that the trustee had the right to vest himself with an absolute estate in the trust property. Mallon's Est., 345 Pa. 115.

Accountant, a trust company, during the administration of the trust, effected 27 leases, 20 itself, 2 through an independent agency and 5 through a subsidiary real estate corporation. The fees paid to the latter and the independent agency were the same. A beneficiary filed exceptions on the ground that the trustee was without right to engage or pay for the services of its subsidiary company, basing its contention on the Restatement, Trusts, section 170, subsections 1 and 2. Held, dismissing the exceptions, that the burden was on the accountant to show that dealing with its subsidiary did not work to the injury or disadvantage of the trust which burden was fully met. Fink's Est., 34 Berks 87.

In the absence of fraud, a trust company will not be surcharged for loss on a mortgage investment where the only breach of trust is the acquisition of the trust investment from the commercial department of the bank. 

Where the commercial department of a bank held a second lien on which it foreclosed, it became its duty to pay the underlying mortgage held by the trust department in order to avoid self-dealing, and having failed to do so, the bank

39 The practice of having the same institution act as banker for a bond issue, and as trustee of the mortgage securing the bonds, is of doubtful propriety, but the trustee cannot, ordinarily, be required to pay over to the bondholders its profit upon sale of the bonds.

Thompson v. Fitzgerald, 4 Fay. 71, af'd in 344 Pa. 90.

The conduct of a trustee in purchasing investments for the trust from himself, without more, does not constitute fraud and is not a sufficient reason for reviewing an adjudication of a trustee's account after the expiration of more than five years.

There is no more duty upon a trustee, upon the filing of an account, to inform the beneficiaries that it purchased certain of the assets of the trust from itself, than there is to disclose any other grounds of objection, such as facts which would show imprudence in making or watching an investment, or the omission of debits, or improper credits; when an account is filed the trustee and the beneficiaries become adversaries, like other litigants, and it is the beneficiaries' duty to make inquiry for the facts upon which possible objections might be founded; but the fiduciary should not make any effort to conceal the existing factual situation. Colladay's Est. (No. 2), 33 D. & C. 507, af'd in 333 Pa. 218.

A reasonable degree of viligance and the exercise of good faith is the standard of a trustee's duty. Hudock's Est., 5 Cam. 151.

When a fiduciary undertakes to transfer assets from an estate wherein he is co-fiduciary to himself as sole fiduciary of another estate, a very heavy burden is imposed upon him to demonstrate that the transaction is fair and just and that the investment thus acquired is safe and sound. 

Where an experienced attorney who is co-executor of an estate, transfers a mortgage therein to himself as sole trustee for the estate of two minors despite his admitted knowledge that both the owner of the premises and a mortgage broker had experienced difficulty in placing the mortgage, without independent reappraisement, relying solely upon a personal inspection of the premises and previous sales of the property, he will be surcharged for any loss resulting from the investment. Connell's Est., 32 D. & C. 20.

Austin's Est., 5 Fay. 41, 44 D. & C. 249.

A surcharge will not be imposed upon a fiduciary for mere errors of judgment, but only to compensate beneficiaries for loss caused by the fiduciary's want of due care. Miller's Est., 345 Pa. 91.

A trustee is liable for supine negligence or wilful default, but he will not be surcharged for a loss which has occurred in case he has exercised common skill, common prudence and common caution. Smith's Est., 332 Pa. 581; Beaver Tr. 

Co.'s App., 146 Super. 545; Hudock's Est., 5 Cam. 151.

A trustee has the duty of making only such investments as a prudent man would make, having primarily in view the preservation of the estate and the amount and legality of the income to be derived. Thompson v. Fitzgerald, 4 Fay. 71, af'd in 344 Pa. 90.

Exceptions to the account of a trustee, seeking to deny the accountant the right to offer mortgage investments in distribution of the balance of the account, on the grounds, variously applying to the particular investments, that the investments were illegal, improper and improvident, that the accountant had an interest in the transactions adverse to the estate, that the interest rate on one mortgage was reduced improperly, and that there were no appraisals when certain of the investments were made for the trust, were properly dismissed, under all the evidence in the case. Swindell's Est., 332 Pa. 161.

A trustee will not be held personally liable for an honest exercise of a discretionary power, in the absence of supine negligence or willful default. 

The propriety of an investment must be judged as it appeared at the time it was made, and not as viewed in the light of subsequent events. 

If a trust investment is properly questioned, the discretion exercised by the trustee will be scrutinized in the light of the will and of the Fiduciaries Act, and the primary inquiry will be whether he has performed according to the recognized standard applied to the facts that existed at the time of the investment. 

Croll's Est., 55 York 6.

The broad general principle governing trustees in the investment of trust money is that all that is required of a trustee is common skill, common prudence and common caution, and he is not liable when he acts in good faith as others du with their own property. Smith's Est., 46 Lanc. 625.

The propriety of an investment must be judged as it appeared at the time it was made and not as viewed in the light of subsequent events. 

If fair, free from fraud and collusion, directors of a fiduciary bank may make appraisements of securities held by a trust company as fiduciary. 

Appraisals of mortgaged real estate for the purpose of determining the propriety of mortgages as trust investments, which are fair, free of fraud and were made by well qualified appraisers, are not rendered invalid by the fact that they were made by directors of the trustee rather than by so-called disinterested third parties. Seager's Est., 340 Pa. 73, af'g 18 Leh. 274.

Generally speaking, a fiduciary in making a mortgage investment is entitled under the Act of April 26, 1929, P. L. 817, to rely upon an appraisement made by any competent appraiser, who may be in its employment, and need not look beyond the appraisement unless circumstances come to its notice which tend to discredit the appraisement.

The fact that an appraiser, who valued a property at $115,000 for the purpose of making a mortgage investmeent, had two months before appraised the property at only $65,000, when the fiduciary was considering its value in relationship to an existing smaller mortgage thereon, does not constitute such a circumstance as tends to discredit the later appraisement, where the appraiser testifies that his second appraisement was more full and careful than the first. Beutel's Est., 45 D. & C. 418, af'd in 347 Pa. 237.

Failure of a trust company to cause an appraisal of real estate to be made at or about the date of placing the mortgage thereon is proper ground for entering a surcharge.

Where by an appraisal made subsequent to placing the mortgage it is obvious that the security is inadequate, a bank will be surcharged for failure to take proper action thereafter. Austin's Est., 5 Fay. 41, 44 D. & C. 249.

The fact that the appraisal of a mortgaged property is made by an employee of the corporate fiduciary does not affect its value, in the absence of any showing of fraud or bad faith. Snyder Est., 346 Pa. 615. 

Failure to make a reappraisement of the real estate before making investments in mortgage participations is immaterial where there has been no change in the value of the real estate.

In the absence of evidence to support a contrary finding it will be presumed that the fair value of the real estate mortgaged is as it was at the time of an appraisal made less than three years before.

The settlors of a trust deposited a sum of money with the trust company under an agreement by which the company was to invest the money "in good first mortgages" and to pay the net income to the settlors' mother during her life; upon her death, one-half "of this fund" was to be paid to each of the settlors or their personal representatives. The trust agreement contained no provisions for revocation of the agreement, payment in cash upon distribution, or guarantee of payment of the principal sum or income. The funds were invested by the trustee in installment mortgage pools which, at the time of distribution, could not be fully liquidated. Held that the trustee was entitled to make distribution in kind under Section 49 (e) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 447). d'Happart's Est., 132 Super. 326.

An exception to a decree of distribution in the orphans' court that distribution should be made in cash and not in participation certificate in a mortgage pool, as the will of decedent did not permit the investment in the mortgage investment fund and in doing so the trustee violated the intention of testatrix, was dismissed, where the trustee was directed to invest the fund in first mortgages and at the termination of the trust the fund was to become a part of her residuary estate. Exceptant failed to meet the burden of proof that the allocation was not within the terms of the will. 

The contention of exceptant that testatrix meant cash when her will provided that upon the termination of the trust estate distribution should be made in cash was without merit, in that the designation of the amount of the fund does not control the character of the distribution nor that it must be in cash. 

The orphans' court, by reason of its comprehensive and intimate knowledge of the trustee's pool, needed no further evidence to determine the proper distribution of decedent's estate and was moved by reasons entirely satisfactory to it, as provided for in section 49 (e) 1 of the fiduciaries act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447. Paul's Est., 87 P. L. J. 437, 88 P. L. J. 337, af'd in 338 Pa. 191.

While the Act of April 26, 1929, P. L. 817, amending section 41 (a) 1 of the 

Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, may authorize investment by an independent fiduciary in trust certificates issued by a trust company against first mortgages, it does not authorize investment in certificates issued against a fund of first mortgages which is not fixed and defined but may be changed from time to time by way of substitution, for such a fund fails to satisfy the requirements of identification and fixation of a trust res and also would involve an illegal delegation of responsibility of investments; nor is investment in certificates issued against such a fund validated by the fact that a trust fund of first mortgages, properly earmarked, is properly set up and the fiduciary's interest therein as trustee duly recorded, so long as the trust company has the right to change the investment.

The Act of April 6, 1925, P. L. 152, authorizing trust companies to assign to their various trust estates participations in a general trust fund of mortgages under certain circumstances, validates mortgage pools as a matter of corporate practice, but in no way authorizes investment in such pools by fiduciaries. Klennert's Est., 37 D. & C. 568.

The purpose of the Act of April 6, 1925, P. L. 152 which allowed a trust com pany to assign to its various trust estates participation certificates in general trust funds of mortgages on real estate, was to permit the investment of odd amounts in mortgage securities and at the same time to spread the risk of unwise selection by giving even a small estate an opportunity to own an interest in a number of mortgages.

The Act of April 6, 1925, P. L. 152, authorizing a trust company to assign to trust estates participation in a general trust fund of mortgages upon real estate securing bonds, is in derogation of the common law of trusts and must be strictly construed. O'Connor v. Hagy, et al., 34 Berks 35. 

Participating mortgage certificates are legal investments for trust funds in Pennsylvania and the designation on the records of a bank of the trust estates participating in a mortgage and the amount of the participation is a sufficient compliance with the Act of Assembly without a designation on the public record of the mortgage. Austin's Est., 5 Fay. 41, 44 D. & C. 249.

A trustee will not be surcharged for losses from mortgages purchased for the trust estate solely because title thereto was originally placed in the name of the trustee individually, where a declaration of trust was immediately executed, proper entries were kept upon the trustee's books, the income was duly accounted for and the mortgage papers duly earmarked, where the life tenant was fully acquainted with the investments, where the trustee, who had been following a generally accepted practice at the time, immediately made a proper change in the title upon realizing its impropriety and where no damage resulted from the technical breach of trust. Myers' Trust, 35 D. & C. 492. 

73 A certificate of participation in a mortgage pool gives the holder a legal interest in the entire trust res; the title to and responsibility for the elements composing the pool are in the trustee, while the certificate holder has an equitable interest in the elements of the pool which include a right to an accounting thereon. 

Arnold's Est., 31 Berks 129.

The complaining beneficiary of the estate was not entitled immediately to a general accounting by the trustee of all the mortgages composing the mortgage pool, where it appeared that a great number of similar trust estates shared in the fund, that an orderly process of litigation was now under way, under the control of the courts, and that an immediate accounting would impose a great expense upon all others having interests in the mortgage pool. Harton's Est., 331 Pa. 507, af'g 86 P. L. J. 13. 

77 The language of statutes permitting fiduciaries to invest in certain classes of securities to escape liability is not mandatory or exclusive. The law does not forbid or make unlawful an investment in securities not of a class expressly authorized by the Acts of Assembly. Where such an investment is made for the trust estate there is not a breach of trust although there may be liability for loss by reason of depreciation. The term "legal" is sometimes freely used as descriptive of investments of a class permitted, and "non-legal" as descriptive of those not expressly permitted. As so used "non-legal" is not synonymous with "illegal" or "forbidden."' Illegal or forbidden investments are such as those named in the original Article 3, Section 22 of the Constitution before it was amended, and purely personal obligations. Illegals have no place in an account and they, and legals illegally held, may be stricken from the account on application. Those not expressly permitted to carry with them liability for loss on depreciation. They will not, however, be stricken from an account and, in the absence of compelling reasons to the contrary, will be carried for liquidation, determination of loss, if any, and determination of liability for such loss. A loss to the estate may be determined by and upon a sale of the asset. be found by judicial determination upon distribution on a final accounting. It

Where a settlor throughout her trust agreement consistently uses the words "pay" and "distribute" in matters pertaining to the distribution of income and principal respectively, she negatives the idea that she intended the final settlement of the trust to be in cash, since an intent to settle in cash must appear in the contract in unequivocal language; and this is true even though the settlor under the terms of the trust agreement requested distribution of a portion of the principal and received her distribution in cash, since the conversion of the principal assets was made with her knowledge and was not intended to operate as a waiver of the trustee's rights under the agreement. Where the settlor of a trust assigned and transferred property to a trustee, in trust to invest and reinvest in first lien mortgages and to pay the net income to the beneficiary, by deed which further provided that at the end of fifteen years the trustee was to pay to the settlor the principal sum in its hands, either in cash or in securities, as he might elect, such deed required the trustee upon termination of the trust to pay to the settlor the present value in cash or securities as the latter might elect, and not the face value of the property originally received. 

Under such deed, there was no obligation of the trustee in addition to the ordinary obligation to exercise common skill, prudence and caution. Lacy's Trust

Where a testator bequeaths a specified sum in trust, authorizes the trustee to invest and reinvest it and to pay over the income to a life beneficiary, and provides that upon the death of the life beneficiary the sum is to be paid to a nephew according to a promise made him, the nephew is not entitled to the specified sum in cash, but only to the principal of the trust fund as it exists at the death of the life tenant. Sentner's Est., 41 D. & C. 417.

In an action of assumpsit, a statement of claim which averred that plaintiff delivered a specified sum of money to defendant bank pursuant to the terms of a receipt, which provided that the money was to be held in trust to pay the net income as specified and that the trust might be terminated and the fund withdrawn at any time upon reasonable notice by plaintiff, and that plaintiff demanded return of the money originally deposited but defendant declined to pay it, was held on appeal not to state a cause of action, since the defendant undertook only to account for the trust property and not to repay the amount deposited. 

Cohen v. Miners Bank &c., 337 Pa. 388.

Where a testator gives express directions as to the security in which the estate is to be invested, it is the duty of the trustee to follow such directions, literally, or make the investments under direction of the court.

If investments by trustees are unnecessarily approved by the court and subsequently challenged for resulting loss, the trustees could still be required to justify the wisdom and propriety of their selection.

The only effect of the failure of a trustee to secure the approval of the court of an investment he is about to make, where such approval is required, is to throw upon the trustee the burden of showing that the investment was such as the law permits, and that, in the light of the circumstances existing at the time it was made, there was no imprudence in making it. Where the trustees of an inter vivos trust manage it exactly in accord with its prescription and with the instructions and approval of the settlor himself, who is one of the trustees, the trustees, after the death of the settlor, cannot be held liable to the beneficiaries of the trust for losses arising from the sale by a pledgee in the exercise of its rights of certain securities put up as collateral for loans. 

Greenhouse's Trust Est., 338 Pa. 144. 

An agreement under the terms of which a trustee accepted a trust, limiting its liability to the amount, "which it shall realize on the said assets agreed to be accepted in kind,' was construed to protect the trustee against any assumption of liability for the full face value of the securities taken over in kind but not to relieve it from its obligation to exercise reasonable care and skill to protect and preserve the trust property. Beaver Tr. Co.'s App. 146 Super. 545.

The power to invest in non-legal securities must clearly appear and cannot rest upon equivocal words or upon conjecture.

The presumption is against the existence of such power, and all doubts are resolved against the party asserting it. 

Where testator directed that the residue of his estate be invested in a trust fund in "good sound securities," it was Held that the trustee was not authorized to purchase a non-legal security. Hale's Est., 347 Pa. 177, rev 'g, 46 D. & C. 351.

A trustee who, in violation of a restriction in the instrument appointing him, invests trust funds in mortgages exceeding two-thirds of the assessed value of the mortgaged permises is not relieved of the burden of proving due care by reason of the fact that subsequently, because of reductions in the mortgages or increases in the assessments, the unpaid balances became less than two-thirds of the then assessed values of the properties and, in the absence of affirmative evidence that at the time of investment the loans were safe, sound, and proper, will be surcharged for any resulting loss. Reyburn 's Est., 43 D. & C. 85.
