The orphans' court has no power to render an advisory opinion as to the duty fa trustee generally in respect of investments, either in proceedings under the niform Declaratory Judgments Act of June 18, 1923 (P. L. 840), or in proceed- 

1gs under Section 49 (e) 2 of the Fiduciaries Act as amended, but is restricted ruling upon matters involved in an actual existing controversy. Rebmann's 

Est., 35 D. & C. 33, af'd in 338 Pa. 120, and see Lee's Est., 40 D. & C. 195, 47 

Lanc. 429, af'd in 342 Pa. 567.

Generally, a cause of action may not be split into parts; until a trustee has arted, has exercised his powers by investing, the court has nothing from which to determine whether his act as a whole shall be confirmed or whether he must bear the loss; there must be a real controversy. 

The orphans' court is without authority to direct the discretion and judgment of a trustee, or to interfere with an effective and binding direction or request by those who, in the event of loss, must bear the loss. 

The petition of a trustee asking the orphans' court for a decree authorizing and directing compliance with a request made by all parties interested in the trust estate, that certain personal assets be sold and invested in shares of stock of enumerated corporations, will be dismissed even though the interested parties agree to accept such shares of stock in kind, and agree to indemnify and protect the trustee against loss and liability for loss. Sternbergh's Est., 31 Berks 41. 

The Court will not attempt to direct a trustee as to what particular securities he should purchase or retain in the trust. Reed's Est., 21 Erie 233.

A guardian petitioned the orphans' court for its approval to retain certain nonlegal corporate stocks under the fiduciaries act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, section 49 (e) 2. Petition dismissed, as the court could not act in an advisory capacity.

The orphans' court was without jurisdiction to entertain a petition, where the facts stated showed no controversy and the purpose was clear that the guardian was seeking to protect himself from a possible surcharge by a court order. Dym 

Ests., 90 P. L. J. 531.

If a trust is properly questioned, the burden of showing the wisdom of propriety of his conduct in making it is on the trustee. It is at that time and in that proceeding that the discretion exercised by him will be scrutinized in the light of the Will and of the Fiduciaries Act. The primary inquiry will be whether he has performed according to the recognized standard applied to the facts that existed at the time of the investment. In considering the matter, a subordinate question in some cases may be involved, (as petitioners claim here) the will shows that the testator enlarged the field of investment and to that extent relieved his trustees from the restrictions imposed by the statute. But it is when the court deals with the principal question that the subordinate one will be decided. Fry's 

Est., 25 Erie 33.

1 A competent beneficiary who, with full knowledge of the facts and of his rights, expressly consents to or affirms an investment by the trustee cannot, in the absence of fraud, thereafter question its propriety. 

Such rule is applicable to the beneficiary of a spendthrift trust as well as of any other trust. Miller's Est., 333 Pa. 116. And see Simmers v. Simmers, 339

2 Laches and acquiescence in a trustee's management of a trust constitute a bar to a person seeking a surcharge. 

In ascertaining whether laches or acquiescence exists, the chancellor considers the circumstances shown.

A long delay in failing to challenge the administration of a trust, during which important witnesses for the trustee die, constitutes laches which is a complete bar to proceedings to surcharge the trustee for its past conduct; and the conduct of parties in interest may also be evidence of their acquiescence in the trustee's management of the estate.

A delay of many years by a beneficiary in objecting to the total amount of principal with which a trustee charged itself, during which time the beneficiary knew or had reason to know the facts, constitutes laches. 

There is no basis for a surcharge against a trustee for failure to charge itself with an item of principal after the exceptant has received his share of it in distribution and has executed a release. Wilbur's Est., 334 Pa. 45.

Since the testimony indicated that the executors operated the farms with the knowledge of the heirs, and that the heirs expressly or impliedly consented thereto, the heirs have no standing to object to losses unless the executors were negligent in the performance of their duty. Longenecker's Est., 54 Dauph. 24.

In this case, it was held that the beneficiaries were not barred from demanding a surcharge, because of acquiescence or laches, where it appeared that they had never affirmatively approved of the unauthorized securities nor received any benefits, that there was nothing to show that they were aware of the presence of the non-legal investments in the trust at any time during the period in question, and that the beneficiaries excepting were remaindermen and the life tenant had died only three months before the filing of the account in question. Lewis' Est., 344 Pa. 586, af'g 42 D. & C. 269.

A beneficiary is not barred by acquiescence and laches from objecting to improper payments made by a trustee simply because she had access to the place

Where a trustee makes a mistake of law as to the extent of his duties or powers as trustee, it is no defense that he relied upon the advice of an attorney, even though the attorney was competent or the trustee reasonably believed he was competent. It is immaterial whether the mistake is as to statutory or commonlaw rule of law or as to the interpretation of a trust instrument. The extent of the duties and powers of a trustee is determined by the rules of law which are applicable to the situation and not the rules which the trustee or his attorney believes to be applicable, and by the terms of the trust as the court may interpret them and not as they may be interpreted by the trustee himself or by his attorney. The subjection of the trustee to liability where he is not at fault in making the mistake may seem harsh. He may, however, escape liability by submitting the matter to the court for instructions. If he is in doubt as to his duties or powers he may thus avoid the risk of acting on his own opinion or that of his attorney. O'Connor v. 94 Findings of fact by the trial judge in a hearing upon a petition for removal of an executor, supported by evidence, are binding on the appellate court, and his decision will not be reversed unless an abuse of discretion on his part appears. Fleming's Est., 135 Super. 423, af'g 32 D. & C. 245.

The removal of a trustee is a matter resting largely within the discretion of the court having jurisdiction over the trust, but an abuse of that discretion renders its exercise subject to review. Crawford's Est., 340 Pa. 187, rev'g 88 P. L. J. 267. 

96 Removal or limitation of a fiduciary appointed by will requires much stronger proof of lack of capacity or fidelity than trustees appointed by the courts. 

Where there is no loss to any of the parties in interest, courts are reluctant to remove fiduciaries appointed by will. Hartman's Est., 331 Pa. 422.

The removal of a trustee is a drastic action, which should be taken only when the estate is actually endangered and intervention is necessary to save trust property. 

Such rule is particularly applicable where the fiduciary is a testamentary trustee who enjoyed the confidence of the settlor of the trust. Crawford's Est., 340 Pa. 187, rev'g 88 P. L. J. 267.

A trustee is not required to exercise more than common skill, common prudence, and common caution in the administration of a trust. 

A mere error of judgment honestly made by a trustee is not ground for his removal. 

Losses incurred by a trustee in the administration of a trust do not in themselves convict him of mismanagement. 

A trustee will not be removed at the mere whim or caprice of a beneficiary; some substantial reason must be shown before a fiduciary will be replaced. 

This rule is particularly applicable where only one beneficiary desires the trustee's removal and that beneficiary represents a minority interest. Barnes' 

Est., 339 Pa. 88. 

98 A trustee will not be denied commissions or removed from office simply because he administered the estate in a somewhat informal manner and failed to obtain proper receipts for expenditures, where he has been vigilant and attentive and produced satisfactory results. Crawford's Est., 340 Pa. 187, rev'g 88 P. L. J. 267.

Fleming's Est., 32 D. & C. 245, af'd in 135 Super. 423.

The jurisdiction of the Orphans' Court, under the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, Section 53 (a)1, to remove an executor and vacate the letters testamentary given him when he is wasting or mismanaging the estate or property under his charge, or when for any reason the interests of the estate or property are likely to be jeopardized by his continuance as executor, may properly be exercised only when a substantial reason is present for such action. 

It is an abuse of discretion for an Orphans' Court to remove a coexecutor unless the situation is one in which the estate is in real danger of substantial loss if the executor is permitted to remain. Glessner's Est., 343 Pa. 370.

The conduct of a fiduciary which shows lack of ability, sincerity, good faith and willingness to cooperate, renders her wholly unfit for the proper administration of the estate and she should be removed. Haak's Est., 24 Erie 65.

Where there was bitterness and lack of confidence in the relations of a minor and her guardian to the extent that the minor would not speak to her guardian, and that an action in the Quarter Sessions had arisen between the guardian and the minor's husband, the guardian was relieved and a new guardian appointed. 

In re Schell, 7 Northumb. 237.

Executors who, without misconduct, have completed administration and have filed final account of all assets, which they hold ready for distribution, will not be removed on petition of distributee because their personal interests in trust inter vivos, created by them and decedent, conflict with interests of estate as to payment of succession taxes, where alternative remedy is available by appointing trustee ad litem. Scholler's Est., 55 Montg. 36.

While friction between a fiduciary and one or more beneficiaries of the trust is not sufficient ground for removal of the fiduciary, it may be taken into consideration with other elements constituting grounds for removal. 

Where a trustee has divorced his wife, the sole life beneficiary of the trust, and has become estranged from his children, the remaindermen, all of whom join in requesting his removal, a condition exists which is not conducive to the best management of the estate, and is a ground for his removal as trustee. 

Mooney's Est., 56 Montg. 1, 37 D. & C. 203. 

8 When a court is called upon to remove a trustee the question in each case is whether the circumstances are such that the continuance of the trustee in office would be detrimental to the trust.

Under section 53 (a) 9 of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, the court may, upon petition filed by a majority of the life tenants, remove a substituted trustee where the relation between the trustee and the life tenants have reached so acrimonious a condition as to make any personal intercourse impossible and to hinder the proper transaction of business between the parties, particularly where such relations are caused by the personal fault of the trustee. 

A substituted trustee may be removed where he has exhibited a hostile and malicious attitude toward the life tenants. Hodgson's Est., 342 Pa. 250.

The orphans' court is a court of limited jurisdiction, having only those powers expressly given it by statute.

The orphans' court does not have jurisdiction to set aside a sheriff's sale of real estate sold under a fieri facias issued out of a court of common pleas upon a judgment obtained therein against a decedent in his or her lifetime. Peterson's 

Est., 146 Super. 87. er Want of jurisdiction due to lack of power in a court to entertain a proceeding cannot be supplied by waiver or consent of parties and such question will be raised by the court of its own motion. Smith's Pet'n, 43 D. & C. 154.

The orphans' Court has no jurisdiction to enforce compliance with the terms of a written agreement made between beneficiaries under the will of a testator. 

Waldron's Est., 3 Fay. 83.

The orphans' court is a court of limited jurisdiction, the extent of which is determined entirely by the Orphans' Court Act of 1917. 

S That act does not confer jurisdiction on that court to direct that real estate conveyed by the decedent in his lifetime to a daughter, subsequently granted letters testamentary on his last will and testament, should be conveyed by her to a trustee for the use and benefit of his heirs and devisees. 

Where the record shows that the decedent died on the second day of May, 1926, and that letters testamentary were granted on May 11, 1926, the Court will grant the fifth prayer of the petition for citation which is as follows: "" 'Why your petitioner should not be given such other relief as equity and justice may require, and decree that an accounting be made by his personal representatives.

Where the orphans' court has found that a trustee has invested trust funds in securities and has taken title in the trustee's individual name, without the beneficiaries' knowledge, it may properly decree that the beneficiaries are entitled to have the investments replaced by cash.

Where such a trustee is an insolvent national bank which is in the course of liquidation, it is not essential in the orphans' court to trace the fund to the receiver; that should be done in the forum having charge of distribution of the assets of the national bank. 

A decree that beneficiaries of a trust are entitled to have a trustee replace investments with cash does not necessarily adjudicate a preference in favor of the beneficiaries. Fenelli's Est., 330 Pa. 499..

It was held that exceptant was barred, as a matter of equity, from recovery of interest on the uninvested balances of the estate held by the trust company in its banking department during specified dates, even if the existence of an enforceable contract to that effect were assumed, where it appeared that exceptant, as a co-trustee was primarily to blame for the failure or delay in making investments. 

The orphans' court, within its sphere, is a court of equity, in which equitable principles apply. Kaufman's Est., 137 Super. 88.

The orphans' court had the right to appoint a successor guardian as requested, where it has acquired jurisdiction over the estate of a feeble-minded person on which it had entertained original jurisdiction prior to the act of May 28, 1907, P. L. 292. Its jurisdiction over this property will continue until it discharges the guardian upon proof that the condition of incompetency no longer exists, either through a return of mental health or through death. 

Since the act of 1907, P. L. 292, jurisdiction rests exclusively in the common pleas courts except in those cases where original jurisdiction had, vested in the orphans' court under the act of June 19, 1901, P. L. 575. Where a court originally obtains and exercises jurisdiction, it will not be overturned or impaired by any subsequent legislation unless prohibitory words are used or must of necessity be implied.

The act of 1907 places jurisdiction in the common pleas courts alone "whenever hereafter'' any person shall become feeble-minded. The wording indicates that the legislature did not intend any retroactive application of the act to deprive the orphans' court of jurisdiction exercised under the act of 1901. Patterson's 

Est., 89 P. L. J. 169, 41 D. & C. 136.

Section 4 of the Act of June 1, 1915, P. L. 661, as amended, which provides that the court of common pleas shall, upon application, make an order for the payment of maintenance to the Commonwealth, "upon the trustee, committee, guardian, or other person who has charge of the estate of any such inmate,'' is not applicable where the ward is deceased.

A claim by the Commonwealth for maintenance of a deceased feeble-minded person must be presented, not to the guardian, but to the administrator of the estate under the jurisdiction of the orphans' court. Frew's Est., 340 Pa. 89, and see Graham's Est., 147 Super. 57, af'g 41 D. & C. 273 (af'd in 346 Pa. 479). 

43 Generally speaking property which has been assigned or conveyed by the decedent after the manner of a gift, confers a title upon the donee or grantee subject to the lawful demands of prior existing creditors of the estate. The executor or administrator, representing these and other interest against the expressed or implied wishes of the decedent himself, if need be, may and ought to procure all assets suitable for discharging demands of this character, but if any balance is left over, it goes not to the next of kin, but to the donee or grantee, for the revocation of any gift for the benefit of creditors of the decedent is only pro tanto. Metzgar's Est., 22 Erie 281, 54 York 197.

Under the Orphans' Court Act of 1917, the jurisdiction of that court extends to and embraces the distribution of assets and surplusage of the estates of decedents among creditors and others interested. Boytor's Est., 130 Super. 591. 

45 The orphans' court has jurisdiction to decide title to real estate when it is incidental to the interpretation of a will. Schollenberger's Est., 5 Sch. Reg. 65.

The orphans' court has no jurisdiction to surcharge an executor for the value of land alleged by creditors to have been fraudulently sold by the decedent during his lifetime. It cannot try titles to real estate nor settle disputes between, living people. Walkinshaw's Est., 11 West. 1. 

47 Under the provisions of Section 9 of the Act of June 7, 1917 (P. L. 363), the orphans' court has exclusive jurisdiction to compel specific execution of a contract made by a decedent to purchase real estate.

When the orphans' court has obtained jurisdiction over a subject matter it should apply the rules and principles of equity and dispose of an incidental question of reformation of a contract. Mellinger's Est., 334 Pa. 180, rev'g 46 

Lanc. 147. And see Schmehl v. Mellinger, 325 Pa. 489.

If the proceedings are simply to enforce the specific performance of a contract to sell real estate, the Orphans' Court is the proper tribunal to require performance, but when the equitable rights of others are concerned which require 17

the exercise of the broad powers of jurisdiction beyond the limited powers of equity of the Orphans' Court, which are conferred entirely by statute, the 

Orphans' Court does not have jurisdiction. Baker's Est., 21 Wash. 37, 39 D. & 

C. 405.

When a case is once within the grasp of the orphans' court the power of the court is only limited by the necessities of the case and its duty to administer equity in accordance with established rules, and the court has power to dispose of all incidental questions arising out of the subject matter within its jurisdiction.

When the orphans' court, in proper proceedings for the specific performance of a decedent's contract to convey real estate, has ordered his executor to convey certain real estate of the decedent, the court has jurisdiction to decree that the liens of judgments entered against the decedent in his lifetime and of his unsecured debts do not bind the real estate conveyed by the executor pursuant to the order of the court. Emig's Est., Eppley's Pet'n, (No. 2), 54 York 122. 

48 The Orphans' Court has no jurisdiction of cases arising between a legatee and a stranger to the estate. Spangler's Est., 11 D. & C. 79. 

50a While a court of common pleas has no jurisdiction over an action of replevin against the executors of a decedent's estate to recover a chattel in the possession of a decedent at his death, it has jurisdiction to determine title to the same chattel in an action upon the replevin bond instituted by the executors against the unsuccessful plaintiff in the first proceeding. Unger v. Hoak, 44 D. & C. 8. 

Possession, actual or constructive, of personal property by a decedent, at the time of her death, suffices to give the Orphans' Court the jurisdictional right of at least a preliminary inquiry into the ultimate question of ownership, and where such possession exists the Orphans' Court will give decedent's executors full and free access to a safety deposit box leased jointly by decedent and another person to the end that they may take and possess its contents and inventory and appraise the same.

In such case the Orphans' Court will enjoin a claimant to property in said safety deposit box from interfering with the decedent's executors in their possession of the contents to the end that ownership may be legally determined. 

Moser's Est., 35 Berks 187. 

51 The duties of a trustee, under the trust and under a collateral agreement with the beneficiary, are distinct and constitute separate relationships. The orphans' court is specifically given jurisdiction over the trust relationship, by Sec. 9 of the Orphans' Court Act of 1917; but no statutory provision gives the court jurisdiction over a relationship which is purely contractual and collateral to the trust.

The orphans' court has no authority under section 9 (b) of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, or under any other statute to authorize a trustee upon receiving indemnification from all parties in interest, to invest the trust estate in a way not authorized by testator, to restrict the trustee's right to sell real estate as given by the testator, or otherwise to alter its authority as granted by the testator.

To require a trustee who is authorized by will to sell real estate in its discretion to obtain the consent of the parties in interest before doing so would be to compel it to delegate the exercise of its discretion which it cannot do. Schumann's Est., 47 D. & C. 139.

A trustee becomes trustee by virtue of the court's appointment; not by virtue of any contract he may have made with the parties in interest guaranteeing a minimum percentage of income. Stinson's Est., 56 Montg. 102, af'd in 143 

Super. 513.

No useful purpose is served by seeking in Equity Court a remedy which has already been sought, and may be obtained, in the Orphans' Court. Campbell v. 

Plummer, 41 Lack. 3.

An action in assumpsit by a practical nurse against a testamentary trustee for services alleged to have been rendered to the cestui que trust, based, not upon any alleged contract on the part of either the trustee or the cestui que trust, but upon the contention that defendant, under the terms of the trust, should have paid the amount claimed in the exercise of his sound discretion, is within the OSS 3D 20 at be

52 The Orphans' Court of York County, Pa., has jurisdiction, when all parties in interest are before it, to order a testamentary trustee under a will probated in York County, to convey real estate which is part of the trust, situate in another state, to persons to whom the testator, in his lifetime, by parol, presented it as a gift.

The validity of a parol gift by a resident of Pennsylvania of real estate in another state, litigated in Pennsylvania, must be determined by the laws of the state where the real estate is situate. 

Under the laws of New Jersey a gift by parol of real estate accompanied by possession and followed by valuable improvements of a permanent nature, which the donee was induced to make by the promise of the gift, is valid, and equity will enforce the gift by a decree ordering a conveyance of the land to the donee. 

Lauck's Pet'n, 57 York 73. 

53 Two persons acquired the entire capital stock of a cemetery association, the purchase being financed by one and the stock of the other held by him as collateral security "until fully paid for, with interest, from the proceeds of the sale of lots of said cemetery," and the one who so financed the purchase died, whereupon, according to the contract, there was to be an inventory and appraisement of the stock with option within thirty days in survivor to purchase and in default a public sale of the stock. 

Held, the purchase price not having been fully paid as agreed upon, the option not having been exercised, there having been a delay of 9 years, a rule to show cause why the decedent's part of the stock should not be sold should be discharged. Sterner Est., 18 Leh. 222.

One who enters into a contract or option to purchase personalty and who subsequently becomes a co-executor of the deceased vendor or optionor may secure specific performance. Rosenthal's Est., 335 Pa. 49, af'g 35 D. & C. 117.

An Orphans' Court has jurisdiction to determine title to assets alleged to belong to the estate of a decedent if the assets are held by one who was acting as agent for the decedent and who claims title thereto by virtue of a gift mortis causa. Where a decedent in his lifetime executes a general power of attorney to his niece and subsequently turns over to her an unendorsed certificate of deposit and the proof relative to his intention is conflicting, the question as to whether or not she was merely acting as his agent or whether he intended to make a gift to her mortis causa is a matter to be determined by the Orphans' Court and not a question for a jury. In such a case where a confidential relationship exists, the burden is on the alleged donee to prove affirmatively that the decedent intended to make a gift to her and testimony by her relatives, who were not related to the decedent, will not be sufficient to establish a valid gift if the testimony is oral and conflicting. Moyer's Est., 47 Lanc. 61. (And see note 40, supra.)

An Orphans' Court has jurisdiction to investigate title to personal property where it was in the possession of the decedent, either actually or presumptively, at the time of his death; if, however, a substantial dispute exists the matter must be submitted to a jury. Moyer's Est. (No. 2), 47 Lanc. 225.

Schoble's Pet'n, 43 D. & C. 459, af'd in 346 Pa. 318.

A petition by the purchaser of real estate at sheriff's sale on a foreclosure to have the mortgagee in possession pro rate the rent for that portion of a month after delivery of the deed to her was dismissed by the orphans' court, where she had affirmed the existing lease, the rent having been made prior to the sheriff's sale. While the orphans' court has no jurisdiction over trusts which arise by opera. tion of law, nor where the relationship established between the parties is solely one of principal and agent, it has jurisdiction over express trusts even though there be no formal trustee and the terms of the trust must be proven by parol evidence. Gorkiewicz's Est., 43 D. & C. 40.

The orphans' court has jurisdiction to determine whether. an express trust was created by certain writings signed by a testator and found among his belongings after his death.

Where a decedent purchased bonds with his own funds, retained the income therefrom for his own purposes and disposed of them in his lifetime, retaining the proceeds, the fact that after his death certain memoranda were found in his handwriting stating that the bonds belonged to his wife, which fact he never communicated to her, is insufficient to raise a trust from the proceeds of the bonds in her favor. Raistrick's Est., 46 D. & C. 225.

Where a trust is created to pay a specified sum yearly to the settlor's former son-in-law upon the latter's agreement that his children may be legally adopted by his former wife and her then husband or by the settlor and, his former wife and her then husband having filed a petition for adoption, the son-in-law contests the adoption, filing an answer and cross petition wherein, while professing to consent to the adoption, he adroitly interposes such conditions as to make it impossible, he thereby loses his right to any benefits under the trust fund. Kolb's 

Trust, 46 D. & C. 259.

Where an attorney, who required the assistance of associate attorneys in other jurisdictions, would, when he received money from a client, estimate the amount that he expected to pay the associate attorney in the future and deposit such sum in an account marked "Collateral," it was held, under all the circumstances, that the fund so deposited did not constitute a trust for the benefit of associate attorneys. 

Since the money was not received from clients with the understanding that a portion of it was to be paid to associate attorneys, and since the amount set aside was determined by the decedent alone, his acts were purely voluntary and amounted to no more than budgeting for an expense which would have to be met in the future, in a sum not yet definitely determined. Humphries' Est., 55 Montg. 211, 44 D. & C. 452. 

A petition filed in the orphans' court alleging that petitioner's deceased husband delivered a certain sum to his son in his lifetime for investment, that he subsequently advised the son that it was his desire that the principal of the fund should go to said son at his death, and that at a still later date, by written instrument, he created a trust in which he directed the son to pay the interest from the fund to petitioner until her death, sufficiently sets forth ground for relief to require the dismissal of preliminary objections thereto. Gorkiewicz's 

Trust, 45 D. & C. 91.

as amended by the Act of April 25, 1935, P. L. 72 and supplemented by the Act of May 22, 1935, P. It is a matter of discretion whether or not jurisdiction will be taken of any particular case.

Parties are not entitled to a declaratory judgment on remote questions, or to aid them in another transaction.

The orphans' court will not entertain a petition for a declaratory judgment to m determine whether capital gains realized upon the sale of a part of the corpus of a trust estate charged with set payments in favor of certain individual annuitants, with remainder of the income and principal to a charitable institution, are liable to payment of the individual annuities in the event that the income should be insufficient therefor, where the admitted purpose of the judgment is to determine whether the Commissioner of Internal Revenue was correct in disallowing a deduction of such capital gains under section 162 (a) of the Revenue Act of 1936: in such case the proper procedure is to prosecute an appeal under the Revenue Act of 1926 from the decision believed to be incorrect. Where a petition for decree of construction of a will is presented to the court of Common Pleas, and where the judges of the court of Common Pleas not only have jurisdiction in that court but are likewise the judges of the Orphans' Court, the question was disposed of as if the petition had been presented to the Orphans' Court, and the entire proceeding was certified from the court of Common Pleas to the Orphans' Court and there entered of record with the proceedings in the estate of the decedent. Houtz's Est., 14 Northumb. 5.

The vital factor in the assumption by the court to render a declaratory judgment is the presence of antagonistic claims indicating imminent and inevitable litigation, coupled with a clear manifestation that the declaration sought will be a practical help in ending the controversy. 

The mere convenience of executors to have a will construed in advance is by no means an adequate reason for invoking the Declaratory Judgment Law. 

Where an executor's account has been filed and is, or soon will be, ready for adjudication and distribution of the balance, the orphans' court does not have jurisdiction to render a declaratory judgment construing the will. 

A petition by a testamentary trustee to the orphans' court asking for the construction of a will in aid of the petitioner's duties to carry out the provisions thereof was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

A testamentary trustee, when in doubt as to the legality of the exercise of his discretionary powers, may apply to the orphans' court for approval of his intended action. In re Loucks Will, 57 York 81.

Where a testator by his will provides, inter alia, that the balance of his resid. uary estate shall be given to his executors to purchase real estate for the purpose of laying out and establishing a public park for the citizens of Lancaster and that then they should deed the same to the City of Lancaster and also provided that the City must first signify its acceptance of the gift by passing an ordinance accepting the same, and the City desiring to accept only one-sixth of the residue presents a petition to the Orphans' Court for a declaratory judgment, averring in the petition that a controversy has arisen as to whether the City could elect to take only one-sixth of the residue or whether the election would have to be such as to consume the entire residue which was denied by the executors in their answer, Held, the Orphans' Court will assume jurisdiction under the provisions of the Uniform Declaratory Judgment Act in order to construe the will and determine the rights of the parties in interest. In such a case the Court will not construe the words of the testator literally, but will construe them according to his real intent and purpose to the effect that he did not contemplate only one tract but one, two or more tracts and that the balance unexpended in establishing such park should be awarded to the contingent remainderman. Musser's Est., 47 

Lanc. 239, 341 Pa. 1.

5 The Statute of Limitations is not a bar to a claim for costs because the order of the Orphans' Court has the dignity and force of a judgment, and the limitation as to judgments is 20 years. Baker's Est., 59 Montg. 199, 48 D. &

C. 163. 

6 The allowance of proper witness fees as a part of the costs to a successful litigant is a matter of course. It is somewhat different in the proof of claim at a hearing in the audit of an account in the Orphans' Court.

The fiduciary may not know whether or not the claim is proper, or even if he personally believes it to be proper, he may not be willing to take the risk of paying it without the protection of an order of court. 

The purpose of a hearing on an audit of a fiduciary's account is to afford the claimant an opportunity to properly prove his claim. In such cases, ordinarily, witness fees are not allowed.

Were a fiduciary with full knowledge of the facts to arbitrarily and without reason to deny a just claim, thereby puting the claimant to unnecessary expense in producing necessary and competent witnesses, a different rule would apply. 

Reed's Est., 24 Erie 256, 56 York 202, 47 D. & C. 422.

Fees of witnesses before an auditor appointed to distribute funds of a decedent will not be paid to parties who were present before the auditor presenting their own claims against the estate or representing as attorneys claims against the estate. Keefer's Est., 3 Northumb. 1.

The matter of fees and expenses of witnesses is now regulated by the Act of 

July 21, 1941 (P. L. 425).

Long's

Costs advanced by counsel in filing a petition for and service of a citation upon executors to file an account will be reimbursed by an award from the estate. Heckman's Est., 57 Montg. 310.

Where legal proceedings become necessary to determine the ownership of a joint bank account and the claimant prevails and the Appellate Court expressly directs the costs to be paid out of the fund in the hands of the accountant, the accountant will not be permitted to charge the costs against the share of the estate which belongs to the successful litigant. 

Where a joint bank account is awarded by the Supreme Court to the surviving party and it is not a part of the estate, but is the property of the survivor and should not be included in the inventory of the decedent's estate. There should be no criticism of an executor when he litigates a debatable question as to the ownership of the property and two judges of the Superior Court dissent from the opinion of the majority awarding a fund to a claimant. Culhane's Est. (No. 3), 22 Erie 62. 

10 The disposition of the costs of a proceeding in the orphans' court concerning a proposed sale of real estate is a matter lying peculiarly within the legal discretion of that court. Cope Trust, 347 Pa. 221.

In a case where a neighbor was named executor in the will, settled up the estate following the death of the sister, and applied the residue to himself, and where exceptions filed to the account were found by an auditor to be without merit and the auditor's finding approved, it was ordered that the exceptants pay the costs of the proceedings.

There is no reason why a party who presents an unfounded action in the Orphans' Court should not be compelled to pay the costs of his litigation as does the losing party in proceeding at law. Mosteller's Est., 7 Northumb. 226.

11 Section 7 of the Declaratory Judgments Act of June 18, 1923 (P. L. 840), as amended, which provides that "all orders, judgments, and decrees under this Act may be reviewed as other orders, judgments, and decrees,'' must be construed in the light of Section 22 (a) of the Orphans' Court Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 

363, limiting the right of appeal to "any party aggrieved by the definitive sentence or decree of any Orphans' Court."

A trustee is not aggrieved by, and may not appeal from, a decree, satisfactory to all the parties in interest, which construes the manner in which the principal of a testamentary trust should be finally distributed and does not threaten the protection of the trust property.

In the absence of some special trust purpose, neither the trustee's abstract interest in seeing the testator's intent carried out, nor his concrete interest in his fees, can prevent the termination of the trust if all the beneficiaries agree to terminate. Musser's Est., 341 Pa. 1 (s. c. 47 Lanc. 239).

An administrator d. b. n. has the right to appeal where the question involved relates to the recovery by the estate of which he is administrator of an asset belonging to it. Krick's Est., 342 Pa. 212.

An appeal from a decree of the orphans' court terminating a trust estate and distributing the principal by one who has no interest in the property which is the subject of the controversy will be quashed. Allen Est., 347 Pa. 364.

The trustees under the will of a decedent are not aggrieved parties, within the meaning of section 22(a) of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 363, and have

$289 

no standing to appeal from a decree directing the executors to invest the funds of the estate in specified securities and to deliver the same to the trustees to be held in trust for the named beneficiaries. Lochrie's Est., 343 Pa. 165. 

11a Where, on appeal to the Superior Court concerned only with the allowance of interest on a prior decree of the orphans' court which, on appeal, was affirmed by the Supreme Court, it appeared that the main questions involved were whether, in the peculiar circumstances of the case, the judgment of the Supreme Court affirming the decree of the lower court, awarding appellees a stated sum of money, without interest, carried interest pending its final determination and whether the administrator of the estate should be held liable for the payment of interest, if allowed, rather than the surety on the appeal bond, the appeal was certified to the Supreme Court because of its fuller knowledge of the issues involved in the original case. Koleff's Est., 148 Super. 519. 

12 Where, on appeal from the decision of the register of wills admitting to probate a certain paper as the will of the decedent, the orphans' court entered an order or decree stating that the appeal was sustained and the probate of the will set aside, such decree was definitive, final and appealable. 

Where the proponent of the will filed a petition for rehearing, and the court granted a rule to show cause, but made no order staying the proceedings, pending the consideration of the rule, the rule for rehearing did not stay the running of the time within which the appeal had to be taken. 

Where no formal disposition of the rule was made, but testimony was taken before the court, and, thereafter, proponent filed a paper specifying grounds for exception to the order of the court sustaining the appeal, after the time prescribed by the rules of court and more than three months after such order had been entered, the court below was without power to extend the time for appeal, and it was immaterial that the court treated the proceeding´pending before it as if it were on exceptions duly filed to its original order, instead of a rule for a rehearing, and dismissed the exceptions and made the original order absolute; the later order was merely a repetition of what had been done and did not afford proponent a second opportunity for appeal. Bobbitt's Est., 131 Super. 386.

Refusal of an application for a reargument in the court below is not reviewable on appeal.

A motion for a reargument, at least in the absence of a stay of proceedings, does not stop the running of the statutory period allowed for appeal. Seem's 

Est., 341 Pa. 198, af 'g 27 North. 101. 

13 An adjudication of an account may not properly be designated as a "final judgment." Snyder Est., 346 Pa. 615.

No judgment or decree is final that does not terminate the litigation. Keasbey's 

Trust Est., 342 Pa. 439. 

14a While the orphans' court may, in its discretion, withhold an order to pay awards made at the adjudication of a decedent's estate, pending an appeal by a claimant whose claim was dismissed, even though the appellant failed to enter the bail necessary to make her appeal a supersedeas under section 4 of the Act of May 19, 1897, P. L. 67, as amended, this discretion will be exercised sparingly and only under exceptional circumstances.

Where an unsuccessful claimant against a decedent's estate has appealed to the Supreme Court but failed to file an appeal bond, and the distributees do not request payment of their awards before the date fixed for argument of the appeal, and on the date fixed for argument appellant has the appeal continued because she has insufficient funds to proceed, a petition for payment of awards filed thereafter will be granted over appellant's objection. Saxton's Est., 38 D. & C. 579. 

18 Where, on appeal from the decision of the register of wills admitting to probate a certain paper as the will of the decedent, the orphans' court entered an order or decree stating that the appeal was sustained and the probate of the will set aside, such decree was definitive, final and appealable. Bobbit's Est., 131 Super. 386.

Where the orphans' court, the account of an administrator having been audited and the matter of distribution reached, stated, in an opinion, that the decision of the register of wills refusing to revoke letters of administration granted to the alleged husband of decedent, implying a finding that he was in fact the surviving spouse of decedent, was conclusive of that issue on distribution; and,

$ 269 

to this order, exceptions were filed, and, subsequently, a report of audit and distribution was also filed; and to this report exceptions were likewise filed, and the court dismissed the exceptions and confirmed the report of audit absolutely by an order which was described as a "definitive decree; "' it was held that the orders prior to the last order were interlocutory, subject to further consideration if exceptions were filed, that the final decree was the one so described in the last order, and that an appeal to the Superior Court was properly taken from such order within the prescribed time. 

An order, to be final, must, in definite terms, dispose of the case as a whole, directing distribution to be made. Boytor's Est., 130 Super. 591.

Where, after an account is filed by a fiduciary and adjudicated by the court, a decree is entered ordering the fiduciary to restate his account, charging himself with a specified sum, this is equivalent to a surcharge, and the decree is a definitive one and appealable. Williams' Est., 338 Pa. 98.

Where, upon petition, a citation upon an executor was issued to show cause why it should not file a final account; and the court made an order, not strictly responsive to the citation, refusing to direct further distribution at the time; and exceptions to this order were dismissed but no final decree was entered, an appeal by petitioners was quashed. 

In such case, the dismissal of the exceptions did not constitute an appealable decree, and an appeal could lie only from the final decree entered in connection with or following the dismissal of the exceptions. Shacklett's Est., 139 Super. 418. 

An appeal will lie to the Supreme Court only from a final or definite decree of the orphans' court.

No judgment or decree is final that does not terminate the litigation. 

A suspension of proceedings for a temporary period is not an appealable order. 

Where the court below dismissed "pro forma" all the exceptions to the adjudication of the account of a trustee under a deed of trust, to await the termination of the proceedings in another county involving a testimentary trust created by the settlor of the trust inter vivos, to determine whether certain moneys had been properly divided between the trust inter vivos and the testamentary trust and whether the former had received all to which it was entitled, an appeal from such order was quashed. Keasbey's Trust Est., 342 Pa. 439 (s. c. 40 

D. & C. 300). 

19 When exceptions are filed to an opinion of the orphans' court disposing of exceptions to a first and partial account of a fiduciary, the Court may reserve its decision upon the exceptions until the filing of the final account. Hardner's 

Est., 21 Erie 116. 

20 A joint appeal by life tenants, whose interests are separate and distinct, is not permissible, but the appellate court may consider the appeal as the appeal of one of the parties. Brown's Est., 343 Pa. 19.

Plaintiffs could not properly object that a joint appeal was taken by the appellants (which included one of the present plaintiffs) from the decree of the orphans' court, which was passed upon by the appellate court in the prior proceeding, instead of two separate appeals, especially where a joint appeal was likewise taken by plaintiffs in the present case. Jones v. Fid.-Phila. Tr. Co., 134 Super. 178.

Orphans' Court, shall hear, try and determine the same as to right and justice may belong, and decree according to the equity thereof: See Hunter's Pa. Orphans' Court Common-place Book, page 947; McCullough's Est. (No. 2), 292
